review_text:
So id have to call this game a mixed bag, the humor and art i love, and the game play loop isnt exactly bad but it becomes stale after a while, i could recommend this game but theres things i would wanna see looked over first not that im saying some things i dont like are the entire point but here we go.

1.Class stacking/level cap: i dont hate the whole "have x different types of unit for a buff" as an idea, but in the late game it takes a goofy turn with levels being capped at 5 so the lower teir tank you have had for longer will always be worse then a higher tier one, but you cant get rid of them because you lose the class buff and you become stuck with it, some classes have less of this problem like cultists because you can have any amount and you get more benefit but most classes seem to hit a point where spamming higher tier units and ignoring the class buff works out best for raw power.

2. Healers: The main form of healing needs a light twist, this is a small gripe but the healers should really be focused on healing the most damaged party members rather then the closet damaged ones, helpful buffs ended up hurting a team because healers starting pumping backliners who took a small amount of damage ruining the point of having them.

3. Paid Mutations: if the currency is shared between shop/food/mutations thats not necessarily a problem, but i cant help but feel that the purchased mutations might be better as something placed in a shop, a lot of people complain about RNG here but i noticed after a while you start to pick out which mutations are the best to buy and every run starts to blend together a bit in doing so, its not a huge deal but it takes away some of the excitement of finding what your looking for.

4.unique quests: Ive played through some of the level quests different characters will give you and i like the idea although you may want to generalize the bonus they give a bit more, tokens are nice if you dont like that particular buff but it feels a bit lame in my opinion when compared to getting something the team can use.

5. Classes themselves: the classes are very neat and i like the style for a lot of them, and this is more of a suggestion then a gripe, but multiclassing characters who have hit level 5 as a sort of second job kinda thing might make things more interesting as well as help push away some of the meta feel about which groups are worth taking and if tiers or buffs are more useful.

Overall i had fun with the game when i first played it, came back after a few months to see how it looked after a bunch of updates and while it isnt bad i cant say id be itching to tell someone to play it, its funny, it looks good, but it lacks replay-ability outside of trying to complete challenges. If mixed were an options for recommend id put it there.

review_text:
AMD Users - Download 24.9.1 at least - Recommend at least 60 fps setting in game, vsync off, AMD Fluid Motion Frames 2 on in your driver configuration.  Game feels way snappier and while it doesn't solve skill lock issues, it definitely helps a little with the latency vibes it was giving off prior.

**Original Review, additional notes below @ 17 hours**
A shameless cash grab, preying on two groups of people: 1) SAO fans who just wanted a good game to drop to fill their hearts with GGO era vibes(This aint it) and 2) Thirsty whales who want skimpy outfits for children.   Even if you can look beyond that, the game runs terrible even on modern high-end hardware, with stutters and a camera that is tied to the mouse, so if you don't play on controller, get ready to feel like you've got .. a syndrome.  In either event, if this wasn't a gift from a friend I would return it right now.  Instead I'll warn anyone who goes to get it that the devs have taken exactly zero feedback from the open network test, and have in fact made some elements worse.  There are now weird shader elements in cutscenes, the UI in the lobby has even more clunky items to slow you down and keep you looking at their other paid options, because you didn't just pay between $60 and $120? for the game which feels like it's just north of an asset flip but not quite a complete indie game.   There is a battlepass which ironically (so far) seems like the only thing that isn't a cash grab but give it time.  They have DLC bundles for gear and aesthetics, and they have a buggy but built in system for getting RNG boosters to give you more drops, which will undoubtedly be in their bundles.  This is the game that all the youtuber game reviewers warn you not to buy.

**17 hour review notes**
Fractured daydream is an appropriate name for the story since it's what I imagine an AI would think up after reading the wikipedia page for SAO.  There's not really any fundamental lore involved, and 90% of the plot is the characters arguing in an attempt to be cute, 5% of the time is regurgitated plot devices and 5% is actually new/specific to this game lore information.  I could spoil the entire 5 chapters in 2 sentences or less.

The game is abysmal for its inability to properly actuate some skills, like where you hafta mash and hold C/L1 to use your unique skill - i don't know if this is supposed to be a feature so you don't accidentally it, but it's a bad UX.  With the user experience being not worthy of a $19.99 pricetag, the idea that I'm playing on a $100+ version of the game seems about as out of touch with reality as the script writer for this plot.  Graphical bugs, text bugs, and combat bugs galore riddle this game, and there's no where to report problems to, no one to send screenshots and information about them back to.

The problem that's a glaring one though, and the one that will 100% kill this game, is the fact that on top of the pay walls, there's not enough players to even fill a group on mid-tier content in advanced access.  I don't think that full release is going to change that dramatically, so when high-tier raids and co-ops are being matched for they're going to be all NPCs, and the end result is going to be near-impossible to complete.  The NPC AI is dumber than starfall's NPC AI, and at least those were comical.  This just feels like the developers were given a directive and they completed it as fast as possible without trying.  It also feels that this was greenlit as another attempt by a C-suite to cashgrab as much as humanly possible on the IP before people give up on it, like companies are doing with just about every other major IP right now.  I'm disappointed, and the players deserve better.  

Shame on you bandai namco.

review_text:
Lost Ruins is a very simple and overall decent action platformer (not a metroidvania) . It is quite generic, feels overall quite solid, and its sprite work is probably the most standout thing about it. The difficulty is not crazy, and the game is easy to cheese, if that's what you want. I played the game for around 6 hours and nearly 100% completed it. If you're looking for something to play, get this on the cheap and it'll kill 6 hours—you could do far worse. 

[h1] Story & Presentation[/h1]
There isn't a whole lot to say about the story. It's not especially deep; the main playthrough has almost zero characterisation almost on any character—they're all quite bland. The premise is you've been summoned from another world and must kill *the things* in order to regain your memories and cue the highly predictable plot twist at the end. There are books scattered about for extra plot too, they're short and much like the story as a whole, don't outstay their welcome. 

In the post-game, a new mode unlocks that lets you play the story through in a different way, with some different characters that have actual personality. I have not finished this, but so far it is slightly more engaging?

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
The gameplay is quite solid, but overly simple to be truly satisfying or anything above "average." You have melee weapons and magic. You have weapons that stab, swing overhead, some that are slow, and some that are fast. Your magic options are spinny balls of ice, fire, electric, or a projectile of those elements. There are a couple more creative ones, like invisibility, absorbing corpses and the like for HP, but again, nothing that'll rock your socks off. 

A positive that the game has is that accessories, and some weapons, have unique effects which are quite impactful and can create many OP or cheese strategies. You won't find boring "+1" attack damage armour, for instance. It's usually +50% bleed, +30% extra damage against orcs, etc. While in some senses these are mundane, they're big increases you can exploit. Some are way more unique, such as getting +1 HP regeneration when wet, or +3 HP regeneration when bleeding, immunity to being frozen and etc. While these are just generic immunities and buffs, they're impactful and you can FEEL their impact on gameplay, which can't be said for every game these days. It makes your choice of accessories quite impactful, and there are a lot of synergies and builds you can go for. It's simple and a bit of fun.

Another thing I liked was the interaction between elements. The game has reactions between elements, such as water being hit with an ice spell will freeze it, doing damage to enemies in it (and yourself). Gasoline can catch fire and deal fire damage. The game even messes with you in places with this, putting jars of gasoline and candles you can accidentally destroy to light yourself on fire. It isn't a complex system, but, like everything else, it's simple and a bit of fun.

[h1] Exploration [/h1]
Lost Ruins has a metroidvania-looking map, but for the most part, it's a long linear corridor to the end. It has branching paths that will reward your exploration with unique accessories and weapons, as described above. There's a decent variety of biomes available as well. It keeps it from being too samey. There's a good mix of enemy types, although all of them are super simple and quite easy to kill overall. They look and feel very good to fight against.

[h1] Bosses & General Combat [/h1]
The bosses in this game have great sprite work and vibrant animations for the most part and feel very alive. Sadly, the complexity of the combat system and their attacks don't reach that same bar of quality, unfortunately. They'll have very few attacks, often 3-4 they'll cycle between, sometimes they'll also just de-aggro and stand in the arena doing nothing while you heal? It's unfortunate.

I played this game on the hardest difficulty available at the start. You take 50% more damage, and critical hits deal more damage to you as well (and statuses stack, like poison). This often meant you pretty much HAD to play perfectly a lot of the time and would go from full health to zero in seconds. Most of the time you lose reams of health in what feel like very unfair ways. You have no invincibility frames, so some attacks can just wombo combo you while you're stunned. If you survive on a sliver of health, good luck, because now you've got 4 stacks of bleed, all lasting 20+ seconds. You can open up the menu and eat all your cheese, cheese it if you will, and get full health again, but this doesn't feel very satisfying. Hard mode in this sense just feels brutally punishing, needing you to play to perfection. I presume normal mode isn't as bad and may even be a complete cake walk. The same that can be said here also applies to general enemy encounters. 

The beginning of the game was quite a bit more brutal as well, having low HP. Critical hits from enemies were the most annoying. Sometimes you just get one-shot from full HP if you get unlucky with an enemy crit. review_text:
A live service game that asks for full price at the door. 

The single player component is 10-15 hours of braindead-easy hack & slash with the typical simplistic writing you normally see in anime crossover games. The single player component alone might be justifiable at $5-10 if you're a big SAO fan.

Multiplayer is lacking in obvious QoL features and endgame content. The playerbase tanked by 90% after the first month and never recovered. Games need 5 players to even start and it's a fight to achieve that. The game's matchmaking was region locked for months and forced most players to figure out they had to switch to the JP server to even find games and then always suffered lag for their trouble. There is no competent way for games to be filled due to all players being skewed between account levels that only affect stat inflation when mechanics could have easily been designed differently to full everyone into a smaller number of queues. review_text:
TGR is another multiplayer focused arcade racing game where the goal is to get your ball in the hole sooner than the rest. While the essence is simple, everything wrapped around this idea makes the game such a joy to play. There are tons of maps with their own gimmicks, plenty of skills to equip, tons of visual customisation options, a lot of in-game activities to focus on for individual progress, different game modes and most of the achievements encourage participation instead of beating others all the time. There is also a decent single player mode where all the maps can be attempted in time trial, including getting up to 3 stars. All of this content is delivered with beautiful graphics and smooth controls. I especially love being able to fly with a car whenever I want and it just feels great. In terms of finding matches, I got 9 out of 10 without caring about being online at busy times, with the European time zone at least. Even though steamdb often shows low activity, the game is carried by game pass users and the rest of the slots are filled by bots. There were a few rare moments where I encountered 4-6 out of 8 slots being real players. Most of the players were of casual-average skill level. You don’t get the sense that the community is too competitive or the sweaty type and it honestly feels great to just enjoy a multiplayer online game on your own terms.

It’s remarkable how polished and bug free the game feels even though you can tell that support was pulled sooner than expected. The golf game modes are the most recent additions and they don’t have any achievements, same can be applied to the last maps released for time trials compared to other maps. This can be seen as a good thing since you’re not forced to spend more time on the game if you don’t want to as a completionist. I’m a bit less forgiving on the game’s balance and 3 specific achievements. The game has a couple of item pickups including two types of rockets, but rockets don’t feel needed as most of the players are focused on getting their balls to the goal. It would have been easy to ignore them if there wasn’t an achievement to shield yourself from 50 rocket attacks. It might not sound like much but I only got 11 naturally in 20 hours because most don’t use it. It isn’t helped that temporary shield is a bit finicky sometimes, a proper shield is dropped randomly and there aren’t enough pickups for bigger maps. The 2 other achievements require you to be in a party lobby with 2-4 players total and start a race. I got extremely lucky to have found a public party lobby with 3 other players. It’s a shame to have those 2 achievements when the rest of the achievements could easily be gotten by joining the default race mode and focus on individual goals such as getting your ball through boost rings x amount of times etc.

You can tell the game was made with care. It’s in a good state despite it not receiving anymore updates. It might not have a long life as an online focused game but it’s a lot of fun and it feels relatively easier to find matches in this game compared to other online games with a small community I have experienced. I got the game through Humble Choice and I was fearing that most of the achievements would be annoying. It wasn’t like that for the most part luckily. The normal price is less than €10 and it’s worth it if you’re willing to enjoy it while it lasts or you weren’t planning on sticking around for long to begin with.

first off, lets start by saying id had high hopes for this game. i actually came from a tiktok in which someone was gallivanting around as a gazelle and it looked like a lot of fun. 

its not. this game is so incredibly unfinished. i dont want to be rude, but i feel its important to be honest. i bought this game because i found ONE positive review. now im submitting for a refund.

flaws:

- everything has to be set to low to run without lag. 
- there is NO FOOD. the one type of food i found as a leopard was an elephant herd, which of course killed me where i stood despite all of my gaming experience. two hits and i was down for the count. even the babies can launch an adult leopard clear across the sand. scenting food doesnt work. seeing an elephant does. 
- theres no sounds to tell you if sniffing (q) works. you may sometimes see water orbs but i only saw that once. 
- if stuck, theres an unstuck button. issue? you have to wait an entire minute to be unstuck from something as simple as a log or a rock. 
- no one plays on the public servers. there is no one on at the times ive checked, making the game seem even more lonely and pointless. 
- baby leopard cubs are so glitchy that you cant run. literally. youre thrown all over trying to. 
- this is a simple detail, but you dont leave footprints in every spot you step. about every three strides do two paws randomly appear.
- sounds of nature when theres nothing else around. birds, rocks, trees - nothing in sight. thought you heard some prey? no, you didnt. 
- the english is poorly translated.
- sometimes when you load in, its just a black screen. nothingness. if thats night, there is no night vision option. 

pros: 

- i LOVE where this could have gone! i see the vision! i admire it! i think the models need some work but are cute. i like the pelt and body options, though i wish they would tell you what you were changing.
- i like the variety of herbivores, and think that more carnivores would be sick! omnivores too! ai or not. 
- the map is huge. its a test map, but it might be too large if theres absolutely no ai to be found, or even other players (all of the maps were empty, though). 

right now i would suggest saving your money if you made it to the bottom of this. TLDR: dont buy it yet. theres hope? but just not right now.

review_text:
As of October 15th of 2024, I have played through this game twice. With Final transmission I totaled 25 hours and I think that is all I am going to give this game.

I bought the game on launch day after many years of waiting: as many who played on pc know, it was a messy and buggy launch. I poward through though and was  greeted with the following.

Story(No spoiler)- I am a massive fan of the deadspace lore and ecstatic for another sci-fi/horror, there are so few in this genre of games/movies that is good, that anything to come out that has the potential to be awesome I am so there for it. At the start of the game the story shows potential and has a intriguing hook, however that hook dies flat and goes nowhere, lacking and more hooks than the current string it started with. This leads up to a rather disappointing ending that kinda apes deadspace 2. In fact a lot of story beats of deadspace is present in Callisto Protocol, almost feeling like a cheap ripoff of the og games, but lacks that unique spark they had.

When it comes to the story, I am taking Deadspace 3's story: stupid love triangle and all, over all of Callisto Protocol.

Graphics/Visuals- The game looks fantastic, looks wonderful. I could not run the game at its max setting as that kind of horsepower is way out of my grasp, but with what I could do this is a cool looking game with nice detailed models. Saying that, I do feel like a lot of environments looked and felt the same as time went on, the only real change up was a [spoiler]Brief stint on the surface and the habitation center with its trees, it was cool~[/spoiler] I Wish those areas were not so small. The guns were also kinda just, Meh. Detailed, but I wont be remembering any of them. 

Gameplay- Alrighty, this is where I start getting quite a bit harsher. I will start with being blunt, This game is not fun to play. It tries a hybrid melee/Tps thing and it just feels lost and nonsensical. Baddies will wait in line to attack you, guns come in to late into the game and feel weak, even with upgrades. Telekinesis Makes its return as the GRP system, it works just the same as in Deadspace, except it has charges and needs battery's to recharge fast. The GRP is the only fun thing about combat, as picking up baddies and yeeting them into a fan will never gets old. 

Melee is down right bland, dodge by holding left or right(interchanging after each blow.) and spamming two or three attacks back, that's all melee encounters. They could have spiced it up with a variety of melee weapons, however you only ever get one at any time. [spoiler]The hammer from the story DLC is much better but the way mobs are just zerging you in that DLC grinds the fun down quick.[/spoiler]

Guns suck, they just feel like pop guns. Its kinda funny saying that, all guns are 3d printed and it feels like it. I played the game on medium difficulty and the guns had hardly any stopping power, needing to empty a clip into a basic mob just to kill them. They were pushing hard for this hybrid combat system, the best way to kill something is to weaken the baddie till the tentacles pop out and shoot the the tentacles for max damage. Getting RE5 vibes..guhh.

I used guns and GRP as much as I could to avoid needing to melee at all. However there are a lot of parts in the game where melee is the only real option. [spoiler]Final transmission. Cough* Cough*[/spoiler]

Healing and recharging the GRP was another part of the game that peeved me off. You need to hold still, open the inventory and use an item. Battery's 1 second, healing makes Jacob kneel down and inject himself for a painful four seconds.. GL needing to heal during large fights, or when you are getting zerged. This sucks.

Last Transmission- [spoiler]Ok this story DLC cemented how I feel about this game. So the good first. The story is OK, it wraps up the game in a nice box. Jacob and the doc do die in the end, but not before sending a massive data pack of all the bad stuff did in the prison to that lady. What I DID like about the story is that we at last get some psychological horror that felt missing from the main game. 
You lose the baton and get it replaced with a awesome fucking hammer that one shot all mobs but one..oh speaking of that..one. The bad. Oh my fucking gosh, how I hate the Biomechanics. So, you remember the robot Security yea? Well, lose the gun and replace it with melee, oh..and send dozens at you with a emp that's super fucking hard to avoid. Lastly, the fucking door lock mini-game.. 5 rings that you need to line up but they keep moving as you try to line another up, I fucking hated it, there's only three but you will remember how much you hate them.[/spoiler]

I tried hard to enjoy this game. I waited so long only to be met with peak mid. I wanted to add this game to my shelf of awesome sci-fi, but I cant and that fucking sucks. I hope for the best for the Dev team and there future games, maybe Callisto Protocol 2, if it ever gets made, will be better.

Not saying you can't be inspired, but they didn't really do anything with it.

I tried maybe ten times and it just didn't feel worth it to try anymore. I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone. I don't know how a game in development for that long has so little to it. It truly is a massive disappointment.

TL,DR: The people who made this game have destroyed it to wring money out of you. Stay far, FAR away.

If you in any way enjoy using mods, enjoy watching modded content, view lets plays with modded content, or prefer single player to multiplayer, do not buy this game.

Bioshock is an excellent game that is very well built, created by innovative, brilliant developers who geniunely love what they do. You can see it in their work. However last week, the publisher of the Bioshock Series, Take Two Interactive, sent a cease and desist order to the developer of the most commonly used mods in another game they developed, GTA V. A mod which thousands of other mods and hundreds of thosands of work hours depend upon. A mod which has existed for ten years, and has only now become the focus of legal action due to Take Two's efforts to increase monetization. This move came on the 5th of June, in what appears to be an attempt to hide this action from public attention as the gaming community is occupied with the E3 conference. 

This game has recieved a continued level of attention and constant exposure to new audiences through the way in which modders have continued to create new and interesting content that is related to this game. Despite this being of net benefit to their sales, Take Two is now betting that they will be able to make more money by cracking down on mod development in order to further monetize the existing player base. In short, they are actively destroying collaborative works and content they have previously allowed, making the singleplayer experience of their game LESS enjoyable, in an effort to wring more money out of players. Considering that a significant percentage of their sales from the PC release of this game (i.e., this version) has come due to interest in using and developing mods, this move is unconscionable. 

Take Two's recent actions represent the very definition of corporate hackery. They are choosing profits over people. There are plenty of other game developers and publishers that do not do this. Go spend your money on their games instead. This decision has utterly ruined the game in my view.

review_text:
I'll start like many other reviews and say that I loved Boneworks (BW). The story in that game was somewhat veiled, but it gradually became more apparent as the story went on. BoneLab is nothing like this. When I watched the promotional videos and whatnot, I thought it would be a story-driven sequel to BW, with similar writing. That is almost the exact opposite of what actually was released. There were some good parts to the game, but they all occurred in about the first hour of play through. I'll divide up my review to (hopefully) make it more readable.

[h1] The Good of BoneLab [/h1]

-It introduces new weapons that are somewhat interesting
-Introduces native support for modding
-Includes an updated physics engine from BW (more about this later)

[h1] The Bad of BoneLab [/h1]

-Absolutely horrible story
           This game started strong, but quickly made me want to toss my headset in the trash. As other reviewers have gone into detail, I won't write much here, but suffice it to say, they suck. The minigames that are forced into the campaign ruin the flow of the story and add nothing to the game. The body changing levels simply make no sense other than showing how well the devs can integrate that system into the game. After playing through the rest of the story, I can confidently say that I didn't use this system more than once. Maybe it would have been better if the system wasn't introduced with only about 15% of the story left.

       The story here was nonexistent and seemed to be a bunch of different ideas all compiled and shoved randomly into a cash-grab disguised as a game. 

-Weird physics system
       While BW had a wonky physics engine sometimes, it was undeniably better than BoneLab's most of the time. In BoneLab, half the time you'll go to climb something, or vault a ledge, and you'll find your legs will catapult you in the opposite direction. This causes you to repeat part, or all, of the level. This is especially tough since you cannot do anything about your leg position, when crouching either doesn't work, or makes your virtual head be glued to the floor, making you unable to move. 

-Overly simple level design
       Once again, BW shines much brighter than this game. BW allowed you to explore every nook and cranny to find hidden items and ammo (more on this later). If you wanted to, however, you could progress through BW fairly quickly without the exploring. BoneLab provides almost no exploration, and even when it does, the "hidden" areas provide essentially nothing. One level specifically has you find a "hidden" spot just to find two chairs and writing on the wall. This makes exploring basically useless. Most levels just force your down the story path as it is literally THE ONLY path you can take, with no dead ends or anything to make people curious. This makes even longer levels seem extremely short and underwhelming. 

-Ammunition/guns
       One question: Why make guns and ammo stay through the levels and remove the option to purchase items with ammo? I basically was extremely stringent on shooting enemies because in BW every bullet mattered. You could buy different weapons, and at the end, you could buy dev tools with your saved ammo. BoneLab lets you keep ammo through the levels, and doesn't give you a way to do anything except shoot things  with it. I wound up finishing the game with large amounts of unused ammo. You will get enough ammo to essentially run the whole game doing nothing but shooting enemies. I could have probably avoided 1.5 hours of game play by simply shooting everything and not worrying about how else to kill things. Also guns are perpetually saved as well, so you can keep the guns you initially get throughout the game. Gun spawns later in the game seem to be worse than those in the earlier levels. 
        Also, the final level gives you a ton of guns and lots of ammo to choose from/pick up. I thought from all these items it would be a huge battle like the clock tower in BW. I get to the end of the level and maybe shot 20 bullets to kill 6 enemies. Unlike in BW, where you either had to buy or find weapons to survive tough enemy waves, BoneLab hands you enough guns and ammo to play through the story five times in the first level. (You can also just play as the heavy and kill everything with one punch)

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
       I really wanted to like this game, but it just does not meet even my lowest expectations. If I had known I'd be spending $40 on a compiled list of tech demos and concept ideas, I would not have bought the game. There is almost no story development or reason to continue playing. In BW, even if you didn't understand the story right away, you felt an urge to lay simply to escape the world. Here it just seems like the developers wanted to show off their programming abilities and get a bunch of money from people that simply wanted a playable game. When I first got into the game, as the levels progressed, it felt more and more like a beta or early-access game. If you have BW, do not waste your money on this unfinished cash-grab.

[h1] TLDR [/h1]

This game is barely more than a compilation of mini-games and bugs. Barely any story, bugs, and little improvement over Boneworks left me feeling disappointed and like I was playing an early-access title. Boneworks was much better in several aspects, and this game takes the franchise back several steps.

I'm guessing this is one of those games that only existing fans of the franchise would appreciate. 
I don't know what Haseo's deal is, nor understand why he is such a bellend, but it makes it horrible to have to play as him. There is absolutely nothing he can't screw up horribly like the chuuni little teenage weed he is.
The gameplay is dull and janky, the pacing is painful, the railroading in places is especially annoying.  The story is near impossible to get invested in because the characters are mostly unpleasant and / or completely clichéd... plus constantly having to log out to check e-mails between every story event is beyond stupid (especially when some of them are basically just "go back to where you were before you logged out"). And don't even get me started on the arena cutscenes... 
. 
I don't know if this would have been considered good back in the Sh!testation 2 days, but if so it hasn't aged well.  The fact it is a port of an old game is the only reason I haven't thus far complained about how trashy the models and animations are... though to be fair I've played older ports on here that looked far better.

As for upsides... there is one. 
Pi. 
Just her. Glasses + B00bs. Even her username references the latter (Japanese pun). The makings of a perfect character.  Even has jiggle-physics in her few cutscenes.  Would be even nicer if it weren't for the low poly-count... and if Haseo wasn't continuously such a dipsh!t to her.


In general though, this game is painful to play, much like a lot of games I've tried recently. I swear I might be put off trying new games entirely if I don't find something good soon.

First things first - you should note this game can be completed in around 1-1.5 hour if you don't know what you're doing or simply don't remember. Much quicker when a solution in mind or on a separate window.

This is an absolutely beautiful video game, one of Amanita's first and best in my opinion.
It does have some usual point and click scenes - the puzzles don't always make complete sense, you do need to do some pixel hunting, and there are (very few - maybe 2-3) timed puzzles which are a bit hard to distinguish (you may think you're just not doing the correct thing).

Even with all its minor flaws, the game is reasonably solvable without a guide, in my opinion (so even though the puzzles don't always "make sense" they're not crazily irrational and out there up to the point of no way of ever finding what to de next).

And most importantly, the world is so irregularly magical and makes it totally worth it, in my opinion. This is due to the simplistic yet fantastic music and graphics (which now look so much prettier in 4k).

review_text:
This game is awful.  Absolutely awful.  Completely unbalanced, terrible characters, and .hack// seems to suffer the same problem as Aliens in that every single piece of media tells the same basic plot over and over and over and over.  The only redeeming factor this collection has is that it's at least the full game at one price instead of making you pay full price three times over to get a full game's worth of content (and, no, each individual piece is NOT a full game's worth).

To get into specifics, the game is completely unbalanced.  The amount of experience you get from enemies is mostly flat the entire game, only determined by your level, and the enemy's level.  Unfortunately this is ramped so high that you generally can level every 2-3 fights.  One dungeon can have a few dozen fights.  The maximum level is 50 per game (so 50, then 100, then 150).  I gained 8 levels in one dungeon run.  So you can massively, massively outpace the story without even trying, you can do it simply by doing the side quests.  On top of that, the damage you do has more to do with the level differences as well than your gear.  This is supposed to make it harder to go to a dungeon that's too high for you, as you'll do minimal damage, but ultimately you really can keep enemies locked long enough to kill them anyway even with a sizable difference.  Not that you need to go after high end enemies.

Gear drops don't match the level of the dungeon either, despite what the game tells you.  Your NPC party members can gain quite a bit of levels as well, to 'catch up' while you're not using them.  However, they won't do anything about gear.  You can have someone join your party in the 30's still wearing level 1 gear because you and you alone determine what they use.  In most RPGs this wouldn't be such an issue, but this game is pretending to be an MMO.  But the other characters are dumber here than in most other RPGs anyway.

The story is laughably bad, the same rehashed plot line of "there's a glitch/not-glitch in The World that gives some users super powers and puts other users in comas" and you're the CHOSEN ONE who also has the power so you can counter it.  But the characters in this are absolutely insufferable.  Their personalities are extremely poorly written to the point of parody of religious zealots, pacifists, psychopaths, and the like.

review_text:
I've been a big fan of Hakuouki since the PSP version came out and I was really looking forward to playing it with all the promised new content. But as much as I love it, I can't recommend this version for multiple reasons.

First: This is not the whole game; it is roughly two thirds of the story and the part that was called the 'common route' in the original game. And it ends when any romance option you may have achieved with your decisions just starts to bloom. Since Edo Blossoms is out already, you can continue on the spot, but you are forced to buy a second game to get the whole story.

Second: It is not a romantic story. As mentioned above, this game covers the ‘common route’ and that means you only get a glimpse of budding romance right before it ends. As it is set in a time when Japan renewed itself in a bloody civil war, there are many dark aspects you will discover. And as if the times weren’t grim enough then, the game adds even more dark stuff to that, so if you are unlucky with your decisions, you can have a very dark, very depressing experience. Also, the game wants to tell the story of the Shinsengumi and their fight in those stormy times, so prepare for a long history lesson. I loved it, but I’m a history geek and quite in love with the past of Japan. I just wanted to warn you in case this is not your cup of tea.

Third: The translation. Oh God, the translation… I know that not everyone knows Japanese and would (or would want to) notice this, but I’m already at the point where it really hurts reading the subtitles. And my Japanese isn’t all that good, so I’m sure there is even more than what I've spotted so far. It’s not only that the men ‘sound’ so much more aggressive and ill-willed in the text and that it often doesn’t fit with how they talk in Japanese. I understand that this may be due to localizing the game for a Western audience. But there are translation mistakes even in really short, easy sentences where the meaning is completely garbled and even some instances where it felt like they had given up on translating altogether and just invented some stuff that seemed fitting for the scene. And even the English sentences often have grammar mistakes that forced me to interpret more than read. I expect more from a VN of this caliber, especially for this price.

And last: Neither the developer nor the publisher seems to have any interest in their game here on Steam apart from how much money it makes them. There are some issues with the performance of the game that are still unaddressed. I didn’t have any issues except for the small bug that the characters don’t say my heroine’s name when using the default ‘Chizuru’. But even that is still open, no response from anyone working on the game as far as I could see in the discussions.

So, even though I love Hakuouki, I can sadly only tell you this: If you are one of the few people who own a PSP, try to find the original game. The translation of that was not perfect either, maybe it wasn’t even good, but sadly it was still better than what we get here. And I still prefer the art of the original game, especially with regard to the uniforms. It was gorgeous. To be fair the art in this new version of the game is one of the few good points it has. It still looks beautiful. But that is not enough, so I have to give this a thumbs down. I’m so sad right now…

So I bought this game during a recent Steam sale and I finally got to experience it and see what all the fuss is about. I went in with the mindset of "Do NOT expect a Dead Space spiritual successor". That is a major mistake, as countless people have already said about this game. Experiencing this game in that "Don't expect Dead Space" mindset really wasn't all that bad, honestly. I definitely don't HATE the game. And I definitely don't think it's irredeemable TRASH, as many make it out to be. I had a good enough time playing through it. I even started a New Game+ run immediately after beating the game. For what it is, I think the game was worth the 20 bucks I paid for it during the sale. I'm not unhappy with the purchase.
However.... HOWEVER.... I do have to agree with all the negative commentary about this game. So many bizarre design decisions with this game. So many design decisions that are outright FRUSTRATING and even infuriating at times. I won't go into detail about all these frustrating and bizarre design decisions. You surely already know. They've been pointed out by countless people since this game released over a year ago. But I definitely agree with all of these complaints. This game had so much potential. It really did. It's a well-made game in overall, but I don't recommend because, after a while, it feels quite repetitive.
I have a hundred of hours played because I've been since half the game was made, and thus with every few updates I came back to see if things had improved. After it's "stable release" I finally gave it more hours and noticed it's really, plainly repetitive.

- after 1 or 2 cities you've already understood the ways and order to get everything going in almost every new city
- going to a different terrain doesn't change anything really, just shifts your strategy a bit and refreshes the city aesthetic (a bit, because the buildings don't change either)
- you don't unlock more advanced stuff throughout the game: everything is available from the first city. You only gain small benefits ("wow, I just got +3% of the speed of road construction, [i]such an improvement![/i])
- if you feel it's enough and you want to spice things up, you can increase the difficulty........ with a game reboot. Seriously? After days and days? Even when there's not much carry-on from city to city?
- some objectives are plainly crazy and virtually impossible to achieve; either because they're crazy hard, or because they don't make sense in the current world anymore - this should be checked and prevented by the game system
- the victory objective is really a joke. play for a long time in EVERY TERRAIN? SERIOUSLY?
- not to mention a lot of other small issues in game mechanics, lack of statistics and lack control that you can find in the game forums...

Bottom-line: nice to spend a couple of days playing and then leave it in the shelf, disappointed with "having" to abandon a game. You deserve more than this.

review_text:
We have one Star Trek MMO.  It should be FAR, FAR, FAR better than this.  It's a tired game that never really gets better.  

You can do pretty much all of the content in a few days and after that, it's rinse and repeat.  They have various reps and currencies you can grind for but, to what end?  To redo the same very small amount of content?  

One would think worlds would be a big feature in a game about space travel and exploration?  Ground content is virtually non-existent, save for a few instanced encounters and those part of their small amount of story arcs.  You can land on planets, but it's a carbon copy of every other with some aesthetic changes here and there.  No chance of open world at all.

Even though it's F2P, they have insidious lockboxes all over the place forcing you to gamble real money if you'd like to acquire an iconic ship from the show you love.   Don't want to gamble?  Buy a ship with real money from their in-game store.  They offer 1-2 ships for in-game grinding once or twice a year, normally novelty non-cannon centric vessels.  If you speak to an STO apologist, they'll tell you you don't need to spend anything and you can grind X currency in game and convert it to Y - Yes you can in some cases, but takes you forever and the actions required to do it are the most tedious and mind numbing things ever.

I preordered this game, have a life time sub, and was waiting to login at midnight when they turned the servers on 10 years ago - I abandoned it shortly after logging in because it was awful.  

I came back after a few years (Legacy of Romulus 'expansion') and it did feel improved, spent a few weeks playing, realised it's an empty feeling and now login once every few months.  

What do most players do with this game?  Space Barbie (basically STO's transmog type thing) or Tweaking Ship Builds to knock up DPS numbers a fraction - DPS that is meaningless in a game that offers very little.

I will say that many of the ship designs are beautiful and it is the only game where you can pilot any number of Star Trek ships.  Pilot is a bit much though, it's micro-machines in space.

I pray one day a major studio will come along and the rights to this will be passed to them so we get a proper, 100% genuine MMO rather than this poor imitation.

review_text:
This game has great potential. It's original, it's provocative, it's surreal. It talks in whispers about life and death. It makes you struggle, get despaired, hopeful - and despaired again. It raises hard questions - whom to save, whether to be "good", what is it to be "good" - so you'll have to make hard choices. It's here not to merely entertain you - it has a more ambitious goal.

However, for me this game failed to live up to its ambitions.

There are 12 days in total. The first 4 to 5 days are great at setting up the atmosphere, characters and mysteries. The mechanics of survival is very challenging but it feels authentic and fair - and fulfilling to overcome. The music, the design, the unsettling world left such a great impression on me that I, without any hesitation, put Pathologic in my personal "top 10 best games ever".

However, next days do not bring almost anything new to the table. The mechanics of survival doesn't change much. It keeps being challenging though - even more so if you didn't excel at gathering right resources in the beginning. A few times I ended up in an absurdly tough spot, where I had to repeat a sequence of actions over and over again till I got it just right to survive. Hello my old friend, Dark Souls. You can reduce difficulty, which I didn't as, well, I trusted the developers: the hardest difficulty is the recommended one.

The characters and mysteries didn't really pay off for me. When the game is great at making plot setups, the stories and characters often lack any meaningful development. While there are some interesting ideas and twists, overall the story doesn't feel complete. Also, while the game makes the point that to solve the mysteries, the player must think for himself rather than follow markers on the map, almost all of the quests are solved exactly by running from one marker to another.

I'll still be waiting for the next part though. Hopefully, the bold and brilliant ideas of Pathologic will get a better execution.

review_text:
This game sits in a rather interesting cross roads of genres. In basic concept and overarching gameplay loop, it's a Metroidvania. You explore a series of rooms making up an interconnected world, defeat bosses and gain upgrades or adjustments to your kit along the way.
That's about as far as the comparison goes however.
The moment to moment gameplay is not like any other Metroidvania, it's combat and attacks are slow and seemingly clunky. The fastest attacks still leave you standing still for a good while, and while you have a dodge roll it's start up and recovery times mean it's not good for much beyond dodging an attack and disengaging, you'll almost always get hit if you attack to counter after rolling. The game is rather difficult initially as a result, though I did play on the Veteran difficulty for my first play through.

However, this kind of gameplay is intentional, and the game is for the most part built around it. It's much less focused on the action of the gameplay, rather it rewards care in exploring the world and taking to careful preparation. The game lacks real upgrades to it, bosses drop stat upgrades or equipment slots rather than new abilities, and throughout the game you'll be collecting an entire variety of spells, weapons and accessories that can drastically modify your loadout and how you can approach situations. Early on the slow nature of combat made me gravitate towards the fastest weapon I could find, but soon I found that using a large heavy weapon was much more successful thanks to the range it gave me and the ability to control the fight by making enemies have to close the distance with me instead, and often times I could kill enemies in one or two hits. The game wants you to be slow and careful, and use the right tool for the job, and you'll be much more successful adjusting what your kit is depending on what you're fighting.

The game does have a bit of a difficulty issue around this though. Being very stingy with money and offering no free heals, the early game is arguably the hardest part of the game as you lack the tools needed to properly strategize and play around the situations in front of you. The first boss was certainly the hardest for me, even with equipment that let me move quickly or heal in her arena, it'd certainly have been even worse if I hadn't explored before approaching her. However by the mid game, with the proper use of consumables and equip loads I was able to start killing bosses in only a handful of hits, with the final boss needing less than ten hits if you set yourself up to deal large amounts of damage. As well, magic started out as a valuable and scarce resource in the early game that slowly became my main method of clearing out mobs once I'd gained items to let me passive regenerate mana in the late game. While being able to fight only with spells was cool, magic is also incredibly strong and much of the game's moment to moment difficulty was diminished. On one hand I was rewarded for gathering and using all the tools I could, but I given the ability to simply roll over any non boss enemy purely with spells. 

Also, dev if you read these, please add some kind of loadout system, often times I had to menu through a cluttered inventory as I wanted to get the achievements for collecting items and it became rather annoying to swap everything out even with a favorite's system. As well, the ability to resave at checkpoint statues instead of having to leave to activate a different one is a much needed QoL change.

Over all, I'd recommend the game. It's not a hack and slash, and shouldn't be approached that way. The art style obviously has a bit of a lewd anime girl trend in a similar vein to Shantae, but I wouldn't say it detracts from the game much and the overall aesthetic and featured art is quite good. There's not much to write home about on the story, it's alright with a decent twist at the end and some of the characters can be amusing or quirky.

review_text:
After an 8-year hiatus, EHM makes its return via early access and while the game is very similar to its most recent iteration, that does not hinder or ruin the experience in any way.  As an early access game, this is a very polished and solid initial effort.

For those who haven't played EHM, the game is a text management sim where you take complete control of a team and attempt to use your skills as a general manager to take your team to glory.  As the game is in early access mode, there are no official licenses or real players.  However, www.ehmtheblueline.com has a very nice roster set, logos, and real team and competition names that provide that.  

Unlike NHL by EA Sports, you are the General Manager and do not control the players during games.  You sign free agents, hire coaches, scouts, and of course, trade as you desire.  Additionally, you can set your lines, practices, and tactics.  You also can promote and demote players between minor leagues and choose how to build your team.  As you're unable to control your players directly, tactics are very important in helping you win games.  The games themselves can be viewed via 2d mode where the players appear as dots with the puck, similar to the initial offerings of Football Manager 8 years ago, before it went 3D.  


The game engine is solid and provides a decent way to watch games and observe your players.  The minor gripe I do have with the game engine is that it does look dated especially compared with how SI has evolved its Football Manager franchise.  Having said that, the fact that this game was developed as a side project by SI mitigates that gripe somewhat.

The menus are cleaner than EHM 2007 although again, not as intuitive as the newest Football Manager games.  The other issue is that the game can only be run in one resolution which means that newer screen owners will not be able to view the game on a full screen.  Hopefully, that will be addressed in a future update.

If you love Football Manager, Out of the Park Baseball, and text sims, you owe yourself the privilege in checking this game out.  For $14,99, you simply can't go wrong.  The more people that purchase this game, the more likely we will see official licenses and future releases.  If you're an armchair hockey fan who thinks, sleeps, and drinks hockey, you definitely need to check this out.  Disappointed that your team continues to build around a questionable core?  Fix it yourself in EHM.  You won't regret it!

The game itself is not very long and can easily be completed in one sitting. It took me around 6 hours to do all missions and collectibles so if you skip that stuff you can easily finish it in only a few. It's a short, deliberately bad story but the whole package has a charm to it. I don't think the short play time is to its detriment though, because a lot of what makes this game appealing gets boring the longer you play.

With the lower price tag it's definitely worth checking out, you can probably even get it on sale for just a few bucks, especially if 3 is your favorite Far Cry, if you're not a fan of the Far Cry formula though don't expect this one to change you mind; it's more Far Cry 3 with a nice aesthetic and a lot of 80's references.

review_text:
For a small team of devs I must say the game is quite fun. It is short but there is some replayability.

THE STORY:
The story is pretty straight forward with some twist and turns here and there which gives is a vague dark souls feeling because nothing is directly told to you and exposition so its fun trying to guess who the big bad is even if its nothing new its refreshing to say the least.

THE ART:
The art style is fun and animated very well. I have no issue with the over-sized pixels as it is more likely an art decision and not a limitation of the dev team. I've seen art styles where the characters have no faces so big pixels should not make or break how the game feels. Its all subjective so if big pixels bother you don't buy it.
With that being said, the big bosses look awesome and are animated gorgeously.

THE GAME PLAY:
There is a learning curve here as to say the game wants you to learn how to play it not apply what you have learned from other platform games like it. The jumping, attacking, dodging, and hit boxes are essentially pixel perfect but they also have what Id like to call real weight to them. You are playing as a girl that is NOT a super hero, so she cant jump really high or dodge at super high speeds, her muscles are puny so swinging weapons would be cumbersome and there for by default clunky. Smaller weapons feel more natural and allow for better movement between attacks. 
Since your movement does not really allow for you to correct mistakes instantly you have to think about how you approach certain situations and what best weapons for the enemies present. The game wants you to think instead of mindlessly cutting through enemies with no regard to the gameplay at all. The gameplay is thoughtful.

OVERALL:
LOST RUINS is in my opinion a solid game, is it worth 20 dollars...Im not sure. The game is complete but short. There are some other modes that essentially add some additional hours to the experience but not truly any new content. However its a fun experiment i think. The small dev team did a good job capturing this particular genre of game and Im happy I picked it up. Hope to see more in the future.

I found the gameplay rather boring, but that's not necessarily the dev's fault--it could just be the format of the game that I'm not used to. Still, you should know going in that all you're going to be doing is walking around, progressing dialogue, and clicking things in the environment. About 1/3 of the way through it became a chore, and I just slogged through to get the rest of the story.

The premise was kind of silly. Changing the memories of people who are about to die? What's the point? But I'm willing to overlook that, there have been plenty of good stories built on a silly premise. I was expecting there to be a twist on that, but no, they really do just alter the memories of people who are about to die for a paycheck, there really isn't anything deeper there.

No, what I'm giving this a negative review for is the story arc itself. I just found it really...unimpressive. I won't give away any spoilers, so all I'll say about the ending is that my reaction was "wait...that's it?" The plot really wasn't that adventurous. For as highly acclaimed as the game is, I was expecting more, and it was a bit of a letdown.

I would recommend purchasing it only when it is on sale. Desperados 3 and Partisans 1941 were far better in my opinion than this game.

name: Dead by Daylight

review_text:
Pros

- Great deal of flexibility with how you want to play the game. Lots of skills, weapons, etc.
- The voice acting is decent.
- The graphics are decent.
- Lots of different side material to try out (hunting, alchemy, dice game, etc).

Cons

- The pacing of the game is all over the place. The tutorial alone is like 4 hours long. Even main quests get stretched out for so long.
- Your choices in the game don't seem to matter all to the storyline. If they do then it only becomes apparent closer to the end of the game. More than 50 hours in and I haven't seen it impact much besides small differences in quest outcomes.
- Following the plot of the game is a challenge because its not clear who is on whose side. 
- There are so many tedious side quests.
- So ... many ... cutscenes.
- The "skills" feel too bloated. It didn't need skills that give percentage increases. Once you go down that path it just adds to the bloat.
- The music is so repetitive. The same song gets played over, and over, and over.

Verdict: 

I think a lot of the praise of this game is a sign of how desperate we all are for a good RPG. This game is like a 7.5/10. It's not terrible but if you don't play it you aren't missing anything major.

I wouldn't recommend it for most people. Even people who play RPGs regularly may not enjoy it and may find themselves bored.

review_text:
I wanted to like this, but there were so many little quality of life and odd choices that it was very hard to get into it. After the first cut-scenes, it felt a lot like an MMO Player Simulator. There are points where you log out of "The World" and have to email people and check webpages about lore and look at forums IN THE GAME. You have an in-game desktop and have fake friends and fake forums / websites. There were also a lot of them. An official forum, an art forum, a forum off of a website. 

It could be interesting, but it just got super tedious. Other things were tedious for it as well. You could get party members but couldn't just manage their inventories. It was another simulation of being an MMO player note. You had to gift them something and then go into their inventory and then use it. It took a lot of separate interactions on separate screens to get other characters upgraded with new equipment. It was also a bit annoying that the dialogue was fairly standard JRPG but was supposed to be coming from "players" of the mmo. Like, those NPC "players" were really invested and roleplaying really hard, all while breaking the 4th wall. It was a bit bizzare with the tone of other elements of the game.  

This game has some interesting things and  I'm sure there are interesting bits to get to, but it never quite vibed with the older JRPG tone I was hoping for. It felt like it was trying to be a few different things at once and it was just tedious in some of the elements of gameplay.

review_text:
To the Moon is a bad video game and a bad story.

Before you flame me please note that my issues with the game extend past its rudimentary gameplay, poor graphics, and nonexistent settings. Also note that I have played several games similar to To the Moon which I will shout out in my review. If you're looking for a good adventure game, just going off of stuff I've both played and are available on Steam, check out the Ace Attorney Trilogy, Zero Escape: The Nonary Games (999 specifically, as that game is fantastic), killer7, or VA-11 Hall-a, and there are loads of other games I haven't played that seem better than this (Telltale's The Walking Dead, Danganronpa, Firewatch, 428, all of the LucasArts games, etc.). Hell, if you're looking for an Adventure game built in RPG Maker, I'd highly recommend OFF over To the Moon, and that game is [i]free[/i] (I have also heard good things about Yume Nikki and Ib, but again, haven't played them)

So let's address the obvious problems everyone already mentions. This game was built in an old version of RPG maker, which means a few things. First off, there are no settings to speak of, so I hope you like playing the game fullscreen with a low resolution, and I also hope you like clunky controls with inconsistent movement speeds. The graphics are also super generic. This isn't even a limitation with RPG Maker, OFF was made in this engine and that game has actual character design and an aesthetic protrayed in its worldbuilding. This is probably controversial, but I don't like the OST, there's a ton of piano songs and while they do provide a moody atmosphere, they largely blend together. As someone who loves video game music and will gladly seek out the music of games I've played, I really have no desire to do so with To the Moon. This is especially hilarious considering one of these piano pieces is a major story element. Once again, OFF had an atmospheric OST, but it was farrrr more unique and thus compelling to listen to on its own (on an aside, I adore its usage of [spoiler]Somewhere Over the Rainbow[/spoiler]). The gameplay basically boils down to running around a clunky RPG overworld to find certain interactables and solving some extremely basic tile puzzles…hell you don’t even play tile puzzles by the end of the game. 

So we're left with one thing: The narrative. The story itself is mostly compelling and has a cool setup: Look through a terminally ill patient’s memories and change them so that they remember themselves being an astronaut and going to the moon before they die. It has a very moody atmosphere and the story at least gives good payoff to the things it sets up. However, the overall tone is suuuuuper melodramatic, like it's actively trying its best to make you sad or emotional because of the music and the events we see the characters go through. But...I honestly don't care about any of that, because the characters and writing are quite poor. The characters are bland as hell and lack much in terms of personality or anything interesting; I can’t recall the names of most of the cast, and I have very little to say about the ones I do remember. While I can tell you about Johnny's life and what he goes through, I can't say anything compelling about him as a person. He uh...likes olives? He wants to go to the moon? His relations to other characters don't matter when they're ridiculously uninteresting: River and Johnny's mother's characters have some good idea but ultimately they aren't enough. The two leads have personality, but they also totally break the game’s serious tone with some really cringe-y writing that sometimes devolves to just referencing things, and it often becomes obvious that this was an indie game made in 2011 (Doctor Who references? Really?). I know it makes sense narratively since this is just another day of work for them, but it doesn’t make for an entertaining experience. And again, they really don't do much beyond that, they don't have any character relations outside of themselves (not even with Johnny tbh), so I don't really feel anything for either of the two leads. Compare them to some of my favorite characters, Phoenix Wright from Ace Attorney and Gillian from Va-11 Hall-a. They are very silly and entertaining characters, yes, but they also have a number of fun and interesting relationships with other, similarly deep members of the cast (Maya, Mia, Edgeworth, and Larry; Jill, Dana, and many customers and randoms), on top of their own depth like Nick's backstory and his motivations to be an attorney, and Gill's connections with Va-11 Hall-a's themes of coming to terms with your past and focusing on the present. To the Moon's characters just don't have any of that...

At least the story, in terms of the events taking place, is good for much of the game…at least until the climax and ending which are [b]awful[/b]. It's both nonsensical and RIDICULOUSLY emotional manipulative. I imagine the devs want you to cry during this sequence, but I was absolutely livid. To get into spoilers, [spoiler]how the HELL is River the one preventing Johnny from going to the Moon, the loss of his brother and subsequent loss of his memory is the real thing keeping from doing so. There is absolutely no reason for her to have been moved to a later part of Johnny's life, and the fact that your partner REFUSES to explain anything while doing this is, also, nonsensical and only serves to add tension through that chase sequence. And then, they segue into this ]emotionally manipulative disappearance sequence with a disgustingly sappy song...ONLY THEN does the game back-pedal on River's disappearance because of course it does, it obviously wasn't going to commit to rubbing out River, the game just wanted you to cry for a bit. Sigh..,I'm not against emotional story moments, but please don't force it and let it make sense (i.e. 999's S*f* Ending). Not like it would've mattered much in this case since, again, I don't feel much of a connection with these characters to begin with. Also, while I'm on story spoilers, the twist that Johnny has a twin brother is pretty dumb[/spoiler]

When I took all of this into account, I realized something…To the Moon has [i]nothing[/i] going for it. The graphics are mid, the gameplay is mid, the soundtrack is mid, and they even managed to botch the story. While it wasn’t a straight-up pain to play throughout, I can’t say I came out of this game with a positive outlook.

If you legitimately cried at this game, I'm glad you were able to find an emotional connection that I couldn't. But also, I'm sure there are plenty of other games that will make you cry harder.

review_text: Such a cute idea to move this to the 1700s, and I love the 2D graphics styling.  In addition, slight changes to cozy farming gameplay was genius (example, quests being optional, proposals not being guaranteed marriage, other characters lives progressing alongside yours, the rotting of food items).  These changes (and many others) actually had me paying attention and learning how to alter my gameplay style instead of it being a rinse and repeat from other games. review_text:
I want to love this, I really do. It's got all the makings of a relaxing low stakes trick game. The controls in theory are well adjusted to the type of game this is and allow for flexibility and player expression, but some bugs and quirks really hold it back. For instance, when certain conditions your buttons will behave different to how they normally do. Your held jump button will sometimes decide that you are intending to do a stunt, forcing you into a trick you don't have the clearance for. On a few occasions when trying to do a running jump from the end of a thin wall it would catapult me into a dive straight to the ground when I was trying to gain more height. There are also some key moves missing. The lack of any sort of wall kick really sticks out, but the wall running and wall climbing mechanics in general are very stiff and rudimentary. Moves requiring multiple held buttons and triggers can often feel stiff and occasionally unreliable, and any moves requiring specific set ups of map geometry like striding and power leaping feel railroaded.

I don't envy the movement system dev. Their task is difficult and I am sure they will improve the flow of the game over time, but in the meantime this doesn't satisfy my parkour itches. Before I go I will say that the area this game shines most is trick lines. If you can take the time to understand the quirks of the movement system and plan out your routes in ways that compliment its strengths and mitigate its weaknesses you can build a line that you can explore with a decent variety of stunts to choose from. But for me, the game just doesn't quite capture that free flowing fantasy.

review_text:
*Warning: spoilers* 

Blend, short and uninspired game.

Lucius is a game about an evil little 6-year-old boy, that apparently is the son of Lucifer himself. The game is all about murdering everyone in your household and covering your tracks so nobody will know that it was you. Do this for around five hours and you beat Lucius. 

There is a lame and cliché story about cultists, the birth of Lucius, his connection with his Devil father and how he came to be the evil boy he is today. The story itself has some potential but when playing the game, it is a wasted effort and feels misplaced. Imagine Tetris for example. You watch a movie about how the blocks can move on their own, how they came to be, and after that, you just place blocks and make rows disappear.

The game play is boring, repetitive and short. You use telekinesis and some sort of pyro thing to casually murder everyone, one at the time, in the manor you live in. Although you go to different places in the manor, it is the only location in the whole game and you cannot free roam. Every day you get a mission and need to follow a specific path. The rest is blocked off. When you arrive on your destination, you play some kind of mini game to setup the murder of the lifeless, empty and generic character that you want to send to the afterlife and then repeat this process a couple of times with some different mini game.

There is nothing else to this game. You repeat the same thing over and over. There is no inventory, no different approaches or different outcomes in a certain scenario and there is no satisfaction whatsoever. It feels, and is, all so scripted and empty, it almost plays like some sort of demo. 

Graphically, the game is all right. The animations and the frame rate are smooth, and for the time, the overall game looks fine. Such as shame and wasted effort for a bad game like this.

The sound is terrible. All the effects and music are more blend than ever. They are ripped straight off some kind of open-source sound board. 

To top it off, the game featured some achievements, which were all ridiculously easy. But, of course, they needed to add a filthy grind achievement, in which you play the game for forty hours….. The game is not even four to five hours long. This meant getting on my tricycle bike, putting a weight on my left arrow key and let the game beat itself. Sad, I know, but I like my games complete, no matter how bad they are.

Overall, Lucius was a boring, blend experience and I hoped it would get better, but sadly, it did not. It is just not worth it. 

Not recommending this one.

UPDATE 2025: In 2022, I experienced the introduction of Bonelab, and upon revisiting it, I’ve gained a deeper understanding of its psychological and visual design choices. The intro sequence was not just an artistic decision but a carefully crafted psychological priming mechanism that subtly manipulates the user’s emotional state through a series of deliberate psychological triggers.

Step 1: Embodiment and Self-Identification

The experience begins with the player standing in front of a mirror. This is not just a simple reflection—it’s an embodiment technique, reinforcing the connection between the user and their avatar. By seeing themselves in the mirror, users are subtly grounded in the virtual space, making subsequent experiences feel more personal, immersive, and inescapable.

This step ensures that what happens next feels like it is happening to "you"—not just a character in a game. It deepens immersion, making the psychological impact of what follows far more intense.

Step 2: The Light Beams and Lowering the Guard

The next sequence features moving light beams advancing forward—a visual that seems artistic at first but serves a deeper purpose. The forward motion induces a sensation of weightlessness and deep relaxation, lulling the user into a passive state.

This transition is not abrupt but carefully structured to make the shift from light to darkness more jarring and emotionally disruptive. By relaxing the player beforehand, the upcoming events become even more unsettling, as their guard has been lowered without them realizing it.

Step 3: The Dark Void and the Noose

After the light beam sequence, the player is suddenly placed into a dark void—an empty, featureless black space where nothing happens. There is no immediate instruction, no visible escape—just silence and darkness.

This forces the player into a moment of stillness, where they have no choice but to wait. This is a psychological setup—it builds anticipation, uncertainty, and mild discomfort, making the player even more vulnerable when the next event occurs.

Then, without warning, an extremely detailed and unnecessarily hyper-realistic noose swings down from the darkness in front of the player.

The game does not progress unless the player interacts with the noose, puts it around their neck, and hangs themselves. There is no way forward, no alternate path, and no option to refuse. The game locks the player into an explicit, forced simulation of self-harm, offering no explanation, no foreshadowing, and no consent.

This is not a symbolic or artistic moment—it is a direct mechanical requirement to continue the game. The player is placed in a controlled environment where their only option is to comply.

Step 4: Sudden Shift to Public Judgment

Immediately after this forced act, the player is ripped from the dark void and thrown into an entirely new environment—a hyper-realistic open field, suspended above a pit, surrounded by a large crowd of robed figures holding torches, staring up in silence.

This transition is a psychological escalation, shifting the player from internal isolation to external judgment and condemnation. The people in robes evoke ritualistic, cult-like imagery, symbolizing execution, punishment, or mass scrutiny. The shift from solitude to public exposure mimics a nightmare-like distortion of reality, where what was once a personal, silent moment suddenly becomes an inescapable spectacle.

This sequence is designed to be emotionally overwhelming—the rope, the pit, the torches, the judgmental figures—all working together to amplify distress and psychological discomfort. Whether intentional or not, the message is clear: there is no escape, only the weight of what has just occurred.

Step 5: A Completely Disconnected, Aimless Gameplay Loop

Yet, what follows is perhaps the most telling part—after this highly distressing and manipulative introduction, there is no context.

The story doesn’t continue in a logical way. Instead, the player is thrown into a disconnected sandbox mode where they must complete all the doors and solve a complicated crane minigame that, for some players, takes hours to figure out.

This minigame has no explanation and is purposefully complicated, creating a scenario where players feel utterly lost. The difficulty and lack of guidance appear designed to make the user doubt their mental abilities, as if the traumatic intro sequence has disoriented them to the point of cognitive dysfunction. This additional layer of distress serves to deepen the psychological manipulation, leading some players to question whether they are thinking correctly or if something is wrong with them.

Only after completing this unrelated obstacle does the actual narrative of the game begin.

This is not normal game design. It suggests that the intro was never meant to be a cohesive part of the story. It stands alone as an isolated psychological experience, its sole function being to plant disturbing imagery and force players through an emotionally jarring sequence before dumping them into a completely unrelated gameplay loop. The fact that the story only resumes much later, after prolonged and aimless wandering, further proves that this opening was meant to serve a separate purpose.

Final Thoughts: A Masterclass in Psychological Manipulation

For anyone struggling in real life, this sequence can be extremely distressing. The way it is structured is not accidental—it is designed to manipulate emotions, create an intrusive association, and provoke a deep psychological response. The lack of warnings or context only adds to its potential for harm, as users are drawn into a carefully controlled mental state before they even realize what is happening.

Looking back, the entire sequence was a masterclass in psychological priming—using embodiment, relaxation, contrast, and hyper-realistic detail to guide the user’s mind in a specific direction, even before they are fully aware of it. The lack of transparency about these psychological techniques raises serious ethical concerns, as they are implemented in a way that maximizes emotional vulnerability without consent.

This isn’t just an unsettling experience—it’s an intentional psychological manipulation disguised as artistic storytelling.

Don't touch this game.

The issue isn't the game itself; which is great. The issue is a complete lack of customer support when you engage through STEAM.

It has this really cool link that permits you to automatically generate an account for the game through STEAM. As soon as you do, however, you run into a myriad of problems and wind up on a customer support blacklist.

To use their "customer support" link, you must have an account through the game developer itself. To have that accound, you must create it on their website. When you do so, you can link it to STEAM; but that means the existing account becomes UNlinked. It appears that they can no longer find your STEAM account and provide you with logon information.

If you go directly to their website and chat, as soon as they find out that you created your account through STEAM, they apologize that there is nothing they can do for you.

I have concerns about products I have purchased with real money that I should have access to, as per the text ("unlocked for all characters on the account") which I don't have. I have purchased two products that were supposed to be made available to all acocunt characters; and they're not. I can't get it fixed because I don't have an account with the game provider. The game provider will give me all the support I want or need -- after I abandon my current account (of which I have invested literally hundreds of dollars AND hours) and start fresh; thus losing every bit of my investment.
