review_text:
IMSCARED has a few original ideas, but really fell flat in the end. There are different environments that you traipse through, each with a different atmosphere, but nothing felt intuitive or exciting. Sometimes there's a hidden key you haven't found, and sometimes you have to go check out files that the game is creating on your desktop. Sometimes you even have to close and restart the game yourself to continue. The fact that the game never communicates what you have to do to advance can sometimes create situations in which you're not sure if you should be looking around harder because you missed something, or if you should write a five page essay and submit it to the game. The fourth wall bits are interesting but poorly implemented for a cohesive horror experience.

The story is weak and vague, the graphics have a nice style but make text illegible, and the jumpscares were mostly unnecessary. Some parts of the game rely on sound within a 3D soundscape, and sound seems to originate in one position but does not change relative to your movement. Certain actions like climbing a ladder or printing tickets have a gratingly loud volume for no reason. 

Many achievements were very arbitrary, and ended up being necessary to finish the game. Oh, and if you want to go back to get the achievements, have fun figuring out the ridiculous hallway hub. 2 doors go to 2 areas, one door with a pickup is needed to access a password screen to get to 2 other areas. It's as dumb as it sounds. 

IMGLAD that I didn't pay more than $4, which still seems too steep for the overall quality of this "game,"  or waste more than 2 hours getting achievements to see the loud, lame ending. It's an experience, but one that I could have lived just fine without.

review_text:
I gotta say, for a game bundle that is functionally free, these are fantastic.

I got hooked quickly. The puzzles are, for the most part, very intuitive. You're generally given enough clues to be able to solve them, and there's no complicated crafting system for combining items. In terms of buying hints, the star points system is resource management rather than a penalty; it's very easy to stockpile earned stars since the majority of puzzles are reasonable to solve on your own. For certain puzzles, if you have 30 stars, you can even skip them entirely.

Having to wait for keys to regenerate so that I can unlock more chapters is a bit annoying on weekends, but it offers me a natural stopping point on weeknights. Most of the chapters have enough content in them that it doesn't just feel like a cheap trick to get you to pay for more keys (though the earlier games are worse when it comes to intuitiveness and content amount). I can understand the developer needing to hold back players from just consuming ALL the content at once considering it's GOOD content that *can* be played entirely for free if you're patient enough.

Pro Tip: If you're ever feeling lost on what your objective is, check the title of the hint box. It'll usually clue you in on what puzzle you should be working on solving.

--

Editing to add individual game opinions (spoiler-free):

- Something I discovered after finished this bundle via desktop is there's even more individual games by the developer available in the iOS app store. That led me to discover that some of the adventures in this bundle set were repurposed from the app store games. When played individually on the app, there's no paywalling--the chapters are short with barely any content per chapter BUT they're all unlocked. Games such as Midnight Carnival and Haunted Hunt are annoying to play within the bundle because they weren't originally made with a paywall in mind.

- I will say about Haunted Hunt that it has a fantastic magic system and a super compelling story. Using the shapeshifting is integral to solving the puzzles in a very interesting way.

- On the flip side, Cursed Crown was frustrating for me. The magic system feels tacked on in a way that you forget to use it. Neither the story nor the characters were particularly compelling either.

- I love Mirror Man. There's a nice variety of puzzles, and it never felt stale for me. The horror flavor is nice too (I've already devoured every Rusty Lake game), and if you can handle occasional jump scares (which are just there to give you a little controlled scare without asking for a response), you should be fine with this one

- I hate Allied Spies. Many of the puzzles are either timed or require timing. Too much reliance on reflexes. I had to use up a LOT of stars to skip puzzles that were just effing impossible for me to manage

- Legend of the Stones duology is mehhhhh. Very repetitive puzzles with the board pieces and then the boss battles. The latter of which is timed. I had to skip many of the boss battles because I just couldn't handle it

- The Detective Kate series is decent. It's a whole lot of copaganda, but if you can get past that, the puzzles are reasonable for a straight-forward murder mystery series. Chapter lengths vary wildly though. But I can say the Trapmaker adventures are fun since it gives an excuse for literal escape rooms.

- Painted Worlds has some mechanics and puzzles that are unique to itself, and I mostly enjoyed it. There was ONE puzzle that required clicking the screen in a reflex test that couldn't be skipped, and it was so frustrating that I rage quit for a while. I had to switch my setup from touchpad to a mouse just to get past it. 

- The Squire's Tale surprised me with how much I didn't hate it. The first chapter has a puzzle-battle against some goblins, and I was worried this would be a core mechanic throughout the adventure. Thankfully it's not so! I was also very pleased that the final boss battle was not reflex-based. 

- Adventures that I enjoyed, though I don't have any specific commentary on them: Psychic Squad, The Sultan's Inventor, Lost Ruins series 

- The Puzzle Pack is just 6 of the same puzzles for every chapter, which gets monotonous after a while. Supposedly it offers guidance/Easter Eggs for the Covenant, but that information slid right off of me

- Covenant is the only paid game (hints are free and chapters all unlocked). After having gone through hundreds of hours playing everything else, I paid for it as a gift to the developers. And given how short the chapters are and how horrible a few of the puzzles end up being, I don't think the game itself is worth the $7. For example, the final "boss battle" is an arcade style mini-game (boo hiss) that does not function as a puzzle. There's also TWO puzzle hints in the game that require AUDIO, which makes them non-accessible to deaf/HoH people and anyone like me, who turned off all audio for personal reasons and was like wtf is going on. With all that said, at least the game offers some replay-ability based on the NPCs you choose, which changes the flavor of the ending and varies up how much background information you learn.

They appear to really be in touch with their game community, and I very much respect and appreciate that.

review_text:
The Callisto Protocol is such a waste of time, I'm not even sure I want to dedicate mine to review it frankly...but I must inform people; 

The Callisto Protocol is essentialy an amalgamation of poorly designed and badly executed game mechanics that went half-cooked from its conception to the game release; what kinda works in it, it's just because the same hands that made TCP also did [u]the game[/u] that took massive "inspiration" from, which is pretty peculiar seeing that the guy in charge, in retrospective, tried to do THE SAME damn game all over again, giving it another name. From the plot to some mechanics, the similarities are so uncanny, that I can't even classify it as a "spiritual successor".

The melee combat system with the baton has no excuses to be this bad; the worst mechanic in the game by far, which extends every single fight, on hard difficulty, by at least thirty seconds in which you have to dodge and attack without any effort at all in the hope it will all end sooner than later. It gets repetitive after the second encounter if you do not implement anything else with it, but it is almost mandatory to go full melee, because of the scarcity of ammo and resources found in some chapters of the game. At least some weapons feel powerful despite enemies being very lacking in diversity, not offering much of a challenge throught-out the game.

Can't say nothing bad about graphics, we are so far above what we used to look at a few years back, that now, with the high fidelity and the photorealism, good graphics are not a novelty anymore for big companies rather than just something pretty to look at, if the game doesn't just stand on itself, and The Callisto Protocol got too many downsides for that. It runs a bit poorly, as it was already established in the launch days, and even tho it has been fixed somehow in time, it still stutters in some scenarios.

The story starts decently and it is generally interesting on paper but you're almost left out of it as the protagonist for so long, that it starts to feel like it is dragged out, until it fades in an anti-climatic ending if you don't play one of the DLCs that exists only to delve into important details omitted in the base game (and by omitted details I mean that the game goes from one hundred to zero mph in the frame of a minute leaving you with a bitter taste in your mouth, without much explanation). 

Overall a sluggish, forgettable and uninspired experience, if not one of the most useless games I've ever played. It doesn't almost never happen to me, but I had to force myself to finish it while rushing to the end because it was unbereable to keep playing, yet I still wanted to see where the story lead. 

It's so ironic to me that the same year came out the Dead Space Remake too, and it's so much better in every aspect if inevitably compared to The Callisto Protocol, which doesn't manage to check anything positively in spite of Dead Space. 

If you value your time, this is a [b] big skip[/b]. You'll thank me later.

Six years later and I finally decided it was time for a change. I went back to school and rejoined the third grade, but this time it was worse. I now live happily in a mansion with my seven wives, twelve super-cars, and billions of dollars.

Thank you "Samorost 2", I will be forever grateful to you.

review_text:
I was really hoping that the dev would continue adding to the promising foundation that this game has but unfortunately that is not likely to happen.

In its current state building up your first village is an enjoyable experience and quite challenging, but once you get over that first hurdle and can spread to other tiles it becomes a major bore. The difficulty takes a sharp decline even on the hardest setting as you can easily get ahead of the corruption in new tiles by sending enough resources with your nomads. 

Positives:
•	Core village building feels great and watching your villages grow is rewarding.
•	Magic system is a great twist and allows for a more active role during tense situations.
•	Art style is simple but endearing.

Negatives:
•	Corruption (the enemy) is simplistic with limited enemy types.
•	Difficulty scaling is wonky due to an incomplete feeling “end game”.
•	Builder AI can be frustrating as they hold no priority and will all rush the same buildings together.

Ideally, I would have loved to see more enemy types start appearing as time goes on or as more tiles are colonised. Some sort of research tree mixed into the progression to complement an adapting enemy would make this a solid tower defence/colony sim.

*update 13/6/21*
It looks like the dev has made an announcement that development will continue, hopefully the game will receive some much needed love. As it stands my review is still valid for the current version as of this update.

Hiveswap: Act 2 is a game riddled with bugs, detrimental shortcuts, and tedious gameplay. When I first played and finished this game I was fine with it, but looking back I realize that most of my enjoyment came from the visuals and dialogue rather than any other part. The actual game part of it is downright embarrassing for a project thats been in development for almost a decade now.

The main gameplay is basically the same as the first act of Hiveswap. It works fine and I don't have any complaints about how it's laid out. What I DO have a problem with is the inane bullshittery that is the puzzles. You can barely apply logic to most of these puzzles, they're that bad. It either comes down to using every single item you have on every single object in the room or talking to every single character in the room again even if it seems like they dont have anything else to say. You cannot make it through this game on your own without using hints, because nothing you do makes any sense. The trial portion of the game shares similar problems, with the evidence needed to progress often not being clear. The worst part of the game however is definitely the final portion. It is quite literally nothing but backtracking over and over again. You have to go down the map about six different times during this section, and there's no way to quickly get to a location. You have to manually walk ALL THE WAY BACK. If that wasn't bad enough, the last time you do this is completely pointless. It's literally only done so you can get out of a certain room so an event can play out. After all of that, the game ends with another trial-and-error puzzle that ends anticlimactically. This is such a major step down from the first game's simpler design. It doesn't help that alongside this you have tons of bugs as well as entire story scenes just cut out completely leading to bad pacing.

In the end though, I think the worst part about this game is the fact that they actively refused to credit the people involved with this project. The Homestuck team stated on Twitter that they'd purposely not included the credits and are going to add them "as launch hype dies down". This is scummy, terrible behavior from this crew and I would recommend not giving them money until they fix this and credit their goddamn workers.

Don't let shitty business decisions go unpunished,

review_text:
Out of the hundreds of games in my library, I dont think I've ever played such a repetitive, frustrating, overhyped game in my life. All 18 hours I've spent in this game were not remotely fun or interesting, only frustrating, counter-intuitive, unbelievable and just flat out boring. I got this game on sale and still wish I could refund it.

First of all, the game is optimized terribly. I have a pretty high end computer and I still get massive frame drops just walking around the boring, cookie cutter world and every time I enter a tiny little warehouse it takes like 5 seconds to load while opening the door. My computer runs games that look twice as good and have twice the amount of resources exponentially better than this game. Also. (and this is probably the biggest issue that is making it impossible to finish the game even if I wanted to,) this game claims to have full controller support and that is simply not true. The D pad does not work in menu's, I constantly have to disconnect and re-connect my controller in-game to get it to start working again (I have never had to do this in any other games with native controller support,) and the game will not register the input of the left and right triggers or mouse buttons. Meaning I am completely unable to fight, pick locks, zoom in or out on the map, etc. After trying for hours to fix the problem on my own, I emailed Icepick customer support and politely asked them if they had any suggestions for me to try or if they could look into patching this issue, that was over a month ago and they have completely ignored me. Shoddy game, in addition to shoddy customer support.

There are countless other features of this game that are just utterly infuriating and not in any way entertaining. I love difficult games, I've played all of the From software games and love grinding away at a difficult challenge for the euphoric feeling of finally beating a difficult boss or area, this game is not like that at all. For example, you character in this game is severely diabetic (apparently.) I starved to death about 5 in game hours after I ate a loaf of bread, a fish, 2 eggs, and a glass of milk, all of which cost like 2000 dollars. Extremely unrealistic and breaks any semblance of immersion. So when I die, I am then told by the annoying theatre guy that from now on I'm going to starve to death EVEN FASTER. How fun! Also, apparently staying up all night will make you just suddenly fall over and die. Again, super unbelievable, immersion breaking, and just plain stupid and frustrating. 

The trailer for this game makes it seem like it will be way more exciting and action packed than it is. It shows basically all the most dramatic parts of the game and does not represent what the vast majority of the experience is. 95 percent of this game is just walking/running around this boring little town with identical looking buildings while listening to your character huff and puff, getting trapped in an endless amount of dead end back yards because the knee-high rock wall is to tall to step over, so that you can talk to all these boring, identical looking characters that dont even speak, just have text underneath like a skyrim mod that didnt bother to put in voice acting. All of these characters say the same cryptic, irrelevant, esoteric nonsense that feels like it was pulled straight out of a 14 year old emo kids diary or off of Jaeden Smiths twitter. "The town represents the body, and the body needs blood to survive, and the spirit is in the blood, Barakh. Therefore find the spirit of the town, and you will find its body, and your path will be illuminated etc etc." 

The audio in this game is super weird as well, not in a good way. When I am in a plague ridden area of town, you hear the same identical scream on a 4-8 second loop and it just sounds fake and again breaks any semblance of immersion which is apparently supposed to be a defining feature of this game. The soundtrack, while pretty atmospheric and eerie at first, plays over and over and over during all your hours just wandering around the map to the point of driving you nuts and wanting to turn the music volume all the way down. 

Stealth in this game is an absolute joke. It doesnt even exist. You can be in a completely empty apartment building, in an empty room with no windows, about to take 4 dollars out of a nightstand or take a dead guys organ, but somehow "they'll know" it was you who took it despite there being not a single soul around to see it. I've mentioned immersion breaking right?

I spent so many hours trying to like this game mainly because it had so many good reviews I figured I must just be looking at it the wrong way, doing something wrong, not having enough patience, not getting the point etc, so I kept trying and trying to see where the fun or any form of enjoyment or curiosity about the bland story would start to sink in, and it just got progressively more frustrating the longer I played it to the point of now having zero interest in getting any farther whatsoever in addition to not being able to complete the story with my left and right triggers and mouse buttons not working. I also cant bring myself to recommend giving your money to a studio whose customer support wont even bother answering a consumers question with a simple "sorry you're having this problem, we'll look into it" or even "we dont know how to fix it."

 I truly mean it when I say this is the most disappointing game I have ever played, in almost every aspect.

review_text:
The intro to Just Cause 3: Shooting rockets while standing on an airplane flying over a war zone
The intro to Just Cause 4: "Follow the pipes Rico"

I haven't experienced the same crashing or technical issues others have, my gameplay has been rather smooth and unproblematic. Instead, I'm focusing my review on one thing: the fun factor, something JC4 distinctly lacks. The Just Cause franchise has evolved into a very clear gamplay loop: blow something up, go to the next thing to blow up, repeat. Just Cause 4 massively neglects the first half of that gameplay loop, there's far less to blow up in this game. On a technicality there's the same amount, but in reality there's no reason to do anything, so you won't do it. Why blow up a massive propane tank if you don't need to? You won't, you'd rather use that rocket on a helicopter. 

Just Cause 4 is an excellent game, but it feels gray compared to the colorful and explosive world of Just Cause 3. The movement is the same, so the core gameplay loop is undeniably worse in exchange for better graphics and more advanced systems. The comparison can be summarized in one sentence.

[u]Just Cause 4 is more impressive, but Just Cause 3 is more fun[/u]

This game is a love letter to the Jet Set Radio series, and even includes original music from Hideaki Naganuma. The artstyle, music, and setting are also a strong hook for fans of those games, and there are tons of collectibles to be found and some of them are very well hidden. I only have 3 real gripes with the game:

1 - The trick system is very simplistic. You have all of 3 options to choose from and a small boost trick.
2 - The story is, way, way too short. If you scoop this game up definitely pace yourself and take your time exploring and gathering collectibles.
3 - The cops get old fast. As you progress thru the game and begin spraypainting you'll attract the attention of the cops and you'll wish you could press a large red button that turns them all off. There are mechanics in the game designed to help you shake them off but it doesn't make them any less of a fun tax.

All in all it's enjoyable, but short. Wait for a sale before grabbing it imo.

Overall the graphics and physics are miles better and I recommend the game simply for those reasons as well as the mods and sandbox.

review_text:
I enjoyed this a lot more than i thought i would. It's not the most groundbreaking horror shooter ever made, but its atmosphere and gameplay are both extremely solid.

Combat is slow and tactical, the mechanic of enemies merging with fresh corpses to become stronger is interesting but underused, the weapons all feel good to use and they each have a modified version that works completely differently, which is nice for variety and replayability.

The story is very obtuse and can be hard to follow but the smaller bits of lore and character building make the whole thing a lot easier to enjoy. The environments are mostly typical horror game stuff but are all very lovingly modelled and detailed. The lack of polish dub is a little sad considering how rooted in that country's culture the game seems to be, but this is a minor gripe.

My biggest gripe with the game is the fact that hard mode is only unlocked after beating the game once; if you've played games like this before the default difficulty will definitely feel too easy. 
Pleeaaaaaaase game developers i beg you stop doing this

review_text: I have over 30 hours in-game now and have encountered a few game-breaking glitches. Often, after dying, you will glitch out and be unable to shoot or turn your head. The only workaround is to pause, redeploy, or be killed. When switching between weapons, the sights sometimes glitch and display the perspective of the previous weapon, making aiming difficult. Occasionally, after reloading and switching between a special ability, the gun will not be reloaded when you attempt to shoot, leaving you scrambling to load a new magazine while bugs swarm your face. I've also respawned into a glitch where you're endlessly falling through the map and dying because the spawn area is cluttered with walls built by the team. This drained my team's tickets—about seven times less—until the game finally managed to spawn me in. Many of the weapons, including the primary assault rifle, feel underpowered, so each kill of a "standard bug" isn't very satisfying. I've tried all the classes in the game, and most of their weapons and abilities also feel weak, almost like a gimmick, especially when you've seen the original movie and the devastation an AR can cause to a bug. It takes an entire magazine to kill a single bug, even with the auto-shotgun (unless you hit a weak spot), which makes the kill feel pretty lame. People have spoken online in reviews about how they need to change the way the Galactic War Mode or whatever its called works. By making it more of a turn based war claiming bug planets by way of battle. After a planet has been claimed you go to the next planet and the next until the campaign is completed. That would make the Horde mode make more sense if after a mission is failed the team is gathered to a point on the planet to defend like "the Alamo" until swept off planet by a dropship. Then the team is regathered, you go back to the same planet, and fight again to claim it, planet by planet until the war is finally done. I really feel like the game could use dismemberment similar to the movies. Bug arms and legs getting physically shot off by your gain fire depending on the body part you target, then the bugs movement could be slowed down. Also, the marines could once in a while be picked up by certain stronger bugs, and torn apart limb by limb. I feel it would feel more like the movies if it was so. Casper Van Dien or "Rico" could also be used to narrate the Galactic war missions, and dont lock players out if they're in a clan or not. There's much work to be done here, but I have faith that they can make it great. There's so much untapped potential in this game.

review_text:
I really want to recommend this game as a hockey fan, but I just can't in its current state. It certainly has its moments, and it [i] almost [/i] has that addictive quality that great roguelikes have, but it has some absolute glaring issues that make it incredibly frustrating to play beyond Act 1. 

[b] Issue #1: The AI [/b] 
The teammate AI is a mixed bag. In some ways it works well; it's clear that effort was taken to ensure that it plays well in the offensive zone, with the AI-controlled players reliably getting in position to receive cross-seam passes. The issues with the AI become more obvious when you don't have the puck. The AI seems to have no concept of "last man back", and will charge straight towards the puck carrier in the neutral zone. This frequently gives your opponent scoring chances, and I'd wager at least half of the goals I allowed were scored at least in part due to this. 
The other annoying issue is how bad the AI is at moving to get the puck. The bots aren't very good at predicting where the puck is going, often completely missing what should be an easy rebound to bang home. This is compounded by how awkward it is to pick up bouncing pucks. 

[b] Issue #2: The Opponents [/b] 
The early opponents are just basic teams with simple themes. As the run progresses, the opponents get more varied and interesting, but also much worse to play against. In Act 3, teams are spamming their special abilities so much it becomes impossible to play with any strategy or skill; I beat the 'final boss' team by just dumping the puck and trying to win the faceoff. This is boring, but anything else is nearly impossible because otherwise your players are more often than not knocked out. These teams should provide a challenge, but are really just a slog. 

[b] Issue #3: The Progression [/b]
Tape to Tape draws massive inspiration from Slay the Spire, but seems to completely miss what makes that game so addictive. In StS, winning a run with a character unlocks the next level of Ascension for that character, which is essentially a slightly-harder version of the run you just beat. As the player improves, the game offers harder and harder challenges to match them, which makes them want to keep coming back for 'one more run.' In Tape to Tape, you get currency to buy upgrades between runs to make the game easier, which kills the feeling of wanting to come back to do it all over again. 

[b] Issue #4: The Content [/b] 
I can cut the game some slack as an early access indie title, but that doesn't change the fact there's just not enough content for the price right now. You play almost the exact same teams in the exact same order every time. Other roguelikes like StS put players into completely different builds and scenarios every run, but Tape to Tape starts to feels repetitive after just a few hours. There's a decent variety of starting abilities for the player to use, but they're mostly totally useless by Act 3 anyway. 

So yeah. I want to love this game, but it's incredibly frustrating and repetitive in it's current state. Losing runs rarely felt like the consequence of a mistake but instead the result of janky mechanics or pure RNG (I once outshot an opponent 25-to-1 and lost...) I sincerely hope these issues are addressed, because the core of this game could be awesome if it were improved upon further.

review_text:
The only other game I can think of that fails at Dead Space this hard is Dead Space 3. This was clearly put together by a producer that said "I can do it better" that went on to prove that he in fact could not do it better, in the most incompetent way possible. This feels like a vertical slice early development prototype that's been stretched to 10 hours. I suspect that some of the current problems come from attempting to "patch" problems that are fundamentally broken. A certain Yahtzee Crowshaw nails why this is a horrible game in a much more creative way than I ever could but I'll try. 

tl;dr Combat is boring, movement is clunky, difficulty is achieved through by being a cheater, and the story is a poorly done version of Dead Space, and there's little exploration or branching paths

First off, yes this game is Dead Space, no matter what anyone says. Regular Joe doing a regular job? Check. An out of the way facility in a place people aren't going to look? Check. A corporation with a facility out on the edge of space so people can't watch what they're doing? Check. A shadowy religious organization that infiltrates the company and uses it to its own means? Check. That organization releasing a zombie outbreak because it fits in with their beliefs? Check. Holographic HUD on the character? Check. Vaguely Japenese writing all over the place? Check. 

The entire plot is Dead Space with the nuance removed and the obvious being spelled out in minute detail. There's a log in the game that says "I don't know why they want to stop terraforming after spending billions, its like they don't want people here, wink, wink, wink". You don't care about the characters either. One character naturally dies, I didn't care because he wasn't helping.

How is it not like Dead Space? They took all the good things, chucked them in the garbage and replaced them with features a senior game design student would put together over a semester.

Movement is slow and clunky. It takes forever to turn around, even with the mouse settings maxed out. And you randomly run into walls or trip over random objects. Either the hit boxes are off or the Jacob has some undiagnosed illness.

The combat is boring and inconsistent.  Its got 3 main problems, weapon handling, how difficulty is achieved, and the variety of tactics. 

It really shouldn't be "melee focused" it should be "only one weapon at a time focused". I died a couple of times early on and for the life of me couldn't figure out why. It was because the weapon stowing and switching is gawdawully slow and inconsistent. The pistol will come up and you can ADS in a flash. On the other hand you can bake a cake in the time it takes to stow the thing or switch. The baton, you know the thing was built around, is slow at everything. Including getting unstowed. Oh and it'll get [i][b]stowed all the time without you having a choice in the matter[/b][/i]. So you either have to see an enemy coming from far off, or you need to be able to have it ready at all times for it to be useful. The overall effect is that switching from one weapon to the next can take 5 or 6 seconds. Which will get you killed.

And who the f*** thought the [u]quick[/u] weapons switch was quick or a good idea? Over the last 30 years we've converged on few different ways to cleanly select the type of weapon from a pistol to a shotgun. It takes 4 separate button clicks to switch between both of the weapons the game gives you.

Enemy AI is dumb. Enemy's will come straight at you, with the ranged enemies planted in place. Close range you'll do melee. Which is the same sequence of steps for each fight, dodge once or twice, attack 2 or 3 times, repeat until enemy dead. If you're at a distance you can just chuck objects at enemies until they go down, or use the pistol. No thought or effort required. 

To give you any sort of challenge the game has to cheat. It loves forced damage. You'll have enemies that pop out of boxes and piles of goo on the ground. You can't do anything about the ones that pop out of boxes. It got so bad I was just spamming E whenever I opened a box. Some of the piles of goo you can see but they're placed in awkward positions to where you can't it them with rapid flying object or the pistol. And then there's the games favorite trick, dropping an enemy immediately behind you without any sort of clue that it's happening. Of course enemy placement is 100% scripted, so once you die you know when it where, when, and what's going to happen. Die once, kill them second time. At least Dead Space would drop enemies into areas you already cleared. 

There are some other minor issues that could be overlooked if everything else weren't so bad. The facial animations are just this side of the uncanny valley, like early talking stone CGI. The game is very linear. The story feels like its still at the outline stage. And the game is still still buggy, I had to restart a couple of times because a bug stopped me in my tracks.

I give this game a 71% rating: it's nice, nothing great, but nothing really bad either. It is probably a higher rating than it should only because I have been playing the whole series of We Were Here with the same good friend of mine, and now it is a very cosy and pleasant journey we keep having. For someone who is expecting a lot from an Escape Room/Coop Puzzle type of game, you would probably rate this lower (around the 50% mark), but for someone who never played a single game like that, has a good friend online, a couple of hours tonight and a few dollars... this is a really nice little game!

Admittedly the game is a bit clunky, the difficulty balance is all over the place (very easy puzzle, then suddenly stressful, then suddenly VERY hard and abstract, then suddenly based on skill and platform abilities...) and the length is very, very short (one evening). Also, the music and narration tend to be annoying and tedious, and there is close to no story.
But beside that? the environments are lovely and quite crafted, the overall vibe is reminiscent to Disney Parks Pirates of the Caribbean or Sea of Thieves, some puzzle like the last one are very imaginative and original, and getting all the achievements should still be a bit of a challenge for you and your friend.
...and less than 5 bucks!

So, sure, compared to the original series? this is probably the weakest of the bunch. But if you don't care and want to know what this series is about, I reckon it is an interesting entry nonetheless. I wonder if this is going to be a spin off series with additional chapters?...

review_text:
I would recommend scorn as a very disturbing and atmospheric experience but as a game it has quite a few shortcomings that might turn off a lot of players. The puzzle and exploration aspects were very good but if you treat the game as a shooter it would be an unforgiving and frustrating way to play it. There is a disparity here with what the game excels at and what it mishandles almost to the point where I wonder if there should be combat at all. I have found through my playthrough that it's possible to ignore a large majority of threats if you hang back and let them pass to wherever they are trying to go. That does remedy what I think is the biggest problem with the game, and maybe even helps flesh out the world with creatures that become part of the level design instead of things to shoot at.

The game is at its best when you are exploring the world and solving puzzles to progress, which is what most of the game is anyway especially in the first half. There isn't a plot exactly, you wake up as a nameless being making their way through the locations in the game. Everything is vague, there never seemed to be a story to follow. It made the game feel like a walking simulator through a disgusting yet gorgeous Giger-esque world. I can describe it as an industrious complex that has fallen to ruin. The machines are bio-mechanical and everything that is left alive appears to be in some kind of agony. You scoop creatures from egg-like pods, killing them for their body parts. Tools you get are screwed into your flesh, blood coming from the wounds you now have. Even the weapons are some flesh and metal thing you rip apart and reconfigure to the few weapons you have. I found I enjoyed the game just by watching how horrible the world is and how you interact with it, trying to work out what all of the machines you discover are really for.

Disappointing. It had great potential but it's hampered by design decisions and polish.
My biggest gripe is that it doesn't feel like there's any payoff, trying to be tactical or sneaky to reach some nice sniping position just for enemies to immediately hide and know exactly where you are. Sadly it plays best just mindlessly shooting at whatever you see without any plan of attack.
 - For being a sniper game you're actively discouraged from sniping. As soon as they find a body, they immediately know approximately where you are and will hide behind cover. No more fun except for boring peekaboo
 - Movement is janky and you'll get stuck on and in terrain when crouched or prone
 - Drone can be fun, but they made it somewhat op for marking, so they tried nerfing it by adding broken mechanics with signal jammers. It randomly just crashes in some areas without a jammer and sometimes work just fine in areas with a jammer. Sometimes you get a screen effect that indicate that it's being jammed, most often it just randomly crashes and you get a "Drone lost" message
 - Lots of focus on special ammo during tutorial, but so far I haven't seen any need for it. It's also inconvenient to equip, having to unlock relatively expensive nodes or mag on the weapons
 - Enemy snipers are quite annoying, hiding where you rarely find them before engaging, and once a single enemy is alerted snipers will locate you almost immediately
 - Finally, no saves! There are checkpoints which randomly trigger. Did you spend 20 minutes carefully clearing a site only to get shot by an enemy hiding somewhere when you though it was clear and were looting? Have fun doing it all again.

If you haven't, try the Sniper Elite series instead

review_text:
Actual game is pretty fun, but there are a few things that hold it back. Namely, sloppy parkour and an un-skippable "warmup" before the actual game starts, every time. By sloppy parkour, I mean that the player's speed is often useless against enemies. With enough practice, you can go extremely fast, but the enemies are unable to keep up. Meaning that a lot of the time, you wallrun into an arena, kill one or two enemies in the air, and then are forced to sluggishly jump around on the ground in order to deal with the rest. Ground movement speed is also far too low. I get that you go faster in the air, but the speed at which the player walks is honestly just anti-fun garbage atm. Combine that with less than accurate wallrunning detection, buggy monkey bars and speed boosts, and a bugged door that doesn't work half the time and you have the worst part of the game, "the void". A parkour tutorial is fine, but it should be reserved for a help menu or the tutorial already present. Having to do the same 3-4 parkour layouts every time you start a run is awful for everyone. It's too difficult (and buggy) for new players, and irritating for experienced ones. Half the time you'll spend 10 minutes on the parkour and then close the game because of how bad the hit detection is. It's also worth mentioning that the maps are not randomly generated. Despite being a roguelike, the game has set levels that you'll have to go through every single time you play it. Set levels + unskippable buggy parkour = not very replayable. I really, really want to like this game, but atm, it's far too sluggish and irritating to fully recommend.

TLDR: Gunplay is fun, game looks great, but the parkour and unskippable tutorials make the game sluggish and a chore to play. I truly believe that the game will become better if given enough time, though.

TLDR: this is an interactive art-book with no overarching plot, nor satisfactory explanation to things that happen/exist there. Buy on discount if you are into the aesthetics of it

Design, sounds and gameplay are great, I wouldn't say that the combat is very bad, its a bit clunky, but I wouldn't expect more from a primarily horror game.
The very big problem I have with this game is with its plot and world. The creators are saying that they tried to tell a story using level design primarily. And its actually pretty cool, your surroundings do tell a lot about this world, however a lot of things are left over for you to deduce - what are those thingies sticking there, why are the bodies located here, how exactly the way we come into this place is tied to the rest of the game, and what was that thing in the ending of the game? Throughout the game I was trying to piece everything together, but I thought that after finishing it, I can just go online and see what this game was really about. Sure enough, there is an art book, where the authors of the game open it up more and explain stuff. And here is the very bad part - there is no explanation given to most of the questions I had for this game! There is stuff in this game, that they talk about, that has little to no reason to be in this game. I enjoy story-driven games, especially ones with emotional weight and unique narrative structure. To The Moon definitely tries to be one of those—but for me, it didn’t quite land.

This game is a novel, a very interactive one, which is great! You walk around as Eva and Neil, piecing together memories and playing through a handful of puzzles and minigames.

Honestly? The best part of the game was the doctors. Eva and Neil are genuinely fun characters. Neil’s bad jokes actually got me chuckling, and I loved all the little references and unexpected scenes that came with them. They were the heart of the game for me—I found myself more invested in their banter than the main storyline.

Now, the story...

It’s told backwards, which can work well in certain games or films—but here, it made everything feel a bit predictable. It's a string of explanations instead of a gradual journey to a grand finale.

Despite the constant reminders that “John is our client,” I couldn’t help but focus on River. All her quiet efforts to make John remember. It wasn’t his fault, of course. His memories were buried too deep. But it felt like River never truly got a chance to be understood.

And that ending...

Spoiler ahead.
[spoiler]In the end, River got to the moon alone—despite everything she tried to do to reconnect with him. It broke me a little. Not because it was tragic, but because it felt unresolved. Unfair.[/spoiler]

So, while I can see why To The Moon resonates with so many people, it just didn’t hit me the same way. The characters had charm, and the concept is genuinely touching—but the execution left me feeling distant.

review_text:
I really like lethal league and lethal league blaze, so when this game was announced I was pretty exited for it. I guess Team Reptile is just a one trick pony tho cause this game is kinda terrible. I really and truly do not understand the praise this game has received.

We'll start with the gameplay. As a game that's main focus is moving around a level and "collecting" things and graffiti spots, the movement sure is atrocious in this game. Everything feels far too slow for how big the levels are, and in many levels if you fall down trying to get a collectible you have to spend minutes working your way back to where you were to try again. The boost jump feels very inprecise. Sometimes you'll snap to a rail from downtown, other times you will literally just clip through it.

The trick system is a joke. It is almost impossible to actually drop a combo once you know the mechanics of the game. Other than building multiplier by riding on billboards and rails across the level, there is no reason to pick one trick over another, leading to just spamming random tricks because it literally doesn't matter.

There are three movement options, inline skates, BMX, and skateboard. Although there might as well just be one because there is no discernable difference between any of them and all of them play exactly the same.

Each level just consists of running around a big ugly and empty world throwing up graffiti (each one requiring a qte that takes you out of the flow of riding) until the local crew gives you a braindead simple challenge to do. Once you do all the challenges they have you have to do a score attack against the rival crew. As stated earlier tricking and comboing is so braindead easy in this game that this will never be a challenge.

There is also the questionable decision to include "combat." Combat is in quotes because I have a hard time even calling it that. After you throw up about 2 pieces of graffiti the game spawns endless waves of cops that sometimes get in the way, but you can mostly ignore. Each time your "heat" goes up there is a cutscene that shows what rank of cops are coming to run towards you unmenacingly, yet another thing to ruin the flow of riding around. There are a few instances where the game forces you to fight the cops, and these parts are by far the worst part of the game. I don't think I could describe with words the "combat" in a way that would do justice to how terrible it is.

This game is also horrendously ugly. The graphics look like they have been ripped straight out of a PS1 game, and are the stylization is ugly and does not make up for the bad graphics. I'm assuming this was done to emulate jet set radio, but I think there could have been a way to keep the spirit of the artstyle instead of just making it look the same as a game from 2000.

The story is dumb. Its a nonsensical plot about a world where everyone does a crappy dance while they're standing there waiting to give someone a quest because they put some doodles on a bunch of walls. The writing is awful, the characters are terrible, overall bad time on this front.

The only saving grace in this game is the music, which is mostly fantastic. That being said each area seems to cycle between 3 tracks, so it gets repetitive pretty quick.

If you want a fun game that plays with skating and utilizes tricking in a fun and interesting way play Rollerdrome

If you want a collectathon/platformer play Mario or something idk

If you want a beat em up play literally any other one cause the combat will be better no matter what you pick.

If you want to play this game for the music... don't. Youtube exists.

While although I love a good story, and I love a good setting, Bioshock didn't provide that for me. It is probably already well established that the game has boring shooting mechanics, and a poor RPG system at best, but I also felt that although it could be VERY beautiful at some points, the setting is lackluster. Rooms look similar to me, and there is nothing enjoyable about spending most of the game in cramped hallways. The story, the other talked-about part of this game, is also kind of lackluster, not because it relies on you looting the audio books to enjoy it, but because even if you still do that, the story is very much something that feels disjointed, like you are playing a different game. The story that your character goes through is delivered in a less than gripping fashion, and the lore found in the audiobooks feels unconnected to your own story.

I love a good story and good lore in games, and I really enjoy a nice setting, but only if it has a reason to be there (take another game from 2K, Spec Ops: The Line, a game with audio logs that explain your setting beautifully). The game sometimes shows you some beautiful parts of Rapture, but doesn't show you them enough.  It doesn't help that the sound and music are sub-par, and can even take away your immersion into the world, where it should be helping it. This is a game that is worth it on sale if you really want to play it, but if you are looking for a game that deserves the metacritic score that this game got, look elsewhere.

review_text:
Do you want to relive the joys of Action Man comics you read when you were 5? The plot of Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts is for you! Join the devoted fandom, including all 45% of people who actually completed the first mission, according to achievements. Enjoy infinite replayability as the borked checkpoint system forces you to go back through areas you cleared out entirely before you were suddenly sniped by a black spot half a kilometer away! Live the thrill of starting missions from scratch when you inevitably hit "restart mission" instead of "restart from checkpoint" for the third time, because the menu has both tabs right next to each other.

Challenge yourself with in game additional tasks that push you past the bounds of what you feel you can accomplish and, indeed, what the developers can reasonably expect anybody to achieve with the moveset and ruleset afforded to you. I particularly love how these challenges contradict each other, with "kill the target from 300 metres away" and "complete the mission using only a knife" being afforded to you in the same mission. This brilliant decision gives you an opportunity to further appreciate the boring levels as you trudge through them multiple times to get the completion above 50%. 

I love how you can sometimes spend ages scouring the map to find your target, only to find that they haven't spawned in yet. It gives you ample time to appreciate the clumsy movement system, invisible walls, and climbing mechanics that will fail and drop you to your death as often as they work. Once, a target spawned right behind me inside a cloud of red smoke and gunned me down before I could even spot him. This was an incredible display of this game's incredible AI which, apart from this spot of physics-defying genius, largely involved ignoring me as I shoot their comrade in the head mid conversation, and they stand there gawking for several seconds waiting for their turn. Sometimes, I can crouch walk right through their line of sight without issue and other times I find them suddenly spotting me from across the map without warning and alerting the entire base. 



EDIT: So I didn't expect this salty little rant to blow up as it did and somehow end up as one of the highest rated reviews. In the interest of fairness, I should also comment on some things I liked because this game isn't as terrible as I made it out to be above. While there are many more little frustrations I have not yet mentioned, I will still list some of the pros below. The things it does well, it does REALLY well. If this sort of thing appeals to you then it may be worth your time if you can abide the frustrations.  

I like how some aspects of the mission can change when attempted a second time. I am sure that will keep things fresh for those going for 100%

The actual sniping is excellent, simulating realism while still being very accessible. It is very satisfying to curve a bullet around a barrier to hit an enemy who thinks they are hiding.

Levels are enormous and open. Huge compounds can be approached from a number of different viable positions.

Bottom line: Worth playing if you love survival horror. Just be ready for some mission fatigue and a slow-burn story.

review_text:
World of Goo is a physics puzzle game where you control a collection of goo particles, and try to get them into a pipe. Building structures by connecting balls of goo together is how you get them to the finish pipe. The unused balls crawl along your structure, and then into the pipe to end each level.

The physics feel great. The unused balls of goo crawling along your structure have mass, not just the components of the structure. Shifting them around is the key to some puzzles. The structures never break from their own weight, only bend, which saves a lot of frustration. Gravity is consistent between levels, except for a short sequence of levels where unique gravity for the level is the main component of the puzzle.

The humor is excellent. Your adventure is narrated by a series of signs written by a character identified only as "the Sign Painter." Their exasperated/humorous narration of the goo traveling through the world lends a lot of charm to the world. The game is very self aware that it is a game, breaking the fourth wall multiple times, each time to great effect.

Puzzle design is good. Challenging at times, but very well designed. Each puzzle takes a few minutes at most to figure out a way to do it, with most having more than one solution. Much more time could be spent on this game than I spent if one wanted to optimize the levels.

There are multiple different types of goo balls introduced through the game, each of which interacts with the environment in a different way. Each one is interesting and unique, and does not overstay its welcome.

Overall, I would recommend this game. I did get it has part of a HumbleBundle, so not sure if I would by it on its own.

review_text:
"Scorn is a game where you get to experience the abject horror of being a sentient cow on its way to slaughter. Machines beyond your ability to understand line your path. You can't comprehend of what or why any of the horrors you see are. All you know is that they simply happen, outside of your control or input."

Scorn is an expedition from the nightmares of H. R. Giger and Z. Beksiński.

It begins without context, there is no narrator or clear clues of what happens or has happened, you do not know where you are, you do not know who or what you are, it is taken for granted that we have a purpose, but we do not know what it is or what it was, you just wake up and walk endlessly through a post-apocalyptic and desolate world, as if you were seeing the ashes of a past civilization. It is through the progression of the game that we are told in broad strokes the meanings and purposes, however, there remains a huge room for interpretation.

The strong point is the artistic design, deeply inspired by works such as Alien, Dune and Prometheus. Scorn seeks to engage and captivate the audience through its landscapes, atmospheres, environments and sound pieces.

Its worst “flaw” is the combat; it feels monotonous and in certain areas tedious, however, it can be counteracted by playing strategically, once you learn to know when to shoot and when to run away the gameplay becomes more fluid. The game does not force you to kill the base enemies in order to continue, a single shot is enough to stun them and take advantage of that moment to bypass them, this allows the progression of the game to be more satisfying and enjoyable. (From a subjective perspective, this section is consistent with what it wants to transmit; it does not have to be polished to be captivating, nor does it have to shine in its mechanical aspect to be a masterpiece. If the environment is crude it is timely and appropriate for the gameplay to be crude as well).

Absolutely recommended.

review_text:
Starship Troopers initially launched with great promise, giving players hope that there are still developers committed to creating truly engaging games. Unfortunately, that promise has steadily declined over time, and with the release of patch 1.6, the game has reached a breaking point.

At present, the game is effectively unplayable. Severe server lag and massive ping spikes are commonplace affecting every player in a match. Characters warp across the map during connection issues, creating a frustrating and unstable experience.

Core gameplay mechanics are also broken across multiple classes. For example:

- Medic: healing bots fail to revive teammates, and healing stims have no effect.
- HMG: the deployable shield no longer functions as intended.
- To many jumps in a row and you die
- Random death if you stay on the drop shop too long
- Falling through map 
- death times start at 15 seconds instead of 60 no matter what

Enemy AI: drones can easily bypass defence and one-shot players, while warriors stack in ways that glitch player models, preventing them from reloading or firing.

The result of the newest patch shows a game that feels unfinished and untested, leaving players discouraged and unable to enjoy what once showed so much potential. It’s disappointing to see a title that began with promise reduced to this state, and it raises serious concerns about developer priorities and long-term commitment.

It's not worth the time or money, even on sale.

review_text:
If you're a fan of Stealth Real Time Strategy genre, just get this game. It's super good. This genre is not that popular, we should support it as much as we can.
If you're a newcomer to this genre, so am I. In fact, I've never played any RTS game, let alone a stealth RTS. And I loved every moment I've had with this game. 

- The story is what I would call "nicely done". It's not a literature masterpiece by any means, which is not a bad thing at all. It's interesting enough to make you feel interested, and the characters all have their own appeal. I admit, some of the dialogues could be delivered better. The characters are quirky and a little cringy at times, but I feel like that's part of the charm. I actually found myself emotionally invested towards the characters, especially towards the later half of the game. Can't lie, the ending made me kinda sad for a bit lmao

- The gameplay is what you'd expect from a stealth strategy game. I really liked stealth, but I have also never played any strategy games, especially RTS. And this game gave me the best introduction to the genre. By the end of the game, I can't help but feel excited to play more games just like Shadow Tactics. It's exactly what I wanted in a stealth game. Observation, tactical planning, decision making, and execution. It feels so damn satisfying when you take your time to craft a plan, execute it, fail, refining your strategy, and finally succeeding in the end. It's like playing chess, or solving an elaborate puzzle.

- The characters all have their own sets of tools and traits which can be combined to tackle an obstacle, but sometimes there are levels where one character is clearly better than the others, and can be used for every situation. Though this is not a fatal flaw, since you can choose to be more creative with your approach. On my first playthrough, i rarely used Takuma, feeling him to be a liability due to his weaknesses, but on my second playthrough, I found myself using him more, which in turn helped me discover more creative ways to solve a level. Because that's what the game is all about. Creative problem solving! 

There are some clear flaws, though. The camera and controls. The camera can become awkward or downright frustrating, especially at the far edges of levels. The controls, while manageable, can sometimes feel clunky and unresponsive. For example, if you click on an unreachable spot, your characters will stop moving entirely, which could lead to detections. Similarly, moving multiple characters to a single location can cause them to collide, slowing down their movement or even exposing one of them unintentionally. The shadow mode is also a bit underwhelming, and I usually only found myself using them when I'm just trying to be fancy with my tactics. Because of the enemies' pathing and predictable viewcones, sometimes all you need is time and patience. If you don't mind taking it slow, you can finish some levels without ever using shadow mode. 

[h3] Summary [/h3]
[b] Gameplay: 8/10. [/b] Good level design, lots of opportunities to make different plans and strategies. Wonky camera and controls which takes some time getting used to.
[b] Story: 8/10. [/b] Very good. Characters are interesting, and the story is simple but sweet.
[b] Visuals: 9/10. [/b] Very appealing aesthetics and visuals. Game graphics look timeless, probably will still look good in the year 2050.
[b] Replayability: 7/10. [/b] The level stays the same, but the badges and achievements urges you to replay the game, but with different gameplans and approach.

Definitely recommend. Many thanks to the developers for giving me an awesome introduction to this genre!

review_text:
This is the first of two games, if you want the full experience you MUST buy both this and Edo Blossoms.

Now, onto the review. Hakuoki is a very popular series of otome games that has gotten various rewrites and ports throughout the years. It's extremely popular in Japan, and it's known for being what truly brought otome and visual novels to the west as a niche market medium that's only gotten more and more popular since. 

This version of Hakuoki has 12 routes, and they're as follows (written in family name, given name): Hijikata Toshizo, Okita Souji, Saito Hajime, Toudou Heisuke, Harada Sanosuke, Chikage Kazama... (those are the original routes!) then we have three routes of characters already introduced in the original storyline, they are: Sanan Keisuke, Nagakura Shinpachi, Yamazaki Susumu. Then, to top it all off, there's three new routes: Iba Hachiro, Souma Kazue, and Sakamoto Ryouma. The final route possible is Yukimura (you!) alone, which would make it 13... but it really isn't a route honestly, you're just more or less along for the ride. 

Each route offers different perspectives and events (more so in Edo Blossoms than here) but it's still well worth it to play each route that interests you. The only downside to doing so is having to replay the common route present in this game, Kyoto Winds has a very long common route with a branching narrative to whichever bachelor you decide to pursue... or end up pursuing by chance.

There's enough eligible men in this where anyone can find someone who interests them, but if I'm being completely honest... there's not much romance in Kyoto Winds, it's mainly a focus on the historical aspects of the Shinsengumi and their journey up until the point they leave for Edo. 

There's some fantasy implemented to change things up, of course... I don't want to spoil anything, but it's definitely an interesting take on something you'd expect to be overdone. 

The way this has been translated is really good, especially relative to other visual novel releases on Steam. Don't get me wrong, there's the occasional oddly worded sentence or spelling mistake, but it isn't common to see throughout any of the routes, very rarely do they stick out. 

All in all, if you enjoy historical visual novels or otome games, this is well worth the price. There's plenty of men to choose from, this incorporates some bonus content from previous releases, and the art is absolutely gorgeous from the sprites to the CGs to the opening and ending movies.

review_text:
This game is so weird and cool and has left a lasting impression on me. It started slow and came off as pretentious on the surface which turned me away at first, but once the story gets going in earnest it becomes very engaging and immersive, and a lot of necessary questions get answered. I was addicted by the middle and very satisfied by the end. Now it lives rent free in my head and I'm hooked on the aesthetic.

I think the dialogue could do with being slightly less flowery, and the intro slightly less slow, but they do give the game this uncanny and surreal feeling. It's like the whole thing is a dream, or you're playing The Truman Show. It was difficult for me to tell what was scripted and what was emergent or coincidence.

The art, character design, models, UI, music, sound effects, and map design all are 10/10 for what they are. I am fascinated by a lot of the ideas in the lore too. The town is this perfect mix of cozy and nostalgic, while also being alien and horrifying. I also liked the animation and voice acting, despite both being very sparse.

It can be frustratingly difficult at certain points, but it does throw in breathers every once in a while. After I finally finished the game it all felt worth it. If you hate missing things or being on time crunches this will be a very unpleasant experience.

review_text:
If you really enjoyed the first game, be aware that this one is a completely different experience. Instead of rooms full of a multitude of objects that can be interacted with lots of different ways with funny dialogue, Act 2 focuses much more on character dialogue, the rooms being otherwise mostly empty and with little opportunity to use your items. If you enjoyed the Hiveswap Friendsim, you might like this new dialogue-focused approach; otherwise you will probably find a lot of this game quite boring. Friendsim fans should also be aware that the Friendsim's story has zero effect on how the characters are portrayed in this game, so you shouldn't expect this to be anything like a true sequel to Friendsim either.

Beyond that, it's obvious this Act of the game is an unfinished product. It's quite evident that a lot of content has been cut from the first few rooms of the game, which are also the largest. Among this cut content are the characters Zebede and Charun, who were advertised as Act 2 characters years ago and were included in promotional art for the game even within a month of the game's release. No explanation has been given for why these characters in particular are simply absent from the finished product, but a rushed release is quite apparent.

Even beyond the content that was obviously originally in the game and then removed, a lot of Act 2's features are half finished, and features from Act 1 are totally missing. The Chittr or Prongle social media mechanic that has been advertised since before even the release of Act 1 is almost non existent, being used only for a single scene plus some minor gags early in the game - and need it be stated that we are now halfway through the originally planned length of Hiveswap. Despite Act 2 having a lot of puzzles that are much more difficult than Act 1, the sparkles that indicated useful items in the first Act are now gone. Instead you will be expected to use the hint feature, which for some reason only works for one of the two playable characters.

The game looks quite good, and aside from some inconsistent and at times hard to understand GUI, it functions mostly how a point and click adventure game should function. However those expecting the tight, witty writing from the original Homestuck and Act 1 should probably try looking elsewhere. And unfortunately, so should anyone expecting their money to be going toward an actual finished product worthy of the years it took to hit shelves.

review_text:
Sometimes games just don't vibe with you, but you play them anyway, because they were in the Humble Choice selection and looked ... interesting? Touted as a 3D action platformer by users ... 

What it really is is "Tony Hawks with graffiti grinds and bad combat".

You go around the stylized world to grind on rails and smear your graffiti over the graffiti of other crews. You do tricks, boost around, and fight the police ... and read the terrible dialogue to get the "story" moving. Grinding isn't really anything cool, though, the game does everything for you automatically. There are no "tricks" to speak of. You just press B,X,Y alternatively to accrue points. For nothing. 

The first part is actually not that bad, but it doesn't feel impactful, because actually doing tricks is meaningless. It only fills your "combo" meter, which in turn gives you boost. The real reason to do all this is to grind, pardon the pun, REP. Earn enough REP and you can challenge a rival crew and progress the game.

While you do that police keep endlessly spawning the more you "vandalize" the city. You can defeat them in melee combat with your "tricks", so you keep pressing B,X,Y, sometimes spraying them with paint to momentarily blind them ... or you just ignore them, because they seem to keep endlessly spawning, as I said, and can't really do much, at least not at first, I'd assume. The foot soldiers really are powerless.

I'll give the game points for some originality, and for sticking to its theme, and also for its selection of music, which isn't really my genre, but it's obviously fitting, and that's that. I remember vaguely that there's a series of games very similar to this. Jet Set Radio, now that I've looked it up. If you're the kind of person that has played these games and really enjoyed them, and you're desperately looking for an unofficial sequel, then this might be it. Personally, I just don't like grinding fucking REP as the main activity in any game. Definitely the weirdest game I've played this year, though ... or one of them, at least.

If it were focussed more on the tricks, I might actually not dislike it that much. BUT, it's overwhelmingly positive, and most likely that means that fans of this type of game got EXACTLY what they wanted, so I'll give it that. Just take this review from someone who apparently wasn't a Jet Set Radio fan to begin with before you buy a "3D action platformer" fpr 40 bucks!

Let the Jester awards commence, because this game's "fan base" seems to not take criticism well. ;)

EDIT: Nope, nope. I've played about half of it now and I CANNOT recommend it. If you really want to play Hakuouki, try Aksys' versions on 3DS, PSP or PS3.

I've never left a negative review of an otome game like this, and I didn't think I'd advise against Hakuouki in my entire life, but here goes.

They censored Kimigiku's status as an oiran -- a courtesan -- to a "geigi", or geisha. The translation has been changed in certain spots and is much poorer, with a typo right in the first few minutes of the game.

Chizuru seems dumbed down, screaming things in all-caps, and even more timid than before. This is partially to blame because the game has been lengthened. In some cases the extra scenes are welcome, in others it feels like pointless padding to make the game longer. But the more she talks, she gets more indecisive and it gets boring.

They added plenty of scenes that made it drag and drag unnecessarily. But, then, bafflingly, they cut and altered certain scenes. Scenes such as when Nagakura and Harada are speaking of the coming war -- changing this in favor of Chizuru doing silent expo-speak.

The new music is awful, and is way too modern in certain places. The battle music is a form of techno, for god's sake. It's 1864!

I think it's part of a plan to "youth up" the game. The achievements for this game are impossibly annoying -- memes and slang like "New guy, who dis?" and "Still a better love story than". That and the techno REALLY make me think that they're trying to sell this to a younger crowd.

But Hakuouki has always been timeless, and if someone is too immature that they can't play a game without sharp, techno battle music and have the characters using more slang -- Harada says "like" as in, like, the way I just used it -- then they shouldn't be playing Hakuouki in the first place.

And the new characters are boring, droll and take up too much time. I kept skipping through their parts.

The only GOOD thing is that there are more scenes with the original characters -- the five main Shinsengumi and Kazama -- and you can now romance the other 3 Shinsengumi characters: Sanan, Yamazaki and Nagakura.


One more thing? Kyoto Winds + Edo Blossoms are one whole game if you purchase the 3DS, PSP or PS3 version. So you're not shelling out tons of money for what is supposed to be one entire game.

____

What is there, really, to say about Hakuouki? Other than, if you're an otome fan, this is an essential game. The artwork is beyond amazing, the story is richer than the best chocolate, and the routes are so emotionally involving that you'll feel sucked into it all. You'll laugh, you'll sob, characters will die, they'll leave their "brothers" behind as life goes on... It's quite moving.

I've loved Hakuouki for a decade now, since high school, when the anime came out and I streamed the fansub. Then when it came out, I had the Limited Deluxe Edition for the PSP. I'm just glad I'm able to continue playing this beautiful and romantic game long after my little portable console died.

If you love anything otome that Idea Factory has put out, or if you love otome games period, and somehow haven't played Hakuouki yet, do so. It's like a rite of passage.

It's worth it at any price.

TLDR: Not a bad game, but extremely rough around the edges.

For the pro's, everything in this game works. The wind and range systems are neat, the UI is clean and easy to use, watching your shots land feels satisfying. Unfortunately, the awful enemy AI and zero interesting objectives make playing a repetitive and uninteresting experience.

Enemy alerts in this game are global, meaning that when one enemy is alerted, all enemies in the area will suddenly know exactly where you are. This does not combo well with the instant-kill snipers, or full auto enemies, who have almost perfect accuracy regardless of your range from them. This creates a frustrating loop where you will often be shot down from across the map by enemies who had no realistic way of knowing your position.

This combined with the lack of interesting enemies, completely broken ledge grab system, pointless and annoying exfil system, lack of manual saves, useless gadgets, and cookie cutter story make this game feel outright rushed to completion. The bones of a good game are here, and if on heavy sale it's probably still worth buying, but overall SGWC is an unimpressive mess of a sniper game that feels clunky in every aspect.

review_text:
I've finally bit the bullet and purchased it. I've refunded it. 

Why? A simple reason: the price.

40 euros for a title like this seems too much to me. Unworthy of the available quantity of content, sadly.

Quality? Absolutely gorgeous and grim which very few games nails perfectly nowadays even if the market is seemingly bloated.

I have high respect for the devs who seem very in touch with the community and have clearly shown effort in their craft, but again, 40 euros for a very limited roguelike is too much.

I would have given it a 10/10 if it was a 20 euros title: i'm already seeing it with tens of thousands of Overwhelmingly Positive reviews if it was the case. But it's 40 instead, and that's why i think many people are doubting the purchase (me included).

Gunplay is good, locations are great, gameplay loop is fun, however it seems short and with limited stuff to unlock, hiding behind a "difficulty levels" excuse called "Gnosis". Essentially, you start at default difficulty until you decide to invest some points in Gnosis and increasing the difficulty scaling, unlocking new zones and areas.

All cool and smart in theory, but in reality i was quickly done with 2 of the 4 total zones available (2 more coming with future updates) in 2 hours. Increasing enemy pattern and spawns and a couple doors locked behind upgrades doesn't cut it for me, it's still too few, too expensive to justify it.

Sadly, Steam only allows refunds inside the 2 hours bracket and i would have very much liked to keep playing and see how much longer the "Gnosis" would have extended the game, but in my gaming experience i think i was kinda see where it was going.

SO, IN SHORT:

Great game, great atmosphere, too little content, too expensive.

As usual, i'll come back when it'll be finished and hopefully with a juicier discount.

review_text:
There are two requirements for you to better enjoy Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts: The first would be for the player to see this game as something a bit different from the traditional Sniper Elite games as well older Sniper Ghost Warrior games. The second requirement is patience. Excel at these two and you will be having some fun with the game.

With only 5 maps for you to play, at first it seems short but we are talking about big maps with 5 or more different objectives scattered across the map. How you approach it is entirely up to you. The tutorial is brief and short so don’t be shy to repeat it if you did not get aiming on your first try. I tried to go full stealth at the start but later on some sections I was using all the possible firepower at my will. It’s not the way I wanted or intended to play the game but with some issues with checkpoints and a not-so-clever AI, it made me switch playstyles. Still, there was fun to be had. The game looks good and plays well in general, perhaps a bit of optimization could help not push my hardware so much but I’ve managed just fine.

Around the 10 hour mark I finished all missions, going for all contracts in each map, on the easier difficulty, while also ignoring specific challenges or collectibles. Trying to be on the lookout for collectibles everywhere in a game where stealth plays a big part makes no sense. There’s also a false sense of open world. While you can roam at your own pace if you try to climb a mountain or find a well hidden area in the forest, you may see the classic “warning, land mines” causing you to fail instantly.
