review_text:
Turbo Golf Racing is very simple, especially in this state of Early Access with 30 courses available for solo play.  These are divided into three sets of ten holes, which you must complete within a set time limit.  There are three time goals for each hole, each rewarding a star for finishing under that time, and your access to additional holes is unlocked by earning stars in previous holes.  At the time of this review, I have two stars on every hole, which is basically required to access/complete all 30 holes.  Going back and earning that third star is a challenge I look forward to in my future spare time.

But all of this solo play is mere practice for the online golf game that awaits once you have learned how to play golf with a fancy sports car or truck.  Vehicle choice is limited for now, but you do unlock new vehicles through normal level-up progression. Regardless of your finishing position you will still earn XP and Gears during each match; the former increasing your level and earning you a prize at each tier, while the latter is used as currency for the in-game store where you can buy visual upgrades for your car, ball, and other flashy effects.  While not as vast as the parts selection in Rocket League, at least in Turbo Golf Racing you are actually earning “real stuff” and not silly blueprints that only unlock the privilege of buying later with real money.

Nearly all of the upgrades are visual in nature; a new paint job, a flashy spoiler, or a dangerous looking plow for the front of the vehicle to knock the ball around.  Some upgrades (Cores) do offer limited performance boosts, but these are nicely balanced with their own negative effects; like increasing your boost speed at the cost of slowing down how fast the meter refills.  Basically, the entire game is about the skill of the player and not the capabilities of the car, but it is still fun to mix and match up to two Cores per vehicle and see how it affects your game.

Controls are pretty excellent, at least when playing with a gamepad, and Turbo Golf Racing “feels” exactly like Rocket League with the same turbo, e-brake, drift, and jump mechanics.  There are fun “secrets” to figure out like getting a boost off the starting line or flipping your car to create a momentary shield to protect from a rocket attack.  The game does require more precision than Rocket League.  In that game you just hit the ball in the general direction of the net and there was a chance it would go in.  Here, you are going to need to hit the ball 20-30 times or more just to get it to the hole, so each shot needs to be accurate otherwise you end up chasing the ball around...

review_text:
This game blew my mind. 
I bought it on sale, not really expecting much but damn. I should probably mention that I have no former experience or knowledge of the Hakuoki series (I've somehow missed it through all these years), yet I was equally, or perhaps even more impressed with this series than those who have played it before. 

Firstly, the artwork is in a league of its own. I've played a few visual novels but very few, especially PC ones, match up to the artwork in this. It's simply beautiful. The colouring in the CGs and proportions of the characters are amazing, unlike the many anime-inspired art pieces with their overly-lanky proportions and flat colouring.

The voice acting in this is also breath taking. If you're not a fan of it, there's always the option to switch it off but holy cow, I love it. I'm a fairly fast reader, so I almost always finish reading before the part gets read out but the thing is, I found myself waiting for the voice acting to finish because I just love their voices - Kazama's in particular. 

One thing I will say is that this game is pretty history and plot heavy, not much romance if any in it (though different routes differ slightly on this), so if you're getting this in the hopes of the typical cheesy, k-drama romance, you're out of luck. I personally love history but have never really been interested in East Asian history, especially Japanese history. This game changed that. 
There's also a lot of Japanese terms and keywords which are kept logged in the encylopedia - I found the sheer number of them to be confusing, but as I replayed the game to experience the different routes, I gradually got used to it and made more sense the more I played. The same could be said for the number of characters. There's 12 guys to choose from, plus a fair few side characters, which made it hard at the start to remember who was who (bearing in mind I have no prior knowledge of this game and have very little experience with the Japanese language). Of course, this wasn't so much as an issue when I replayed it more. 

If I had to be nit-picky, I would also put the MC's personality down as more of a con than a pro. It can be a little infuritating how unable she is to stand up for and protect herself, always relying on the members of the Shinsengumi. It's as if she's playing damsel in distress and is simply doting on guys to save her, instead of actually attempting to defend herself. [spoiler]She does actually learn some swordsmanship techniques through Kondou in a number of routes, albeit not much, but enough for self defence. Even so, we do not see her put these new skills in use at all further in the storyline.[/spoiler] Her character plays by many tropes in otome games - special snowflake, damsel in distress, a little dense at the best of times - and if those tropes are really something you can't stand, this may not be the best series for you. However, being completely honest from my standpoint, I've played many otome games with far worse MCs, whose traits are far more exaggerated. Although the MC in this game is a little infuriating and annoying at times, it's not really a factor that affected my enjoyment of this game and because of this, I still hold this game very highly. 

On the whole, I think this game has good replay value and I would highly recommend this. There are some repetitive bits that get a little tedious, but nothing the cheeky skip button can't fix. Overall, it's incredibly well thought through and is definitely up there in the realm of visual novels and otome. Even if you're not into the otome stuff, I would still suggest giving this a go. It's worth every penny, even if not on sale. 
I am now sucked into an angsty af series urgh wtf-.-

This game is truly a great send up to Jet Set Radio and JSRF but for my 2 cents it misses some key things to really make it feel like it's own game. 

New Amsterdam... just doesn't feel distinct. I can't play a area and feel like i'm in a Dutch future city. It's feels more like an extension of Tokyo-to. And finally... Where my prof. K man???? ok this is a minor gripe but a pirate DJ giving us lowdowns instead of reading what the characters say would be phenomenal.

Dispite that, this is a grand game and deserves a playthrough but with that distinct-ness missing... I don't feel compelled to come back to the game anytime soon... that makes me sad.

review_text:
We Were Here Expeditions: The Friendship is a two person co-op puzzle game where you must work with a friend to escape an abandoned amusement park. There are three different puzzle rooms that must be solved via communication with your partner. 

Overall, I found this title to be the best of the entire series, which is somewhat amusing given it was free for a weekend and of the titles listed for a price, it's the cheapest. It is relatively short (comparable to the first title in the series, which is/has been always free to play). Whereas other titles in this series feature much less clear puzzles, each puzzle in this game was more obvious. Now, you might think that takes away some of the fun, but I found it didn't. Instead, it allows you to focus on solving the puzzle as opposed to trying to figure out what the puzzle even is to begin with. 

One playthrough took ~2 hours and a second playthrough for achievements (getting the max score for each puzzle) took another ~2 hours (mostly due to some RNG in the second puzzle). If a co-op puzzle game sounds like something you'd enjoy, I'd recommend this game. That said, I definitely recommend playing the original as it is free and will give you a good sense of the type of gameplay you'll be getting into.

review_text:
The simple crux of playing Left 4 Dead is that Left 4 Dead 2 exists. The sequel has more of just about everything, with nearly all of this game's content included. This game has fewer campaigns, fewer extra modes, and fewer weapons (including a complete lack of melee weapons). I've seen some favor this game for its atmosphere. Indeed, Left 4 Dead takes itself more seriously, skewer closer to its horror inspiration. But I suppose that's not why I play either Left 4 Dead game, especially given that both are multiplayer-oriented experiences. When playing with friends, much of the tonal nuance is inevitably lost.
I will concede that, from my estimation, this game's default lighting solution is far more playable than the sequel's. You'll still find plenty of pitch-black rooms, but it's not as prohibitive.
If I can praise anything unequivocally, it's this game's opening cinematic, which expertly introduces you to so many key gameplay elements, such as the various special infected to expect and the car alarms.
As I see it, there's no reason to play this game when you can get basically all of its content in the sequel, on top of everything it adds. This game has few advantages over its successor to justify choosing it over the sequel.

I was sad after finishing Dead Space recently, so I decided to give this a shot. 
If it were a movie (and the structure of Calisto Protocol uses cinematic narratives, aesthetics, and techniques), I would say it's a mediocre but entertaining product that becomes a bit repetitive towards the end and fully abandons the theme of the main character's personality breakdown as it approaches the end credits. I would also say that it is a slightly sloppy, spiritual successor to Dead Space with some great moments and ideas. If it were a movie, I would recommend it because I would recommend entertainment where you can turn off your brain and forgive a few things. I hate leaving bad reviews... (warning: possible spoilers)

Just Cause 4 is the weakest game in the series on many levels. Here's some of the worst issues:

1. Story: ...or the lack of one. You get a quick glimpse of the main bad guy at the start of the game, a quick exchange with his second-in-command a short while later, then nothing. No interaction with the enemy until the very end of the game. There is some interactions with friendly NPCs, but 90% of the game is non-interactive. 

2. Missions/Goals: There is a main quest line but it is incredibly brief. However, to perform some of these quests, the game forces you to go out and clear some regions. Clearing regions is the only real game play here.

3. Weapons/Vehicles/Tools: To be honest, I played the entire way through with the automatic rifle I started with and a grenade launcher. Every other weapon had limitations that made them nonviable. As always, the grappling hook and call for gun/vehicle drops and location drops makes up the bulk of world traversal.

4. Graphics/Characters/Environments/Etc.: Very, very dated. Feels and looks like a lot of recycled assets from previous versions.

This game ruined my faith in the Just Cause series. I'm going to be very cautious when/if I see JC5 drop here on Steam. I'll watch game play videos and read a few reviews, but I won't buy it just on brand recognition.

review_text: To the Moon is an interactive novel that uses brilliant and unique ideas into storytelling and this game's story is one I don't see myself forgetting for quite a while. The only problem with this game is the aspects that make it a game since there is none. As previously stated it is an interactive novel and it is PURELY an interactive novel and features no gameplay whatsoever. Even though I was fully aware of how this game would play out like that and was perfectly fine with playing an interactive novel (I love the Phoenix Wright games) I couldn't help but feel utterly dissapointed in this game hence the "not recommended" review. The whole thing just feels like it's in the wrong format, it doesn't feel like it should be a game. The only thing that differentiates this as a game from anything else is the segments where you have to walk around and interact with stuff until the story progresses and you go back to reading again. These segments were an ABSOLUTE CHORE; they were so unbelievably boring the only reason I was doing them was to progress and get to the next point in the game. The game also features cheap puzzles called momento puzzles that offer no fun value whatsoever and are so astoundingly unoriginal. In my personal opinion To the Moon should of been made as an animated short or perhaps even an animated movie, it feels like something that would fit in a Hayao Miyazaki movie. I do not dislike this game I just don't recommend buying it and I usually absolutely despise saying this but perhaps this game is best experienced by a Let's Player on YouTube. If you want to support Free Bird Games by buying this game then feel free to do so but for me this game didn't feel like it was worth the small amount of money it was to buy it.

I wish they wouldn't have started over in 2020 and speed developed the game in around two years. This universe deserves to be fleshed out.

That's what I'm left with when I think of this game, how much it is one of a kind, how much it has stuck with me after finishing it and how much I wish there were more to it. I respect if this was their vision, but I can't help but feel like they wish they could've included more as well. Worth it on sale, but for most, probably will leave you feeling disappointed.

review_text:
I have many mixed feelings about Scorn. 

In many ways, I love it. It's a dark journey through a haunting nightmare realm, heavily inspired by the unsettling works of H.R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński. Every building and machine is a disgusting yet oddly beautiful amalgamation of technology and living flesh, and traversing the game feels like a biomechanical fever dream. The sound design is on point as well, from the sickly squelching of inserting a key to the muffled cries of a disfigured humanoid. Honestly, Scorn is one of the most visually and audibly distinct games I've ever played, and I applaud Ebb Software for creating something so unique.

However, the actual game-play of Scorn is... Not the best. There's no map, so it's easy to get lost in the labyrinth of hallways. Many of the puzzles are quite hard, and you can spend hours trying to solve them and never get anywhere. And don't get me started on the combat. Why do enemies take so much health? Why do you have so little ammo and healing items, and why are the refill stations single use only? I know survival horror is all about feeling helpless against horrific monsters, but there's a big difference between feeling helpless and actually being helpless.

All in all, I feel that while Scorn suffers from a lot of bad choices in game-play, it's a good start for a new studio. Ebb Software had a clear artistic vision, and they definitely achieved it. I would say that I high hopes for  this little Serbian game studio in the future, but unfortunately it seems like they've been shut down since November 2023, which is a damn shame, since I would have loved to see what they do next.

review_text:
This is coming from the perspective of someone that played NHL GM Modes up to NHL 14. The games after that, except maybe for NHL 15 on the PS3 and X-Box 360 didn't improve anything in GM Mode, so I came in knowing the ins and outs of the GM Mode in the NHL games at their peak regarding simulation. This is also after one full season, so look at this reason.

As far as realism, I would say it is fairly decent, but obviously it cannot be 100% accurate, as it cannot always predict when players will have off or good seasons. In my season with the Kings, I made it into the finals in year one and faced the Tampa Bay Lightning. While initially unrealistic, Tampa didn't have Stamkos most of the year and almost made the playoffs, and in this game Kopitar and Gaborik had good years, as the Kings main problem was scoring, not allowing goals, even when Budaj was the starter. As for the simulation engine, the best testament to it's realism is being able to watch and coach the games. How you do this is your own choice. I believe you can have the games be coached by an AI, but that takes the fun out of the game in a way. And this indirectly leads to this game's double edged sword: time. While you become more accustomed to the day to day job of a general manager/coach, there is a heavy amount of time to be invested in a single season of this game. As I said earlier, I only played one full season (including the playoffs) and it took me over 20 hours. However, this one season was definitely fun as I got closer to the team and was satisfied with the simulation and the way stats worked for the most part, and the many coaching options the game gives you. The trading system is also very interesting as it allows you to offer a player to the league and see what offers teams give you. The spread of trade rumors also adds to the fun of the situation.

Another great thing about this game and being able to coach them and watch them, is the addition of the amount of personality that goes into this game. This was best characterized by a series I had with the San Jose Sharks. In I believe it was game 2 or 3, the Kings were pounding the Sharks, and I remember us having 7 goals or something crazy at the end of the game. After the first or second period, Drew Doughty was injured by a Sharks player and I went crazy and adjusted a lot of my players so that they could fight and have them target Sharks players like Couture and the guy that injured Drew, who seemed to be some nobody. At the beginning of the third, a line brawl broke out and even the goalies joined in, though this would cost Quick a suspension and the Sharks backup would get the suspension, not Jones as he was pulled. After the line brawl I'm not sure if a fight broke out in the game, but it was a crazy moment, one you literally cannot have in EA NHL GM Modes. Drew came back for the next game and we lost the next game, but it wasn't the fault of the goaltender as we didn't get enough done in regulation. In the end, we won the series in seven games. To me, this is what a rivalry series was supposed to feel like, crazy, intense, hard-fought, and brutal. This single series made me fall in love with the game.

So should you or should you not buy this game? While I've only played one season all the way, I definitely enjoyed that one season. I cannot accurately judge player growth as I haven't invested much time into the game. From what I experienced, if you're willing to invest time into this game and want a realistic hockey sim, go for it, this may be the best one out there, but I haven't played Franchise Hockey Manager 3 so I can't compare it to that game. If you're not patient enough to essentially "play" as the coach then this game may not be for you. 

One more thing, you need to download NHL rosters from the workshop if you want to use those.

tl;dr If you're willing to invest time into a realistic hockey sim, this game is for you as it adds a ton of personality to being a general manager. If you aren't patient enough, maybe manager games aren't for you.

Over the years Star Trek Online has settled into the role of being the ultimate Star Trek fan simulator, in my opinion. There is an original story and world that exists here. For you, there is the option to basically play any ship (especially if it was one of the main 3: Federation, Klingon, Romulan) that appeared in cannon or original star trek online ship of your dreams. Same goes for weapons and crew looks.

You basically fly around with the ship and crew of your dreams within this star trek universe. New stuff is added regularly from various pieces of star trek. That is why the community is still here or comes back from time to time. I use the Alita class with basic star trek online style uniforms, weapons, and gear, so it was easy to straiten out my head cannon dreams.

That being said, there is a lot of things locked behind pay walls for various reasons. Some are much much frendlier (regular 1 time cash shop stuff with benefits) than others (loot boxes). Some things are borderline impossible to get without spending a ton of money or effort. With over 12 years on this game I can also tell you it was easier to grind for what you wanted in the past than now, but there is enough free stuff and other goodies to ensure that you aren't gear locked out of the standard story and side missions. The important thing, ships, fairly easy and/or strait forward; but not always cheap.

Overall if you ever wanted to do star trek stuff using your own dream ship and crew in the equipment you want, this is THE place to do it.

- Movement speed and Mobility options are meh if compared with the dynamic. Strafe speed is garbage.
- You can dash, you can jump. Can you dash-jump? Nope. Can you dash in midair? Nope.
- Melee attack has a huge recharge... why? And discharged melee doesn't even push back enemies.
[strike]- Reload blocks your escape options: no dashes, spells, or melee to interrupt that. No, the shockwave ear is not an option as it doesn't work at all xD[/strike] Okay, my bad, maybe that was a bug in state machine.
- The balance seems on the multiplayer side of things, but you must play alone.
- Why there is no "Gears of War"-style fast reloads? That would fit this gameplay nicely.
- You cannot chain dashes, jumps, attacks, weapon switches, etc. into a doom dance - everything seems to have a way too long delay before the next action.
- Stamina system in general: High HP = High Stamina, low HP or got hurt way too much - PP-Tiny Stamina (less chances to survive). Can be removed and nobody will cry about it.
- Enemies spawn next to your face or around you... interesting, why this was never a feature in Souls games? Because that sucks.
- There are 3 types of weapons by distance: long, medium, and close. But in reality there are only two as the damage falloff by the distance is HUGE, like 200 vs 5!!! (Like come on! This is not an MMO) So, remember: long is medium, and everything else is close range.
- Enemies are way too spongy and there is no way to +1 your weapon. SRSLY, common goons must die in one headshot from a fricking stakegun. SPONGE != HARDCORE.
- No icons on minimap for ammo or health if they are out from the chest - why?
- Pushed into pits with full health = your run is over - again, why???
- I died nearly 10 times from being pushed or simply sliding into a pit in that cave with a timer, just to get 14 GOLD and one rusty dagger that never worked - very generous, devs.
- I feel like you must play only on MEDIUM range with such low mobility, poor stamina system, severe damage dropoff, and FRICKING REACH of enemies' attacks!
- Leveling system... just put everything into HP and "Healing". Not like that will make a difference, but at least you will be able to craft more stuff with actual usage.
- No STAT-based weapon scaling - funny that devs picked a lot of junk from other games, but forgot about something useful.
- Even after 6 hours I still don't know what that small text in the left bottom corner reads - that is one hell of a poopy Italic UX. Use ICONS next to that text, we don't have time to read small italic text, for the love of sanity.
- Abilities, HP, and stamina must be indicated near the aim-cross. They have low contrast, bad placement, and poor usability.
- For an "Extraction shooter" there is NO LOOT in zones.
- "We got fancy graphics, but our gameplay is outdated AF," and because of all that colourful UE5 glory I can't see shit, but enemies still can shoot from the trees and VFX.
- Enemies can shoot at you from the distance you cannot deal enough damage to them - why?
- Too many "WTF moments" like: 
    -- "Ah, you unlocked the 'asdawacaesvss 2'? Here, now all enemies are permanently stronger, have fun!"
    -- "The 'flying-guard-crap' blocked your way, you must destroy its small crapy energy sources somewhere on the map! One is blue, and one is red... for some reason. Remember that you don't have much time at all on this map!" <- seriously, how to destroy that red one? I tried shooting, melee, spell, and demonic, but nothing worked!
    -- "Ah, here goes the hunt or something, run and save your sanity while we spawn endless mobs around you! By the way, portals will not open when enemies are near <3" <- Sorry, but this is a straight idiocy. Why do you block portals? Is the timer not enough?!

Like with many "Souls-likes", this game has many "features" but without actual understanding of how they must work and if needed here at all. 

- A good souls-like has a tight and fair balance with good scaling, it always allows you to overgrind the location and beat it with ease. Here, everything is tight up just to make things HARDER, not more challenging or rewarding - bad game design.
- A good rogue-like has overpowered combos and give chances to cheese the session. Here... again, good combo is MANDATORY just to play normaly. The "Pain vs Reward" is on the very poor side.
- A good extraction shooter gives a ton of loot to collect and loose. And here we have only ~5-20 GOLD and EXP.

[spoiler][h2]A free advice for idea-poor devs:[/h2]
- Make a "weapon parts" system where we, players, can craft our own gear with different rarity, stats, and effects, and hide all this crap into chests and enemies. Barrels, triggers, receivers, sigils, etc.
- Raise players' mobility. Even Ogryn from W40k Darktide moves faster and smoother than our witch-hunter. Leave "slow and realistic" movement in 2014 with DS2.
- Raise players' aggressiveness with parry and HP return by dealing damage to enemies aka Bloodborne.
- More in the comments.[/spoiler]

review_text:
[h1]Review[/h1] 
I was waiting for this game. I was hyped up but then sadly saw the reviews. I got the game gifted because I love horror games with combat. I finally decided to play it and decided that I actually enjoyed the game. 

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Forget that the game is a dead space clone. Forget that the games system is in every way inferior. It has everything that dead space has but less. The only feature that is new is a melee combat system. In contrast to other people i deem it at decent and serviceable but not in the context of the games structure.
I played the game on hard difficulty, which makes enemies take 2-3 melee combos or more to die. You dodge automatically by holding the dodge button, there is a block button that makes you get damage thus being absolutely useless aside the fact that it does not make you dodge in a direction. This is useful when trying to melee combat multiple enemies. Upgrading your weapon increases damage and the chance to break enemies’ arms or outright give you a kill animation. Basically, a must. Ranged Weapons can be upgraded too but that’s not as useful to do. You cannot decide what to upgrade first, making you get useless upgrades like less recoil for a revolver first. Also, for some reason you have the need to do an animation when switching weapons. They don’t change themself that much, since you are in melee combat most of the time the weapons just serve to reduce enemy count and later finish mutating enemies.

At 40-50% of the game, the melee combat gets more tedious. If you play on hard, it’s almost impossible to melee kill an enemy without them mutating. This means they change into a harder enemy, regaining health. Therefore, you either use ammo or have to fight an enemy with twice as much health again, repeating the same dodge and attack pattern.

Otherwise, the gameplay loop about the exploring and pressing on is good. There is usually always a change of location, you don’t get bored by same looking rooms. There are no puzzles at all, and the game is very linear. Its hard to figure out which path is the intended one and which gives additional rewards and loops back again.

The melee combat itself gives satisfaction. The animations are punchy, hard and fantastic to look at. Each combat encounter is a decision between being able to maybe stealth it a bit, take out 1-2 enemies in melee or deciding which enemy to kill with scarce ammo. Ammo is scarce making melee the main combat tool.
In general, I never got bored from my playthrough although the “just” serviceable combat system and linear structure of the levels say the opposite. I never got stuck and while you can die easily a checkpoint is rarely far away. Funnily enough there is a horde mode that shows that the combat system, with enough ammo and lower health enemies, can work very well. Enemies are just too few, too long to beat and recourses are too scares to waste.

[u]Story[/u]
You get to a prison colony on a moon for x reason and a biological virus gets out for y reason. Thats it. Goal is to try to escape and explore more of the colony. The latter part is more interesting as it offers various set pieces and memorable levels. This part is the only one that i deem being very, very good in this game.

[u]Sound[/u]
I did not find the OST in any way memorable. Neither the voice acting nor any other things. Weapons are also serviceable, sound effects are decent, aside melee sfx which are absolutely brilliant.

[u]Graphics[/u]
It looks great and from the stutters people complained about: i have had 0 in 2025. Experiences may vary. Game just looks absolutely great. Variety in level design, enemies and animations. While there is that 1-2 kill animation that you see over and over again, there are a few more rare ones that get you by surprise, especially those that cover the main character getting killed.

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR[/u]
It’s an ok game. There are many decisions that are questionable, tying in a melee combat system into a survival horror game plus a ranged combat system with scarce recourses is a unique approach and difficult. They failed. Instead of making the melee combat system rewarding to use, it’s easy to get into but you can never really do much to make it work in a way that it isn’t tedious. It quickly becomes repetitive. It doesn’t help that it has the modern game design philosophy of making all animations long and repetitive, including long vent crawling sequences. Yet the gameplay loop is serviceable, it’s not so bad that its frustrating and the level design is good. Its one of the few games where I wanted to see what the game would throw at me next, while also being able to recall places in the game after finishing it. I would recommend it, but barely. Since there will be never a sequel as it was a massive flop they never have the chance to remake their mistakes.

review_text:
Tape to Tape is a wonderful game that has a lot of potential. As a Roguelite, it has this arcade kind of feel that you just love from ice hockey. In it, Tape to Tape has a lot replay value in the campaign as you have to keep grinding on it. On expert difficulty or any difficulty, the run ends if you lose an elite game or a boss level which makes it extremely challenging. And then you have to start all the way back over from Act 1.

Gameplay wise, I love it so much as I said before. My only thing is: I wish they had a little bit stronger of a poke check. But it's not really a complaint because that would change the entire landscape of the game, if they listened to me and did that. You can still poke check a little bit, which I love already. Body checking the way they have it is awesome. I think this is a game that a lot of hockey fans of this genre will start to fall back on. And once there is an online multiplayer to it, watch out! I cannot wait for that.

review_text: While this game may have been good at one point, I can not recommend anyone purchase it in 2022.  Why?  The game will not save my progress.  It shows the save symbol in the bottom corner, but if I quit the game and come back to it, I have to restart at the beginning of the game, tutorial and all. review_text:
[h1] A Fan's Preamble[/h1]

I wanna make it clear that I care immensely about this game. Or at least it's franchise, Phantasy Star has always been one of my favorite game series. Phantasy Star Online on the Dreamcast especially is a game that I loved playing as a child. At the time, I didn't even realize online co-op was something possible, let alone the games selling point. Despite this, the gameplay itself was so satisfying, with it's relative simplicity. Even today the combat still has some amazing staying power, and being able to play that game online now thanks to private servers feels like finding a hidden passage in your childhood home.

It was a wild ride between PSO2's localization to NGS, But finally, this game is at a point where I feel a review is warranted.

The most recent update as of this review was being tentatively called the "Ultra Evolution Update" before release. Which is a title more loaded than Jeff Bezo's wallet. Before the update, the lead developer came out and said that this is how they intended the game to be released on day one. Meaning that despite the game being branded "Ver. 2", it is effectively version 1.0.0.

So here we are. For all intents and purposes, the game has exited it's early access and is a "finished" product. So after most of the bugs, drama, and insane content droughts, is the game worth playing?

Well, you've already seen my answer. So let's talk about why:

[h1] Combat[/h1]

Firstly and most importantly, the combat is incredibly BORING. Despite having seemingly simpler combat, PSO achieved a fun system by making it heavily timing focused. Giving combat a nice rhythm. PSO2 made this timing more forgiving, but NGS has completely ditched this important aspect in exchange for focusing entirely on making attacks "look flashy". This flashy presentation, and increased combat abilities make the gameplay seem more in depth on the surface, but is in fact so shallow that the game gives you an "AUTO FIGHT" button that you can simply hold down to win. Even without this cruise control gameplay, trying to play the game skillfully amounts to very little more than cycling through which button you hold down.

It's doesn't help that most enemies are either worthless trash, or annoying damage sponges. The standard enemy  feels like it takes 30 seconds to whack away at until they keel over. In PSO, a foe like this would be a miniboss. Something that was an actual threat. Rather than the most basic enemy you find everywhere.

[h1] Progression[/h1]

Second most important aspect of a good MMO is a game's progression. AKA, how it feels to get stronger through the game, or, the enjoyability of grinding. Another way of thinking of it is how the game escalates. In this aspect the game still falls flat on it's face.

The dungeon crawling of previous games was a large part of previous games identity. With NGS, the removal of this shows how much heavy lifting that gameplay "format" was doing.

Grinding entails running around a small room, killing monsters, until the big monsters come out, repeating ad nauseum. The drops of these monsters are so minuscule and rare, that you might as well be collecting wads of gum in a McDonald's Drive-thru. Same also goes with their EXP payouts, which compounds this games massive issues with leveling.

Throughout the games 4-5 hour story, (which we will talk about next) you go from level 1 to level 60. With the current max being 70 (soon to be 75) Most of this leveling is skipped through massive EXP payouts skipping upwards of 10-20 levels at a time. However, it should be noted that levels in this game are mostly just an arbitrary number to lock you out of content. Paling in comparison to how important levels were in PSO2 let alone PSO where the massive dopamine rush of a level up was aided by [url=https://youtu.be/zQQ9bnksTPE] the best level-up jingle mankind ever created [/url]. It's almost as if the developers knew they made leveling a chore, and decided they could simulate the dopamine hit from previous game by force-feeding tons of levels at once.

[h1] Story[/h1]

NGS's story is at best a 4-5 hour affair. And any extra time spent is because of you being arbitrarily locked from progressing until you reach a certain power level. The actual plot consists of you -an amnesia ridden, silent protagonist- and two, one note, waifu-bait, party members (Aina and Manon), going from region to region solving problems that have no real bearing on an overarching plot or theme. Never do you face actual conflict because, as the protagonist, you are a perfect paragon of infinite power. Never flinching, even when facing revelations that should rock your world.  [spoiler] I.E. Being a test tube baby. [/spoiler] You never get a chance to role play the character you want to be. As you are almost always given dialogue choices that mean the exact same thing, to which characters respond in the exact same way regardless of choice. It's so insane how railroaded your character is in the story. So much so, that I would've preferred not having any dialogue options, so as to make the cutscenes shorter and, more bearable.

I could rant for hours on how terrible the story is, but I'm hitting the character limit so lets move on:

It's worth covering the new stuff in this game that was apparently worthy of calling it "Ver 2" so lets go over those:

 [h1] Cell-Shading [/h1]

This blatant attempt to make the game more superficially similar to Genshit Impact is an addition that completely destroys what little visual identity this game still had. You see, the filter gives all the games character that soft look which cell-shading excels at. However, it does nothing to the surrounding world. Making the characters clash with the environment to an extreme degree. It's about as jarring as it would be to see an actual anime character walking around in the real world.

Okay, with that, lets talk about the actual big new thing in this update:

 [h1] Creative Spaces[/h1]

Creative spaces were added to the game as a response to the massive player requests for personal quarters to make a comeback from PSO2. However, it seems the devs didn't understand why people wanted this feature, so creative spaces are a massive over correction to the perceived "hole" in the game.

Creative spaces throw out the apartment you were given to decorate in PSO2 and replaces it with a whole island. Far more space, and far more flexibility is given to you to create the home you want. And surprisingly, it doesn't require you a premium account to actually have fun with the feature.

Don't get me wrong, creative spaces are very fun to build in and to explore. So fun. in fact. that it overshadows the ACTUAL GAME attached. Even so, the creative spaces aren't anything that other games haven't done before. This is no better than freaking Disney Infinity's sandbox.

 [h1] Closing Thoughts (and TL;DR) [/h1]

everything about this game is a crying shame. I had spent over 1500 hours on PSO2 in one year even before it made it to Steam. And as a Hardcore fan of this franchise, I only barely reached half of that playtime In NGS's two year lifespan. Even so, a not insignificant amount of those hours are from me getting so bored I leave the computer and accidentally leave it idle overnight.

on a meta level, SEGA as a company has destroyed everything that gave them notoriety and made them a company of some renown. The only thing they are known for at this point is a blue hedgehog, and even that is a point of contention. At this point, supporting their products is nothing short of Stockholm syndrome believing that maybe, just maybe, things will get better.

As such, I'll still be passively watching this game, hoping either that this company comes to their senses and rebuilds this game from the ground up. Or that the game is finally laid to rest, allowing this series to end, and be at peace.

TL;DR: Not worth a passing look, Genshin Impact respects you more than this game.

review_text:
Fun and brief. Worth picking up on sale, for sure. I finished my first playthrough on hard mode after just a handful of hours, no guides or breaks needed.

Enemies are varied, but extraordinarily simple. Most have exactly one unique attack; a handful of larger minions have two; bosses have, by and large, three per phase. Their art is well-styled and cohesive. All enemies have tells and consistent AI. The bosses are all young women that embody various fetishes, like slime girls, succubi, and a few other less-decent ones, but only the art plays off of that; the limited conversations and lore are completely nonsexual (with the exception of one comedic quest giver who exists to reference erotica from The Elder Scrolls).

It controls like a classic post-SotN Castlevania game, with a few exceptions. The most notable is that swinging a weapon cancels all sideways momentum and controls. Startup and end lag is significant on most weapons, and you'll have to learn how to approach and disengage from each enemy individually. Back dashes are replaced with a Souls-like dodge with very forgiving i-frames and infinite uses.

While I've heard complaints about the combat feeling slow or unwieldy, I enjoyed it. Some enemies or bosses are fast enough to swing twice before the slowest weapons can swing once, but they're rare. (Plus, slow weapons are going to be the least flexible -- why should you be able to tackle every threat that exists using only a greatsword?)

While this game is tagged as a Metroidvania, you don't collect new movement options, there are no secretly-breakable walls, and the game is entirely linear with no necessary backtracking. Attack options (weapons and spells) are collected or bought throughout the game, including in one-screen optional areas that are barely hidden. Puzzles are simple and small.

The developers also describe the game as "survival", but I disagree. Free, unlimited, unconditional regeneration is available before the first boss (for a toggleable penalty to max HP that you can switch off once you're healed), there's a checkpoint every third or fourth screen, and unless you choose the permadeath difficulty, you can simply treat the consumables as you always do: as things to be hoarded and unused.

Lastly, I very much like the flexibility offered by the environment. Acid on the ground will poison you, but if you light it on fire, it will burn anything that touches it until it's exhausted. Casting ice spells in water will indefinitely chill it to damaging levels for both you and foes. Certain surfaces and regions are "sticky" and slow you down. It's all intuitive, and it's neither over- nor under-used.

Overall, heartily recommended. It's a cute fusion of gameplay elements that doesn't overstay its welcome.

review_text:
I'm 41, and I cannot recommend this game.  Despite others my age who've raved about how good this is. If you have an actual life - and enjoy seeing your playtime into a game recognized, avoid this. For the record, I'm not bad at FPS's. I loved Doom Eternal, Far Cry 3, Crysis, Bioshock. They say this game is like dark souls and destiny. Well, truth be told, I didn't really think Destiny was all that great when it came out. - Bungie really popularized the whole idea of cramming RPG mechanics into an FPS action genre. It just felt dumb and unnecessary - I worked at a gamestop when that game released. And I triggered quite a few kids sharing my opinion lol.  Shooting stuff and seeing negative numbers spew out of an enemy while depleting their health bar just looks so f***ing stupid, sorry guys.  So there's one big aspect that ruined this game for me.  Mainly though, this is just a difficult and punishing waste of time that reminds me that I'm way out of touch, more than any other game I've ever played. I don't really play many roguelites in general. But I do have a few favorites recently; battleshapers, Entropy Effect, and a few others.  Why did I buy Witchfire?  - It looked f***ing awesome.  Why question the purchase with so many rave reviews?  Well, I blame myself for reading just a couple of the sycophantic reviews of this game on steam before pulling the trigger. I think roguelites are one of the worst things to happen to modern gaming, aside from microtransactions and the GAS concept.  When did we decide that cutting content into a fraction of what would normally be required to be considered a full game was acceptable in a game?  I guess it's seen as ok, just as long as there's randomly generated enemies and a level-up system to feed the dopamine-addicted youth. Eat it up. This game has all that s*** and more.  There's a lot more to love here...
This game's atmosphere is amazing. The graphics are 10/10. As good, or better than any AAA game on the market. This is a bright beacon of light to see. I almost considered not requesting a refund just because of all the hard work the small team spent on this game. There's an amazing soundtrack/background.  Solid sound effects.  Smart enemies. I would have loved it otherwise, had it not been such a punishing game. Make it an open world game, or a linear story - either is fine. I would love this game.  But the difficulty level is obsurd!  Plus, paired with the fact that if you don't make it out, your entire time devoted is null; You loose all your "witch power" and progress/ power ups because you never made it out.  Nah. Sorry.  With 2 boys who constantly hound me to play overwatch, and a pretty healthy marriage I've kept going, this game offers nothing of value for me because it decided that my time isn't worthwhile, especially if I'm not up to the demands of this ridiculous game structure and its lore.  ANY Time invested into anything when you're 41 means something! Why the f*** do I want to die over and over getting my a$$ handed to me!?  For real. I could not make it through 1 f***ing quest. NOT 1. lol. 10+ tries. I guess I suck and this game. It wasn't designed for me. But for all you nerds in dire need of dark atmosphere who found dark souls and destiny to be "revolutionary", or if you're just a dopamine addict with some appreciation for the occult, THIS is the game for you.  If you're 41 and you have a life, I would say avoid this, but f***-it - give this game a try - or instead, find a good movie to see with your spouse. Your choice.  Big takeaway here is that your time is mostly useless unless you know all this fantasy RPG roguelite bulls***, or just need more of that sweet dopamine.

review_text:
The concept is almost exactly where I've always wanted to see a sports game roguelite/RPG to be, but there's a lot of work that needs to be done on the gameplay loop and the flow.

A single loss can frustratingly put you out of a good run, which is something most roguelikes and roguelites generally avoid unless there's a significant payoff to the risk. An example would be an instant-death upgrade in a roguelite game until you "purify" it to receive a bonus to a stat.

Auto-changing characters is VERY frustrating, because there doesn't appear to be any rhyme or reason to what character is selected. I think this can be alleviated if I were to change characters with the right thumb stick? The problem though, is nearly every sports game out there offers auto-character selection that prefers near the puck, which has thus far not been my experience in the game.

The enemy goalie is MUCH better than mine. I'm not sure if this is balance-based, but I know it's not skill as the sheer number of shots I take to goals is much larger than the computer. We're talking like 25 to 1 versus 8 to 2. Even if they were all trash shots on my part, that's kind of bizarre.

It'd be nice to see the AI teammates doing a bit more. Right now they may occasionally throw a check out there, but that's pretty much it. They also have a terrible habit where ALL OF THEM of migrate to the side of the rink I'm on, providing me with no one to pass to for a backdoor shot.

The game seems to favor wholesale stat increases for the "non-all stars" much more than the all stars, but there's not much to do with that unless you're controlling said non-all star--which I do, because they, again, often have far better stats in the late game.

Early access though, so I imagine a lot of the kinks will be worked out, and anything that isn't may just be a problem I see that others don't. It's fun, but not a lot of replay value at the moment. It'd be cool to see a franchise mode or something.

review_text:
Dead by Daylight is not an easy or beginner-friendly game by any means. The biggest flaw? It desperately needs an updated tutorial and practice mode. New players have no way to rehearse basic skills like flashlight saves, flash bangs, loops, or facing specific killers. In custom matches, you can only fight bot survivors as killer—never the other way around.

I’ve introduced this game to several friends; 90% quit within their first week. The learning curve is brutal and full of odd mechanics (like having to line up exactly 90° for a fast vault). After nearly a decade, the same issues remain—tunneling and slugging still dominate matches, making the solo experience miserable. Solo queue players are punished by design, since survivors can’t communicate beyond basic gestures (“come here” or “follow me”).

The developers seem to prioritize new content over stability, balance, or beginner accessibility. The business cycle feels predictable: announce a new killer, generate hype, attract new buyers, they realize how unforgiving the game is—and then they leave.

A notable example I would like to point out is Dead by Daylight hasn’t been forced to evolve for nearly 10 years due to lack of major sustainable competition. Until Behaviour Interactive adds quality-of-life features that support new and solo players, I can’t recommend this game to anyone starting fresh.

Verdict: Great concept, deeply flawed execution. 6/10 for veterans, 2/10 for newcomers 

 [Overall]: Not recommended

this game gets so frustrating for many reasons.

The controls are absolute ASS. On mouse and keyboard, i have such a hard time believing how miserable the controls are. It's just as difficult to create your own key bindings because I don't know any of the moves, abilities, etc.

Manually adjusting the camera movement AND rotation while trying to move your character, place a trap, pick up a body, or whatever, just feels like the dildo of god thrusting into your backside.

You can also completely brick a playthrough on a map with an unlucky quick save. For example: map 3, i reached the point of playing as the Samurai. I was stealthy, killed a bunch of bad guys, then hid in a bush and quicksaved. Immediately after, one foot print made it right outside the bush and two enemies + 2 more behind me now insta kill me every time on this save. My last quick save was before I even got the key.

This game has good ideas, but the execution sucks IMO.

review_text:
I have a lot I could say about this so I'll keep it as brief as I can. This is good! One of the highest recommendations I'll give for something I played this year.

But I'm not gonna lie, I think there's a lot of factors that make it good to me specifically, that I think the average person might not be as into:

First of all, elephant in the room, the entire style of this game is insane. Every aspect of the game is curated to a specific "y2k" aesthetic that I am absolutely obsessed with. All of the art, all of the music, every detail is incredibly on point. To the degree that this genuinely feels like it could have released in 2004 or something, which is both a positive and negative, but I think is definitely what they were going for. 

Second, in terms of gameplay, the thing I can compare it most to (other than Jet Set Radio, which it's of course connected to), is Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, another game I famously enjoy a lot haha.

Just to rattle off some negatives though - All of the songs are great, but there's only about 20-25 of them in the game, so you end up hearing a lot of them over and over in an 11 hour playthrough. Additionally, some of the gameplay feels a liiiitle jank, which kind of plays into the 'feeling like it came out in 2004' factor. This could potentially be a skill issue I guess if you wanted to be lame but it just made some sections of the platforming feel very unsatisfying when you miss one step and lose like minutes of progress.

There's objectively a story here which is honestly interesting enough to work for me but the "voice acting," if you could even call it that, makes it a little more difficult to get into.

All in all, I think this is absolutely worth a play because it's so very singular in every aspect, but it wouldn't be winning anyone's GOTY awards or anything

review_text: After completing SH2:Remake from Bloober I was anxiously awaiting Cronos after its announcement trailer. I like many others love Dead Space and have always longed for something to fill that void, so Cronos looked promising. That being said, Cronos The New Dawn is an atmospheric, creepy, intense, and excellent survival horror experience. Survival Horror in the true sense- low resources, encounters that feel like life or death, and heart pumping bosses that really have you barely getting by with ammo. The difficulty is perfectly balanced, the more you play the more you understand how to handle situations best and although challenging at the start, by the end you are cruising by enemies. The story is interesting enough, the general mystery behind the disease and its relevancy to your character are what kept me engaged and the multiple endings and new game+ make replayability worth it. Definitely pick this up if you love horror, for it definitely is a standout amongst the current options out there right now! 2/2 for Bloober and I am happy they can be trusted within the horror space! Finally, performance was fine on my end, played through high settings 60 FPS and had no crashes or terrible hiccups, the occasional stutter when loading certain areas, but quickly smoothed over so nothing frustratingly bad.

Doesn't work. Either let a player fully strave and move unrealistic or keep the characters movement consistent with the horizontal axis from where the player came from not a mix of both. 
With a game as ridiculously fast as this it would be great if I zoom past an 
enemy be able to face it and shoot it and when I press like... Left then actually go left. 

now the game still does this but in a strafe form that either takes years or shortly defending on your speed. Now on its own giving how forging this game is, sure you can forgive it and just say "get good" which is fair. 
Perhaps with an hour of gameplay I wouldn't be able to judge the controls just yet, but that is where the flaw of the stages come in. You fall so easily in this game and for a game about speed and control and parkour u kinda don't want to fall to keep the speed and momentum going, sure if you play the game well u can probably go around this but for a new player like me that isn't used to controls like this its just such a massive turn off. 

(little edit)
(I know it works more like this if you ONLY hold the directional key because I ALWAYS hold W but this makes stuff like wall jumping just... too much. Especially if you fall and you get teleported ALL the way back and not just at 
the last place u were. Now the dev got checkpoints to counter this but they are way too 
far apart and should actually just put one after every enemy beacon.

review_text:
I'm so sad. I love this series so much, the nostalgia alone from the opening cutscenes gives me chills. Seeing it remastered in HD is literally a wet dream come true.

However, this is a poor port (as of right now). The game on its base settings moves VERY slow. The cutscene's, dialog, movement all look like they've been set to 1/2 speed. I have tried adjusting the settings after doing some comment digging. Turning off shadows, anti-aliasing and playing in windowed bordeless mode on 1280 x 720 does infact fix the 1/2 game speed issue. The game will run smooth as butter after that, but you end up sacraficing (at least I do) a large unused portion of your pc screen.

For how big a fan I am I was willing to make that sacrafice for overall playability.

Now here comes the dealbreaker. The crashes.

This port REGULARLY crashes during cutscenes. The good news is it isn't consistent from what i've experienced (it never just walled and crash during one specific part of a cutscene or dialog), but thats also bad news all the same. You never know when it will crash, or when the crash is coming. You just know it will be during a cutscene if it does, and not all cutscenes seem to trigger a crash. 

To add salt to the wound, the way this game is set up, you do not have the capability to save in the middle of "Areas" (or dungeons if you want to call them that). You can save either before or after leaving an area. Area's (not all of them but mandatory ones needed to progress the stoy) have cutscene's! So imagine running 2/3rds of an Area just for the game to crash during a cutscene at the end of it. With no way to save mid Area, you have to literally restart the game, and repeat the area- in the hopes the cutscene wont trigger the crash, with no garuntee.

...And well you see, the way my bank account is set up- REFUND!

P.S. In all honesty this would be a 10/10 for me if the bugs are fixed. Fix the 1/2 speed game issue, and fix the crash issue. My fear is that, as i've seen with a lot of ports- they get released and essentially forgotten, with either ridculous wait times for patches to be rolled out, or no patches ever being released at all.

I'm STILL waiting for Nier to be patched to working status.

I get this was barely added to steam, so I'm not that upset- but I will be refunding this and checking in to see if/when a patch rolls out to fix these issues. Then I will definitely buy this again in a heartbeat.

review_text:
A remastered collection of an old PS2 RPG series, .hack//G.U. Last Recode is an interesting game that does some things right but also, quite a few things wrong and unfortunately for me these flaws ended up sucking away the enjoyment I had from the game. I will try to explain but please keep in mind that I am completely new to this series, so for old fans and people familliar with the franchise the game will probably be far more enjoyable and worth of your time.

Also an important thing for newcomers: make sure to check the extras, as they include numerous text and video files explaining not only the lore and world of the game, but also the storyline of the previous series (not currently on steam) so you can better dive into Last Recode!

So,
We are introduced to a pretty interesting concept, a "game within a game", taking the role of Haseo, a player of the famous fictional MMO "The World" who, after a series of mysterious and unfortunate events, is on a revenge quest in this virtual world, searching for his nemesis, making friends and enemies along the way.
The game does a marvellous job at immersing you into this concept with the main menu being your "desktop" where you log into the game. There are Forums full of players discussing events and rumors, emails that you can receive and occasionaly exchange discussions, a fanart blog and even browsing through the occasional update of news clips, articles and various other tidbits that explore more of the world (real or virtual) that our hero Haseo lives in. It even has a fully animated web series that updates episodes after you made some progress! The immersion the game offers in this aspect is really one of the most impressive and enjoyable parts of HackGU! 

The visual presentation of the game is also of very high quality with the upscaled graphics and new lighting enhancing the already impressive (for its time) graphics (with cinematic cell shaded cutsenes looking incredible for what is actually a PS2 game) and the same can also be done for the audio department that offers some really great music tracks, from the calm poetic music of the green lush fields, to the ominous choirs of old temples.
having the choice to pick a Japanese dub is always welcome too!

As I mentioned earlier, the story is also quit eengaging and interesting although sometimes a bit convoluted, but despite the problems i have with the actual gameplay (which i will discuss next) i was curious to see how things will turn out in this weird mix of sci-fi and MMO culture. Fair warning though, our protagonist Haseo starts as one of the most extremely unlikeable protagonists i've ever seen in a videogame and his unnecessarily edgy, mean-spirited and childish personality carries for most of the entire 1st part of the trilogy before having a massive improvement during the second part. Thank God!

So it seems that i am gushing for the games presentation and the interesting things it attempts. Then why the negative opinion? Simply put, the horribly repetitive and uninspired gameplay and the way the devs decided to tell the story through it. Full of filler and padding. It's not a case of gameplay "not aging well" - i have no problem playing older or more grindier JRPGs - but even in its time of release back then, i feel this one is not designed very well.

Imagine this:
All three main games in this collection dedicate a large chuck of the story in you advancing through a tournament. 
You log in the MMO. 
Watch a cutscene. 
Clear a dungeon that is the same looking corridor you've seen for the 50th time. (it takes ages to see just a small change/variety in the backgrounds)
Enter the tounrament. Win a round.
Log out to read an email so you can trigger the next story cutscene.
Log in again and clear a filler dungeon so you can progress a short cutscene.
Log out to read an email that tells you to Log in.
Log in and fight a tournamernt round. 
Log out to read an email that tells you to log in.
Log in to enter and finish a filler dungeon so you can again trigger the next round of the tournament/story segment.
Log out to read emails.
Log in to enter the tournament round.
And it' s not just one tournament. Once I became champion during the first part, the 2nd and 3d parts introduce a new one that I need to finish again and again.
Even when there is no tournament, reperat the log in - log out - filler dungeons.

See where this is going? Now multiply this for almost the entirety of three 20hour-each games. 
I was in - what I believe - the middle of the third installment, so close to the end of the main story when I realized I  just couldn't have any more patience for this ordeal when for the 100th time an important character forced me to go with him and spend 30 minutes clearing another random dungeon so he can then decide to talk to me, in a dialog session that barely lasts 1 minute saying stuff that rarely are important to the actual story (sometimes are completely unrelated!) and then forcing me to log out again, read an email AGAIN and repeat the process again...

And it's a shame because underneath all this exhausting filler and repetitive missions they do have a fascinating world to explore but we barely see new locations and surprises along the way. There are plenty of quests and interesting things you can do, like customizing your weapons, riding and customizing a bike, becoming a bounty hunter, things that will give you countlless extra hours of gameplay but all these are part of the same-looking dungeons and worst of all, the difficulty of the game is so unbalanced, you can become so easily powerful, that half of these systems do not matter in the end.

So in the end, perhaps this game is not for me. But from what I can understand, it is a game that caters first and foremost to the fans of the franchise. If you are an old HackGU fan and have any reservation whether this rermaster is good, it is actually really good. The port is fantastic, i haven't encountered bugs and it offers the definitive version of the games, accompanied by tons of extras, (even a parody segment) and most importantly a short but all new 4th chapter that, from what i read, offers a nice epilog.

It seems this review has been quite confusing. if you are a HackGU fan, definitely try this updated version, you will enjoy it. And apparently a lot of newcomers enjoy it too! I am still feeling very reserved to recommend this game to people not familliar with it.
As a story, it is intriguing, fun and soemtimes exciting (but cosidering this is supposedly taking place within an MMO, it does not always make sense!). The immersion is done wonderfully!
As a game, I feel it has many flaws that keep it from being very enjoyable and I am not sure I would return to experience it again in the future.

this virtual world, searching for his nemesis, making friends and enemies along the way. the game does a marvellous job at immersing you into this concept with the main menu being your desktop where you log into the game. there are forums full of players discussing events and rumors, emails that you can receive and occasionaly exchange discussions, a fanart blog and even browsing through the occasional update of news clips, articles and various other tidbits that explore more of the world real or virtual that our hero haseo lives in. it even has a fully animated web series that updates episodes after you made some progress! the immersion the game offers in this aspect is really one of the most impressive and enjoyable parts of hackgu! the visual presentation of the game is also of very high quality with the upscaled graphics and new lighting enhancing the already impressive for its time graphics with cinematic cell shaded cutsenes looking incredible for what is actually a ps2 game and the same can also be done for the audio department that offers some really great music tracks, from the calm poetic music of the green lush fields, to the ominous choirs of old temples. having the choice to pick a japanese dub is always welcome too! as i mentioned earlier, the story is also quit eengaging and interesting although sometimes a bit convoluted, but despite the problems i have with the actual gameplay which i will discuss next i was curious to see how things will turn out in this weird mix of sci-fi and mmo culture. fair warning though, our protagonist haseo starts as one of the most extremely unlikeable protagonists i've ever seen in a videogame and his unnecessarily edgy, mean-spirited and childish personality carries for most of the entire 1st part of the trilogy before having a massive improvement during the second part. thank god! so it seems that i am gushing for the games presentation and the interesting things it attempts. then why the negative opinion? simply put, the horribly repetitive and uninspired gameplay and the way the devs decided to tell the story through it. full of filler and padding. it's not a case of gameplay not aging well - i have no problem playing older or more grindier jrpgs - but even in its time of release back then, i feel this one is not designed very well. imagine this all three main games in this collection dedicate a large chuck of the story in you advancing through a tournament. you log in the mmo. watch a cutscene. clear a dungeon that is the same looking corridor you've seen for the 50th time. it takes ages to see just a small change variety in the backgrounds enter the tounrament. win a round. log out to read an email so you can trigger the next story cutscene. log in again and clear a filler dungeon so you can progress a short cutscene. log out to read an email that tells you to log in. log in and fight a tournamernt round. log out to read an email that tells you to log in. log in to enter and finish a filler dungeon so you can again trigger the next round of the tournament story segment. log out to read emails. log in to enter the tournament round. and it' s not just one tournament. once i became champion during the first part, the 2nd and 3d parts introduce a new one that i need to finish again and again. even when there is no tournament, reperat the log in - log out - filler dungeons. see where this is going? now multiply this for almost the entirety of three 20hour-each games. i was in - what i believe - the middle of the third installment, so close to the end of the main story when i realized i just couldn't have any more patience for this ordeal when for the 100th time an important character forced me to go with him and spend 30 minutes clearing another random dungeon so he can then decide to talk to me, in a dialog session that barely lasts 1 minute saying stuff that rarely are important to the actual story sometimes are completely unrelated! and then forcing me to log out again, read an email again and repeat the process again... and it's a shame because underneath all this exhausting filler and repetitive missions they do have a fascinating world to explore but we barely see new locations and surprises along the way. there are plenty of quests and interesting things you can do, like customizing your weapons, riding and customizing a bike, becoming a bounty hunter, things that will give you countlless extra hours of gameplay but all these are part of the same-looking dungeons and worst of all, the difficulty of the game is so unbalanced, you can become so easily powerful, that half of these systems do not matter in the end. so in the end, perhaps this game is not for me. but from what i can understand, it is a game that caters first and foremost to the fans of the franchise. if you are an old hackgu fan and have any reservation whether this rermaster is good, it is actually really good. the port is fantastic, i haven't encountered bugs and it offers the definitive version of the games, accompanied by tons of extras, even a parody segment and most importantly a short but all new 4th chapter that, from what i read, offers a nice epilog. it seems this review has been quite confusing. if you are a hackgu fan, definitely try this updated version, you will enjoy it. and apparently a lot of newcomers enjoy it too! i am still feeling very reserved to recommend this game to people not familliar with it. as a story, it is intriguing, fun and soemtimes exciting but cosidering this is supposedly taking place within an mmo, it does not always make sense! . the immersion is done wonderfully! as a game, i feel it has many flaws that keep it from being very enjoyable and i am not sure i would return to experience it again in the future.

review_text:
I got the game for less than £5.

It's amazing. I am only on Day 5 (there is 12) as of writing, but it's fantastic.
The atmosphere and noises are perfect, although in the first few days some didn't make much sense (you hear wailing a lot, but in the first few days there is no pandemic so it was a bit confusing). Afterwards though, it was brilliant. 
I try to limit my spoilers, I only looked up what some mechanics were because it was confusing me (and I am the type of person who likes understanding mechanics). The story has been unspoiled though and I intend to keep it that way until the end. 
I play on the "Intended" difficulty, but it's nice that they included easier options and customisability for those that struggle with games. So far, on Day 5, I can see the game ramping up in difficulty, and I'm most not looking forward to [spoiler]the water gradually turning off and having to be fixed.[/spoiler] This is great though, as it keeps you tense. 
I don't think it is impossibly hard, I actually think sleeping and eating mechanics are fairly lenient (although it does sting having to sleep and not having time to do things, but that is part of the game and story). 
I'm not sure how I feel about [spoiler] children's caches [/spoiler] as I feel it hinges too much on you being forced to remember where they all are, and I have been tempted to just google where the rare ones are each day. 

Also, I must say, I wrote this out and posted it and then realised I forgot this. The writing is fantastic. For Russian developers, it is incredibly well-written in English. Really surprisingly so. The story is great, and at first you will be confused, you won't understand anything. This is intentional, you will gradually begin picking up on the world and understanding it as the game progresses (if you read the dialogue, anyway). It is even immersive in that aspect as you are given choices a lot of the time to say "I know this" or "I have no idea what you are talking about" and that changes their response. This is such an excellent feature for repeat playthroughs or just anyone getting into the game who may have played the others or watched a video or anything. I've not seen this utilised in any other game, it is so simple and yet so immersive. 

I usually review AFTER completing a game, but this one is just fantastic, and a great length too. 

Only issues: The performance was awful at first, I believe because of the Unity Engine. There was a fix for this that worked for me though:  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2847169669
This literally boosted my GPU usage from 50% to 100% and I had +100fps more. 
The other is that I believe they said the Bachelor story (the original game had 3 stories/characters) is coming "in the foreseeable future..." back in 2020. I understand COVID and everything occurred, but with the map already being built and everything, 3 years for another story (and still seemingly no sight of it being near) is very long. The base game and story is fantastic on its own though. It'll be nice to replay as the Bachelor story when it does come out, as well as the Changeling after that.  
All of that said, it seems the studio fell on fairly hard times (https://teletype.in/@icepicklodge/QC8lkECDPqZ), they also appear to want the two next stories to be more like new games than reskins of the Haruspex - this is really admirable. I suppose none of this is really an "issue" and I wish them luck.

Anyway, £29.50 is a bit steep, but I'd say even for like £15 it is amazing. I got it for less than £5, and saw it just go up for even less. I feel like I've scammed the developers, it really is amazing.

The game is not bad, but i have my motives to not recommend it.

The good part of this game is the story line is good and has a nice background to it. During gameplay you get to know the characters personalities and dark secrets, and putting it against them.
It's a good concept overall and the deaths are gory and cool to watch.

Now aside from the random FPS drops, the bad part comes with the gameplay.
I spent way more time finding items and running around the house than actually planning and setting up the death of someone. By chapter 7 i already knew the house pretty well, still it was still very frustrating to find objects or know what step to take next in some cases. The hints help but it lacks a lot of information the player should know.
For such a linear type of game it should guide the player better throughtout the puzzles rather than frustrate him/her.

I am the type of player that does not use walkthroughs, and during gameplay i have to say the game bored me more than excite me. 
A game should never make the player need to search for walkthroughs to guide them, but because this game was so messy guiding the player, i would sugest to anyone who does purchase it, to not make the same mistake i did and just follow a walkthrough.
I think anyone would rather have a 3 hour game with plenty of cool things happening than a 11 hour game that makes me wander around 80% of the time and entertain me 20% of the time.

4/10  (Meh)

review_text:
I quite enjoyed this to begin with but there's not much to experience. The game is an autobattler where you have a little army of guys that you equip with tools, each granting them a class. As they survive they get better at their weapon and survival will depend on class synergies such as defenders taking hits to protect melee units, and melee protecting fragile ranged units.

Each floor has a number of encounters and each win grants you tokens that can be spent on people, equipment, or food. Each move between rooms costs food and if you run out you have to sacrifice people to feed the survivors. As you can imagine there's a balancing act. There is also a skill tree which tends to be central to tipping the balance on a run.

It's a fun premise but relies heavily on the equipment you find, though I was surprised how quickly I managed to roll up a reasonable enough team and beat the game. Also the only unlocks are for different starting teams which is a bit frivolous, there's nothing of substance to gain from playing multiple times sadly.

A nice concept and good start but there's much more untapped potential here waiting to be accessed.
