review_text:
Graphics
An interesting environment that raises questions. After the initial WTF, everything is more or less the same. There's only a handful of impressive/memorable moments. Body horror/gross-out is part of the draw, but isn't used very much. A few graphical errors with weapons and puzzles can be fixed with a restart.

Audio
Generally of excellent quality. Music is sparse, but effective at enhancing the moment. Ambient noise instills fear of what might be lurking behind every corner. Directional audio seemed unreliable at times. Could not hear some enemies until they had seen me.

Puzzles
This is not a puzzle game.

There are maybe five (5) "puzzles" to "solve." Most of them I "solved" as I was trying to learn the rules of the "puzzle." I've seen reviews that mention being "filtered" by these puzzles.
Unless you are extremely impatient, I doubt you could fail to "solve" the "puzzles."

Combat
This is not a combat game.

You are slow, firing is slow, switching weapons is slow, reloading is slow, healing is slow, ammo is sparse, health is sparse, and the damage you do is low.
You almost never need to use your weapons because encountering enemies is rare and they are easily avoidable. That is, until you are suddenly surrounded. 

Stealth
This is not a stealth game.

There is no way to hide from most enemies, other than running far away.
Hiding from enemies in tight quarters is tedious and unreliable.

Story
There is no catharsis to be found here.

Conclusion
This is a walking simulator.

The description on the store page is completely inaccurate. I think steam should force them to change it and offer extended refunds. This game took like a decade to make. I payed $35 for this.

review_text: I see a lot of reviews for this game that say "not recommended" and then have like 4k hours and 100 in the last week lol. The game is a bit rough around the edges, no doubt, but it has something that keeps me (and those other whiners) coming back. Yes, Sega could make the game a bit more consumer friendly and they could make the menus a bit easier to navigate, but you're not going to find a better f2p MMO. The combat is very fluid and smooth and, once you learn it, very rewarding. The classes all (for the most part) have engaging mechanics and fun gameplay, though a bit of balancing is in order. Content is a bit slow, but that's nothing new. The people that played classic PSO2 Global don't understand that the game they received at launch already had 8 years worth of JP content that was drip-fed to the Japanese playerbase. If you're looking for a hardcore, competitive MMO where you can be a sweaty tryhard, this probably isn't the one for you. If you're looking for a casual MMO with the best fashion and character customization that exists (and you're a weeb), this is the game for you.

review_text:
This game is very entertaining and is able to run well on many systems, however, due to the number of effects, unoptimized configs and lockdown of graphical settings, it is not as customizable nor optimized as older Source games, such as Half-life 2, Counter-Strike: Source or even Team Fortress 2.
At this point, pretty much all Source games support OpenGL rendering, which is much faster than the proprietary renderers such DirectX (or Direct3D), even the decent DX9 and 8, however, this support is only included for Linux (and other operating systems similar to ones using Linux); while I would definetely understand gatekeeping this performance (and security) to make people more attracted to free operating systems, I do not believe this is something done for activism/raising awareness, rather just a decision for convenience, which costs basically 75% of performance for Windows users and, even if the Windows version also used OpenGL, Linux, BSD and other free oprating systems would still vastly outperform Windows.

I see this game to be vastly superior to its sequel (Left 4 Dead 2), containing more cohesive and better visuals, better performance, better characters and better campaigns. The darker visuals are ideal to the slower (when compared to Left 4 Dead 2's) gameplay.
Left 4 Dead lacks some additions later implemented into Left 4 Dead 2, however, not to its detriment. Such as lack of melee weapons, less zombies and less special infected, it makes Left 4 Dead much less of a zombie killing sandbox and much more cohesive with its lore and ambience. The disparity between difficulties is not obvious and might be subjective, but Left 4 Dead is less ridiculous than its sequel in relation to that; they both are definetely unfair, technically, considering you're one man (or four if you count your team) fighting hordes of zombies, but zombies in the first game are less janky, lesser in number, while still being threatening since you have no OP melees.

review_text:
If the game is on a deep sale, then it's worth it.

Combat is a bit of a downgrade from KCD1 amazingly, and even that was clunky. Hit registration is inconsistent, and you are forced back to being just as bad at combat as Henry was in KCD1 just to make the game "challenging". Continuing on this vein, the best way to win fights are with master strikes, but Henry for some reason acts like he hasn't spent an entire game before wearing any armor or sword fighting and lasts about 4-5 swings before he's gassed out and needs to breathe (even without wearing armor). Generally your best bet when fighting is just to parry everything, maybe get a master strike if the game feels generous, then wail on the NPC when they're gassed out. In short, the 1v1 fights feel boring. If you're fighting more than one person then it just depends on how lucky you are since the NPCs like to teleport through themselves to hit you through other NPCs

There are multiple instances where you have little to no control and are put into extremely frustrating situations for no real good reason. For example, as you're on the verge of entering Act 2 you are forced to fight a battle with no armor, and if you try to equip armor picked up from fallen foes the game just goes "lol no go yank your pizzle".

Narrative is a downgrade from the first game and has even more significant plot holes and is plainly predictable. The story is not that rewarding for time investment or how much frustration it puts you through. KCD1 had issues with random bandit encounters and they have made it even worse. You literally can have just started the game and have absolutely nothing, and you will randomly encounter 2-6 bandits and one of them will be wearing platemail. The game likes to tell you you can run, but it rarely works. The AI also does not have proper scaling - bandits are just as good of swordsmen as lords.

Lastly there are some stability issues with the game even running on a "launch a spaceshuttle" grade computer. Audio randomly doesn't work in cutscenes, you'll also get screwed up lighting, or some instances where the entire screen randomly goes black in one specific spot.

All this aside, the game is beautiful. It has that going for it at least.

review_text:
I’ve got a lot of mixed feelings about this game. Every time I play it, I catch myself wondering, why the hell am I even playing this? And then it hits me that’s the point. The game fully commits to simulating dread, despair, and hopelessness.

I went in determined to save everyone, to have the most optimal playthrough possible. Instead, I kept failing, failing to save those around me, and failing to save myself. That cycle of failure isn’t just frustrating, it’s thematically intentional, and it forces you to reflect. There’s a surprising amount to take away from the experience it even made me question my own worldview, and it’s rare these days for a video game to push me that far.

As for the gameplay itself, it’s serviceable at best. The combat feels like Skyrim with an even worse stamina system, especially when you’re starving, thirsty, and some lunatic decides to test you. But despite all that, I keep coming back. I’m on my fourth playthrough now and still haven’t completed the game in the “traditional” sense.

The art direction is really good, and encapsulates the themes of the game. Whoever designed some of the building's though has got to have a history with psychedelics, cause they are crazy to say the least. 

This game is absolutely for a niche audience. Honestly, I don’t think most people will enjoy it because it isn’t really designed to be enjoyed. It’s designed to be endured, to be experienced.

review_text:
Where Winds Meet – Feedback So Far

I’m absolutely loving Where Winds Meet so far. The story is fantastic, the visuals are a straight 10/10 and the character models and customization options are some of the best I’ve seen in any game. Weapon designs are incredibly well done and the variety keeps combat interesting. Overall gameplay feels smooth, steady and consistently engaging.

That said, there are a few areas that could make the experience even better:

Energy Costs for Bosses and POIs: The current energy system can feel a bit restrictive. Either reducing the energy required or offering more frequent or accessible ways to earn energy would make exploration and boss encounters flow more naturally.*

Healing in PvP Bounties: Healing feels a little overtuned in PvP bounty fights. Either lowering the effectiveness or adding a mechanic that allows players to interrupt or temporarily disable healing would help keep battles fair and skill-based.*

RNG on Weapon and Armor Rolls: The RNG system can feel punishing. While god rolls shouldn’t be easy, having gear roll poorly 99 out of 100 times makes progression feel more frustrating than rewarding. Slightly improving the balance here would go a long way without removing the challenge.*

Overall, the foundation of the game is amazing and refining these systems would help it reach its full potential. Looking forward to seeing how the game evolves!

review_text:
For a game that touts itself as "the ultimate medieval adventure" and presents as a simulation, there are some wild design decisions that are pulling at the seams of my enjoyment. Surprisingly few dialogue options are presented during what could be interesting moments; Henry can take some bewildering turns in conversation, turning a short, reasonable response into a Shakespearean tirade aimed at the straight-faced NPC. Pebbles *refuses* to keep either of you alive by galloping past small bands of bandits, never mind that a horse wouldn't know a "bandit" from anyone else on the road. Need to "dig a grave" for a quest? No, the tool tip says that you need to "rob the grave". Starving, I directed Henry to nab a piece of bread while crouched (and therefore stealthy) in a closed room, only to find that some clairvoyant guard sensed the movement of gluten up a flight of stairs and through a wall, immediately moving to cut Henry down. On average, fights are three-to-one against Henry: bandits travel almost exclusively in threes, unexpected quest combat pits a lone Henry against at least two enemies at a time, and every tavern fight somehow sees Henry outflanked on all sides.

I'm all for slower, more deliberate gameplay with deep mechanics and rewards for paying close attention, but the inconsistency of the experience thus far tells me that it's more than a learning curve that keeps derailing my precious, sacred immersion.

review_text:
[h2] Good game to play if you're willing to have your eyes get scarred over with the horrid, abominable, degenerate looks some people have the gall to flaunt in public. [/h2]

[h3] Gameplay [/h3]

The game is really just a standard action RPG where levels don't really matter other than minor stat increments and dictating what gear you can and cannot equip. If you've ever played NieR: Automata, imagine that game but with combat that's about half as complex.

[h3] Content [/h3]

The content of the game is alright for someone starting out, but once you get the story finished and have grinded up to a modern weapon and armors, there's almost nothing worth doing anymore outside of dailies and grabbing regional valuables (a more beneficial and lucrative equivalent of mint collecting for those who know). Lots of players treat this game as a glorified chat room for this reason, and the next topic.

[h3] Phashion and Sunk Cost Fallacy [/h3]

The fashion is absolutely the main pull of this game, and if anyone tells you differently then they need better gameplay standards. The level of character customization in this game is (as far as I know) unmatched in any other games in this genre and of this multiplayer capacity. It's unlikely you'll find yourself dissatisfied unless you have very specific fashion taste, or are looking to cosplay a character whose outfit has no similar analogs in this game.

As you can likely guess, the majority of phashion is locked behind a paywall. You should expect to break out your bank card or do a LOT of grinding (player shop allows paid phashion to be purchased through a grindable in-game currency, but people love to overprice) if you have anything you want that's even remotely popular. Doesn't help that all (even "free") phashion is locked behind a gacha system. 

Most of the aforementioned chat room players are probably only still around because they've spent too much money on the game to bow out now.

[h3] Community [/h3]

This game's community is borderline insufferable at times. I highly suggest any new players start on Ship 1 or 2. I don't know from personal experience but I have heard bad things about ship 3 and 4 folks.

[h2] So, should you play this game? [/h2]

As someone who has spent over 2,500 hours in the PlayStation port, I've thoroughly enjoyed most of my time with the game. I came in with no expectations as someone with no prior experience with the Phantasy Star series, and so wasn't disappointed.

With that being said though, even though I recommend the game, I don't suggest playing it unless you're not susceptible to FOMO, and/or have friends who play. This game is not worth spending money on, but it can be fun.

review_text:
I don't have a ton to say on this one. I can fill a review page after just half an hour with some games, but here, I don't have a lot of complaints [i]or[/i] compliments. I'll get the latter out of the way first: the music is nice, the graphics are pleasant, the sound is good, and the user interface shows things off pretty well.

As for complaints, it largely comes to personal preference, I think. I will state, however, that I am a big fan of stealth in games, so this definitely falls in the realm of something that interested me, as opposed to me reviewing a football game or something else I was "fated" to dislike, almost guaranteed. One minor complaint is that I didn't feel like the controls were terribly intuitive, but the on-screen prompts addressed that well enough that it wasn't a deal-breaker for me.

What did turn me off completely, however, is that the game felt - to me - more like a puzzle game dressed as a stealth game than anything else, and while I like puzzles, constant trial-and-error start/restart quickloads on killing various enemies in an area until you kill the one or two enemies whose deaths won't alert everyone else in the area...it just really put me off. 

For instance, one mission has you hopping on top of carts and cliffs to avoid detection, but you need to kill specific guards, and to get to them, you have to take out every guard who can see them, or at least distract them long enough to kill and hide the body. There is a stream with guards and civilians across it who have pretty good vision distance, and it becomes a game of finding the one or two people who can't be seen to take them out, before moving along, taking out person after person until you're done. Also, killing civilians can lead to fail states, so this complicates matters.

Technically, I suppose that to some extent this falls under the category of I'm a wuss and I found it too difficult. However, [i]could[/i] I beat it? Sure! It's stealth, so with enough quicksaves, quickloads, and patience, eventually I would overcome the enemies. It would just take me a long time. Am I going to bother continuing, however? No, because I was never having fun while playing this game at any point. I am not playing it for the enjoyment of others, so if I'm having a bad time even after several hours, it would be a terrible idea for me to press on. At this point, cutting my financial losses and moving on to try to find another game that can make me happy is my best course of action.

If stealth games where you might get the feeling that there are very few "solutions" - much like how puzzle games typically work - don't sound like something you'd enjoy, then you might avoid this. I prefer a bit more freeform with my stealth takedowns with the game being less anal about vision cones. The Arkham games, Metal Gear Solid stuff, Deus Ex Human Revolution, Vampire the Masquerade Bloodlines and other games delighted me when it comes to stealth, but Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun seemed more intersted in policing my stealth than me having a good time sneaking around.

review_text:
I'm normally a huge fan of looter-shooters, but this game missed the mark for me.

Combat feels fast and responsive enough for a top-down shooter, but the camera and visuals and can be difficult to follow. I frequently found myself confusing enemies with teammates because of the art style and jerky camera movements. Menus, talent trees, combat, controls, and the world map have a very simplified, almost mobile (Android/iOS) feel to them. Not necessarily a negative, but worth pointing out.

The forced multiplayer was the nail in the coffin for me. I'm glad other people enjoy it, but I'm not investing time in another game that has to be played with strangers if my friends aren't online. The game even forces you to wait on other players to join before starting some mission types, or puts you in a mission that's partially complete because another group is already halfway through the stage. In fact, my very first mission after unlocking the world map dropped me into someone else's group, so I would have to re-run the stage to know how it even starts.

Update: I've been informed by the developer that the forced multiplayer I experienced is a known bug. The Private option to play solo should be working, soon.

review_text:
After waiting 2 years after the release of Callisto Protocol i decided I might as well give it a try. Surely, I thought, they have fixed all the problems by now. Boy, was I wrong! Fortunately, I purchased it on a Black Friday sale so I am only out $18. I'm a little disappointed in Steam. They denied me a refund even though I have purchased many, many games from them over the past 10+ years and have never requested a refund on anything. They denied my request because I had played for 8 hours. Most of that 8 hours was spent just trying to get the the game playable. I never got that far into the game due to all the lock ups, screen freezes and corrupted game saves. Oh well, so much for rewarding a long time customer.

I honestly don't know how any retailer in good conscience would even sell this game. Let me assure you, I have played many current day games on my current PC which has an 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-11700F processor and an Nvidia GeForce 3060TI GPU. I've never had any problems. It's not the Champion of Gaming PCs, but it certainly should be  very capable of playing Callisto albeit not on ultimate settings. I couldn't even get it to play reliably on low settings.

In a nutshell, the issues I had were severe stuttering, total lockups and totally corrupted games saves (both automatic and manual). If I needed to restart the game for any reason I would have to spend 30 minutes or longer trying to find a game save that would actually load. It usually meant  starting the game over again and again and again. Hence, even though I had 8 hours of game time, I only had about 45 minutes of game progress when I finally threw in the towel.

I know some people will say they had no such experience and successfully played the game. If you are one of those I am happy for you. I know there are also many that are in the same boat as myself. Anyway, if you want to roll the dice, give it a try. I would not recommend this game unless you really like to gamble with your money, or someone gives it to you for free, or you just like to tinker with things to see if you can make them work. If that's you, good luck.

The only really positive things I have to say about this game are the atmospheres and aesthetics. It takes on a really nice feel of samurai-era Japan, and most of the levels (that I got up to) feel nice in art choice. And, well, everything else is either average or really, really bad. Each of the five characters all feel like anime trope stereotypes, including Edgy Swordsman, Humble but Loud Big Guy, Underage Goofy Girl, Funny Old Guy, and Hot Lady. Even in Japanese, the voice acting is atrocious; especially the main villain, who sounds like he should be the dub for someone like, Vector from Despicable Me instead of someone who's supposed to be this mysterious mastermind. I can only imagine how bad the English is...

Gameplay-wise, i mean, it's all been done before. Everyone likes to scream "OH!!!!11!! BREATHING LIVING WORLD!!!" when in reality there's like, 4 different enemy types, and they all go through predictable and readable cycles that take a minute maximum to track. The main difficulty of this game feels inflated by just putting a bunch of people in one area rather than making areas feel challenging and interesting, but there are a few exceptions.

I got this game for four dollars (USD) and that feels about the right price. If you bought this at full price, lol. If you're planning on getting this anyways, wait until it's four dollars again.

(OH, one more thing I forgot to add, every time you boot up this game one of the developer cards is this really annoying crying 4-year-old that feels equivalent to a flashbang to your ears. It's like, Mimimi studios or something, idk)

review_text:
DID SOMEONE SAY DEAD SPACE?!?!?


Seriously it's very hard to talk about this game and not mention dead space, considering how much this gane is hellbent on making you remember dead space, which for sure is a much much better game.

I was actually quite excited for this game when it was first announced but when the reviews dropped it instantly killed my hype, doubley so when dead space the remake came out to universal acclaim, and whilst I'm glad I've now finally played it I can safely say the reviews are right, this game isn't really that good despite some really nice graphics.

So before I start moaning too much I do want to say this is probably one of the best looking games I've played and it ran beautifully on my machine, the voice acting as well is really incredible and the overall presentation can't be denied, it's a shame the games world isn't really expanded on because it is presented in a fantastic way. I also can't really complain that this game is bad, it plays well, it runs well and looks incredible. It's one of those awkward games that is stuck on the edge of a thumbs up or down but ultimately I'm giving it a thumbs down.

I really didn't like a few things that being the combat, enemy design, story and atmosphere unfortunately that's the bulk of the game. 

The enemies are so uninspiring and bland that it really kills all tension the game has, the vast majority of time it'll be zombies...just zombies, when you have a cool sci-fi setting you can go crazy with awesome aliens or lovecraftian horror but no we get zombies, oh and a few enemies originally cut from dead space. 

Combat is so bad, it has some fun 3rd person shooting and completely rips off the Kinesis from dead space, the guns are very generic but they at least feel good to shoot, however the main bulk of this game is melee combat which in my honest opinion is just shit, it's spammy with no sense of skill and you are able to cheese it so easy by dodging. It's a system that was patched after launch because it just wasn't right and what we have now just feels so dumb because you just fight one enemy at a time, it really brings this game down and with ammo being so expensive it's a system you will constantly have to engage with. 

I won't spoil the story but have you seen aliens or are you aware of weyland yutani? Well then it's exactly what you expect, yano dead space was cool because it had the marker and cults and body horror and it was all in service to the genuinely interesting plot whilst this game, stuff just happens and it's all hand waved away at the end in one of the most tepid reveals I've experienced in a while. Is this the result of this game originally having ties to PUBG which they backtracked on late on development? Yeah probably but it sucks and the whole setting is wasted. 

I think for me the biggest deal breaker is that this game isn't scary and relies too heavily on cheap jumpscares which don't work and nostalgia from dead space, look at the end of the day if this game is going to spend 90% of the time reminding me of a better game and then 10% of the time annoying me then I'll just go play the better series. Not the worst game I've played and some will enjoy this a fair bit but for me a waste of potential.

So To the Moon is one of those games that seemed to have a pretty unanimously positive customer perspective.  The reviews of this game cumulate at a very high rating, noting that it's "simple...full of heart", "absolutely beautiful", and as put by Eurogamer: "How do I explain why it's brilliant without spoiling what makes it so?"  The conclusion that can be drawn from these reviews is that To the Moon is a touching story game with little actual gameplay (since the actual gameplay isn't mentioned anywhere).  OH BOY.  Regardless, I had played some games like that before and I had actually enjoyed them, so I grabbed this at a low price and decided to complete it.  My conclusion after beating it:

To the Moon is an absolutely awful game that I believe would have been much more interesting had it been made in to a graphic novel or animated film.  The few game elements that exist are very poorly executed.  Movement itself can be frustrating and glitchy when using a mouse (I frequently found my character not responding as I expected when clicking where I wanted him to go, and at one point I had managed to walk in to the clouds and I could not get down), the search quests are horrid, and all of the other 'minigames' are trivial and completely out of place.  So, if the bare-bones gameplay elements are minimal and poorly-executed, why bother making this a game at all?  You spend most of your time clicking through conversations anyway; does that make things any more interesting?  I don't think it does at all, and by the end of the 4th hour I was completely overwhelmed at how tiring To the Moon was.  I can't believe that a GAME reviewed by GAME CRITICS recieved such high ratings for nothing other than its PLOT when the GAMEPLAY was this horrid.

Now I don't think anyone beat To the Moon and said to his or herself: "To the Moon was one of the most invigorating gameplay experience of the past year" or anything close to that, so the game was made great by the story (as shown by other reviewers).  Now I must admit that through most of the game I was very touched by the events that transpired; I will reluctantly admit that I teared up at a few moments.  The journey to the end, in terms of plot, was very respectable and  despite the childish "charm" of all the characters and the "click through the words" cutscenes I managed to actually enjoy that particular element.  I would never have given the game a 10/10, but perhaps a 6/7/8.  That was until I beat the damn thing

(SPOILERS BELOW)

To the Moon's story fails in how it wraps up the tale that it tells. You essentially spend the entire game re-living various aspects of a man's life in order to determine why he wants to go to the moon, seeing all of the experiences he'd had over the years that shaped who he was, suffered through major hardships of his life only to erase those from his memory at the end of the game so you can complete your job.  I practically threw my hands up in the air in disbelief when I realized that's how the game was going to end.  The ONLY REDEEMING ASPECT that To the Moon had going for it was smuthered out in the last minutes of this awful title and I would not recommend it to you unless you are the kind of person that likes to marvel at laughably bad titles.  

Bring on the hate, Steam.

review_text:
I guess, seeing trailers a lot of people may get an impression that Lucius is something like sandbox killing game... a Hitman game with demonic powers. Sadly - it's not.

In a game, you play a role of Lucius, a young boy, who - thanks to his Grandfather's occult involvement - posses demonic powers. Each month, he's visited by Lucifer himself and each month he has to kill a new target.
It's an interesting, if not slightly controversial concept, which should have allowed for wide spectrum of possibilities. And even first 3 of the chapters show a fair amount of potential that this game should have used to maximum.

Well, the main problem of the game is that - there are no alternative solutions to a problem. After 5 or 6 missions, you realize that - even though "the playground" is getting bigger and bigger - the concept and possibilities the game gives you stay exactly the same. This essentially makes the game just a shallow adventure game, where player's task isn't to find the best way to kill a target, but finding a way that developer's designed.... even if it doesn't make a lot of sense. And so - in later levels, you're running back and forth, through a gigantic mansion, trying to find that one object that you need to finish up your task, only to find something that is as big as rock or battery(!). This alone wouldn't be so bad, if the game gave you enough hints on what you're looking for or what you have to do, but that isn't a case.

Not only that - the game sometimes doesn't even fallow the rules of "smart level design" and places many objects that you have to use in shadows and badly lighten places - the type of places, where a player is least likely going to look for them. I remember being stuck in chapter 10 for good 10 minutes, only to realize that objects I was looking for were hanging on the wall - the only place in the entire the room, that was in the shadows. Finally, the design on a mansion itself is extremely confusing and it's going to take good few hours, before you're going to learn where to go, to not run in circles.

From all of that, you may get an impression that I completely hated the game. That isn't the case. When everything was going fine and I had any idea what to do, where to find it etc. - the game was fairly entertaining. And storyline - even though, idea behind it felt flat on its face after 7 chapters - kept me interested enough to keep playing till the very end. The number of achievements also helped quite a bit, making me feel rewarded even for the most minor of tasks.

When it comes to graphics - Lucius looks decent. It's more or less something that I'd except from a game of this calibre. There are few textures that don't look right and few places in a house, that feel empty, but it isn't anything game breaking. Character animations sometimes look a little stiff - especially facial animation could use some work. There are also some weird problems with optimization, where a framerate drops in some areas for no obvious reason, but - once again - because it isn't really an action game, I don't consider it a major problem.

Lucius also has a decent music. Although, by the end of the game, you'll hear each of the tracks way too many times. Sound assets are good and fitting for the most part. Voice acting however is a mixed bag. I've played an English version and I personally wouldn't say that for the most part actors are doing a bad job. It's more of a case that script they had to work with and lines they had to deliver aren't very good. It's also obvious for me that in many places, they weren't given enough directions on how should they play their roles, which results in some hilarious conversations in few parts of the game.

Bottom line - I'd avoid Lucius for the price of 20€ or even 10€. However - with 75% discount, I could recommend it to people that like adventure games or simply don't mind checking walkthroughs. It's a 6-8hrs long mediocre game, that sometimes shows its potential, but at the same time - is flawed with problems.

It feels like the company was scrambling to squeeze whatever money they could out of whatever that was. I waited ages to pick it up at a very deep discount and still feel ripped off. If you can get it for free, I could barely recommend you play it. My OCD wouldn’t let me buy it and not finish it, but let me save you the trouble:

This DLC has almost zero story content, and the “ending” was a total disappointment. Now that that’s out of the way, the level design is complete trash compared to the main game. The gun combat was completely gutted in favor of a badly implemented, shoehorned melee weapon that feels clunky at best. You’re then pushed into using a single button for the rest of the game: the "heavy hit." That’s it. Forget using anything else.

They also messed with the combat. The bad camera angles and poor hit detection will get you killed a lot. By the end, it felt like I was just moving from room to room, getting swarmed, clearing enemies, and moving on.

Such a shame. I went in blind on purpose and was very disappointed. If I can save even one person from buying this rubbish, then it was worth writing this. It’s a money grab, pure and simple. If you really want to know what happens, just watch the cutscenes on YouTube and save yourself the money and frustration.

I wish I had better news. It’s so sad to see them fall so far.

review_text:
Graphics and sound are spot on. The atmosphere is excellent and the story is right up my alley; think the movie Twelve Monkeys meets Resident Evil/Dead Space.

The gameplay, on the other hand, isn't great. I could complain about the clunky handling, the limited inventory space, and the linear level layouts, but my main gripe is just how stingy this game is with ammunition. When I mean stingy, I mean ridiculously stingy. I'm no slouch when it comes to survival horror. I know conservation is key, but this borders on downright tedious. Even with fully charged shots (which I'll get to in a second), every enemy takes a pounding before going down, soaking up what precious few bullets you have while yielding diminishing returns, if any drop at all (shoot four bullets, get two back if you're lucky).

Which brings me to the gunplay. I despise charged shots, and you have to charge every shot if you want to stretch your measly ammo across encounters. Every gun I've found so far has charged shots, and while you can shoot enemies without charging, your bullets basically bounce off them; meaning not only does every bullet count but every charged bullet counts even more. It's downright obnoxious. 

My final complaint is with the upgrade system and how this one is just so uninspired. Upgrading weapons boils down to spend energy (game's currency) and purchase the next level of damage, reload speed, charge speed, stability, or capacity. Your suit, on the other hand, requires special items to upgrade, and these are far more scarce. Worse, upgrades are progression capped, meaning you can't save up and max your weapon's firepower first and then move to something else, not that you could really afford to do that anyway with how limited resources are.

All in all, Cronos has an intriguing enough story and atmosphere, but as far as gameplay and survival horror goes, it doesn't really bring anything new to the table or expand on existing concepts of the genre. Compared to something like Dead Space, for instance, which was made almost twenty years ago and from which Cronos clearly draws inspiration, it feels extremely bland and rudimentary in its design and mechanics. Even the enemies are just generic flesh nasties who lazily whack at you, pitting their predictable attacks against your sluggish movement. 

Cronos isn't a terrible game, it's just not all that great either; and when you slap a $60 price tag on your game, going toe to toe with a backlog of stellar classics in the genre, graphics alone just won't cut it. If you can grab this game on sale for $30-40, it's probably a fair deal.

Side thought, but I never understood why more games didn't try going down the 12 Monkeys route. Great movie, if you haven't seen it.

[i] Originally posted on October 28, 2013 [/i]

To The Moon's core concept, a dying man trying to fulfill a final wish through memory-based technology, is simultaneously compelling from a science fiction perspective, and deeply sad. I bought the game because it was well reviewed, and because that concept intrigued me. However I found myself unable to finish it due to several key frustrations.

Chief among these is the game's uneven tone. The game's writing constantly alternates between inappropriate or ill-conceived humor, and scenes that are supposed to tug at your heartstrings in a frankly very sappy manner. But that sappiness is what we're playing for, and buying into, so it's very disconcerting to have so many flat attempts at humorous asides completely break the mood. While there were some charming moments that made me laugh, and I certainly appreciate the proper and necessary usage of comic relief, the game's designers took it several steps too far. Furthermore, the game's retro art style and JRPG interface really limits the emotional impact of the narrative, and doesn't really bring anything to the table on it's own.

One particularly frustrating aspect of this is the asinine gameplay, involving fetch quests, idiotic "memory-breaking" activities, and totally inappropriate JRPG-style fight scenes. What little gameplay is present is not really very enjoyable. It's enough to make one question whether this story would be better told in a different medium. Dear Esther, another game that was very short, focused on narrative, and had minimal gameplay, at least existed in a 3D engine and had some really beautiful visuals. Dear Esther also didn't force you to play silly minigames in order to advance the narrative.

A bright spot in To The Moon is the soundtrack, which, if you're in the mood for sentimentality, really hits the spot. However it's better enjoyed without the game getting in the way. To be honest, I would recommend that people simply watch an LP of the game rather than play it, and skip over the "gamey" sequences. Or just read a plot summary while listening to the soundtrack, and maybe look up a couple of key sequences on YouTube. Either option would be far less frustrating than actually playing the game.

review_text:
Callisto Protocol: A Missed Opportunity

So, I just finished Callisto Protocol, and I gotta say, it’s one of the most disappointing games I’ve played in a while. This is supposed to be the spiritual successor to Dead Space? LMAO, no. Let me break this mess down for you.

1. Graphics and Atmosphere
Okay, I’ll give it credit where it’s due—the graphics are insane. The lighting, the textures, and the overall aesthetic are top-tier. The game looks like it was designed to flex next-gen capabilities, and yeah, it nails the creepy space-prison vibe. But atmosphere isn’t enough when everything else feels half-baked. Pretty visuals don’t fix shallow gameplay.

2. Combat System
What the hell is this combat system? It’s clunky, repetitive, and feels more like a bad boxing game than a survival horror title. The dodge mechanic is so poorly explained and implemented that half the time you’re just eating hits because the game doesn’t communicate what you’re supposed to do. And don’t even get me started on the stick-wiggling melee mechanics—it’s like they tried to reinvent the wheel and ended up with a square.

3. Lack of Innovation
This is 2023, and we’re still rehashing Dead Space ideas? The story is generic “corporation bad” sci-fi nonsense we’ve seen a hundred times before. The enemy designs are uninspired, the scares are predictable, and the “survival” elements boil down to resource scarcity instead of meaningful tension. It doesn’t innovate; it imitates, and not even well.

4. Performance Issues
Even on a beast of a PC, this thing chugs harder than a frat bro at a kegger. Stuttering, frame drops, and weird glitches plague the experience. It’s like they decided to skip QA and said, “Eh, we’ll patch it later.” Classic AAA move.

5. Linear AF
The level design is painfully linear. There’s no real exploration or freedom—just a series of corridors with scripted events. It feels like playing a rollercoaster rather than an actual game. Compare this to something like Dead Space, where backtracking and exploration were rewarded. Here, it’s just, “Go down hallway, kill things, repeat.”

6. Lack of Replayability
Once you’ve slogged through the story, there’s zero incentive to come back. No real alternate modes, no meaningful unlocks, no reason to endure that awful combat system again. It’s a one-and-done experience.

Final Thoughts
Callisto Protocol is a classic case of all style, no substance. It’s like they thought the Dead Space name and a pretty coat of paint would carry them through, but the gameplay just doesn’t hold up. If you’re looking for actual survival horror, you’re better off replaying Dead Space or trying something like Resident Evil 2 Remake. Callisto Protocol is the kind of game you buy on sale—or better yet, avoid altogether.

Final Score: 5/10 (and that’s being generous for the visuals alone).

review_text:
I got this game for free from a cereal box many years ago, and it was one of the first PC games I ever played, so it was cool to revisit the game again after all these years. There are lots of aspects of this game that do feel quite old, but it's still quite fun.

You're given a set of different scenarios and maps, and asked to build a profitable theme park by placing paths, stalls, decorations, and rides. it's quite entertaining to go from a large empty plot of land to a bustling theme park filled with hundreds of guests. It's a good thing it's so entertaining to watch though, as there tends to be a lot of waiting in this game, as you often run out of money and must wait for the park to make enough money back to build the next large ride. Additionally, although there's a good variety of different maps and scenarios which present different challenges, building a park tends to be pretty similar each time, so the game starts to feel quite repetitive after a while.

The game uses an isometric view, which gives it that iconic look you're probably familiar with, and it works fine most of the time, but it can be annoying to try and see things sometimes, as foliage or rides often get in the way. Things tend to be fairly small as well, which also makes things a bit hard to see. The UI also uses windows for everything, which makes it feel quite old, and can make keeping things organized a bit of a nightmare sometimes. Once you adjust the settings and controls to your liking and get used to everything, it's not too bad though.

If you do end up getting this game, I'd highly recommend checking out [url=openrct2.org/]OpenRCT2[/url], an open-source re-implementation of RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 that adds new features and fixes bugs, and helps the game feel not quite as old.  I didn't run into any bugs while playing game and it ran fairly well, which was likely due to the fixes made by OpenRCT2. You can even launch OpenRCT2 through Steam and let Steam track your playtime if you set the launch options for this game to the OpenRCT2 executable like so:
[code]"C:\...\OpenRCT2\openrct2.exe" %COMMAND%[/code]

TLDR: If you're bored of Rocket, you might really dig this game called Turbo Golf Racing (TGR). It's got a similar vibe but with way more depth.

Full Review:

Turbo Golf Racing is a super fast and crazy fun game that mixes golf and racing into one epic experience. You hop into a rocket-powered car and use your skills to conquer challenging courses, all while trying to be the first to sink your ball.

The game is easy to pick up and play, but don't be fooled—it's got way more to it than meets the eye. You'll have to master your boost and make use of power-ups scattered throughout the courses. All in all, Turbo Golf Racing is an amazing game that caters to both golf and racing fans. It's fast, fun, and challenging—guaranteed to keep you entertained for hours.

Here are some things I really loved about Turbo Golf Racing:

The gameplay is insanely fun and addictive.
The courses are challenging and diverse.
The power-ups add an extra layer of excitement.
It's easy to jump right in, but there's surprising depth and strategy.
You can enjoy it solo or with friends.
The progression system is well thought out and rewarding.
If you're tired of RL or Golf With Friends and want something fresh and exhilarating, I can't recommend Turbo Golf Racing enough. It's an absolute blast that'll keep you hooked for hours on end.

review_text:
The Callisto Protocol – A Visually Stunning Horror Game with Room for Improvement

Developer: Striking Distance Studios
Release Date: December 2, 2022
Platforms: PS5, Xbox Series X/S, PC

Overview

The Callisto Protocol is a third-person survival horror game set in the distant future, where you play as Jacob Lee, a prison guard caught in the middle of a deadly outbreak that transforms prisoners into terrifying monsters. Initially released in late 2022, the game received criticism for its combat mechanics and repetitive gameplay. However, a series of post-launch updates have enhanced the overall experience, improving combat fluidity and enemy variety. While The Callisto Protocol remains visually stunning and atmospheric, it still faces some challenges in terms of gameplay variety and story depth.

What Makes It Great?

✅ Visually Stunning & Atmospheric Design
The Callisto Protocol is still one of the best-looking horror games out there. The updated visuals in 2025 continue to impress, with incredible environmental detail and atmospheric lighting that perfectly sets the mood for its terrifying world. The game does an excellent job of creating a claustrophobic, oppressive environment that feels truly alive, with every hallway and dark corner evoking a sense of dread. Even now, the visuals are a highlight, immersing players in a gripping, unsettling world.

✅ Brutal Combat & Gore (Post-Launch Improvements)
The combat in The Callisto Protocol has seen several improvements since launch. The fighting mechanics now feel smoother and more responsive, with the brutal dismemberment system remaining a key draw. The violence and gore remain impactful, making every enemy encounter feel satisfying. Although still not perfect, the combat is more fluid than it was at launch, with the improvements making the brutal confrontations more engaging and less frustrating.

✅ Intense Horror Atmosphere
The game continues to excel in creating a spine-chilling atmosphere. With the dark, decaying setting of Black Iron Prison, the terror is palpable throughout. The sound design is a key contributor to the experience, keeping players on edge with its eerie audio cues, distant growls, and the unsettling ambiance of the prison. The combination of atmospheric visuals and sound design creates a feeling of constant fear that works well, even years after the game’s original release.

✅ Immersive Sound Design
Sound plays a huge role in the tension of The Callisto Protocol. From the creaking metal of the prison to the bone-chilling growls of monstrous enemies lurking around every corner, the sound design effectively enhances the horror experience. The use of ambient noise, the subtle but unnerving hum of machinery, and the sudden intensity of enemy sounds keep you on constant alert, making every encounter feel more terrifying. Even with the visuals being top-notch, it’s the sound that truly heightens the sense of dread in this world.

✅ Environmental Storytelling
While the main story leaves much to be desired, the environmental storytelling has always been one of the game’s strongest points. In 2025, the game’s world feels even more detailed and filled with lore, with remnants of the past scattered throughout the prison. These small, environmental clues help paint a picture of the chaos that unfolded before you arrived, adding depth and mystery to the experience. The setting remains a crucial element that elevates the atmosphere and offers a richer understanding of the world.

What Could Be Better?

❌ Combat Mechanics Still Feel Stiff
While post-launch updates have made combat more fluid, it’s still not without its issues. The reliance on melee combat can sometimes feel unresponsive, especially in intense situations where precision is key. Dodging feels awkward at times, and facing multiple enemies can still lead to frustrating moments. The combat mechanics have improved, but they still lack the polish that would make encounters feel more dynamic and satisfying.

❌ Weak Story & Characters
Despite the game’s strong atmosphere, the story remains underwhelming. Jacob Lee, the protagonist, and the supporting characters still lack depth, with the narrative falling into familiar tropes. The plot, while serviceable, doesn’t have the emotional weight or complexity that would make it stand out. Even with updates and patches, the story still feels like a missed opportunity, and the characters don’t leave a lasting impact.

❌ Repetitive Gameplay Loop
While some improvements have been made to combat and enemy variety, the core gameplay loop still feels repetitive. Much of the game revolves around navigating linear levels, fighting off waves of enemies, and solving basic puzzles. This repetition can become tiresome, particularly as the game progresses. The updates have helped to make the gameplay slightly more engaging, but it still lacks the variety needed to keep it fresh throughout.

❌ Limited Enemy Variety & AI Issues
Despite some updates to enemy AI and variety, the game still suffers from a lack of diversity in enemy types. Many enemies share similar attack patterns, leading to repetitive encounters. The AI can also be inconsistent, with enemies sometimes behaving predictably. While some improvements have been made in the post-launch period, the enemy encounters still lack the variety needed to keep players on their toes.

Final Verdict
⭐ 7/10 – A Visually Stunning Game with Solid Horror Elements but Room for Improvement

The Callisto Protocol remains a visually stunning and atmospheric horror game, with some notable improvements in combat fluidity and enemy variety since its original release. The game’s brutal combat, terrifying atmosphere, immersive sound design, and environmental storytelling continue to shine, but it still struggles with repetitive gameplay and a weak narrative. While the post-launch updates have made the experience smoother, The Callisto Protocol still doesn’t reach its full potential. For horror fans and those looking for a visually captivating game, it’s worth playing, but it falls short of greatness.

review_text:
[h1] Cronos: The New Dawn — A Gem of Atmospheric Horror [/h1]

A game that truly respects the player: exploration is rewarding, labyrinthine without ever becoming frustrating, and the overall pacing is excellent.
The horror leans on tension, silence, and fear of the unknown rather than jumpscares. The techno-futuristic brutalist aesthetic, the colossal panoramas, and the Cronenberg-style monsters create a world that is both coherent, beautiful, and deeply unsettling.

The cryptic storytelling — drawing from Dante, Lovecraft, greek mythos, and ancient astronaut theories — is a delight for anyone who enjoys piecing a narrative together from fragments.

Solid gameplay, punchy weapons, and cinematic level design. Only the boss fights slightly break the immersion.
Special mention for the Integrity Scanner, a brilliant idea that is both useful and anxiety-inducing.

Don’t rush this game. Let yourself sink into its atmosphere, its lighting, its silence, and its desperate beauty.

9/10 – A rare artistic experience, memorable and profoundly immersive.

review_text: Felt like a Dead Space fangame. The central enemy gimmick to replace "cut off their limbs" is "kill them before they merge" which is trivial to do so merging basically never happens (I think the stat screen at the end of my play-through showed 15 merged enemies over an eight-hour playthrough and hundreds of things killed). It has a stomp like Dead Space which is pointless as dead enemies do not give loot and your melee opens crates fine. There's no equivalent to the kinesis or stasis modules so combat is very by-rote and won't change from the start of the game with the handgun to the end of the game where you will in all likelihood still be using the handgun. The plot is a fairly standard post-apocalyptic time-travel story that doesn't really go anywhere interesting. The atmosphere is the saving grace. Get it on sale.

review_text:
I thought a lot how to really put it. A work of art, an animated drama novel, survival game as it supposed to be, and so on. All of it just won't do. Then I recalled a conversation with a friend, which we had in times of struggles. And so I found my own words to describe it.
"Life is never fair. What are you going to do about it?"

The game itself, as an actual game, is not the masterpiece of technology, even slightly flawed visually and mechanically, but in a way that does not breaks the impression, and with amount of meticulously thought through, immersive details, you may not even notice most of technical jankiness. Despite technical perfection never being game's main strength, it still uses all it could for building of very impressive, immersive atmosphere.

The story is.. wild, to say the least. Despite seemingly simple premise, it is full of human characters, interactions, motivation, and events, outright worthy of Dostoevsky novel. The game openly invites you to participate in intrigues, opinions, grudges and motivations of characters who actually resemble humans, with their own stories and angles.

Survival is hard. Really hard. As many reviewers already mentioned, it is hard up to the point of being unfair. It is so, but there's a thing - it is hard not because of technical difficulties, or because the game outright cheats you. It is hard because the game directly says to you - it is all about your own decisions, take it or leave it. There will be no hand-holding, there will be no justice, there will be no happy ending. Life is never fair, and you are just one pawn among many in fate's hands. What are you going to do about it?

In fact, the game says so to properly condition you - there will be hints, but you have to be aware to spot them. There will be help, but it will cost you dearly. There will be decisions which you see as definitely right ones, which will lead to disasters just because you are so used to narrow vision, used to fairytales of heroism, so you can't often see the full picture. The game pulls the rug under you feet constantly not because it is strictly unfair, but to genuinely challenge you - life is never fair. Your decision could be in fact not yours, just someone's whisper in your mind which you heard. Unfolding events could be not in your control, since you are never the center of human world, just a part of it. Your own prosperity could be not something granted due to "rights and privileges", but something you have to fight for. All you have in your life - your own judgement, and your actions, which you throw at fate and see if you can wipe this wicked grin from Death's face. What are you going to do about it? You are nothing but an actor on life's stage, and all you can do - is to play your role as you see fit.

The game will mock you openly, taunt you, suggest you to put it away, to play something easier, where after each learned hop and trick some master would reward with tiny piece of mental sugar. Don't listen to it, carry on, and think - if you're an actor in grand theatre of Life and Death, it does not matters how badly you perform, as long as you perform genuinely, tapping into your own emotions and creativity, finding your own ways in the face of unbearable or even impossible odds. It is a game about you.

Wherever you are, dear player, and whatever moment of life you're in, never give up on life, even when struggling with something seemingly impossible to defeat. Only after delving deep into pits of desperation and hopelessness, you may truly learn how to appreciate little moments of your life, appreciate people around you, and the fact that life's play is not about achievements. It is about your own story.

Life is never fair. But it is always about what you are going to do with it.

review_text:
Honestly, A very fun game. Loved pretty much every bit of it. I created custom avatars for VRC so after hearing about this game with custom avatar support I was all ears. Started playing it a little after release (via alternative methods 🏴‍☠️) I had so much fun. After the SteamVR update that broke the hands (and being a few patches behind) I purchased (even after finishing the game) so that I could get the fix and still had fun even after. It gets a little stale after you finish out the campaign and play some of the top mods. But I always keep coming back. This game even got me to write a nice little custom (Based on SLZ's URP Lit) shader for outlines, matcaps, decal, panosphere, Unity standard Metallic/Smoothness maps, separate AO maps, and more on avatars.



Atleast once a week (or 2) i'll find myself back on here experimenting with different loadouts, being dumb in the sandbox or modded levels, importing even more avatars and burn a nice 2 or so hours. Love the gunplay and I'll even throw some "tacticool" elements in there.

There is even a (melonloader) mod that adds multiplayer support! Though i only played it with a friend once and I was on desktop mode since my controllers were charging. But it seems to work out pretty well. Some say public lobbies are a rat's nests though, so public lobbies are a "at your own risk".

If you liked Boneworks at all i'm sure you'll like this one. H*ll someone even imported the entire boneworks campaign into this game and its almost 1 to 1.

review_text:
I am disappointed.

The style is good. The music is tight. The graffiti is cool. The tricks are neat. The movement is smooth.

But there is absolutely zero challenge, zero stakes, zero tension.

ALL of the characters are flatter than cardboard and ALL the cutscenes are boring, slow-paced, and lacking interesting angles. There are no characters that get me hyped like DJ Professor K did, and no character or mechanic to really make you feel like you're a part of the game world like DJ Professor K did. All of the unlockable characters aside from story ones have a few lines of dialogue and then just chill at your place forever. There isn't even any unique selection dialogue or special tricks only they can do, they are just glorified skins.

The cops are sterile and useless, yet are always presented as this incredible insurmountable force in all the cutscenes. The snipers are pitiful and going in a straight line is enough to throw them off. Instantly defeating any cop with a midair spray makes them incredibly easy to kill in batches. The bosses are incredibly easy to dodge and damage (and the normal cops are too of course). Health refills quickly and makes any mistakes overtly easy to correct. Everything feels completely unearned with the lack of stakes and ruins whatever tension could have been introduced with some of the cooler setpieces.

All 3 of the movement styles (board, skates, bike) handle [i]exactly the same[/i] with the only minute differences being 1) what special secret areas you can arbitrarily trigger and 2) the speed/duration of manuals, plus extra manual tricks you can do on the board. You can't ride backwards on skates (JSR staple) or bikes, and you can't ride goofy on boards. You always land perfectly and straight on regardless of what your state is midair; even JSR had the courtesy to spin you around if you would have landed weird. I get it's a style to have the game flow like this, but with such a focus on tricking, making it inconsequential to spam tricks is just pitiful. In fact, so much as touching a surface that so much as resembles stairs forces you into walking state and kills your combo—this is actually the only failure state I think the game has when it comes to the trick system, and even then it's a mere slap on the wrist. Actually being on foot at all is an inherent disadvantage and there is no reason for it to even be implemented. They axed the Soap shoes grind despite the animation still being in the game and I am pissed; no shoes grind makes on foot even more useless.

The 3 trick buttons are completely interchangable between eachother and on all movement styles, with the exact same durations and functionality; just spam all 3 buttons in linear sequence and you always get max points, it's brainless. If you dont care about getting max points (they are are plentiful and piss easy to acquire) then just spam one or two instead. Boost tricks are broken and can be used to effortlessly continue any combo forever, or gain max speed in exchange for a small and easily recouped piece of meter in the very same combo + meter gain multiplier you just extended.

Spraypainting is a fucking pain in the ass and was only cool the first time. It is actually possible to fail the spray minigame if you wait around for like 30 seconds but you can immediately start it again and get no penalty. The only incentive to spraying anything specific is achievements or personal taste. Once again, no failure states: just wiggle stick in a circle a few times so the annoying gameplay stoppage goes away.

The entire game is over-tutorialized and hand-holdy despite the fact they never tell you you can break into the secret areas or spray cops in the air, arguably two of the most useful abilities in the game (well the first isn't if you don't care about secrets). The game never tells you about the grounded trick jump but it's actually required to get a specific spray for completionism sake. Even if you dance on a Cyber pad (god what a fucking stupid name) before your idiotic mary sue of a gang partner tells you you can Cyber, nothing happens and you have to wait for his dumb ass to patronizingly tell you about them.

Many of the locales (and characters) are ripped from JSR[F] 1:1 in terms of aesthetics and prominent design. For example, the bus station and the hideout look like they could have been beta stages for JSR. Most of the grinds flow well but the fast speeds you can reach occasionally makes it difficult to continue combos with the props given, and there's rarely incentive to go max speed. 

I could keep fucking going but I'll probably hit the character limit.

Suffice to say: Game's fun if you turn your brain off, but severely lacking and I am very disappointed. If you want to relive JSR this'll do it, but it does little new and doesn't really push boundaries with what it does do. Honestly just go play JSRF.

review_text:
The game's narrative is hollow and the game/level design is not intuitive. Once you get to the lab after a half hour, you just get dropped in and are left to figure it out for the most part. They don't tell you what to do because it's part of the puzzle. It just ends up being frustrating and down right annoying at times because it gives you 0 context on what you're supposed to be doing. As soon as you feel like you get a hold of what's going on, then you're given too many options in the lab; none of which are really that compelling. Just give the player a HUD and tell them what the fuck they're supposed to do, maybe even a health bar instead of shitty vignette that you can hardly see. 

That being said, it has the best physics engine in VR so if you want to see an example of the most advanced game in the space other than HL:Alyx, then Bonelabs has it. However, what made Alyx so compelling is a good narrative and level design so its not impossible to get started and you're not trying to master the physics and figure out what the fuck you're supposed to do to advance the game at the same time. That coupled with the fact that playing VR for more than half an hour makes most people sick leaves this game falling flat on its face as just challenging and annoying. 

They made this game for people who play Boneworks all the time instead of taking the opportunity to bring new players into the space and hold their hands to show them the true capabilities of VR. Instead it's a game designed for VR "Experts" that left a bad taste in my mouth and after about an hour it becomes frustrating and exhausting. Hopefully the modding scene makes this game more palatable in the future but for now I'm hard-pressed to recommend this to anyone who doesn't play VR games all the time.

Music was dull never grabbing my attention. I was expecting some grand sinister classical music playing while trying to figure out how to kill someone with it going to a climatic crescendo in the same way as THE OMEN movies. Instead i don't even remember if there was any music.

There were also a few annoying bugs which for a game that came out in 2012 should have been resolved by now.

Since this is supposed to be the best one in the series i will be giving the other games a pass.

review_text: This game will have you saying "why the fuck is this working like this?" for you to google the issue you're having only to find out it was intentional and not tutorialized. I'd say incorporate some Hitman mechanics when it comes to assassination opportunities, which are present in the next game and that is a welcome change, give better sensitivity options so that non-sniper weapons don't feel like a pain to use without the lock-on aim assist, have some helpful toggles like holding down buttons for different functions. Overall I actually don't think this game is worth your time, you would probably find more enjoyment just playing the 2nd installment, as you aren't missing anything important story wise, and the gameplay formulas couldn't be more similar.

review_text:
tl;dr: I enjoyed this game much more than I expected, though it's far from perfect. I would recommend it to most horror-action fans, just maybe wait for a sale

Pros:
-Weapons are satisfying to use
-Pretty interesting story
-Graphics are fantastic
-The gore/body horror is genuinely horrendous and gross (if you're into that)
-Most of the technical issues with the PC port seem to be a thing of the past
-Determining which path is the main one for progression and which is for secrets isn't usually immediately obvious (good if you're tired of modern games holding your hand like I am)

Cons:
-Melee combat isn't as bad as some people make it out to be, but it is pretty shallow
-Waaaay too much use of "press forward" gameplay to hide loading screens (shimmying through crevices, crawling through vents, etc.)
-Money seems to be doled out pretty thinly. I explored any secret I could find, and I still feel like I don't have much in my new-game+ playthrough
-Without spoiling anything, there's a moment in the game that's filled with a certain enemy type that's not very fun to deal with (not horrible, just tedious)
-Sometimes non-essential items seem to just fall through the floor or disappear
-The checkpoint system can be pretty unreliable. I've quit the game after seeing that the game saved my progress moments ago, only to have to replay those sections again when I boot the game back up. Never anything major like replaying entire chapters, but I had to replay parts of the game a few times
-Related to the last part, I think there's something wrong with the checkpoint/credentials/save-data validation, because there were a few weird things that happened in the main menu (asked to read the EULA again upon booting, telling me I had unlocked New-Game+ after quitting to the main menu DURING my NG+ playthough, etc.). Again, never anything major, as I was able to fix even the "worst" issue just by closing and reopening the game

Overall this game was a lot of fun at its best, but could be pretty annoying/tedious at its worst. Aside from graphics, it lacks the polish and attention to detail that Dead Space has, but I found that I enjoyed this game more the less I compared it to Dead Space, despite the obvious parallels. While the gameplay itself is far from groundbreaking, I enjoyed it way more than I expected, and feel a lot (but not all) of the criticism I've heard online was too harsh. Granted I got this game on a huge sale (85% off), but I'm glad I played it. Maybe I would be much more critical if I bought it at full price

review_text:
I have followed this game since its infancy and watched as the developer has inched closer and closer to a 1.0-release. I have spent hours and hours on this game after its release and had loads of fun. Right now, however, Im sad to say that Im really disappointed and, frankly, fed up. Here is why:

My latest game was on the easiest difficulty following a strategy of cornering the corruption and building strong defences with mazes and towers, as one does. Countering most threats, curtain walls and ballista towers are the way to go, Ive found. I had made a good bit of progress (~30 days), funneling the baddies past a long line of upgraded towers and building up my town in parallell to the defenses. Once I got the "It feels ominous"-message, I knew that the Blood moon-event was about to occur and so, with the corruption-meter less than 1/4 way filled, I prepared to do some serious blood-slime squashing. It was going just fine, when suddenly, the mobs start attacking the walls containing the corruption and punctures them. In a matter of minutes, 3/4 of the map is covered by the corruption and the map is basically lost. What the fork? I could have sworn I read that, as long as there is a "reasonable" way out of the walls, the mobs would not attack them. Does this suddenly just change once this blased event happens?

Dear developer, I wish to have a relaxing time with your game, playing the traditional mode against actual mobs (i.e. not the peaceful mode) without mucking about tailoring a specific config just for me (i.e. custom mode). How in the World does one do this if the core mechanic (i.e. tower defense, maze-wall construction) just gets thrown out the window once the blood moon randomly starts? If I want a challenge, I`ll go with the nightmare mode. I, for one, really dont. Feeling like I have utterly wasted my time on this, here are a couple of suggestions:

1. Rebalance the blood moon event.
2. Remove the blood moon event from the traditional game mode.

review_text:
I do not recommend this game except for die-hard fans of the series, and they shouldn't play the game without a walkthrough.  Most of the same problems with Yakuza 4 are in this game, so read that review for those things.  I played all the way through it on Normal difficulty.

However, they introduced new problems with this game, mostly linked to switching characters.  First, DO NOT get any of the locker keys with Haruka.  During the playthrough, you can't move things from her item box to other character AT ALL.  For instance, the Chunk of Ash needed to make a specific weapon - if you get it with Haruka, kiss it goodbye, because you can't get it any other way.

Second, the minigames cheat like hell this time, worse that Yakuza 4.  Sometimes your phone will tell you you have bad luck - believe it.  Sometimes it tells you you'll have good luck - DO NOT BELIEVE IT.  I like playing the Koi Koi card game, and on a "good luck" day, I got my ass handed to me and had to reload (and I play well enough to be able to score 9 platinum plates in a row, over 13000 points worth).  If you're going for 100% completion, you'll need over 20 million yen, because several of the weapons you need to craft are 800k - 1000k in price.  You'll need to gamble.  Save before gambling.

Fishing is basically impossible without a FAQ.  Getting the Maguro and Squid (not bait) for the weapons required a Google search.  Trying to do it on your own is not guaranteed, because you can get several types of fish and junk items with the same bait in the same range depending on day or night - bait costs add up, and selling fish doesn't make enough to buy more bait unless you catch a huge fish like a marlin or coelacanth.

The billiards and dart games get too hard at the advanced level, even with good dart parts.  It was better in Yakuza 0 where you got the best darts by buying them at the pawn shop, and when the game didn't mess with your aim in billiards - in short, it cheats a LOT.  And forget air hockey on the hard level - the only way to score is with heat shots, and the game loves to make you to chuck your puck in your own goal for no reason.

No pachinko or slots for the Remastered version is unfair, considering the PlayStation version still has it, and they have other gambling games like poker, blackjack, roulette, etc.

Winning at the gambling tables is more of a risk than the previous game, so keep those win items handy, and use them appropriately to win the most money.  The lack of save points make it a long run back to the casino, and you get in fights along the way, which is irritating considering the Kiwami 1 and 2 games allowed you to save anywhere.

But the worst thing about this game, by far and away, is the Coliseum.  You have to get to around 200 rank points just to break the top 10, and you only get 3 points a match (3 fights per tournament, 1 point per win).  It takes forever, but worse than that, once you get there, you get beaten to a pulp.  I'm not a young gamer - I'm good at this game, but even I have endurance limits.  When you break the top 10, the #1 guy cheats ALL THE TIME.  How?  Mohammed Ali style - when you start beating on him and gaining heat, he grabs you, and half your heat disappears before your pounding the A button will make him let go.  He does this EVERY time you gain heat.  My only match with him went around 10 - 15 minutes on him alone, not even counting the first two hard fights.  I DAMAGED my wrist and arm because I was constantly pounding the A keep to stop him from throwing me.  That's never happened to me before, ever.  My arm was so hot I couldn't keep it up.  He finally destroyed me, and that's the last time I'll ever play the Coliseum in Yakuza 5 again - probably the last time I'll ever play the game, period.  I love the story and the general mechanics, but they made it far too hard on Normal difficulty.  It was impossible for me to win, with an inventory full of Stamiman Sparks (full heal, full heat).  That should never have happened, especially with Saejima.  Oh, and you can't get any of the missable items at the Coliseum (nor levels to get Spirit Orbs), so it's not really worth it except for 100% completion.

But it did, and it happened again with the 2-on-1 fight in the Dojo with the baseball guy - they literally would not let me get a single hit in.  Without Kiryu's reversals and counterattacks, I just got beat to hell.  Saejima was the easiest to win with, and Kiryu was easy enough, but with the baseball guy it was impossible.  I gave up on Akiyama because of what happened with the baseball guy.

The Amon fight was even worst than the Coliseum.  I got through the first three all right, but with Kiryu, I got wiped.  Not only did it grab me all the time, draining all my heat, but I couldn't grab him back, EVER.  That's cheating.  Worse, when I switched to my no-break katana, I could not hit him without heat actions.  I managed to get the guy down to green, and it uncorked everything it had, blocking everything I did, unable to grab, it hit me with unblockables to the legs, and finished doing two of the main character's super moves BACK TO BACK.  I didn't stand a chance at that point.  Remember, this is supposed to be NORMAL mode.

No, you don't have to fight those battles.  I finished the game because I'd had enough of the AI cheating - the final story fight was easier by far, and I didn't even use any items to win it.  That's what made me angry.  The game shouldn't be this hard at Normal level, and it's not fun.  The inability to transfer items is not fun.  The game cheating at the minigames is not fun.  Yakuza 0, K1, K2 were fun, they didn't cheat so much.  Once you got all the skills, you were expected to maul everything in Normal mode.  Not in this game.

One last thing:  If you have no rhythm, and you hate games like Dance Dance Revolution and Guitar Hero, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME.  Haruka's story is all about getting into dance battles, and the interface sucks.  Not only are button presses needed to be done in time with the music, you have to use the D-pad to chose which line you need to press the buttons on (there's 4 of them).  It's actually far worse than the usual too-fast karaoke minigame.  I don't do well with DDR-type games, but I barely made it through.  There is an Amon dance battle near the end - I tried it, it was the hard version of Haruka's initial song (twice as many buttons to mash), and after three unsuccessful tries, I gave up.  It's too hard for me, just like the karaoke stuff.  I never get 100% because of this stuff, and I hate that it's so hard, especially since you MUST succeed at these to advance the storyline.  I only managed it because the story mission difficulty remains at medium throughout.  It's quite generous considering how many presses I missed.  Too bad the Amon fight couldn't have been like that.  Poor QA in not getting things level for Normal mode.

So, don't play this unless you're a fan of the story and you're willing to skip 100% completion.  Play at your own risk.  It took two days for my arm to recover, and that was only playing games with my other hand (I'm lucky I use my mouse left-handed).  Stay away from the Coliseum, it's broken.  Save before doing the Coliseum, Amon or the Dojo fights, or you may burn all your items and still lose.  Same with the gambling.  If it's going to cheat, you might as well cheat by saving early and often.  If you have rhythm problems, take breaks between dance battles.  Save before every one.  Good luck, you'll need it if you play this game.
