review_text:
Let me start off by saying that this is kind of a mixed review

The fact that there is a rogue lite game for hockey is so insane to me still, playing the game for the first time and seeing the creativity for the levels, individual  character perks, and  artefacts for the team is amazing. 


Played this game as a solo player experience and appreciated how it's not one of those roguelites where you don't have to play it twenty times before you can comfortably progress through the game, and after awhile started playing with friends who made the experience even better as there are many funny interactions in trying to communicate and strategize how to score against what seems to be the best blocker in the world. The enemies you go through are all pretty unique from each other with just  having different abilities, and the boss of each act is fantastic.

The upgrades, skills, and characters you can unlock with points you get through playing the game is also nice, but it can be quite of a grind to unlock them all, personally I didn't mind the grind you would need to buy everything. 


Now let me tell you why this is a mixed review, and why I even decided to type this. 

I love roguelite games, and getting every achievement in many games, so I am well known with unfortunate situations that may occur or just losing a run due to being a bad player, however what am I supposed to do when the enemy team shoots from across the field and scores because my goalie has to be the worst human alive. 


Honestly it's crazy to me how well programmed the opponents goalie is the way you can shoot 50 times at goal and get maybe 3-4 goals. Meanwhile the opponent shot across the stage for fun, just for laughs, my goalie doesn't move, doesn't attempt to block, and now i'm down a score because of this. The straw that broke the camels back for me had to be when (spoilers ahead for the first act boss) the ref who assist the team, grabbed the puck half screen, tossed it towards my goalie, and my goalie let it go for free. Currently working on the last achievement in the game, but this was so extremely frustrating because I feel like it's such a common occurrence. This game is amazing and the fact that a terrible goalie is usually what makes the experience horrible is such a shame, because it really is a great experience. I don't mind if they score because they shot it closely, made a trick pass shot, etc. But if I get scored on because they shot the puck at the slowest speed possible, and i visually see my goalie not do anything, I want to quit out so fast. 


Anyways this game is still an amazing experience if you can get past that and a great challenge, fun times as well with friends. I would still recommend playing this game, but just know you may or may not be speechless after a goal determines your run while you're learning the game

review_text:
[b]A cult classic adventure game you must try before Samorost 3[/b]

Samorost 2 is a sequel to the original free-to-play Samorost, an online Flash cult classic game created by Jakub Dvorsky long time ago. This sequel has been developed by Amanita Design (Jakub Dvorsky's indie game studio), same company responsible for other well-known titles such as Machinarium or CHUCHEL. Samorost 2 is a great point-and-click adventure game where once again, you play as the same small gnome character from the first game, on a quest to save your stolen dog. Along the way you’ll encounter some very bizarre and stranger creatures. 

Short and simple, this is a game you can complete in a single afternoon. As in the previous game, the player moves from one enchanting level to another after solving inventive puzzles or overcoming obstacles. Most puzzles are just pixel hunts, because essentially all you need to do is hit the few hotspots in the right order. Sadly, the lack of a proper hint system makes some ilolligical parts quite hard but in the other hand some of them are pretty obvious as well.

The world you explore is so enchanting, with the same art direction as the original with touches of Asian influence. The game's backgrounds often combine organic with inorganic elements and  each scene in the game contains movement, and the creatures, gadgets, plants and insects are beautifully animated. There is hardly any text or dialog in the game and little voice-acting in form of non-legible utterances. The music was composed by Tomáš Dvořák, and like what he did for the previous game, the soundtracks in Samorost 2 are pleasant to listen to.

All in all, this game as a single piece isn't so bad but neither so great. However, Samorost is a worthy series that fully deserves your support. You would like to play this one and the original game title before to really go for Samorost 3, a real masterpiece from the new era.

review_text:
I really tried to like this game; I had heard nothing but praise towards this for years so finally this sale I decided it was time to get it but I really just did not like it at all. So here is why:

First lets start with the surface level reasons, the stuff that hurts enjoyment but could be looked over by those who enjoy it:
Controls: The controls are just plain bad, if you use the keyboard the map is designed in a grid (as in 1 press up goes one block) however the actual design of the area does not make this clear, causing keyboard controls to feel floaty, as if when you let go of the button the character will continue moving until they reach the next grid block. The mouse controls a little better with characters auto moving to where you click, but when switching surfaces or rooms they will randomly stop despite having more to move towards; overall it just controls poorly.
Art Style: I know this one is just an opinion and I'm sure many will disagree but I just really don't like the art style; I can't really put a finger on why but it just rubs me the wrong way.

So now for the more pressing reasons why I don't like this:
Dialogue: This game isn't funny; the character's say cutesy jokes and puns so so often (especially Dr. Watts) but they just arent funny, I cringed through so much of it. Overtime these characters progress and make jokes less often but it just feels like a blatantly obvious way of showing chracter progression, take a bland character and make them say jokes then stop saying jokes and it will make it feel like they differed greatly.
Emotion: All of the big emotional moments felt pointlessly manipulative; often having important bits of information or character motivation hidden simply for a twist later.
Theme: I also disagree with the point the game tries to push about manipulating the past to be happy but I wont go into detail because spoilers.
Ludonarrative Dissonance: The primary gameplay mechanic is finding these glowing orbs to go deeper into memories, but how does wandering around looking for glowing orbs relate to the themes of manipulating the past or memories what so ever? These things are completely arbitrary, if there aren't enough inspectable objects in the room to attach orbs to the game will literally just give you them for walking around.

Overall I really disliked this game, I really wanted to like it, and I have heard nothing but positive regard from others but I just cannot see why. And it isn't just a matter of me not usually playing this sort of game, all of my favorite games are the artsy slow type that your 'average gamer' would hate (Her Story, Gone Home, Pathologic, etc) but this just did not click with me.

I jump into this game for some space Barbie. Fly around in my ship and maybe do a misison or three. Beyond that I don't recommend this game. Nostalgia hits hard but you're better spending your time/money elsewhere.

This game blew me away! I was going into this expecting Left 4 Dead in VR and not much else (which isn't a bad thing) but there's just so many more mechanics on top of the base game to keep it fresh with a lot of replay value.

If you'd like to see gameplay you can skip into my video https://youtu.be/X56JKuSyASw

Basically you replay levels to find secrets, get money and unlock new weapons / weapon mods. 
There's shops in the middle of levels that you can buy items at, or avoid spending to earn the most money possible (which is SUPER RISKY on harder difficulties).
There's also a cool mechanic where a less experienced VR player might prefer to reload their gun by sliding it over the ammo belt, but if you're used to physically reloading, you gain extra money from kills by doing so. The game is littered with fun little features like this!

I haven't played much and I already know that After the Fall is a MUST-HAVE VR game, ESPECIALLY if you have friends to play with :)

review_text:
What a bunch of wasted potential.
I started Callisto Protocol with a clear head and no real expectations, being both a fan of survival horrors and sci-fi genre in general. I have finished the base game [spoiler](and if I buy a DLC, call 112 because I got a stroke)[/spoiler] but from half of it I felt forced to do so and I can not recommend the game.
I have played a game on hardcore difficulty and from what I have noticed it has a lot of good ideas but everything seems to be... half baked.

1. Melee aspect of the game is interesting at the start unless you understand that almost every single fight is "dodge 2 or 3 times, couple of light attacks, repeat till enemy is dead", the dreaded mutation is actually making the fight only slower because nothing changes except for enemies health. Are you afraid to be ganked by a group of enemies? Well, no need to worry because they always form a queue waiting for a beat-up, just like in old Assassin's Creed and even if the other enemy decides to focus on you, the one you are fighting right now will back out and wait in line.

2. Projectile weapons suck because outside of special "QTE" like moment during the fight they do unsatisfactory amount of damage and you need to save ammo for the "bosses", which 3/4 times is the same enemy with the same attack pattern that will absolutely shred you in melee combat.

3. Do you remember the amazing idea of limb cutting in Dead Space? This one has it too but it does absolutely nothing except changing the attack pattern to one dodge only when the enemy has one limb! Amazing, isn't it?

4. The plot is a standard set of genre cliches which is not bad in itself, but yet again, it's half baked. Most of the story is rushed with nothing explained particularly well, and the Callisto apparently has an atmosphere, snowfall, bearable temperatures (protagonist survives more than 10-15 seconds without a mask which would be death sentence in hard vacuum), EARTH LIKE GRAVITY while in real life it has roughly 12% of it. But hey, it got explained in one 2 sentence video log - you might not even find it if you are not careful - with a magical word "TERRAFORMED". And no, if you expect the rest of the story to make more sense, you are very naive.

5. Level design is for worms, I mean 90% of a level is a linear tunnel and rarely present junctions usually allow you additional 2-5 minutes of exploration.

6. Jacob, the protagonist, has basically no personality whatsoever, which is amazing because Dead Space 1 Isaac Clarke was mute, yet he was more likeable than this guy. Half of the game I couldn't even remember his name and I am pretty certain I will forget it by tomorrow. At least he dies in cool, Mortal Kombat like fashion.

7. Bugs, bugs, bugs. My favourite one is the art of chair- and bedomancy, you can use the gravity gun to push enemies on top of furniture, if the game detects they are in spot they are not supposed to be, they will instantly die. Saved me a lot of ammo! Also, some enemies without eyes can't see you, others have sonar vision. There is no consequence in the enemy design at all.

8. Game economy. Out of 5 guns available in base game, you are handed only 2, the rest of it you can print in crafting station, which is nice but I couldn't afford it even once, split between GRP, melee upgrades and a constant supply of ammo for bosses (maybe I went into wrong "build" but the game never warned me I am making a mistake, it actually encouraged use of melee for the most of playthrough.

5. This one is subjective but I, not even once, felt dread or fright, even a little chill playing it. I still remember the chills of exploring Dead Space Ishimura or Alien Isolation's Space Station, I still remember the clip I emptied because one of supposed victims raised a hand to me pleading for help in the first game, and the alt+F4 combined with a real life scream in one moment of the second game... This one? I felt hopeful for the first half, irritated for the second.

6. Biophages are "we have necromorphs at home". Nothing else to say.

7. The good stuff: graphics (if you care) is mostly consistent and playing it on ultra was eye candy. It contained Licorice and anise, but still.

So, [b]to sum up that wall of text[/b], I am truly disappointed, it was supposed to be a new Dead Space, and all I have is hollow, ill-judged game, where every piece of puzzle of making a nice experience is theoretically here, but if you look closely, every piece of it is cut improperly.

Shame...

review_text:
As of the Webgrave update, I can no longer recommend this game. The stat system was significantly nerfed such that, at my same level of 455 prior to the update, I now have 45% less health, 60% less stamina and earn 2.5x less witchfire. You also carry two less healing elixirs for a total of three instead of the previous five. Moreover, each elixir heals you for significantly less while enemies still hit you for the same amount of damage. You can remedy part of this with their new rosary system in which you equip rosary beads, however the stat based ones are weak, you can only equip a few at a time, and they are scattered throughout each map or perhaps earned in other ways.

I feel it is important to continue the discussion around difficulty in gaming and the accessibility challenges it presents. I'm no stranger to difficult games - I've completed Dark Souls, Dark Souls 3, Bloodborne, Sekiro, and Elden Ring to name a few. But I feel these games established a standard of difficulty that can exclude certain players. Witchfire is a difficult and demanding game. But I had found a way round this by leveling up my character, pushing him higher and higher so I could enjoy the game. Even my playstyle changed - I was a long ranged, passive player at early levels, using sniper rifles and freeze spells to slow my enemies. I evolved to blasting my way into enemy camps and taking the challenge head on. But I could do so with the strength I had earned from the levels I earned. 

To make matters worse, the Gnosis difficulty curve system the game incorporates is essential to fully level up to even make it to the end of the game. If I'm struggling at Gnosis level 3 in the current form after the update, then in conjunction with your stat changes I no longer stand a chance on completing the game.

One of the most iconic, if not the most iconic, FPS games is Doom and, too this day, continues to have difficulty levels allowing everyone to access it at a pace that is comfortable to them. The developers of Witchfire have said that they changed their stat system because higher level players were essentially "playing with cheats." I find this statement bizarre. If I'm having fun, what does it matter? The prior stat system allowed everyone to play as they wanted - you could level up as much or as little as you wanted. There was even a video posted by the developers of a very talented player who completed an incredible challenge. Players will always find ways to challenge themselves within the limitations of the game.

I'm more sad and disappointed I have to let this game go. I was following it for years prior to its release. I bought it day one on Epic and bought it again when it came to Steam. I was having so much fun. It breaks my heart to change to a negative review. But this is a warning to casual and even mid-core players who may not enjoy the steep difficulty adjustments with minimal payoff from the new stat system.

Original Review:
I was walking around Irongate Castle in awe of the visuals, the small details, and the atmosphere. The music, audio, sound design - it's all on point. The roguelite aspect and the gameplay loop is absolutely perfect - the player isn't Doomguy with infinite stamina or access to countless healing items, but with limitations to his character which are entirely fitting in this grimdark world. That said, player movement is smooth, responsive, and in close partnership with each weapon - it is a delight to play. Everything is stitched together in such an outstanding way and is always authentic to the world around it.

The developers are also 100% engaged to feedback and have such an honest way about communicating that it is such a breath of fresh air. That said, they are also committed to their vision of this game and they've maintained such an excellent balance with player feedback.

This game is a labour of love. And it shows. I wish them nothing but the best venturing forward from Epic EA to Steam EA.

i was a long ranged, passive player at early levels, using sniper rifles and freeze spells to slow my enemies. i evolved to blasting my way into enemy camps and taking the challenge head on. but i could do so with the strength i had earned from the levels i earned. to make matters worse, the gnosis difficulty curve system the game incorporates is essential to fully level up to even make it to the end of the game. if i'm struggling at gnosis level 3 in the current form after the update, then in conjunction with your stat changes i no longer stand a chance on completing the game. one of the most iconic, if not the most iconic, fps games is doom and, too this day, continues to have difficulty levels allowing everyone to access it at a pace that is comfortable to them. the developers of witchfire have said that they changed their stat system because higher level players were essentially playing with cheats. i find this statement bizarre. if i'm having fun, what does it matter? the prior stat system allowed everyone to play as they wanted - you could level up as much or as little as you wanted. there was even a video posted by the developers of a very talented player who completed an incredible challenge. players will always find ways to challenge themselves within the limitations of the game. i'm more sad and disappointed i have to let this game go. i was following it for years prior to its release. i bought it day one on epic and bought it again when it came to steam. i was having so much fun. it breaks my heart to change to a negative review. but this is a warning to casual and even mid-core players who may not enjoy the steep difficulty adjustments with minimal payoff from the new stat system. original review i was walking around irongate castle in awe of the visuals, the small details, and the atmosphere. the music, audio, sound design - it's all on point. the roguelite aspect and the gameplay loop is absolutely perfect - the player isn't doomguy with infinite stamina or access to countless healing items, but with limitations to his character which are entirely fitting in this grimdark world. that said, player movement is smooth, responsive, and in close partnership with each weapon - it is a delight to play. everything is stitched together in such an outstanding way and is always authentic to the world around it. the developers are also 100 engaged to feedback and have such an honest way about communicating that it is such a breath of fresh air. that said, they are also committed to their vision of this game and they've maintained such an excellent balance with player feedback. this game is a labour of love. and it shows. i wish them nothing but the best venturing forward from epic ea to steam ea.

review_text:
In the beginning I thought this game was very good because of its high rating, but I soon found out that it's not at all what I expected. Its as if the devs died half way through making the game, but instead of someone finishing the game, they just released it. It has so much potential and looks incredible, but there are some things in the game that make me question the mental state of the game devs. (I will also be comparing some things to the game sniper elite, which is very similar to this game.)

1.You can't tell that your getting shot. I know it doesn't sound like much, but once you play the game you'll find out how important it is. In average video games when you're shot, you will be able to see visible movement on your screen to make it realistic. You might also see your view get bloody and darker, and hear your player hurt or bullets hitting your player. In this game, when you get shot, nothing happens, your view and sound is perfectly normal and fine. This is pretty annoying because you might hear gunshots far away from you and all of a sudden your dead even though you didn't know they were shooting you.

2.You might say, "That's stupid, it doesn't matter if your view doesn't change, you will still be able to see your hp bar". Not in this fucking game. They decided to make the hp bar a tiny little line on the bottom of your screen. Yes, you can read it, but it is extremely annoying that its not bigger like in most games. 

3. This game is confusing. This game has a unique playing style that they expect you to know the second you play it. It's very similar to the game sniper elite but worse. One of the most confusing things in this game is figuring where your tasks are. But this is nothing compared to your map and you enemies. In this game, you can't see your enemies unless they're in completely out in the open, or 5 feet away from you. Now in games like these were you can't see your enemies for shit, they usually have a mini map, except the mini map in this game is very bad. enemies don't come up as dots like they do in sniper elite, they just show the general direction of them. You might also say "well that's why you mark them with your binoculars". That's where I get to 4.

4. Binoculars don't work properly. In sniper elite, you click an enemy to mark it. In Sniper ghost warriors, if you see an enemy, you can't mark them unless their head is showing, which is stupid. Another shit thing about binoculars is that there sensitivity is extremely slow when fully zoomed out. This is not that big of a deal, but its still annoying.

5. There is no quick saving. After you get killed by an enemy which you didn't even realize was shooting at you, you load into an ancient save and loose all of your progress.

In conclusion, I really wish this game was better. I love the way it looks and feels, but it seems that the devs didn't give a shit about some of the things in this game. Thankfully I didn't buy this game for that much, but I still think I wasted my money. Hopefully they make changes to this game to make it more playable.

The game brought up a lot of nostalgia for me. GU was one of my favorite series growing up but this is a really poor port. Combat and the speed at which you gain experience has been reworked in a way that is worse than the PS2 version. Levels used to matter: you couldn't fight enemeis 15 levels higher than yourself but now it possible to breeze through dungeuons that are 20 levels higher than you once you reach a certain point in the game. You also gain experience significantly faster, so fast that youll be overleveled for story content even if your just playing story quests. These two factors completely remove ANY challenge from the game.

There's also several technical problems with the game: a significant amount of PC users have been experiencing trouble with the games audio; where the audio stutters or for some, the audio for dialogue isn't present.

A short timeline of playing this game:

1. Booted Up Game
2. Game Crashed and gave me a superlong logfile.
3. Rebooted game. Game froze, appeared to crash, then recovered.
4. Chose Traditional mode.
5. With nothing to guide my choice, chose a spot on the map arbitarily.
6. Mouse map scrolling not being inverted feels completely unnatural.
Checks settings for some way to change this, seems there is no setting.
7. Notices that the settings menu doesn't seem to cause the game to pause/stop the music.
8. Not being able to pause causing some anxiety. If traditional mode is an introduction to the game, why can't something be be done to stop all action and sounds so that doesn't distact from learning the game?
9. I am instructed to build a camp, I do so.
10. Assigned some workers to harvest different resources. How many? Who knows. Were the workers I sent to harvest crystal diverted from the other resources I told them to harvest earlier? Who knows. I could look, maybe, but there's already so much stuff happening on the screen, that, with the weird mouse handling is an inspiration to not be thorough about this.
11. Checks internet for help. Doesn't help much. Six minutes pass. No pop ups occur, although a previous pop-up proclaimed that pop ups would be numerous.
12. Finding it hard to focus on the tiny font now.
13. "There's going to be monsters at some point, right?" *checks defense build menu* --- can't build anything. Builds storage building instead.
14. Can't build more until camp is "upgraded" --- Upgrades camp.   What are the tradeoffs of using the required resources for camp upgrades and not something else? 
15. A pop-up occurs about my storage. Says something about using the bottom left of the screen to allocate workers to it. Can't find the way to do this.
16. Unsucessfully consults internet again.
17. Concludes that while I am not sure what I am supposed to be doing in this game, I am sure that figuring that out will take me more than two hours, thus:
18 Refunds game.

Verdict: Wait until it's done.

review_text:
I do recommend this game as it scratches a fantastic sniping itch that the likes of Sniper Elite have made famous. 

To my mind, the game excels in two key areas:
1) The sniping is fantastic; there is a little skill involved with the wind gauge but it isn't hard to master yet it feels great right up to the last shot. 
2) The level design is intricate enough to allow multiple paths to your objective so it makes you feel more like a smart assassin, planning the kill, rather than a linear assassin (doing what the game tells you). 

There were one or two bugs in my play-through but nothing extreme and certainly nothing that took me out of the experience. 

Lastly, I would counter some of the "angry" reviews that comment on how poor the AI is and that it "immediately knows where you are when you shoot". That is simply not the case. The enemies have three states of existence: passive, alerted, hunting. 

Passive is the default state where they will wander around "guarding". Now, if you take an enemy out from range but someone sees them die or discovers the body, the enemy will become alerted and they will all run for cover. In this state, they get out binoculars and intermittently peak over their cover to try to locate you. If you can kill them all without being spotted, they will simply never shoot you and if you are placed well, you can wipe them all out whilst they are alerted. 

Now, if you are spotted (by binoculars or, more likely, enemy snipers) then they will all converge on your position to try and kill you. The armoured enemies will start shooting in your general direction and whilst it might feel that they have godly aim, they don't and you can easily reposition. 

This is where I would then actively turn to defence to praise because, if you reposition, the enemy will converge on the spot they last knew you to be in and you can effectively give them the slip and start shooting from another location. 

All in all, if you set up well, know your routes of retreat and advance, and fully scan the target zone then you'll have a blast in this game and feel like a god-tier sniper.

review_text:
The visuals, artistry, the mystery world, all of that is awesome, but... 
And that's a big but; I still would not recommend it. Here's why.

Apparently, the game has been released unfinished after more than 10 years in the making, and the gameplay mechanics, especially combat, have been made clunky and too hard on purpose to make the game feel longer: 
- The dodging action has been cut on purpose to make the player dodge by strafing only or avoid combat entirely by sneaking around the enemies
- The [spoiler]health recharge tanks[/spoiler] have been made less than half empty on purpose
- Checkpoints (and that's what grinds me most) that fit the world's lore are missing, where the player could safe his progress, but instead the checkpoints are invisible, arbitrarily placed and too far apart. When the player dies, they never know where they spawn again and what needs to be done once again
- Exploration takes unnecessarily long just to show that something bad happened to the world without anything actually meaningful to discover other than striking landscapes and visceral visuals

Placing fewer, more unique enemies and making them harder, or longer to defeat would have made much more sense and would require the player to be more strategic, analytical and patient. I would have imagined unique enemies having some nasty, gory, gigeresque visceral attacks, as the world's alien biology seems to be out of control. Instead: shout the ugly spitting things in the face; repeat until dead. Some enemies look like they weren't initially planned attacking the player at all, hence the only attack they use is spitting; very easy to implement, much more annoying in combat. Either the combat was slapped on the otherwise fascinating game, or it was left finished. It isn't fun and feels out of place.

I am [b]very[/b] disappointed. Unless you are tolerant to frustration and enjoy games like Dark Souls that game will not be fun. You have been warned.

review_text:
To address the obvious and most frequently asked question: no this game is not trying to be an alternative to Hell Divers 2 (HD2), nor vice versa.  While there are some similarities in enemy types and sci-fi setting, Starship Troopers: Extermination (SST:E) is a game with a very different gameplay and overall experience.  HD2 is a casual sci-fi shooter where the coop and squad loadouts are open-ended: players can choose to pick synergistic kits and work together cooperatively, but they can also zoom off to objectives on their own and remain viable (assuming the player is experienced and armed with the right equipment).  SST:E by comparison is a much more hardcore coop shooter, where players pick one of several defined roles and the teamplay and coordination is required in order to complete the mission.  It is very, very easy for the mission to be failed in this game if teams dont cooperate; quite often the mission will fail even if the teams do cooperate.  This game puts a huge emphasis on teamwork and the gameplay and player fun factor can truly suffer if that teamwork is lacking.

The game modes, player classes and emphasis on teamwork make this a unique and interesting the game.  However, I would not recommend buying this game in its current state.  The game is unstable and poorly optimized - i've had several crashes in the 8 or so hours at the time of this review and I see massive FPS drops when the bug attacks reach full force.  The matchmaking is absolutely horrible - there is no server list for players to browse through, rather they rely on matchmaking that randomly places the player with other randoms.  Players can use friend groups (for Steam, Xbox, PS) to join up with other players, but the process is way more complicated than it ought to be.  With the exception of some building tutorials, there is no real tutorial system to teach new players about the different game modes or class types. 
 There are other random glitches the player will encounter throughout - weapons loadouts constantly resetting for classes, getting stuck on dead bugs or terrain.

This game has potential, but it needs a lot of work and refinement in order to be considered truly playable.  Im not sure if OWI has the patience or the financial inclination to put the necessary work into this game.  I'd advise new players to wait and see.

I refunded it for now, but I’ll keep an eye on its future updates.

review_text:
Solid meh/10.
It's a 4 player cooperative shooter. It only has a few maps. In every map you walk for a bit, go into some arena area, tentacles close it down, shoot zombies, move to next arena area, repeat until the boss fight, which you just kite till it is dead.
There is a horrible lack of variation in enemies, every map plays exactly the same and has the same boss fight.
Lore and story is very lackluster, dialogues are extremely amateurish, might as well have left it out completely and focused more on the game itself.
On higher difficulties you get the same enemies with a bit of an ice crust as armor which makes them harder to kill.
Gunplay is interesting with "advanced reloading" where you actually have to eject and replace your magazine and then chamber the first round. But the game is build around arcade slap to the chest and finished reloading style, manual reloads cripple your ability to win on higher difficulties and make it impossible to dual wield.
Ammo management is more important than shooting, which is an annoying mechanic trying to force you to memorize/plan ammo box retrieving.
If you play alone you get 3 AI player which are so terrible they cannot even manage on low difficulty. I was able to play it just fine on veteran alone but you just wonder why you bring these guys at all.
Matchmaking is kind of a mess; for beginners you can quick join but you will probably be dropped in a extreme difficulty game which is not fun for anyone to try with your noob gear, I was not able to find players in matchmaking at veteran. Maybe player base is just not big enough anymore.
All in all it feels a bit like an early access game that still needs a bit of polish and experimenting.

review_text:
Pathologic 2 surpasses its video game identity into a beautiful work of art, similar to a great novel. This game sucked me into it's world and made me connect with it and the characters in a way I never have before in other games. The more I learned about the world and the characters the more alive it all became. I started to care for these people as if they were my own friends and loved ones. This game is a masterful mix of love, mystery, connection, dread, horror, melancholy, bittersweet happiness, and more. It is truly a symphony of themes and emotions. The design of the world, its characters, the sounds, and the music creates a brilliant atmosphere that ranges from beautiful and sweet to chilling and horrendous. 

In classic survival-horror fashion you will have to manage resources, explore and learn about the world, and uncover the mysteries of the town and it's inhabitants. This game is incredibly difficult; I spent most of the game on the brink of starvation and exhaustion but it only enriched the experience. It's not meant to be easy, you are meant to struggle along and push yourself to keep going against all odds.

review_text:
[h3]The Corridor Protocol[/h3]
Amazing visuals can't hide the fact that [i]The Callisto Protocol[/i] feels ancient and a chore to play. From the archaic audio logs scattered about to the slow movement speed and awful combat, it's all very clunky and derivative. There's nothing here you haven't seen before. 

Everything about it feels unearned as well. The cheap jump scares (that you see coming from a mile away), the nonsensical story, the unlikable characters, the awful pacing, the uninteresting environments, etc. None of it sticks and it boggles the mind that they expected to turn this into some multi-game spanning IP (with it being a [i]PUBG[/i] tie-in no less?). 

It's a pale imitation of [i]Dead Space[/i] at best, one that lacks all the nuance of that title. Instead it's quite literally in your face (on multiple occasions you'll have some character or enemy scream at the camera) and the audio design especially was a real low point for me in that regard. After the first few chapters the general experience does get somewhat better as you get into the rhythm of it all but ultimately I was glad It was over after about 8 hours of play.

review_text:
[u]In short:[/u] To the Moon is a flawed narrative with a few (rather badly executed) game elements tacked on. I appreciate some interesting concepts and themes, but there are also some glaring problems with the writing. The soundtrack is very good, but did not compensate for my general frustration with the game. Even for 3.5 hours of playtime (and some free DLC on top) the full asking-price strikes me as ridiculous, but at least the sale and bundle discounts are substantial.

[u]In long:[/u] This is a game made in RPG Maker. [b][u]Gameplay[/u][/b] mainly consists in advancing dialogue prompts. Every few minutes you have to explore a restricted area and find 5 clues, followed by a miniscule tile-flipping puzzle. The exploration parts handle badly. Movement seems to be tile based and is only possible laterally (not diagonally). I found myself constantly getting hung up on various objects and characters as it is often entirely unclear which areas are traversible (invisible walls, some flowers cannot be stepped on while others can, some characters block while others are ghosts, etc). There is no indication which objects (clues) are interactable, so you'll end up pressing your character against every surface in hopes that something might happen. About half-way through the game this mechanic is phased out and other, strange and very jarring gameplay segments are tacked on (horse riding, whack-a-mole, action segment with dodging and shooting, even a real-world trivia question with its own ugly interface to enter an answer).

In terms of [b][u]technical aspects[/u][/b] the situation is equally dire. The game starts in full-screen and has zero options. No volume control, no resolution control, no built-in windowed mode (Alt-Enter puts the game in a tiny fixed-resolution window). It messes with your mouse sensitivity, to the point where I found it only playable with keyboard. The main mechanic is going through dialogue and for the most part one click/press fills out the current box and the second advances to the next text box. Towards the end this just flat-out stops working for about 20 minutes, forcing you to sit through the text slowly appearing, even if you could read a lot faster. There were no game-breaking bugs or crashes, but it's just made very cheaply and sloppily.

Alright, let's be honest, nobody's playing this for the amazing gameplay, so let's finally delve into the [b][u]writing[/u][/b] and start with the [u]good parts[/u]: The basic premise is already in the marketing material - You're travelling backwards through a dying man's memories to figure out how to implant a faux memory of him getting to the moon. The concept of gradually revealing what made him his current self is intriguing. I enjoyed following the various constants through-out his life like friends or tastes. Most of his memories revolve around his relationship with the love of his life, who happens to be a non-neurotypical woman. This is an interesting and generally underrepresented theme. I found most of their interactions to be endearing. Very rarely the game might also timidly explore almost philosophical questions (who gets to decide the value of one's own life, everyone wishes they were brought up differently, etc.), although these aspects aren't really spelled out in the dialogue (which is not a bad thing either).
These rare highlights are unfortunately eclipsed by the much more frequent [u]bad writing[/u]: The player characters (scientists) are very inconsistent and seem to freely swap traits. There are very frequent boundary transgressions. The game does a poor job of separating the memory world from the in-game "real" world and quite often even shatters the fouth wall to the actual real world in painful ways. The pop-culture references are cringy and strangely out-of-place (the game often alludes to the plot taking place decades in the future). Frequent attempts at humour rarely fit and even interfere with sombre or romantic moments. Nonsensical events take place, just for the sake of blatantly lampshading later parts of the game. The plot is mostly advanced through contrivances and deus ex machina interventions. Even so almost all the twists are predicable. Except for the ending, where the game goes over-the-top and pulls the rug out from everything that has happened previously by introducing severe mental illenesses to characters who previously seemed quite healthy. The resolution then comes through a completely artificial conflict between the two scientists. For me it felt like the last 45min just absolutely went off the rail. The writers even managed to retroactively break the quite well-rounded character of the wife ([spoiler]Why would she fold hundreds of origami rabbits instead of simply confronting him about his faulty memory? She's not the type to drop subtle hints and hope for him to miraculously improve after he stood with her through her diagnosis. She should be used to having better memory and a more rational appraoch than him and not fall into a deep crisis over it.[/spoiler])
The game even mentions that an in-universe film called "To the Moon" might be considered pretentious - but how about fixing your plot instead of lampshading its flaws? There are several inaccuracies and insanities, which can be explained by much of the game taking place within (faulty) memories. But that honestly gave me the impression of lazy writing more than I found it a compelling and well thought-out explanation. This also highlights how nothing we see can be taken for granted, as it is only based on the subjective view of one character. I found several other characters more interesting than the main patient, but we are stuck to his memories. The premise, some themes and characters were quite interesting, the over-all writing was just a bit too aimless and not well-rounded enough. I think the last twist was honestly too much and I could have done without it.

In [b][u]conclusion[/u][/b] the game's music is really good, the visuals are decent and the writing is compelling, smart or cute at times. On the other hand the gameplay is severely lacking, the technical implementation is terrible and the writing is often contrived and painfully tone-deaf. I can see lots of good seeds, but the over-all result far too often made me groan in frustration to be able to recommend it. The full price seems ridiculously expensive to me, but with various sale and bundle discounts I think it comes down to a very reasonable level if you still want to check out what all the fuzz is about.

characters who previously seemed quite healthy. the resolution then comes through a completely artificial conflict between the two scientists. for me it felt like the last 45min just absolutely went off the rail. the writers even managed to retroactively break the quite well-rounded character of the wife spoiler why would she fold hundreds of origami rabbits instead of simply confronting him about his faulty memory? she's not the type to drop subtle hints and hope for him to miraculously improve after he stood with her through her diagnosis. she should be used to having better memory and fixing your plot instead of lampshading its flaws? there are several inaccuracies and insanities, which can be explained by much of the game taking place within faulty memories. but that honestly gave review_text:
You know those MMOs that get bought by other companies that milk them for every cent they can before shutting down the servers once all the players have been driven off? Undoing quality of life changes, making gacha the main content between "major" updates, "major" updates that are feeling more rushed and unfinished every time (they sped-run their own story in the latest update), doing the most half-assed job possible on everything from collabs to repeatable challenges? That's what happened to PSO2, except Sega never sold it. They did it themselves.

At this point I'm only here because of character customization and cross-platform play with friends. And character customization is getting worse all the time. All the outfits look like they're designed by the same guy, they're all variations on the same few themes, the best outfits are still from the base game. And there's zero quality assurance process. They slap them on a rail-thin character model and call it good, because they don't work on any other variation of the character model, textures glitch out or things balloon up like there's antigravity built in. I should mention the disappointing collabs, with a handful of items packed in with dozens of rerun items just to make you spend more money. And in the latest collab you couldn't even change the outfit color or turn off accessories, two of the main selling points of NGS's alleged customization upgrades. It's pathetic what this game has become.

Edit April 2023: I still don't recommend this game to new players, but the most recent update finally advanced the story to a place that feels... okay. Not great, but okay. Let's see how the June update changes the gameplay and repeatable content loops.

After what felt like an endless search, I finally found Adventure Escape Mysteries, a story-driven puzzle game that’s actually free to play! It’s everything I’d been looking for: a mix of compelling stories and clever puzzles that lets you feel like a detective, uncovering secrets and solving mysteries one clue at a time.

The game has a variety of stories, each with its own vibe—murder mysteries, supernatural adventures, you name it. The puzzles aren’t just random challenges either—they’re woven into the plot in a way that makes solving them feel rewarding and adds to the story’s momentum.

One of the best parts is that most stories are completely free, which is honestly hard to find in this kind of game. But heads-up: some premium stories do require a purchase to unlock. It can be a bit of a bummer if you’re hoping for everything to be free, but the quality and depth make it feel worth it to me. Plus, there’s so much free content that it doesn’t feel like you’re missing out if you decide not to pay.

Overall, I’d say Adventure Escape Mysteries finally delivers on the promise of a great, free story puzzle game. With its balance of engaging storytelling, cool art, and satisfying puzzles, it’s definitely worth downloading if you’re into mysteries and love solving problems!

This is mostly about NGS, because if I talk about, Base it'll be what most persons have already said about it. 

Fair warning, it's just gonna get rambly and incoherent.

I really don't know how to really put my thoughts on here without immediately sounding negative, so I'm just gonna talk about the things that I do love about NGS first and foremost. The game's combat is amazing, each of the classes feel engaging and interesting in their own way and they're all fun especially when you find the class that clicks with you. Character Customization is one of the best out there. It's so easy to just spend a load of time in the salon, and it's not a joke when most persons say "Salon is the real end game". The customization options is vast. 

And well, that's it. That's all the positives. Because past that, it is just a slew of just rinse and repeat FOMO events, content that gets stale quickly even if you pace yourself. Speaking of pace, if you're a new player, just get ready for the game to speed run you from level 1 straight to 90, because apparently Sega realized that there's nothing to do in the early stages of the game and they'd rather you go straight to whatever end game "content" they have. Y'know Duel quests are cool and interesting i wonder whats the barrier of entry to it? Having separate pieces of gear FOR EACH FUCKING PHASE. Oh the open world is pretty cool and interesting I wonder if there's hidden mysterie--- No. The whole place is empty there's no wonders to explore there. You can take cool screenshots tho, so there's that ig? There's like some of the content that I enjoy outside of Urgent Quests, but like,. it gets stale really quick, because it's mostly just "Here's this new this you can farm shit for". I've taken 3-4months breaks from this game at least 3 times time, and every time I come back, it really doesn't take much to catch up because nothing much been added. The game is just kinda...stagnant to me. 

Though as of me writing this, I haven't gotten to try to Card game or even M.A.R.S and I was hyped for M.A.R.S because using AIS in base was cool as fuck, but I kinda just, don't care. This game doesn't give me much a reason to care. 

tl:dr game turned into ass and i don't like it . Made some cool friends tho(Most of whom quit)

Am I still going to play this game? Yeah most likely, this isn't even cost sunk fallacy, I just want to be there if / when this game gets good again. That an I still have shit I wanna do on the base game

What was usually a loud and busy household was instead replaced with a quiet and calm environment on account of everyone at work. 

I had purchased this game months before but hadn't gotten around to playing it yet. With it being around 7:30-8:00 am, my usual online acquaintances were asleep and unavailable. I briefly checked the online games I play casually to see if there were any populated servers, but I had no such luck. 

Sitting there with the day ahead of me I began mindlessly scrolling through my Games Library, when I saw this game not yet installed. I went over to the Store Catalog and searched it up to remind myself of what kind of game this was. 
After viewing the trailers, to say I was enticed would be an understatement. 

I enthusiastically clicked on the install button and fixed myself a warm cup of coffee. Back at my mothers she did not use a traditional coffee maker, but rather a Tassimo single cup coffee. I was never fond of the coffee or the brands my mother preferred, but this was my best option. After adding one small teaspoon of sugar and a generous splash of milk, I briskly stirred my coffee and headed back to my bedroom. 

The installation was complete and I quickly immersed myself in the story. Playing the character Lucius was quite enjoyable; devious tricks and plans to sabotage peoples lives and being able to kill them in creative ways was truly exciting. I admire the developers creativity and their ability to execute the deaths so well. I found the story rich for the characters and I was impressed with the amount of details that went into each of them, as well as into the environment. There was a lot of depth in the characters as well as the objectives. I'm not the most intelligent Gamer™, and found some tasks too tricky, but luckily I had google on my side to help me execute these murders. 

During my gameplay experience I took a brief intermission in the early afternoon to try something I hadn't ever before: Skip The Dishes. Now, I'm familiar with ordering delivery Chinese or pizza over the phone, and even online, but the idea of having a stranger not affiliated with the franchise bringing me my food, independently of the store? It was a bit unnerving, but I was hungry and determined to obtain Wendy's sweet sweet Chili. The ordering and delivery went better than expected, and I excitedly ate my chili while continuing with the game, which also was still easy and enjoyable. 

I found the ending to this game very rewarding, and I anticipate on purchasing the 2nd and 3rd game for Lucius. I hope this review helped and I truly could not recommend this game enough.

review_text:
Game Review: BioShock
Score: 2/10 - An Ideological Assault Disguised as Entertainment

BioShock presents itself as a thrilling narrative experience set in the underwater utopia of Rapture, but beneath its surface lies a relentless barrage of liberal ideology that aggressively undermines traditional American family values. This critically acclaimed title is nothing short of an ideological weapon, promoting a worldview that glorifies individualism while systematically dismantling the very principles that hold families and communities together.

A Relentless Push of Liberal Ideology
From the moment players descend into the depths of Rapture, they are bombarded with a narrative steeped in the philosophy of objectivism and libertarian ideals, which are often masked as high-minded discussions on freedom and choice. However, what BioShock fails to recognize is that unchecked individualism and an obsession with personal gain lead to societal decay. The game’s premise, which champions self-interest above all, echoes a distinctly liberal agenda that prioritizes the individual over the community.

Throughout the game, players encounter characters and factions that embody the extremes of these ideologies. The anarchic environment of Rapture is a testament to the dangers of a system that allows for the absolute freedom of the individual at the expense of social cohesion. This relentless focus on personal power and autonomy directly contradicts the values that have traditionally fostered strong family units, such as sacrifice, cooperation, and mutual support.

Undermining Traditional Family Values
BioShock not only promotes a hollow version of freedom but also actively assaults the very foundations of American family values. The narrative’s descent into chaos and moral ambiguity reflects a troubling disdain for the ideals of loyalty and commitment that have historically strengthened family bonds. The characters in Rapture are often depicted as self-serving and morally bankrupt, showcasing a world where personal gain trumps familial loyalty.

Moreover, the game presents relationships as transactional and manipulative rather than supportive and nurturing. The emphasis on betrayal and self-interest leaves little room for the love and respect that are vital to healthy family dynamics. By painting a picture of a world where individuals are isolated in their pursuits, BioShock encourages players to view relationships through a cynical lens, reinforcing the notion that traditional family structures are obsolete or irrelevant.

Conclusion: A Disturbing Message Wrapped in an Engaging Package
While BioShock is often lauded for its rich storytelling and immersive world, it ultimately serves as a disturbing critique of American values. The relentless promotion of liberal ideologies and the undermining of family structures position it as a dangerous piece of entertainment that leaves a lasting impact on its audience.

In an era where media can shape perceptions and influence beliefs, BioShock stands as a glaring example of how even the most celebrated games can perpetuate narratives that erode the very fabric of society. If you’re seeking a game that celebrates traditional values, community, and the importance of family, BioShock is a journey best left unexplored.

review_text:
[h1]If this game goes 100% off on sale it's already too expensive.[/h1]

Pathologic 2 had the potential to be an outstanding hidden gem but in the end, it suffers from the same bloody fate as many other brilliant games out there: [b]f*cking terrible devs doing an utterly bad job in order to delive a pinch more of challenge so they're able to brag about their game being difficult (even if the cost is ruining it entirely), forgetting to test their own game and squash bugs instead of adding more useless dialog throughout the empty town you find yourself in.[/b]

Pathologic itself is complex, unforgiving if playing as intended, mind twisting, narrative-driven feturing an ocean of text and strange language, and 100% psychological horror. You will get lost many times, lose opportunities many times, but after all you realize that's the catch.
And that's fine. It is supposed to be difficult. The set up prepares you for a miserable experience since the very beginning, and it warns a dozen times you are to get the grip of things instead of being led by the hand.

HOWEVER, as no game is perfect, you find out soon that Pathologic 2 has some game-killing, deadly serious defective systems:

1. Basic needs. While the whole world feels unnatural but somehow very realistic at the same time (put aside the lack of character model diversity), basic needs are very very very very poorly handled, tearing down immersion. Artemy needs to eat barrells of food per day and drink gallons of water if he is to not die while sleeping - which can absolutely happen - and the food is UNGODLY expensive. I mean, yeah, the town is facing a huge shortage of many products but that's not possibly an excuse. You struggle to make 1k coins, then you find out a fish that heals a laughable amount of hunger [b]and recovers no health at all[/b] costs you nearly 700 coins.
As one would expect, jumping and running consumes stamina by a lot, bringing even more variables to mess with need meters. Turns up to be awful as hell when we barely have enough daytime to explore and uncover the world around us, summed with the f*cked up mindless economy system they implemented here.

2. [b]Death. Dying DOES NOT take away even 1% of your exhaustion (not to be confused with stamina), leading to scenarios where you can be HARD LOCKED WITHIN A DEATH LOOP if you have no healing items in your inventory. I guess it is just too hard for russians to use their brains and acknowledge the fact that when you move a respawning character back to the last saving point while giving a random death penalty but no chance to heal, no chance to search for items or sleep (you can't sleep in any bed/bedroll/couch you find) WITH NO PREVIOUS WARNING ABOUT IT, you frustrate them. Would be better to make it permadeath and clarify the real importance of dealing with exhaustion above all.
I've been gaming since '97 and I can't really remember a game that failed so miserably in the SIMPLEST MISSION that is respawning a character.[/b]

3. Performance issues. Notorious and gross. Devs say recommended settings are a 16GB RAM rig with NVIDIA GeForce GTX 970 plus an intermediate 3GHz processor but mind you: even far more powerful PC owners reported stutterings and issues that shouldn't happen. Yes it is a beautiful and demanding game indeed, but f*cking ugly optimized.
If you face crashes, textures not rendering correctly and less than 50fps with even minimum requirements, check out forums on how to fix those by changing params directly inside Pathologic 2 files.

4. Bugs. You won't immerse yourself in a town where you fight a spreading plague; you will be fighting [b]all unsolved bugs devs were too lazy to NOT MESS WITH during this REMAKE.[/b] I mean yeah, let's make a remake, but let's not touch any glitch, bug or whatever.
I promptly lost interest in Pathologic 2 due to 2 unnaceptable bugs for a game like this where loading a previous game does not erase your death (yeah I know it is laughable but, remember: russian devs. They have no clue): first was a guy teleporting right behind my back and stabbing me to death in a single hit while I had half HP left as soon as I opened a random door. Second was a guy crossing a prop barrier a.k.a invisible wall when I was chasing him.

Devs made the impossible true: failing miserably at a game that is 95% talking to people, trading, walking, collecting herbs and fast travelling. If I bought my 7yo son an Unity license he would come up with a better game, like everyone else around here could.

If you still want to play this overpriced garbage, then read about how every core mechanic works and avoid playing vanilla Imago difficulty. There's a mod that do what devs apparently couldn't (aside from being humans with more than 10 IQ), fixing game balance by a bit.

review_text:
Incredibly boring horror shooter / slasher. The ranged combat feels bad but the game is clearly not meant to be played relying on your guns alone but instead using a mix of melee and ranged attacks. So that would be fine if the melee combat felt any better. Unfortunately, it matches that level of excitement.
Blocking and dodging happens pretty much automatically as you only have to hold a direction (back for block, sides for dodging). This means every single encounter will play the exact same way. You'll hit 2 - 3 times, shoot, dodge once or twice, then hit again. Repeat until dead.

Same for the GRP glove, which enables you to grab objects and enemies and hurl them around. At least, this way you can end combat a lot quicker.

review_text:
I don’t say this often, but The Callisto Protocol is a bad game. It may be priced like a AAA game, but it feels like a janky indie game that spent most of its budget on graphics.

Imagine you finally get to a safe room. You see an upgrade machine and you upgrade your gear, watching the stutter animation. Feeling prepared you decide to continue on. You see a branch in the path and choose to go left. After slowly walking for what feels like multiple minutes until you drop down a hole that you can not climb back up. You are now locked in a room of zombies with seemingly no way back. Carefully, you kill them all, easily dodging all melee attacks in the dodging system that requires no skill or timing while weaving in attacks. Unfortunately, a spitter hits you with its spit during the dodge animation, because that is a thing that can happen in this game. Luckily you don’t die and you manage to kill the spitter as well. You find some loot, including a collectible as well as a vent that you slowly crawl through when the game freezes for half a second and you know there’s going to be a jump scare. BAM! A zombie runs past the outside of the vent, but you’re not scared, you knew it was going to happen. After escaping the vent, you find yourself back near the branch in the path. You take the other route and find another room filled with zombies. After killing a few of them, the game freezes for another half second and you know another jump scare is going to happen. BAM! Something has grabbed your arm and you have to do a quick time event. Luckily you easily defeat the event and continue on. You see a zombie off in the distance. You run to it and smack it once with your baton. It goes to attack and you easily dodge its attacks, but then suddenly the game freezes for half a second. Is this another jump scare mid fight? No. It was just a regular stutter, but this time when the stutter ends you see yourself already dead. That’s fine, you think to yourself. Surely this game had a recent checkpoint. No. It did not. You are back in the safe room. No collectible, no weapon upgrades. You’re a little annoyed, but the game does offer manual saves, so it’s really your fault for relying on auto saves, right? You repeat the sequence. But this time make a manual save after getting the collectible and returning to the main path. You make your way back to your nemesis for revenge. Even though you know you can normally get 3 or more hits in between enemy attacks, you decide to play it safe and only hit twice. You gracefully dodge the first round of attacks. You smack it once. You click to smack again, but then right before contact it rapidly attacks. You shift your fingers to press dodge, but it’s too late. Even though you hit first, the enemy doesn’t flinch. It hits, but because of your attack animation you cannot dodge and your dead. That’s fine, you made a manual save, right? Wrong. Manual saves are meaningless in this game. You’re still back at the safe house, no weapon upgrades, no collectibles.

This is pretty much the Callisto Protocol. One of the worst checkpoint systems I’ve ever seen. A combat system that has some neat ideas, but could use some polish, and a ton of stutters and performance issues. While some areas ignore the V-Sync cap and hover around 150, others struggle to hit 30. Regardless, most areas have small stutter much of the time and even bigger stutters are fairly frequent. The story is fine. I have not beat the game so I don’t know exactly what will happen, but in the almsot 4.5 hour’s I’ve played, I cannot say the story is super intriguing. Zombies have taken over and it’s probably thanks to an evil scientist. 

The game also started by asking you to purchase DLC, before you even see the title screen for the first time, which is pretty annoying, has a horrible laid out graphics settings menu, and seems to have no way to adjust FOV. I do think there could be a good game in here, it just needs a lot of polish, quality of life changes, and maybe some tweaks to movement speed.

review_text:
World of Goo Review

Ahh, this is probably the first video game I have ever played. EVER. I still remember the times where my cousin and I would play this game on his iPad (1st Gen), having so much fun. Remembering this, I gave World of Goo a shot, and boy howdy did I instantly fall in love with this game.

World of Goo is a physics game on building Goo structures to reach a certain goal. Usually, this is a pipe that you need to build to, but on the last levels of each world (there are 6, including the Epilogue and the World of Goo Headquarters), there is a different objective to advance the story line. The levels aren't overly difficult, they're just difficult enough to intrigue you, but not to rage-quit the game. I really enjoyed this game.

On every level (except the first), the Sign Painter (A.K.A. The Sign Writer, SignPaintr4evr, [spoiler]The Telescope Operator[/spoiler]) writes messages on signs. They can either give tips, advance the story line or simply be humorous. If I were being honest, I would not have been able to complete the game if it wasn't for this mysterious, funny and slightly creepy (he can see you even though his messages come in the form of SIGNS. Give me a break) man/woman that is the Sign Painter.

Every once in a while, you can encounter different types of Goo. Some worlds are completely based on that specific goo. One example is the Green (Ivy) Goo. These types of Goo have 3 attachment 'arms' and can detach from the Goo structure if you so wish to. In the words of the Sign Painter: '[i]Maybe they have commitment anxiety, I'm not sure, but it looks like they can be easily detached from each other.[/i]'

The story line completely revolves around one company: The World of Goo Company. This is the company responsible for controlling (not making) and modifying different types of Goo. Once you complete a certain amount of levels, you unlock a special world: The World of Goo Headquarters. This is where all your goo get placed when they go into the pipes. Once again, in the words of the Sign Painter: '[i]As you complete levels, the Goo Balls you collect are sent here. How nice to see them again! Though they seem to have lost their essence[/i].' The World of Goo Corporation refine the Goo into a special type of Goo before sending it into the world. The special Goo Balls (which I will call WOG Goo) are kind of a mix between the normal Goo and the Green Goo; they can detach from the structure, like the Green Goo, but they have similar colouring and the same amount of attachment arms as the normal Goo. In this world, you have only one goal: build UP (or do nothing). [spoiler]And you can totally obliterate the Headquarters near the end of the game.[/spoiler]

The story line is great. The animation and sprites are even more so, and the puzzles in the game are really clever and fun. 2D Boy did a great job with their games (they also made Little Inferno, the game which had the trailer that is scary, Human Resource Machine and 7 Billion Humans). I thoroughly enjoyed this game. If you want a puzzling but intriguing and fun gaming experience, why not play World of Goo?

review_text:
[h2]Briefly:[/h2]
There's fun to be had as long as you plan on ignoring the achievements, or if you enjoy achievements that require a punishing level of perfectionism to obtain. For me, that isn't the case.

[h2]More fully:[/h2]
The game [i]itself[/i] is good. It's decently creative and has personality, and the puzzles are challenging but solveable. So far so good.

But, if you're someone who bothers with achievements or otherwise cares about them, it becomes quickly frustrating. So, not so good.

Out of 8 achievements:
 - 1 is for passing the game
 - 1 is for doing something unusual on a specific level
 - The other 6 of are finnicky, nitpicky, perfectionist achievements only earned on passing [b]every[/b] level in a chapter with much more restrictive requirements (for which you get an "OCD flag")

It was this third point that soured the game for me. Because I do care about completing a reasonable percentage of achievements for each game I play (50-75% for most, unless I really like the game, then it's 75-100%). Unfortunately, these 6 achievements take a [i][b]disproportionate[/b][/i] amount of time [i]beyond[/i] simply playing the game decently well and passing it—and they make up 3/4 of the achievements obtainable.

It was after I spent hours in the the first chapter getting OCD flags for the first 10 levels (failing over and over on the 10th) that I started to ask myself why I was spending so much time at something I was coming to hate.

I realized that I was wasting my time and not enjoying myself, all for the sake of getting achievements in a game where the designers set them up in such a way that they punish the casual player.

I [i]might[/i] come back to it at some point and at least finish it, but it'll take a while for my distaste to fade.

review_text:
It took me a long time to finally sit down and play this game. Now that I am away from home and only have my crappy laptop to play games I thought I'd give this one a try. I love the graphics and the one song that accompanies most (all?) of the scenes.
Sadly, the game didn't do it for me though. The story (that most people loved!) is okay but not more. There are a few fundamental problems that made this game not really enjoyable. First of all, the controlls are HORRIBLE. You almost only play with your mouse (movement, interaction) which is tedious to say the least. Then there is this one annoying minigame you have to complete over and over again in the first Act (click the squares). Not rewarding in any way, just annoying. In Act 2 this specific minigame is replaced by other, equally bad "quests" (catch someone while riding a horse etc, shoot weird zombie people????). These quests almost made me rage quit. The controlls here become even worse for some reason and at some point I was only smashing buttons hoping to move on in the story.
The quest that you have to do over and over again (collecting memories) is tedious and boring and extremely repetitive...

But what bothered me the most was the was the story was told. John's life is told backwards and many "secrets" are only revealed later on. Which lead to me having forgotten most of them at their reveal since I didn't really get the problem in the first place. I never really got an emotional connection to the two love story characters either. Also had to look up the "tragic mistake" in their relationship that I wouldn't have gotten otherwise. The (good) ending also felt kinda forced to me as the whole story was really melancholic and tragic only for everything to be resolved in the end. The game also didn't want to end. There is cutscene after cutscene in the last 1-2 hours, most of which would not have been necessary imo, it just dragged on.
The last scene was kinda nice and a good ending for John but it didn't feel like the right ending to the story of the game for some reason.

I was a bit disappointed by the game tbh, all the positive reviews made me hope for a more enjoyable experience. But don't let my review discourage you, many people liked To the moon, it just wasn't for me.

review_text:
I've tried coming back to this a few times, hoping something will change since it's early access but every time I just end up sorely disappointed and uninstall the game. In blunt terms, it just feels like the devs don't know what in God's name they're doing. 

The game feels like it's got a serious identity crisis going on. On one hand, it feels like it wants to be a run and gun FPS with an emphasis on exploration. On the other hand, it also feels like it's trying to be like Dark Souls, where mobility is limited due to a stamina system, even the weakest enemies hit like a truck, and regaining health is limited to a very limited consumable. When you take combat encounters that are clearly designed to take a fast and loose approach in the vein of Painkiller or Serious Sam and then slap on a mobility system where you move fairly slow and have to rely on dodging which consumes stamina, then throw the fact that restoring health is limited to using healing elixrs, of which you can only carry a very small amount and are an extremely rare drop on the field, it just doesn't work. There's a reason why good run and gun shooters are usually generous with health items. 

Then there's the weapons. The weapons have a lot of potential. They've got some pretty cool designs and they're fun to shoot. The issue is their damage drop off is ludicrous. Having damage drop off outside a weapon's effective range is common and fine but the issue is that in Witchfire the rate at which damage drops off is just ridiculous.  If you're more than a couple inches outside your weapon's effective range, the damage your gun does instantly drops down to 1.

Then there's the sort of parry system it's got going on. Basically if you dodge while near an enemy a circle appears near them that you can shoot to stun them for a few seconds. It's pretty clear the devs want you to make heavy use of this but at the same time it's extremely finnicky. I've tried all sorts of things with it and the best I can figure it boils down to "it works when it feels like working".

At this point I'd say your best bet is to just skip out on this one. The game has been in Early Access for a while now and I really can't see the devs making any changes to address the issues with the game m

[h1] Spoiler-free review [/h1]

This game has a unique feel, a unique atmosphere. It’s [b]bleak[/b], [b]disturbing[/b] and [b]intriguing[/b].
You have to figure things out for [b]yourself[/b] (the universe, the story, the puzzles).
There is no hand holding and the [b]puzzles[/b] are enjoyable.

It’s a bit on the [b]short[/b] side. A second playthrough is nice to catch up on some details.
I found the weapon combat to be mostly meh … It’s ok I guess once you approach combat as puzzles (as you have limited ammo).
Some environments can be a bit hard to navigate (at least, on a first playthrough).
There are no specific performance issues to note except … there is [b]DX12 initial shader compilation stutter[/b].


[h1] Should you buy it ? [/h1]

Well … I think this game is worth it on a [b]sale IF you are interested in the art[/b] and the atmosphere of the game. It’s a pretty short experience with just a handful of puzzles. You have to piece the story together yourself and it’s [b]open to interpretation[/b]. 
The [b]visuals[/b] (the artstyle) is really what sets this game apart from others.

In this action adventure we play a young girl who has been teleported to a castle. In the process, we have completely lost our memory. Soon we cross a fantasy realm full of monsters and hard-to-conquer bosses to find out how to get back to our old world.

Lost Ruins is a 2D action adventure game in pixel style, in which we can attack our enemies with a variety of swords, axes and other medieval weapons. Soon we'll also learn spells to burn enemies or heal ourselves. The game teaches us to use the environment to achieve our objectives. Flammable liquids burst into flames when they come into contact with burning lanterns or fireballs, ice magic freezes waters. The game's focus is less on frantic jumping passages and more on combat and managing life,magic points, and our inventory.

review_text:
Really solid survival horror entry from Bloober. It doesn't necessarily innovate much with combat and gameplay mechanics, taking a lot from Resident Evil, which is actually fine. What distinguishes it from the rest is definitely the setting and locations chosen - those are very strong and for the majority of the game they ramp up in all the right ways. As someone who is familiar with the real life places the action happens (and you can find at least 4 of the main inspirations in Cracow - the home city of Bloober) the locations visited in game added a lot of extra atmosphere and fun. But even without that aspect, the world crafted from an amalgamation of body/space horror and 1981-1988 Cracow presents a very strong reason to play the game.

From the technical standpoint it's impressive for an AA game and some of the use of lighting is top notch and RTX gives some bang for your buck - however I had to enable DLSS to have smoother framerate as it sometimes chops, like a lot of UE5 games. Also, unless you are really good with shooting using controller, I would strongly recommend keyboard and mouse.

Briefly on difficulty/gameplay - the game has decent variety in arsenal and passives to choose from, although acquisition of both is quite stretched out throughout all the game chapters - to really have fun with the variety you will have to touch NG+. The balance of resources/ammo scarcity is quite impressive and very well fine tuned - it was always never too much, never too little. The game is challenging and there is no easy mode, but from my experience not to the extent that would cross into annoying or tedious.

As far as the story goes, at some point it seemingly pivots into an unexpected direction, but by the end once you think about what happened and piece it all together it does make sense. Very much similar to movie [spoiler]12 Monkeys[/spoiler]. Overall it is intriguing and keeps you going smoothly.

Now, some negatives. I think most of them are down to this being an AA game that punches above its weight at Resident Evils and alike. Something you will notice is that after about halfway of the game there is less "new" monsters - altered versions of some you've seen before but by that point you should be familiar with most types. 
The worst part of the game are bossfights - the game reuses same/very similar a boss and a mechanic upwards of 4 times and another boss you will run into two times. There is only one "real" unique boss in the game, quite far into the playtime.

Overall, worth a recommendation - the locations, setting, lore and exploration are very fun and the game is worth the money asked in my eyes. A must if you are a fan of survival shooters or live in Nowa Huta :D
