review_text:
(Mild Spoilers) This game is terrible. Not only are the controls clunky, the characters obnoxious, and the gameplay tedious at times, but it's also grossly ableist. It's made very clear that River is autistic, but the game never even uses the word "autism" and makes it seem like it's a bad word. They keep referring to it as "her condition" and going on and on about how hard it is for her husband, John, to tolerate her. Mind you, these two are supposed to be in love. He explicitly refuses to learn about her "condition" when given the opportunity, and also makes it clear that he only started going out with her because she was "weird" and "unique" and he didn't want to be "boring" so he uses her to make himself appear more interesting.

I found out after playing that the creator has donated to Autism Speaks in the past. It seems he has since learned about the criticisms against Autism Speaks and no longer supports them. I think it's great that he acknowledged his mistake in supporting them, but he still has a lot to learn about autism. It's clear that he did not reach out to the autistic community during the development of this game.

It's very problematic, and honestly even if it wasn't, it's still a terrible story. It tries to be funny, then romantic, then heartbreaking, then creepy, round and round again, failing at each. By the end of the game, I hated all but a few side characters and River. I felt little more than annoyance during my playthrough. The ending was so unsatisfying, and there were a few loose threads that are never acknowledged (perhaps in a sequel but I'm not sticking around to find out).

I did enjoy the soundtrack and the visuals, and I liked the idea of going through someone's memories in reverse order. The main premise sounded really interesting and could have been done very well. I typically love games that involve facing the reality of death and questions of morality. This one, however, was a miss. I would not recommend this game to anyone.

review_text:
Game's worth about 20-30 hours if you're going for 100% completion, but otherwise you'll likely only get about 8-12 hours worth from the story, and a lot of the story is wasted on repetitive cut scenes and a serviceable story. 

For most people I'd honestly recommend waiting for a sale to make it worth it. The game is a TON of fun, but at 40$ it's not really worth the intro price it offers for its 'main' content, but with a sale of 20-40% off it'd be very much so worth it to buy the game. 

The trick system is very shallow, very easy to maintain and get a ridiculously high score. Once you understand the systems, it's honestly just yourself sabotaging yourself if you manage to lose a good chain, or you hit a set of stairs (Which auto-force you off your skates regardless if you land on the flat part or the actual stairs themselves.) Once you get the combo system down, all the challenge of movement goes out the window. 

But part of the problem comes from the lack of clarity of various mechanics. There's a lot of people that don't know you can use Inline Skates to break glass by gliding on it beneath you, or that you can use a skateboard on firehydrants to get extra air. That bicycles open unique garages, or that running has a singular attack (Carthweel) that chains into a super-jump for getting over / on top of obstacles. The complete lack of clarity and ambiguity the game left in these regards means you might be frustrated until you find the answer yourself through sheer luck, or by looking up an answer to it online.

The game feels like it really missed out from genuine QoL testing and a lack of understanding. Everytime you're bombing an area, you'll be constantly forced to re-watch the same introduction cutscene. The minimap is abysmal at best, not marking anything of import on it even once you obtain the map. Bathroom stalls are used to change your outfit as well as to dump infamy to get the police off you. Cipher gatherings are supposed to change characters and Taxi locations don't auto-unlock based on area; meaning you likely won't unlock the Taxi's until you want to use one in the post-game, only to find that you haven't unlocked any because the usual expectation that the fast travel system would be a baseline unlock actually requires you to do so individually (And also to find them.) 

But nothing important is put on the map itself, aside from tag spots, once you unlock the map. There's no effective way of tracking your collectibles you've gathered. There's constant glitches on points for bombing each area. 

Not only that, the story really only focuses on a small group. There's a few obscure optional characters but unlike JSRF, you never really feel like they're 'part of the process' of playing, rather they feel like out-of-the-way optional sidequests with trivially easy objectives to complete. They don't show up in your hideout, which is a real bummer because genuinely your hideout feels desolate and empty. 

Light Edit here: Recently the characters I've had unlocked HAVE started to appear in the hideout. Not sure why they didn't before. Place still feels empty, but it's a nice improvement, regardless, that a number are there now.

Unfortunately, the game has a huge lack of genuine challenge to it due to how easy it is to gather points in each area, the characters themselves are pretty lackluster overall and the cast - while at end-game is rather diverse, you likely won't really be playing as anyone other than the titular three you see from the get go. I can't in good faith recommend the game at 40$, but at about 30$ I think it'd be a good indie dev game. If you really love JSRF, it would be a great title to add to your collection, but be ready for the fair number of bugs and frustrqation with key mechanics that may come with it. 

It's still a good fun ride, either way.

In this wonderfully ridiculous world, you sprint through spooky barns, abandoned schools, and other questionable real-estate listings while rummaging through chests like a confused raccoon. Your main mission? Fix giant generators that look like they were built by someone who almost passed shop class.

Just when you're feeling proud of your mechanical brilliance—BAM!—you turn around and there stands a huge, sweaty ogre of a killer, sprinting at you with a weapon like he’s late for his shift. Next thing you know, you’re hanging from a giant meat hook right through your chest. But don’t worry! It’s totally fine. Your teammates, including the 40-kg anime girl with zero upper-body strength, can just yoink you off the hook like it’s nothing. And of course, you won’t bleed out, because none of this obeys the laws of biology—only the laws of chaos and pure gamer spirit.

Dead by Daylight: where logic goes to die, but the fun absolutely doesn’t.

review_text:
At first glance, Just Cause 4 is stunningly beautiful and undeniably fun. The massive open world, filled with lush landscapes and explosive possibilities, promises endless hours of entertainment. The game's signature over-the-top action and creative use of the grappling hook initially deliver an exhilarating experience.

However, this potential quickly unravels due to one glaring flaw: the puzzles. The sheer volume of puzzles, combined with the lack of meaningful hints or guidance, makes progression a frustrating ordeal. The game often throws you into complex scenarios with no explanation, leaving you to fumble around until something works. This lack of clarity turns what should be a rewarding experience into a tedious chore.

Adding to the frustration is the overwhelming number of key controls. With so many functions mapped to different buttons, the game becomes needlessly complicated, especially for new players. Instead of feeling like a capable action hero, you're left wrestling with the controls in critical moments.

Ultimately, Just Cause 4 sabotages itself. What could have been an enjoyable, action-packed adventure is marred by poor design choices that prioritize complexity over fun. It's a shame, because the game's potential is undeniable—but it’s hard to appreciate when the experience is bogged down by unnecessary frustrations.

review_text:
This game is one of my personal favorite entries in the series. It's story is admittedly overly complicated and messy, but it still worked for me. It's cheesy, on the nose with its themes, and I bought into so badly. 

The game is split into 5 segments, each with a different main character.  The stand out portions to me are Kiryu, Haruka, and the new character Shinada. Kiryu and Haruka are pretty understandably enjoyable-- they have a lot of history in the series and this game focuses a lot on how they are managing, with this being the first game ever where they are not together. And it's crazy how much you can see this affect them in different ways-- Kiryu, in finding himself completely lost without her, and Haruka in knowing that her entire family is watching her debut. It really tugs at your heartstrings in every way.

Shinada came straight out of left field-- he's a loveable idiot that really brought a sense of outsider POV into the entire mess of a game, and I really enjoyed his presence. He also taught me how to play the baseball minigame properly after 6 games, lol.

Great great great game. They should add more DDR gameplay in the future.

review_text:
It is genuinely hard to describe how little there is to do in New Genesis. Anything I could say will sound like I'm leaving half of the things out. I'll instead make the statement that there is pretty much nothing meaningful you can do that doesn't just loop back into the cosmetics and social chat-room play style. You will be provided gear that is good enough for anything. You will be boosted to the max level through the story. There are the cocoons of course, but those are one-and-done. Once you're powerful, there's nothing to use this power on. There's nothing to fight. Duel quests are maybe the exception, they can give you a source of income, but then the only purpose of this income is to just buy things from other players to dress up your character with.

PSO2 is a completely different story and one of my favorite games of all time. My playtime on steam is less than half of my total playtime, as I played on the Microsoft Store when it was exclusive to that. I would barely recommend that, and if this game looks like it really interests you, go for it. Play the original. The character I've made in PSO2 I haven't changed the design of since before NGS came out, making the purely fashion-themed NGS worthless to me. 

Finally, if you are literally Just looking for a social chatroom and fashion game, I don't really think you'll find a better one than NGS, but they're very predatory with their microtransactions. Most interesting and desirable items are going to come from Scratch Tickets, which are exactly what they sound like. They're just lootboxes, and they cost a significant chunk of money per roll. You can buy these items from other players with the free currency in game, and it's honestly not an impossible task. You can certainly earn enough of the currency to make likely one outfit you really like, though it will be a considerable amount of work, meaning it'd give you something to do in the game. Of course, the best way to get this currency is through buying your own scratch tickets and selling the items, though...

review_text:
I really wanted to like this game but all it ever did was disappoint me
Bonelab feels lackluster, empty, incomplete and almost every thing that made Boneworks feel special and magical was stripped away in this game and nowhere to be found



The long load times:
there have been times where I nearly fell asleep waiting for the game to load and if I wasn't falling asleep then my eyes were getting melted by the seizure inducing loading screens due to the frames bouncing back and forth while loading the next level, sometimes it even appeared upside down. It was to the point where I had to take off the headset due it causing me actual eye pain. Even on an SSD the game still took a really long time to load.



The performance: 
I have never seen such abysmal performance in game as Bonelab constantly crashed SteamVR, Froze my entire computer then crashed everything I had opened then crashed itself, Bonelab is the only game that has ever done that



Boring/Awful level design:
Compared to Boneworks these levels are nothing but a straight line, they are smaller, they are emptier and they are far too linear to the point where little to no player creativity can take place or be had and the "puzzles" were very mediocre compared to Boneworks were every puzzle had full player creativity and every player had their own unique way of solving a puzzle. And some of the levels are so poorly made and so irritating to the point where all I wanted to do was finish the level and get off. Some of the levels that caused this were no other then Level 09 Moon Base and Level 11 The Pillar Climb



Moon Base is and I kid you not, it is a literal sandbox in a campaign and the level is a big empty box with little to no guidance of where to go all while the most most annoying track in the entire game plays in the background. I had to look up where to go and turns out there was a very missable map of where to go. Now it has gotten better as there are jumppads that just lead you to the end and there's are beam of light that shoots up into the sky showing you where the exit is. 



Now before I tear into Pillar Climb I want you to know that it has gotten better but I will be talking about my experience with Pillar Climb when I played it. 

There have only been two times where I wanted to cry due to how annoying and frustrating a thing was in a game, one of them being the last boss in Devil May Cry 4 cause he was really annoying and the second was cause everything that Pillar Climb put me through.

In Pillar climb you start off as a character named Tall and you guessed it he's really tall and the point of this level is to make it to the top and beat up some floating orb but the thing with this level is that you actually don't play as the character that this level was made for as each time you are hit by these little void butterflies you are changed into another character that the level is not built for as you may get characters such as Light, Short and Heavy, none of which will help you in this level in fact all they do is set you back all the way where you started because they are not made for Pillar Climb.

While you're fighting with your body you're also being pecked apart with the void butterflies cause they actually do damage and will kill you and also this annoying turrets that will 2/3 shot you and death in Pillar Climb = a complete restart of the entire level including another 10 minute loading screen.

But my Pillar Climb playthrough was different from most peoples as I did what the game wanted me to and that is modding it and having custom characters and turns out having those custom characters broke the character switching making it so I would never get Light, Short or Heavy, if a bug the game better and helps the player's enjoyment that is a very bad sign.

So after many deaths and many 10 minute loading screens I made it the top and got shot making me enter the Fight For Your Life mechanic and out of pure angyness I started hitting the void orb that was there and turns out that was the thing I meant to do to finish the level. I had to take a break after this level

Nothing in the level was probably tested and if anything it really shows that Stress Level Zero did little to no playtesting before releasing this game and also strangely enough this was at the two hour mark making any refund attempts impossible.



The second last level named Level 13 Ascent was actually pretty good though as it was the closet thing to Boneworks and it's levels, it actually felt like that game was picking up and every character I unlocked during those awful minigames were being used and utilized to the point where I was having as much fun as I did in Boneworks, then it ends It, that's right that's the end of the game then it crashes at the end as the cherry on top. If you ever played Boneworks and saw how Ford looked at the ending cutscene that was exactly how I looked when I finished Bonelab



I heavily discourage anyone from getting this game unless you are getting on the Quest 2/3 as there are far better PCVR games out there for you to enjoy and that values you as a player cause seriously you deserve something better that isn't Stress Level Zero's BONELAB.

If you are one of the few people who do enjoy Bonelab for what it is, then I'm actually truly happy for you, don't let my opinions on Bonelab ruin your fun cause you can always like things even if somebody else doesn't.

review_text:
Cannot recommend this at this state. 

Graphics: Textures are washed-away, hardly any visual effects, only upside is the 3D modelling (Giger'esque graphics are there, Beksinski not so much).

Gameplay: No prompts, no hints, nothing, not even the most basic ones, so you have to check everything first and then solve the puzzles. So basically tinker around until you find the thing you need to move and in what sequence and then move on.

Sound: Pretty poor in it's design. Soundquality is great, but the content is just basic lacklustre dark ambient.

Story: Some say it is in there symbolically, but in practice there is nothing actually, Anyone who thinks there's a deeper meaning to this game are just suffering from severe pareidolia or psychosis.

I'm sincerely hoping there will be a remaster or simply a new IP from Ebb Software that deals with these issues. Stealing someones art style is insufficient to make a game great.

review_text:
Going to be very honest here: I was excited for this game. VERY excited. The market for this genre is thin, and if the dev team actually did anything with it my dream game would have come to life. The problem is, they don't. I think this may be another cash grab early access, or devs that got in over their heads.

Almost a year after release and it's practically identical to its premiere build, if not worse and buggier than before. Animal balancing has been favoring for carnivores since the beginning, which makes being any herbivore downright tedious and unfair -- with even RHINOS AND ELEPHANTS struggling against a couple of lions. 

You may wonder, how did they respond to this consistent criticism? They added a carnivore that one or two shots almost the entire roster. Beautiful.

Speaking of criticism, they do not take any of it well AT ALL. Any critique is seen as a threat, and this is especially showcased in their Discord server. They ignore any questions or feedback they deem "too harsh" or "too unfair", while giving almost nothing in return to the community that backed their Kickstarter and have supported their game for months at a time.

That's funny, considering a majority of the negative and "too harsh" feedback they receive is based on the fact this game's updates are few and far between, and when they DO happen, they break the game even worse than the last patch. Oh, and did you know it has DLC? In Early Access. It's barely even a Beta, and most core game mechanics do not work as intended -- but there's DLC. DLC that is overpriced, and now includes a playable character within them.

The DLC is $15 for a rabbit that cannot eat, drink, or jump -- and they are not offering refunds whatsoever from what I know nor do they seem to care it was released in a completely broken state. I did not buy it personally, but I have seen several others very frustrated by this and it is not the only occurrence of something of this nature from these developers.

For example, for many owners of this game it is not even playable. Upon purchase and installation, it does not launch. It's a common issue, yet it doesn't seem to be very high at all on the dev team's to-do list for development and bug fixes.

This game has a lot of potential -- but until the devs focus less on the money aspect and more on the quality and community, this game will be forgotten when it gains competition from another game of the same idea. At the moment, not worth the price or the time. 

* Will come back and update this review if they heavily improve the things mentioned here.

The art style is very cool. But that’s about it… After finishing the first level I was done. 

The player’s movement is very slow, and there isn’t a way to sprint by default. I tried Keyboard and mouse and a controller but having to hold down a button to move through a level “at a snail’s pace” was frustrating. In the end, Keyboard and Mouse movement felt better but neither option was great. There is no HUD, no compass, no map. The player is expected to walk around randomly to figure out what items are available to interact with, and the order they need to be interacted with, to solve puzzles.

This by itself is fine, but tedious. 

When the game morphed into one of the worlds worst escort missions I was pissed but kept going through the motions.

After another obscure puzzle, steam popped off an achievement and a grotesque cut-scene started. With that, I was done. Maybe if I’d picked this game up a different day there would have been some motivation to keep going but it felt like everything was purposely designed to waste the player’s time

There are several players out there who will love this game and its atmosphere. They will enjoy methodically interacting with random switches and slowly maneuvering around corners; I’m just not one of them. It’s very clear the developers were trying to target a very specific audience.

As it stands, I can’t recommend this title to most people due to the blood and gore imagery alone.

review_text:
Dead Space meets Evil Within during the Covid pandemic. That's pretty much this game. If you didn't like either one of those mentioned titles, you most likely will not enjoy this game. I am barely two hours in, as you can tell, and I'm not too thrilled that I invested the full $59.99 price tag. In fact, I was going to refund the game, but alas, I was 2.2hrs into the game by the time I made that choice. In my honest opinion, you're better off waiting for a 30% discount, at a minimum. 

What's wrong with the game? Well, if you're looking for a scary horror game like I was, this isn't it. In fact, I have only played this in the black of night, windows shut, no lights on, and not even a peep came out of me. So, despite having clear inspiration from Dead Space, it does not deliver in the fear department. You may get spooked, of course. However, I didn't grow up playing horror games, I was always too scared. Hell, I couldn't even get myself to play the OG Tomb Raider games because I feared the water sections having sharks. If I am that easily spooked from horror games and this game does not even do anything to me, it surely won't for you. 

The game has very interesting vibes. I don't want to say indie vibes, because Hollow Knight and Silksong are indie, yet they don't give off the vibes this game does. If you ever played the Lords of the Fallen remake, it gives me the exact vibes. I can't tell you what that means, but perhaps it's the feeling of a game that is made by adequate developers who have vision, yet fail to meet that vision in their execution. I don't know what else to tell you. Not a lot of games I've played give me that vibe, but everyone that did, I ended up not liking at all. And I guess these are the same developers who made The Medium? That too was a generic game that has the exact same vibes. You feel me? We ain't vibing, this game and I. And I fear it's them and not me.

Graphics are solid, but again, it seems like low budget. Game-play is very linear. Too linear, if you ask me. And a lot of the time, you jump down obvious paths that the developers want you to go and can't go back. There's not a lot of exploration, so the little backtracking you end up doing is silly. The enemy's are generic looking and easy to dodge. The only thing that I like about this game is the world building you discover as you listen to audio recordings and read letters left over from citizens. But if that's all I'm enjoying out of the game, that's pretty lame. It's not a bad game by any means, but it's not worth the price they're asking for. If nothing else, it's nice to support the developer for making a new I.P when we're constantly getting sequels or remakes. But do we settle for a generic game and call it a win simply because it's a new I.P? Tough call. 

Ultimately, the game is interesting enough to keep you invested, but it's not doing anything new. It's not pushing the genre forward. It's not blazing its own path. It's playing it safe, while taking inspiration from other games that are far greater than it in every aspect.

review_text:
I’ve watched some of the SAO anime, but I’ve never played any SAO games before. This is actually the first SAO game I’ve tried, and… is this what I get? It wasn’t worth the price I paid at all. I even quit within the first week of playing.

When I decided to buy this game, I wanted a solo SAO game I could play in my free time. I don’t mind games that allow co-op with other players, but this one seems to push it too much. Actually, it doesn’t just push co-op—it requires co-op play only!

For someone like me who prefers playing solo, I could quit as soon as I completed the story, since that’s all the solo mode offers. The rewards don’t really help develop my character much further.

The co-op mode, which is the main focus, just feels like a repetitive grind that quickly becomes boring. It takes a lot of time to play, but most of the rewards are pointless. After nearly 200 hours of trying to stick with it, hoping for some exciting updates, nothing ever came.

I haven’t even mentioned the equipment crafting system yet. It feels like spending all my hard-earned money on a big pile of junk. Nearly every day, I get only 1-2 Epic items out of 100 crafting attempts, and even when they’re Epic, most of them are still practically useless.

I don’t know who thought it was a good idea to limit crafting to just 100 items per day. The drop rates for decent items are already low, and even if there were no daily limit, I still wouldn’t want to grind huge amounts of money just to end up with a pile of junk.
I don’t know if the game will change in the future, but I do hope it does.

In summary, I enjoyed the story and exploring the map at first, but as soon as I realized the co-op mode was just a repetitive grind, I almost wanted to request a refund immediately, but it was already too late.

Fencer spin skill - This skill doesn't proc any other on attack effects, thus any direct attack buffs they get now become redundant as the up time on this skill is MOST of every fight if not all - not a bad ability but ruins others.

Healer attack skill - This allows healers to 'heal' enemies for poison damage BUT it means your healers will now never heal your party, as they will always prioritise attacking.

Extra Mage Attacks - for whatever reason these all come with flat damage values which are great in early game, but very quickly become hinderances to mage DPS and value in late game, as mages will prioritise spending time and mana on these skills whenever available.

Fighters in general - their special ability feels like it actively works against making them effective front liners - though perhaps the intention is to have them work with tanks...

- gameplay is very repetitive. There is like, one type of boss that you fight couple of times and there is also the "main" antagonist, who is absent 99% of the game. I have yet to see all of the features of the game, and yes it IS a fun game, great with other people. HOWEVER- and this is enough to warrant a thumbs down for me- the AI lacks a crucial gameplay function.

So there is a reasonable amount of time you will play with bots during your time with this game. This is because there just aren't a lot of players. There is a specific enemy which requires you to shoot parts of it's body to kill it. Guess what the AI wasn't programmed to do? That's right, shoot those parts. This means that if you get downed, only when that specific enemy is in play, you might as well quit to the lobby because you are locked out of finishing that mission.

It is extremely infuriating and is baffling that a feature like this was introduced without making the AI smart enough to kill it.

Another big issue- Host-only progression. Rewards you only get if you complete the run dead or alive. If the host leaves, it just sends you back to the hub without rewards. I've had players rage quit at the reward screen. The playerbase is awful and it is next to impossible to find consistent, functional matches.

EDIT: I did manage to complete the game. The content is very little and it is one of the most repetitive, one-dimensional games I have ever played. Avoid!

review_text:
[b]“[insert meme from 2015 to 2020 here]”[/b]
[i]-Despot[/i]
[hr][/hr]

Ever jumped in a pool shallow enough you hurt your legs?
Well, playing [b]Despot’s Game[/b] is the game equivalent of that.

[h1]X-Factor[/h1]
The hook of this title are the many animations and enemies the trailer portrays, and the chaos that ensues pitting your little army against the various monsters.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Guide your stragglers room to room to autobattle, get credits to either buy equipment at the shop, food to stave off a hunger mechanic, or upgrades that will affect all characters in the party.

Rinse and repeat for 12 levels and you have this game.

There’s also a hunger mechanic where every time you move from room to room it will deplete a resource, giving you maluses and even a game over if you run dry of food, incentivizing you to build tall, to create through upgrades and gear an elite team of characters, instead of wide.

Another mechanic and maybe the most eyebrow-raising one, is to have many characters each with a different weapon, but in the same weapon category, despite each one being a straight upgrade to the others, in order to unlock/power up, the single class skill for the character.

[h1]Story[/h1]
There is none, Despot is a bored ai overlord that grows jelly-humans in a tube and gets pissy when they beat him at his own game, there’s not much else to it.

[h1]Downsides[/h1]
And here’s the big part of the review:

I expected there to be either more focus on customization, other than a single skill and a few modifiers given by RNG, and more to tactics as both your army and the enemy will just make a beeline to the closest target and autoattack it until it dies.

There’s little to no planning, since the best skills are locked behind RNG drops, and the skills you do have range from the very original “more health” and culminate with the just as original “more attack”.

The hunger mechanic feels tacked on, but fortunately there’s a way to turn it off.

The humor was also something that bogged down the experience, at least for me, and this is purely subjective.
Maybe you like a game where every character is a ADHD kid whose humor could be described by “lol so random, raise your sporks” and “Facebook memes”.

But the biggest problem is how barren the game feels, 

I don’t know how the dev made it... the game feels at the same time barren and “overcrowded”.
Barren because every weapon act the same, there’s just a stat change between them, besides a few having extra abilities to them, and each run being the same set of enemies, locations and bosses.

…ad infinitum.

Congratulations, you just “played” To the Moon.

Jokes aside, this is a well-intentioned game but one that puts all its eggs into one basket: it’s story. It’s a gamble that can pay off if the story is strong enough to carry the rest of the game, but it’s a trick that To the Moon doesn’t quite manage to pull off. 

The story does have its bittersweet finale at the end, but the emotional payoff just wasn’t worth the 4-5 hours of excruciating controls and non-existent gameplay the player has to endure in order to get there. But the biggest crime the game commits is the two lead characters and their insufferable dialogue. They’re obviously there to provide comic relief in what would otherwise be a melancholic and dour story, but their witticisms often fall flat or are delivered at inappropriate times, often both. The best thing about finishing the game was that I wouldn’t have to endure them anymore.

NGS is not Phantasy Star. I do not recommend this game anymore. I actually hate NGS and what its become. I miss when SEGA cared about PSO2

Phantasy Star Online 2 is a fantastic game. This game was its best when it first came to Global and when SEGA kept updating it. I loved PSO2's engaging combat, meaningful story, memorable characters, quest counters, title counters, the lobby, Urgent Quests are really fun. Unfortunately SEGA pushed a lot of content away from PSO2 and they rushed to bring out NGS.

The lifespan for PSO2
USA(only): April 2020 on XBOX ONE, 
USA (only): May 27 2020 on Microsoft store
World Wide: August 5 2020 on Steam
NGS came out for everyone at the same time in June 9th 2021.

review_text:
This game is so close to being fantastic, but I'm afraid the dev's vision of "survive until you die" stands in the way of what the game COULD be. Let me explain.

You start with a great little city builder! Yes, we can quibble about the oddities of farming/water resource management, etc., but it is tremendously satisfying to watch as your village grows and comes alive! Then, the monsters attack. Mostly at night. You transition to a tower defense game, constructing towers and golems to fight the enemy, weaving a maze of walls for the enemy to traverse, holding strong as your villagers cower and attempt to reinforce every defense while balancing seasonal survival needs. This is all very cool... until it's not. 

You WANT to send out a force to counter-attack the enemy base camps. The game isn't designed for that. You WANT to eradicate the threat from every sector of the World Map one by one. But again, that’s not what this game is about. The best you can do is... survive. For awhile. And then die. Yes, you can play on more peaceful settings, but you miss out on the tension which, early on, is really very good. But this game makes me long for more, like the days when I played the Majesty games where you could assemble a bunch of heroes, select a threat, and have them go trounce the enemy (or get trounced if not up to the task). If you play your cards right in Majesty, you can actually win! Here, in Rise to Ruins, you grow until your villagers are defeated, with goals like "Survive 21 days!" as your only incentive to keep going. But why keep going if the end is inevitable and the enemy is guaranteed victory every time?

All defense and no offense creates an artificial limit on what this game COULD be. The potential is there, but ultimately it's a bust for me. Sigh. Back on the shelf of my Steam Library, hoping someday a developer in inspired by the many great elements from this and builds something with a more expansive vision - one with a path to overcome the threat and Rise FROM the Ruins to fight back!

yes... BUT - there's a lot of BUTS with this game (spelled B-U-G-S). See list below.

The good - it's fun with friends. If you like shooting waves of zombies it's entertaining. There's not that much to the game other than slogging through various maps killing zombies. Sometimes I'm not even sure why I like the game. 

The bad / annoying stuff - BUGS. There are LOADS of bugs. Some of them are extremely irritating. Even after the recent update the devs did not fix almost any of the common bugs that have plagued this game. They seemed more interested in nerfing the over-powered weapons. The OP weapons were fun to use, but they did render 95% of the other weapons useless. Now the game seems too hard - it might be difficult to know what weapon configurations are good and how to use them. There are tons of weapon mods, but hard to know how they compare. Running out of ammo is a new problem - an annoying one.  

List of bugs:
- Horde mode - zombies get stuck where you can't find them and the game can't be completed. This is game breaking. I hope they fixed it. It would be easy to have a wave reset or something. 
- Can't talk to players (voice) in your party if they are in a different lobby. There's no text chat
- If someone is in a party, there's no way to contact them (like, if you want to ask if they want to party up with you, or when they'll be done their current round, or anything). You can "nudge" them but that's it.  
- The game hangs / doesn't start if a member of your party leaves as you are loading in, or even if you try to continue to a second map after the first when one player has left. You are forced to restart, and when you do you lose your party members and can't find them again because they're in different lobbies most likely. 
- If the party leader disconnects or leaves, the entire game stops and the remaining three players are forced out without being able to finish the round. 
- New bug - can't seem to pick up partially full ammo mags when dropped 
- Very difficult to know exactly what the chipsets do and how to compare their relative performance (add something to measure in the shooting range perhaps)
- Warheads don't always explode when thrown, and disappear
- Matchmaking - a complete disaster. Hard to say everything wrong with it. Best to bring your own friends. Very hard to get a full party of people who are looking to play the same level and difficulty as you.

review_text:
TLDR: Avoid, especially at current full price it is simply not worth it. 

Huge disappointment and very lackluster content for a allegid £30 game.

My only positives are:

The gunplay feels really good. It’s satisfying to use the weapons and land shots. 

The basic enemy engagements are fun, they are both slow and fast so that you have the chance to enjoy honing your aim and can take some time to enjoy it over the frantic clip empty parts.

I only paid £24, but even that is over what I think this disguised as a AAA early access tile is worth.

Really poor default VR controls. It’s extremely clunky to begin with until you edit them. Yes it’s comfigerable but I shouldn’t need to configure 20 options right out the gate to get it towards what most other games have perfected as a standard.

The missions are too short & there are only 5. Given how simple these “missions” seem, I’m shocked there isn't more.

Safe rooms don’t feel like safe rooms and the dumb arcade machines become unsuable if one of your party hits the door button for the next stage. 

They are clinging to this arcade game style options menu that is cumbersome to use repeatedly and causes more issues than it solves.

The lobby system is appalling. How this passed UX / QA is an absolute mystery to me. In a nutshell,if you, the lobby leader, decide to move away from the arcade machine that allows you to select a mission you have no idea when your party is full and ready to start. Meaning you have multiple lobbeys that you have no control over picking and keep getting put back into the same inactive party / lobby. Stupid.

I have to say, I didn't expect to like this as much as I did. I've never been a big fan of the tony hawk games or anything like that but this is like the idea of those games where someone said "why is all this realism bogging down my fun".

Which is what this game is, just pure distilled fun. Just looking around each area and playing through the story is fun to do and the movement abilities all seem to click into place and work seamlessly. In particular the speed boost you get for leaning into the turn on grinds just feels fantastic. The fact you can do all of these things at high speed while playing on your in game phone without having to give up any control is quite frankly insane and I love it.

Not required at all but I recommend anyone who plays to also mod in some fun characters for your own enjoyment. I personally played almost the whole campaign as carl from athf and it was a lot of fun.

review_text:
Player-side AI all over is terrible. Your players will not check at all unless you get an upgrade that makes them prioritize checking. Check hitboxes are really narrow/wonky, while enemies have very generous hitboxes.

The really damning part is the game will forcibly change which player you are controlling frequently, and commonly at unintuitive moments. The pass button is also hard-bound to the change player button, so if you want to change players and at the same moment one of your players obtains the puck, you will pass it off immediately.

A minor gripe, but one of the abilities is throwing that player's stick to knock some people down. Because you HAVE to control who has the puck and your teammates never use their abilities on their own, you cannot use this ability while maintaining control of the puck ever.

There's a fun game in here but currently it feels like the game is fighting you in places it shouldn't. I can probably recommend this after significant AI, controls, and player autonomy tweaks/overhauls, but I can't recommend it in its current state. It's just an exercise in frustration currently.

review_text:
TL;DR: Playing this while having the worst chest infection imaginable seemed strangely on-brand and really helped settle in the existential dread and despair; I loved it! 10/10!

The game can feel uphill, or even like it's wasting your time at certain sections, but every part of its story and mechanics have been carefully and deliberately - meticulously even - placed to help you embody the role of a surgeon returning to a steppe town, shortly before its descent into a plague. It's dialogue-heavy, with a lot of exploration and pressing survival mechanics, but describing it just like this is both the best way to avoid the unique shock of going in blind, and also feels like an underwhelming description for what is an incredibly fascinating experience to have in a videogame.

The primary downsides I found were performance related; it can take a while to load between deaths and when going inside buildings, and it can stutter and lag a little when crossing loading boundaries, but this isn't toooo bad per se. I found it crashed my game once, but it wasn't that bad. There are a few bugs here and there, but nothing too game-breaking that haven't been highlighted in the community guide!

It definitely won't be for everyone, but definitely play this over Pathologic 1 - unless you're really into seeing more of the ideas of the world itself -, and if you're not sure, give the HBomberguy or MandaloreGaming videos a watch to see if its for you! :) For me, it was bittersweet to finish, it's a rich and unique world full of horrors with moments of hope interspersed between, a story of reconnecting with the place you were born and coming into age and finding meaning amid the horrors of the world. It took me about 40h to go through and finish one full playthrough, and with time, I'll come back and play it again to see if everyone really can be saved. :)

review_text:
[h1] Where The Scorn Don't Shine [/h1]

I wanted to like this game, seeing the trailers made me have so many questions about the world of Scorn and how it works. I understand the developers wanted the story to be told through environment, but there is almost zero deviation of said environment as you are stuck in the same building almost the entirety of the game and leaves you with more questions and none answered. The highlights of the game are pretty much all shown in the trailer and there is no exploration aspect when most paths lead to an locked area or dead end, if anything it's a walking sim. While the game isn't intended at all to be a "shooter", I feel like the variety of weapons speak differently especially with the main focus of the last 1/5th of the game primarily being restricted to "shooting", even having to solve puzzles with your weapon despite the game being "not a shooter". Even then all enemies are way too easy to escape that there is almost no point of having any weapons beside the first tool you get, it seems like the developers couldn't decide whether or not to have guns be in the game but eventually were forced to due to the puzzle design and [spoiler] unnecessary end boss fight [/spoiler]. Just when the game starts getting good, it ends just as abrupt as how the game began. The audio is nice and music is great as expected but the graphics aren't exactly anything to write home about as they are on par with games that came out years ago like Doom or Resident Evil remakes. I feel that if Scorn came out when atmospheric survival horror was more popular it would have been an absolute hit, but this game doesn't do anything defining for that genre gamers haven't already seen.

Overall I can't say I recommend this game, it took me 5 hours to 100% and even on sale for 36$ that is just not worth paying 7$ for each hour of this game and I feel bad for those who have waited years for this. It doesn't seem to shine in any of its aspects, it has plenty of gore but nothing that really gives you the "shock factor" or makes you feel in immediate danger, just monsters making noises crawling around you that can easily be heard and therefore avoided. None of the puzzles were really hard, mostly just fetch quests for other items or doing things in a certain order seemingly to make the game feel longer. The atmosphere is GOOD, if you're okay with seeing what you saw in the trailer for 5 hours and the ending ruined anything that happened in the game. To me there are tons more games that do this genre much better, Abe's odyssey series or Amnesia to name a couple are much more engaging in surreal story telling, art style, exploration, horror, and came out decades ago.

3/10

review_text:
A game I can't enjoy yet it is genius in multiple areas.
There's an era of gaming in the 90's where starting off in a horror scenario with little to no information as to why you're there that this game clearly emulates and does very well.
There are multiple plant and pay offs handled very well. This is the minor of minor spoilers but [spoiler] there is a section where you find a weapon that is also used as a key (essentially). You pick it up off a dead person. You later have a cinematic that leads you to the next area where you no longer have the weapon. You come across another area where a monster (and I'm being literal here) buries itself into your stomach and it's tail is the weapon you just had and just lost. The gap between these moments had no implication on the game at all, you never needed the weapon-key until this belly-creature attachment. But pulling it off a corpse means a whole lot more when you find out the creature in your belly is a life-draining parasite. [/spoiler]
It's small things like this that prove the creators of the game created and respected their lore and took it into account when designing it.

That being said...I don't like this game all that much. The combat is VERY scripted and frustrating at moments, trying to relive what some people found as "tension" in the original Resident Evil 4, where if it's difficult to maneuver you're more likely to panic and thus is a simulation in a horror theme. I've never found this to be effective because frustration and cheap deaths will destroy theming 100% of the time.
The puzzles are built around the protagonist's perspective, in other words all the mechanics of the machinery (loosely using that due to the bio-organic nature of it all) are as much of a mystery to him as it is to you. It's a nice touch at first, because it causes a curiosity to explore and try things out however it becomes clear quickly that the puzzles rely HEAVILY on the player's curiosity because in a game where your movement is very slow (even when running) the puzzles require you to walk back and forth repeatedly in the same level area before you can progress to the next, as if this was another element from the 90's gaming area it attempts to emulate (the dreaded back tracking of "what did I miss?")

In terms of appearance this game is drop-dead gorgeous. The animation of the environment and the...living(?) things in it is near-seamless. The lack of vibrant color allows for certain moments such as "emergency/science lights" to highlight what is important which proves they planned this seemless blend but knew it could cause confusion when on top of a limited exploration a video game can offer. In short, it's literally too beautiful for it's own good. There are times where it somehow breaks the science of reality and makes things seems desolate and claustrophobic at the same time.

However it relies on this a little too much due to the constant re-exploration the puzzles need and the multiple...so many cut-scenes. It handles transitions primarily in 1st person cut-scenes that quickly become annoying as EVERYTHING in this world takes it's sweet time - the protagonist included. The speed that he handles unlocking a door is insufferably slow, most likely in a similar attempt as the aforementioned slow = tension but it falls into the frustrating category fairly fast. Entering a door with a creature that's walking along the ceiling well out of your reach happens in a slow moving cut-scene where I guess the protagonist forgets how to walk because it takes literally 8 seconds for him to walk through it either to show how gorgeous it is and let the ambiance set the tone (which it was doing perfectly before you interrupted it thank you) and to show the creature moving away from you but it takes the entire ceiling in it's movement which is rapid and creepy, there's no way to possibly avoid it. The game relies on it's gorgeous art that it specifically places an immovable camera so you can see what's in it but this is another element that removes the horror aspect because if I was continuing to walk through and saw it move I'd react in game and not have the protection of a cut-scene. Which is hypocritical of me however...because this game loves these cut-scenes so much you can literally die in one. Without major spoilers here you can run through an entire level and succeed just to die in a cut-scene. 

Before ending in a brief summary another commendation this game deserves is Jouni Kalervo Havukainen and the In Slaughter Natives developed an exceptionally visceral, nostalgic, terrifying soundtrack. There is no quip here, it is simply remarkable and they deserve the love they are getting for this score.

In the end it's hard not to see my issue with the game as almost subjective and there is enough well-thought effort and execution in this game that has more love in it's design than most games today that I'm sure there are plenty who pick it up that will rightfully fall in love with it.
I will look forward to the next game this team releases.

While obviously heavily inspired by Dead space It's not nearly as good or fun to play.


The gameplay is simply put, clunky. They really want you to use the melee and evasion system but it doesn't feel good to use and it doesn't help that the camera is stiff, jarring and at some points even nauseating.
Movement is bad and feels stiff. Also lacks a sprint toggle.
Gunplay is very flaccid and usually punishing when used, switching weapons is slow just not very satisfying overall.
Overall the gameplay was repetitive and mediocre.


While graphic wise the game looks gorgeous and realistic, the environments were repetitive and uninspired, i got lost sometimes in a pretty much linear game cause it looked all so similar. And the amount of crawling through vents and shimmying through cracks was so much it became tiresome.
Story was interesting enough but predictable.
The horror elements were alright but the jumpscares were lackluster, although there were some cool transitions into some of the stealth segments.

Would i recommend it? Not really, only if you're a survival horror enthusiast or really like Dead Space to the point you want something similar or new.
It doesn't really deserve a negative or positive review, cause it's neither. once again a mixed option would've been preferred but since i'm leaning more to the negative side that's what it'll be.

The dialogue, the characters’ motivations, and the overall tone are all designed to cater to a younger audience raised on Netflix dramas. Characters have become more likeable, more quippy, and are less grounded in the actual historical mindset of the period. It’s the same trend that’s ruining modern TV and film, where everything is made palatable for the masses at the cost of nuance and authenticity.

I'm not surprised, because if you want to create a successful modern brand, it has to sell well and appeal to as many people as possible. However, I'm not one of those people. 

I’d be more inclined to rate this game positively if it weren't for the fact that the main developers and producers lied about its content. That said, the artists, programmers, and everyone else who put real work into bringing this game to life absolutely deserve recognition for their talent and effort

review_text:
[h1] I [strike]wanted to[/strike] love this game [/h1]

An auto-battler with an ungodly amount of pop-culture references? An awesome art style with fantastic animations? "Sign me up!"

[b]The Expectations[/b]

Game fun character cool

[strike]This game sets itself up with the mechanics of the auto-battlers we've come to love. Relax, and grab things from different factions to build into powerful bonuses, then soup that up further with the extra abilities/modifiers (in this game called mutations) you pick up along the way. A tried-and-true formula at this point! You can even face other players once you've beaten the game, bringing in that competitive element we all love. This all falls apart once you've touched your first playthrough.[/strike]

[b]The Game[/b]

Gameplay nice quite fun very upgrade

[strike]The gameplay loop you'll be put through goes as follows: pick a starting team, walk room to room fighting enemies, and use the tokens you obtain to buy stronger items and strengthen your generic mutations, all while balancing your resources. Not too dissimilar from auto-battlers like Dota Underlords or SnakeRX! But then you start to notice that it IS quite different than those you've played before - and not in a good way. 

Gone are the fun, varied builds, as you're railroaded to putting disposable tanks in the front and forced to focus on upgrading HP and attack speed in the generic mutation tree, so that your team doesn't fall behind. Gone are the fun different abilities amidst the different factions. Excited to see how this level 3 mage item might differ from the level 1 item? That's the baffling part - it doesn't! It only changes the visuals. No matter the item your puny human might be holding, he has the exact same abilities as his other mages or fighters - just an auto-attack. No interesting ability, no variation, just a DIRECT stats upgrade from the previous levels. As well, the only way to level up that boring, singular faction ability is to hold on to weak, inferior, and unupgradable units. This is in no way interesting and is at odds with itself mechanically. I must constantly buy the most expensive item to survive, and yet keep throwing men to the wolves with crappy level 1 and 2 items so that my team even has synergy? You can't combine level 1 items, you can't improve the base guys you put them on, they are simply pure fodder and tedium. The absolute inability for my characters to have relevance outside of my level 4 and 5 characters is ridiculous to me. It's disheartening to want to try out the 5/5 faction bonus, because I know I'll have the slog of bringing along some useless level 1 items to do it.  You don't even get to see a different ability - this character on your team is just an inferior version of something else you have. And even if I give them the benefit of the doubt, that you're supposed to have this revolving door of useless low-level item users that can't survive long enough to level up, when they die in accordance to the gameplay loop the developers designed, you are beholden to a coin flip on whether or not you can even reuse that item or if it disappears into the void for you to have to purchase again for yourself. To design a puzzle, then limit it via coin-flip, is frankly a lazy attempt to get folk to put in more hours due to runs that flat out fail.

Gone is the experimentation, as one simple click can cost you tons of food resources, as the game penalises you for backtracking, and even for simply walking through empty rooms. An odd, tax-like food system exists in this game seemingly only to stop you from backtracking. With multiple ways to spend your currency already, you are forced to drop some on food that your people munch down on in every room - empty or not. Better have lucked out and gone the right way initially, because every empty room your people walk through is as exhausting for them as a battle to the death.

Last, when you're in the midst of having fun, and you're finally at the fight where you die, what is it you want after? Feedback. You want to understand the mechanics of where you died and how to improve, and that's the final place where this game falls flat. There is ZERO feedback. Zero information as to why you are losing - unless it's obvious like the manhacks on the first level that will kill two of your melee units regardless of your choices when you're playing Normal>Classic. You will be soaring, and then you will have to watch your entire team die, or at least dwindle over a few fights, with nothing you can do. Uninteractive, artificially difficult gameplay. You have no player agency when you die, you have nothing to outplay amidst watching them die, no skill to rely on, no meta upgrades to get to improve your next run, you just lose because the game gave you a random stat check you couldn't pass. Yes, I could pick different starting loadouts or lower the difficulty, but that won't give me anymore information as to why the initial team they give is set up to fail against a possible first fight.

And what is the solution to the gripes as seen in the reviews? Focus on health and attack speed upgrades in the generic tree, constantly buy the highest-level items available, put disposable tanks up front, and play on other game modes as apparently the normal mode isn't balanced. These are not proper solutions. If you HAVE to choose an option, then it is no longer an option but a required tax, and there's a good amount of those in this game. To succeed you will have to do similar builds over and over, with little to no variation between your runs as you attempt to find the best ranged items to hide behind your fodder after you realise there's no point to experimenting with faction bonuses.

It's good to shake up the formula, and it's good to question the practices of the auto-battlers of yore to see what they can change and make different, but frankly the changes here do not make for a better game.[/strike]

I would love to re-do this whole thing one day, but I'll sum it up as 'they made this game even better'. These devs are top notch.

[h1]PROS[/h1]

[list]
[*]Beautiful pixel graphics
[*]Incredibly smooth animation
[*]Fun designs, with tons of throwbacks to pop culture
[*]Hilarious dialogue
[*]A passionate team who seem to love what they do
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]

[list]

review_text:
I can't recommend this game for a new player.

That said, if you're looking to get into Star Trek Online then you should be aware of some major things:

While not exceedingly difficult to pick up at the base level, the game doesn't explain its core concepts very well. Core gameplay is divided between a space component and a ground component. Most people prefer the space component, which is fine, but you will need to do both quite commonly if you're going through the story, and very few aspects of either are explained to the player up front. As such, If you want to do well at endgame, you either need to seek out this information externally, have it explained to you by knowledgeable people, or spend a bunch of time on trail and error in a system that hides or doesn't explain the relationship between different gear and abilities and what best synergises.

There is no 'RPG Trinity' despite what the character class system might appear as. All content is DPS focused, with an admittedly wide variety of methods of achieving that DPS. Tactical Captains (Tacs) Usually boost their damage directly. Engineering Captains (Engs) Indirectly boost their DPS and survivability. Science Captains (Scis) usually debuff enemies to boost their own DPS.'Tanks' and 'Healers' don't commonly exist in game, since while tools exist to facilitate those roles, all content still needs things to die moreso then having people tank or heal.

Outside of the core gameplay, you have a loosely 'Star Trek' themed MMO that will probably appeal to you if you liked the shooty combat parts of Star Trek moreso then the philosophical navel-gazing parts. You can fly virtually any ship in Star Trek canon you can think of, but depending on what ship that is, you might need to spend either significant time grinding out the resources for, or a decent amount of money buying outright, the ship you want.

Ships at endgame are priced at $30 USD for a single ship at baseline price. Sales happen, bundles exist, etc. that let you mitigate costs but for the most part any given ship at endgame is gonna be at least that expensive when no sales are currently running.

You don't really need endgame ships to succeed in most content, thankfully, but if you want the most powerful builds, you will need to buy several ships for the gear and abilities they can give you.

While you can grind out the currency used to buy ships in game, this is a time consuming process that needs significant startup resources to get to be at anywhere resembling a decent income rate. Starting this process from nothing can take you literal weeks of playtime to get to a decent point of income on the resource.

On the brighter side, however, the game typically runs 3 events (Anniversary, Summer, Winter) a year that give out an endgame level ship for doing some daily task or another for a few weeks. These tasks usually take a few minutes, and don't need to be ran on consecutive days.

Character customization is fairly decent, but most outfits will cost you money to acquire, even if many are account-wide unlocks you only need to buy once for your account. The age of the game also shows in many aspects here, however, as despite all the options you can't really do too much with faces.

PvP is virtually non-existent. The devs haven't made it a focus in years, and whatever sort of shenaniganry they put out for PvE use is never checked for what it does in the PvP scene, so if you're looking to have unrestricted PvP that isn't an over-the-top pay to win mess, look for a different game.

All that said, the game is Free To Play if you wan't to try it yourself, but if you want to truly excel at the endgame, you'll likely need to pay out either a decent chunk of money or a significant amount of time.

I'm REALLY enjoying Despot's Game save for a few problems.
IT'S EA SO THERE ARE GOING TO BE PROBLEMS AND BALANCING ISSUES THAT I'D IMAGINE WILL BE FIXED
AND I WILL NO DOUBT BE CHANGING IT TO RECOMMENDED BECAUSE I'M REALLY ENJOYING THE GAME.

Pro's 

The art style works really well for the game.
The humour is really funny at times.
The characters you get to use are really good, such as Saitama, Sailormoon, Kylo Ren & Doc Oc.
The sprites and enemy models are great and it's pretty easy to tell who is who and also who they are supposed to be.
I'm genuinely looking forward to seeing the updates, changes and balancing.

Con's
Medics won't heal your front line troops such as your tanks.
Some of the enemy units are WAY too tough.
Eg: You'll be on the 2nd biome and the enemy units will have 2000 hp and there will be 4 of them and they'll slaughter a lot of your troops.

In conclusion, i definitely recommend this game to anoyne that likes a challenge and metriodvania style gameplay, especially if it's on a discount.

review_text:
It's such a shame. 

BONEWORKS was one of the (if not THE) greatest VR games of all time. With how much I enjoyed the first game, and the clear passion that the developers had for IT, I was REALLY excited to see what happened with BONELAB after it was announced.
Let me say it again so it's clear; I LOVED BONEWORKS; this is not me hating both games.

It's BECAUSE I loved BONEWORKS as much as I did that this review hurts all the more.

Tdlr: BONELAB is a buggy mess with absolutely ZERO new ideas to separate it from it predecessor. 

While BONELAB technically does have "new" NPCs and Weapons, they're just either more machine guns, or buggy impact-free shotguns that simply aren't fun to handle.
NPC's are just reskinned Nullmen or Turrets. 

Half of the fun of the original BONEWORKS game was discovering this brand new world you were in, and trying to decipher what the goal of the protagonist actually was!
That's simply not present in BONELAB. You already know what this world is. You as a protagonist simply don't HAVE a goal. 
The new body-swap mechanic (on top of being buggy and broken as hell AND only being unlocked within the LAST HOUR of the game) isn't enough to make players feel like they're experiencing something new at all! It's just VR at different heights, something that VRChat, Chillout, and any VR game with custom characters has been doing for years.

There are two required driving sequences that are either a complete waste of time, being basically a mediocre roller coaster showcase you would have expected to see when VR was first commercially viable; or so ridiculously hard to control that you'll spend more time trying to reorient yourself and your stomach than you will actually driving.

It's clear that the developers had ideas and drive for BONELAB, but clearly not enough to warrant a "full" sequel, and especially not one that COSTS MORE THAN THE FIRST GAME.

Initially, people complained about the first game BONEWORKS; thinking that it was mainly just a tech demo. Obviously, this was wrong; as BONEWORKS actually contained an interesting story, new ideas/characters/USES FOR VR/PERSPECTIVE.
The same argument simply CANNOT be made for BONELAB. It's just BONEWORKS without a story, without new ideas, without interesting use of VR as a medium. BONELAB IS a tech demo of SLZ's new Marrow Engine capabilities. That's not enough for players.

If the game was around $20-25 CAD, I'd feel a little better about it. But, it's $45, which is more than BONEWORKS; and too much for how little there is.

I expected so much better from this game; and it simply couldn't deliver.

I cannot recommend this game as much as i can recommend Just Cause 3

Jet Set Radio is one of my all-time favorite games. This game gets the overall feel and style of JSR down, but it replaces the fun levels with a "rep" system, which doesn't mean anything other than "you must find graffiti hidden throughout the open world in order to open up the next part of the game."

That wouldn't be so bad in small doses, but:

review_text:
Batman Arkham City is the sequel to Arkham Asylum. It does boast with a massive number of collectibles, more enemies, a bigger world as well as more side-missions. Combat and graphics are both a bit smoother than in Arkham Asylum, so game mechanics have improved. This can't make up for the super shallow story and that it's missing any character development or depth though. It feels mostly like comic episodes. Also the start of the game is very strange since Bruce Wayne is running for mayor and put into prison for it (really???). 

The main game is about 16 hours playtime, the DLC "Harley Quinns revenge" about 2 more hours. Below my pro/cons list:

Pro:
+ smoother combat
+ smoother parcour movements
+ smoother graphics
+ bigger open world (city district)
+ more collectibles 
+ OST
+ detailed environment
+ collectible background stories of Gotham

Cons:
- controller portation from console to PC very bad (hundreds of different buttons separately for all kinds of actions)
- bad menu structure for PC
- in-game menu design
- super shallow and boring main story, loosely connected to Arkham Asylum
- story start very strange (Bruce for mayor!?)
- conversations with Joker meaningless
- prison setting strange (a highest security prison in the middle of Gotham???)
- loosely connected quests of main story
- missing face animations (emotions)
- character movements too comicy for my taste
- too much running around in the big city with long distances for missions and items
- grinding for finishing Riddler side mission (collecting 400 pieces, really???)
- DLC level recycling and boring story

Conclusion:
Quantity rather than quality. Arkham City moved much further into the direction of mainstream 3rd person acrade combat. It feels like easy listening songs. The game mechanics have been improved, but good story or depth are nowhere to be seen. The game feels more like grinding and long distance travelling to get finish it rather than offering a captivating plot and story. Rating: 4/10 points

review_text:
I want to love this game so badly. I am a massive trekkie, and this game scratches so many itches perfectly. Space combat is so satisfying to me (though not quite as satisfying as Starfleet Command, it's still solid), as is customizing my crew, my away team, and every aspect of my ship. It all falls into place perfectly at first, even with the spotty ground combat and graphics pop ins. 

Then I level up enough to get a free new ship, and I think, Oh hey, lets see what ships I'll be able to get later on. Then I see all the things that cost the real money currency (Zen), the immense in game currency costs of other ships, the absolutely enormous and rather expensive Zen shop, and all the things designed to push me towards spending cash. And it just kills it for me. Every. Single. Time. 

I've uninstalled this game 7 different times, only to remember the space combat, the story, and the feel of it all, get that itch, and reinstall, then uninstall again within a week. Just, don't cause yourself the same agony. This game is an abusive relationship. Go buy Starfleet Command, or download the Star Trek mod for Sins of a Solar Empire. It may not give you the feeling of having your own captain going to do adventures but like... it's something actually fun in the end that doesn't try to nickle and dime you at every opportunity.

review_text:
[b]Tldr[/b]
After almost 4 years and 100 levels of 'content', I would guess that dev team's core philosophy behind NGS is something along the lines of :

Put in the least amount of effort, recycle content wherever and whenever possible.

Not too concerned about growing the playerbase, the priority is to squeeze the tiny amount of players who have proven that they will tolerate the above and spend significantly and regularly on fashion items.

This is a game that's not very important to us or the company. We just keep the lights on and can continue operating like this for 100's of levels to come. The players will allow us. Most of the proceeds from NGS are invested into other projects.


[b]Level 100 Cap Update[/b]
Sadly, but not particularly surprisingly, most of the things from the old review are still true. I talk about the new stuff here, check the old review towards the end to see more about the game in general.

There still exist weapons with absurd drop rates, but as of lately the devs have been ensuring that there's a weapon option that the player can work towards and grind the materials for. If you play casually, the cost of gearing isn't painful. If you're min maxing, it's not as costly as it was before but the caveats and rng associated with successfully pulling it off still exist.
They story so far in almost 4 years and 100 levels remains lackluster (to put it generously) and is only able to accomplish anything remotely interesting when it key jangles characters from or links to the old game. The new Urgent Quest (equivalent to a raid in other mmo's) is a fight against the Level 100 cap update 'Final' Boss and that along with the scant amount of story, are the only content of what the devs consider a major update. [b]Everything else is recycled content, business as usual for NGS.[/b]

The fight itself leaves a lot to be desired and I wouldn't consider it befitting of a major story update boss. I've seen them design better fights for what would be considered less important bosses in the past few years. For major new raids, mmo devs would usually have an idea of how each class would perform in a fight..for example how Class A will position itself during this phase of the fight or the possible ways Class B might upkeep their damage during this particular attack from the boss. The NGS devs? Well, they do know, what I'm saying is they don't give a fuck. They can't be assed to craft an enjoyable, worthwhile 'final' boss experience for all their players. The content has been getting lazier and lazier and they're always testing how much they can keep recycling. 

I wanna point out that I'm calling this bitch a 'Final' boss according to the presented story beats and heavy implication that there won't be any significant story updates anytime soon, along with the fact that the credits play after as well. Frankly, I believe that they can and probably will go on well past 100 levels in their typical lazy, scripted and soulless fashion of delivering content.


[b]Slightly Older Review[/b]

I can write an essay on this, but I'll keep it brief. 
The two best and most outstanding qualities of this game are its combat and its fashion/character customization. Everything else..and I mean literally everything else about the game is severely lacking and objectively bad, so much so that its frustrating because the aforementioned is really, really good. 
The dev team is very rigid and stubborn and are excrustiatingly slow to balance and update things related to gameplay.

The combat and fashion as I said are the only things the game has going, but if you wanna get into either of them and enjoy them fully, it will require a lot of irl spending. The fashion items and fun emotes and stuff are buyable with ingame money, but the amount of that you will make as free to play would require you to do a mundane activity in game for 8+ hours to afford one, maybe two, items you might be interested in.

If you enjoy gearing and min maxing, then I highly recommend staying away from this game. There are certain weapon drops that are on the level of myths. There's a thing called Fixa which every weapon can have attached to it and it comes in 5 levels and different effect types. They only [b]recently[/b] made it so that the player can recreate this on a weapon that doesn't have it, either by spending a copious amount of free to play resources you accumlate over the course of several months..(for just a rng chance of getting it on one single weapon in the end) or by whaling on the game obscenely hard. Fixa has existed since the game's release and has always been a major point of contention, which took the devs 3 years to even begin to address.

The only way I could recommend this game is if you intend to play it casually on and off. It's arguably perfect for that and can easily be picked up and dropped. The combat is fun and you'll likely find a weapon and class you enjoy playing. All classes function as dps, so if you enjoy playing support in games you might not be as interested. Raids, bosses and whatever else have no real mmo mechanics that require any team oriented strategy..most of the game's strategy is found in optimizing your dps. 

That's about it..and yes, this was brief for how much could be said about the dev team dropping the ball so hard on a game with this much potential. They will never understand the extent to which they harmed and lost the community and following they had going with this franchise. 
Thanks for taking the time to read my review.

review_text:
More content than previous Just Cause games, but somehow worse in every way. It feels like they wanted to focus more on the grappling hook and decided the best way to do that would be to make everything else vastly worse.

There's more weapon variety, but they all feel weak and have tiny ammo pools. Also you only get two weapon slots now, no grenades, and no explosive charges.
There's more vehicle variety, but they have limited ammo, less weapons, and are generally weaker.
You get more supply drops, but the system is clunky and you only get one item per drop instead of a full loadout.
There's more tether functions, but all of them are clunky and weak.
There's more regions, but now instead of blowing stuff up to liberate towns, there's a pseudo-strategy game layer you get more points for by destroying stuff. Which, in practice, means you basically never have a reason to interact with most of the map. There's also missions to unlock liberating regions, but those missions are painfully repetitive.
The interface is not improved or expanded in any way, it's just atrocious.. Also the graphics look like utter garbage in cutscenes.

Which is a shame, because the AI is genuinely much improved, especially the jet AI. The enemy can now effectively use aircraft instead of circling and then crashing into buildings. Sadly, that's literally the only thing they did better.
