review_text:
I bought the original version of Hakuoki for PSP when it was first released in America. I absolutely loved it!  Ever since hearing about Kyoto Winds, I'd hoped for a release on Steam. My wish was granted, thank you Steam! I have played a decent chunk of the beginning so far and below are my impressions of this new version.

Note: Kyoto Winds is NOT the full game of Hakuoki. It has been split in two. I assume this version ends right as the characters leave Kyoto. Part two (Edo Blossoms) is being released spring 2018. With all the added features I personally don't mind the wait. But if you do it's something to keep in mind. Going forward from here:

The translation for this iteration of the game has changed significantly from it's PSP predecessor. Chizuru - the main heroine has a lot more to say and think here. You see the world through her lens now, which can be good or bad. Depending on your preference. Scenarios play out differently as well with added dialouge. It gives a fresh feeling to a farmiliar tale. Slight nitpick ahead. Some of the translation differences I haven't been too keen on but most are spot on. 

Character portraits now blink and their lips move (most of the time) as they speak. It's a nice little detail. It seems hair movement may also come into play down the line, or at least they did in the new opening cinematic. Speaking of characters there are now three new romance options added to the ballot and three additional routes for the characters with smaller roles in the original game. 

The soundtrack change will be known to PSP players immediately. I loved the old score, I really did but the tracks themselves were very short and grew repetative quickly. I found myself turning the music off after a few playthrough routes. Kyoto Winds contains a completely new OST. This new soundtrack has really captured my attention. It's layered and nuanced really setting the tone well. I can't wait to hear more of it in game.

Options: You can adjust the volume level for music voice and sound effects. Furthermore the voice adjusting goes into far more depth than before. Don't like the sound of a particular character's voice? Or is one voice louder than the others?  Now you can adjust character voices individually. I greatly appreciate this!

Overall I'm pleased with the changes that have been made and would recommened this as a worth while purchase to those who have played the original releaase on PSP.

review_text:
Hello my new brother. I know why you're here.

You're here for the pretty pictures.

Go ahead, have another look at those awesome images  and the video. No, really, go ahead. I'll be here waiting for you when you get back. Trust me on this.

Weren't they pretty? Yes indeed they are. So pretty ...

I know. All of us know. Don't be ashamed. We're all like you. We all understand you. We're your friends. We're your new brothers and sisters. All of use came for the pretty pictures also.

Every
      Single
            One

You'll be surprised to hear that there is even a little bit of a game hidden underneath the prettiness. It's not very special, but that doesn't matter. What matters is that the pictures are pretty.

Don't fight it, it's no use. Again: trust me on this, I know. You are going to buy the game at one point or the other. You can not escape it, it's too late for that. The lure of the pretties is just too strong. Maybe today, maybe tomorrow, maybe next year, but one day you'll get the game and become one of us. Yes my brother, all us of have played it. To the bitter end.

And you'll then agree with me that the only thing that matters is how pretty it all is.

One day, also you will have played the game. And you'll know that it's a gigantic exploration of a world so nightmarish, so alien, that nothing makes sense anymore. A slow exploration, a confusing exploration, an exploration that you'll at times despise.

And you'll then know that the game offers a handful of puzzles. Some of those puzzles are hard, some are easy. But all of them will annoy you in some way, frustrate you even. Not having solved a puzzle will frustrate you and solving a puzzle will frustrate you.

And you'll come to know that the game offers a little bit of combat: combat against a small amount of enemies with a small amount of weapons. And that the combat is frustrating, annoying, slow and that you will come to fear it. Hate it? Yes ... I think hate is the right word.

And you'll even come to realise that the game is telling you a story. A story without words. A story that makes no sense. A story that you'll never quite grasp. Because everything is so alien that even the story is too alien for you.

But none of it matters. Because you'll also come to learn that the game is even prettier than what you see here on the store page. It’s pretty because it is ugly and pretty at the same time. Observe my brother!

Yes, you are going to despise the game, scream at it, rage at it, hate the puzzles, despise the exploration, fear the combat. You'll view upon the game with [b]scorn[/b]. Because the game also views upon you with [b]scorn[/b].

And you'll then *see* that you hate the game and the game hates you not because the game is bad, but because the game wants to hate you and wants you to hate it. The scorn *must* be mutual, for love cannot exist without hate and vice versa.

And despite all of this, you're going to continue playing. Because it is just so pretty. Your senses will be so overwhelmed that you'll not feel the torture anymore, you endure, you want even more scorn.

Those are the things that will be. And for us, those are the things that are. We know. Oh yes, we all know.

Become one with us. You know you cannot escape my brother, it's far too late for that.

I see you soon.

review_text:
When I saw the trailer, I was very excited for Bonelab.

I saw there would be a sequel to one of the best VR games, I thought it would be so good. Unfortunately I found it quite disappointing.

In essence, Bonelab is basically just Boneworks physics ported to quest, with very mediocre improvements. No new enemies (with actually different mechanics I mean), or cool mechanics - except for the avatar changing. The avatar switching feature allowed you to switch between body types, which was quite cool, but still not that much for a sequel.

The gameplay compared to Boneworks is practically the same, with the same enemies. The enemies in the last game were quite flawed, they weren't able to go up inclines, or use weapons, except for the one enemy that could, which didn't really have a physics body. Although, the game was still fun. The problem with Bonelab is that it's just the same game but worse.

The maps in Boneworks were large, complex and cool, with unique enemy encounters that were actually interesting and fun. Different sections provided different moods, like the sewer area, being spooky and dark, or the tower, full of interactable objects and enemies. In bonelab the maps were nowhere near as good, basically always just being a room. Or a less detailed open space area. I think this might be because of the limitations of being on Quest.

Although, Bonelab isn't really such a bad experience, the main problem is the fact that the campaign is way too short to be so expensive, especially with so many flaws. The game is just trying to rely on user-generated content, which is really bad for a 39.99$ game.

In conclusion, Bonelab has a short, mediocre campaign with maps that are limited. It has virtually no improvement on gameplay to Boneworks and is just a quest port of Boneworks' physics engine.
Although, I am not saying that you shouldn't buy it, the user-generated content is probably quite good, though it is very disappointing that the last game had such a good campaign, and how Bonelab failed to improve on the mechanics of Boneworks and have an equally good campaign.

TLDR: Bonelab is not a very good improvement on Boneworks, having a worse and shorter campaign. It lacks any actual improvements on the mechanics of Boneworks and fails to address its shortcomings. Though, it can still be a fun game for those who could enjoy its user-generated content.

Edit: it could be worth buying also because of the fact that there is a mod porting the boneworks campaign to it, although I cannot comment on its quality as I have not played that mod. So, I am not sure whether the mod could capture the full experience of Boneworks.

If I had to rate this game, I'd say 3/5 stars

Pros: 
+ bopping sound track
+ you can feel cool as you do tricks and grinds across the city
+ art style nails that jet set feel
+ level design super cool in some areas
+ boost mechanic can be rewarding once you learn its quirks

Cons:
- sound track only has 1-2 songs by the great Hideki Naganuma and they were already released years ago before this game.
- game has no difficulty, combos are pathetically easy to achieve. Leading to most tasks being beat by sitting on a single infinite grind loop smashing the same trick button over and over.
- level design shockingly weak in some areas, 
- bugs and collectibles that were left in, but you can't actually collect?
- collectibles are weak most leading to uninteresting pallet swaps or music you have already heard.
- boost mechanic feels awkward and often kills all your momentum
- story is weak and can be hard to follow
- characters lack strong personality
- DLC is kind of a weak addition

review_text:
**Graphics and Visuals:**
One of the most significant improvements in PSO2: NGS is its graphics and visuals. The game boasts a more modern game engine and offers stunning open-world environments with impressive character models and special effects. The transition from the original PSO2 is remarkable, making for a visually appealing and immersive experience.

**Gameplay:**
PSO2: NGS retains the fast-paced and fluid action combat that fans of the franchise love. The addition of an open-world format gives players the freedom to explore, and the transition between combat and exploration is seamless. The introduction of a new class, the "Hunter," adds further variety to the gameplay, and players can expect intense boss battles and challenging encounters.

**Character Customization:**
The game continues to excel in character customization, allowing players to create unique avatars. There's an array of costumes, accessories, and hairstyles to make your character stand out, and the customization options are quite extensive.

**Story and Lore:**
While the PSO series isn't necessarily known for its deep storytelling, there's still an interesting lore and story to follow in NGS. The game expands on the existing PSO2 universe, offering more context and background to the world and its inhabitants.

review_text:
I was really let down by this entry in the series. It's riddled with bugs, from vehicles freaking out and stuttering all over the place, to randomly clipping through the world, or just random things not working in general. In just 2 hours of playing this game, I saw more bugs than I have in games releasing in alpha with a single developer.
Not only is the game buggy, but the AI is as dumb as a bag of rocks, and they all share a single brain cell. I don't think the AI even knows how to fly helicopters. I've seen them crash into each other, the ground, or anything and everything else around them. When driving, they will straight up drive off cliffs to their death at full speed. I had 3 or 4 in a row drive off one after the other while chasing me, and I didn't even lead them to it.

When it comes to gameplay, it just sucks. I was constantly running out of ammo, and collecting data was extremely frustrating. You can't cancel it, it resets any time you get shot or knocked off of it, and it takes a solid 10 seconds of waiting for the AI to spawn before I'd be able to finish collecting the data. They would then shoot me, causing it to reset again. Having to do that 3 or 4 times each time I had to collect data wasn't fun. The flight controls for the helicopters are horrible as well, and it's not something that you can just fix by changing your controls. It's just how the game is. Unlike most games where you'd expect using your mouse to rotate the helicopters, it doesn't, or it does but really slowly. So rotating around is slow and clunky. It's also really stupid that the AI will shoot missiles at their own helicopters if you're hanging from them. Every time I tried to hijack a helicopter, by the time I'd reach it, it would immediately be hit and take damage.

Another thing that I found frustrating is how many AI they will send after you. You can be swarmed in seconds by a couple helicopters, jets flying overhead dropping bombs, and trucks with mounted guns firing at you. You get overwhelmed so quickly, and when you're just starting out, it isn't fun.

The game also doesn't like showing or telling you what you're supposed to be doing. After completing every mission, I'd be left confused, wondering if I was actually done or not since nothing would pop up or there'd be no dialogue telling me either. If you use the new AR thing that's supposed to light up objectives, it really isn't that helpful and only does anything when the game tells you to use it.

The menus are also confusing and the controls are weird. Why can't I just press "ESC" to go back? Why does it have to be only the delete button? "1" and "2" open the loadout menu, which is another thing that just doesn't work how you'd normally expect it to. When customising loadouts, you have to press and hold enter while using A and D to switch between options. I've never seen any game do their menu like this before. Even navigating the map or the UI in general just doesn't feel right.

I normally don't care about graphics that much, but for a Just Cause game, it is kind of expected to look good. And for something that came out in only 2018, even on very high settings, it looked like Just Cause 2 on the Xbox 360. I was also sad to discover that unlike in Just Cause 3 where you can take down entire bridges, we're back to not being able to do that again, which was one of my favourite things to do. What surprised me the most was how badly the cut scenes looked, somehow they looked worst, it was like I was watching someone else playing the game but on the lowest settings it could have been set to. They should have just animated them instead of doing it all in engine, I know that would have been extra work but at least it would have looked good, unlike what's in the game now. 

For only around 2 hours of playing this game, I had to compress my list of complaints down to a few main points. Overall, I was really let down by this game. It just feels like a cheap knockoff. Even though I bought this game on sale, I'm still going to try and refund it. Even at a price tag of $5 for the base game, and a couple dlc packs, it's just not worth the time to play the game, even if this game was free I'd still avoid it.

review_text:
What, what a complete letdown.

Bonelab doesn't feel like a sequel.  Nearly every element of the game feels like a step backwards from BoneWorks (with the Graphics and Single-Player campaign feeling like the biggest drawbacks).  

First, just to give you my perspective from where I'm coming from.  I didn't purchase BoneLab because I wanted Garry's Mode but for VR.  I played the original BoneWorks and thought the story and presentation was just enough to keep me going.  I fully expected this sequel to flesh things out a bit more and at least up the production values and presentation, as any sequel that costs $40 should.  To my surprise, after finishing the campaign, I got something that felt hollow, disjointed, and completely lacking in presentation and polish.  Graphics-wise, it doesn't seem better than the original.  BoneWorks, to my recollection, had some pretty good set-pieces, and most of the stages had at least some sort of lighting/details in it that made it distinct from each stage.  

With BoneLab, it feels like a collection of stages strung together, with only the most bare bones amount of effort put in the graphics and presentation.  Most stages feature flat, dull lighting and blocky meshes with some very basic texture-mapping.  Hell, I don't think many of the models even use normal-mapping (or at least the flat lighting is causing me to think that).  In addition, most stages felt claustrophobic and very corridor like.  I remember the original BoneWorks having plenty of wide-open spaces to roam around.  

Worse, there doesn't seem to be any new assets in the game.  Nearly every enemy I can recall running into, feels exactly like previous ones in BoneWorks.  As a matter of fact, I think SLZ re-used the same meshes, or downgraded the detail on them.  

Lastly, the single-player campaign didn't have a sense of coherency or overall narrative ark.  There doesn't seem to be any momentum or build-up to a final event, or anything interesting to encounter.  As I mentioned, most stages are corridors and flat, low-texture-mapped walls.  It feels like someone built a basic UT4 game but forgot to add the assets in.  If this was intentional, I don't remember the first game ever being this bad.  Other then that, the plot was completely un-memorable and after I finished it I thought 'that's it'?

Again, I am just coming  from the perspective of someone who liked the first BoneWorks and it's single-layer campaign.  I wasn't interested in this game for the lulz or the mods.  I just wanted a good experience for my $40, but instead it felt like I overpaid by about $35.  I don't know what Stress Level Zero was thinking when they cooked up this sequel and its story.  It really feels unpolished and that lack of effort was put in to rush it out as quickly as possible.  It almost feels like a cash grab.

If you want my opinion on each of the boys/dating routes:

Toshizo Hijikata
The father you always looked up to and admired, who rarely says they're proud of you without a backhanded comment. If you've got neglectful daddy issues, Hijikata's your man.

Souji Okita
He's the reason your mother would tell you "he's only mean because he likes you."
If you like being bullied, degraded, threatened with bodily harm, then heavily flirted with in a confusing mixed-message banter, Okita's more than happy to roast you.

Hajime Saito
Silent, sullen, a man of few words. He's the shy emo kid (even has his hair half in his face). If you want someone that is aloof, but then uncharacteristically dotes you, Saito will leave you on read and get back to you later.

Heisuke Toudou
Very much the "boyish charm" trope. Heisuke reminds me of that boisterous and rakous middle-school type romance. If you want an adventure (and maybe a headache from loud yelling and screaming), Toudou will drag you with him.

Sanosuke Harada
This is the one you take home to mom. He self admits to a colored past, but is one of those rare gems that isn't broken by their experiences and instead turns into someone amazing. He's confident, calm, compassionate, but also a realist, all at the same time. Excellent sense of humor and even more fun when drunk (personally, my ideal guy, 12/10). If you want a husband, marry Harada.

Shinpachi Nagakura
Meat head through-and-though. This is the guy that goes to the YMCA and dead lifts a 350lb rack just so he can slam it on the floor hard enough for all the women sculpting their asses on the elliptical machines to turn and look at him. If your idea of romance is babysitting a massive sack of childishly impulsive muscles, Nagakura would love to showboat for you.

Keisuke Sanan
Sanan is creppy from the very start. With an almost hissing pattern of speech, and those extra sharply squinted eyes, he gives me evil Orochimaru vibes. If you've ever wanted to date the school shooter, Sanan would be happy to tell you his body count.

Susumu Yamazaki
Ponytail mullet boy. The silent protector that lurks in the shadows. Despite being a ninja, he's not very edgey or broody, but rather even tempered and personable. Kind of plain in flavor, but still enjoyed it. If you want mayonaise flavored romance, pick Yamazaki.

Hachiro Iba
Literally a love-sick puppy (I mean, who hasn't heard the story of Hachi?). He can be charmingly forward, and also fiercely protective. If you call his name, I'm sure you'd see his tail wagging. If you want a really good boy, go for Iba.

Kazue Souma
Brown noser. Totally sucks up to the lead characters, and overall was simple-minded as far as character dynamics go. If you used to have a crush on the teacher's pet, date Souma.

Ryouma Sakamoto
As strait as a strait-shooter can get. Incredibly blunt, and to the point. He borders on that obnoxious machismo, but, he has a few moments where he humbles himself. If you want Japanese Johnny Bravo, go for Sakamoto.

Chikage Kazama
Typical "misunderstood bad boy." Says a few poetic things, but is still a deplorable sociopath. If you like guys who are mentally detached with agression issues, Kazama would be happy to kidnap you (repeatedly).

review_text:
Edit 12/26/23

When I first downloaded the game and saw it was ~2gb I was genuinely surprised. How did they manage to fit so much content into such a small package? (btw JSRF compressed is about the same amount, maybe a little more)

....

Then I played the game. There is no content. This game was obviously made for the switch first and everyone else second. It sucks that consoles are what holds games back from their true potential nowadays. And after sitting on the game for a while, modding it (which did improve my perception of the gameplay) and beating it, I have come to the conclusion that I am still right.

I remember when some of the first trailers about this game were coming out back in 21 and they were looking for a voice actress to act as an analogue for DJ Prof. K... They used her for 1 trailer and did nothing else. I really expected a sort of narrator or something similar which would have added some excitement to the story but nope. Yes I am aware that JSR had minimal voice acting but I strongly feel that since this game heavily relies on its story element, it needed that extra assist in the voice department. The same 3 sounds for each character just doesn't cut it. Assets are constantly reused and the game is boring by the third level.

This game is a sad, sad reincarnation of a fantastic series that thankfully is being revived by SEGA. If there's one thing this game did right, it's make SEGA realize the massive mistake they made abandoning Jet Set Radio. 

One thing I did like about the game is the pattern-specific graffiti, that was a cool idea. One thing I absolutely hate in this game is the police system, its not exciting to be chased by the cops, its a major annoyance. (Luckily mods fixed that)

I like Team Reptile, and I think they absolutely nailed the cel-shaded art style. However, a game of this genre shouldn't feel as flat as an arcadey fighting game like LLB does, and so in this aspect, they failed. 

If I had to give a rating for this game out of 10, I'd give it a 5. So buy it half off and have fun.

Or just download an emulator and play Jet Set Radio Future and have some real fun!

review_text:
OPEN LETTER TO THE DEVELOPERS:

A very awesome VR "Left 4 Dead" alike. Changed just enough to make some fresh new mechanics that up play-ability over L4D, IMO. The sad thing is, the difficulty is very, VERY much too hard. I can blow through the entire level on Veteran (normal) difficulty, but when I get to the boss, I get destroyed in very short order. This is in single player, and it doesn't get much better for two players. The higher difficulties are a raging inferno of mass runs of zombies that overwhelm, and bosses that eradicate.

Now here's the BIG problem with all of this: The only way to get the better gear is to play the higher difficulties! I was very excited to farm and play this game, slowly working up to getting better and better gear based on random drop probabilities, but with the "hard" and "hardest" modes being the ONLY way to get most of the good upgrades, you end up stuck at a dead end once you've beaten veteran difficulty a few times! You NEED the better gear to play higher difficulties, and you can't get it without playing them! This chicken and egg dilemma really lowers the replay-ability.

Now, I know, yes I KNOW there will be some people who can stomp through the higher difficulties and have no problem, but you can't make a game for the hardcore players and have it be long-term successful. You need to make the WHOLE game open and accessible to more casual players, like me, to keep us coming back. See my total played time? Yeah, I'm pretty much done at this point. If the loot system was overhauled so I could get better gear without playing the impossible difficulties? I would EASILY have hundreds of hours to sink into this, because everything else is fantastic..

DEVS: THIS UPGRADE SYSTEM IS A HUGE MISTAKE, AND NEEDS TO BE CHANGED ASAP TO KEEP PLAYERS IN YOUR GAME!

review_text:
Might be someones jam, but not mine.  Ground combat I found terrible.  The game does allow you to switch between two combat modes, one more geared for a shooter and one geared for an MMO, but switching between them was tedious and clunky at best.  I found that no matter which mode I was in, I was having difficulty getting anything done.  Shooter mode does not really blend well with interacting with objects, manipulating the environment and using the tools you have.  And MMO mode doe not really blend with a shooter game style.  Plus, ground combat was slow and unsatisfying

Space combat in my opinion was worse.  it felt forced in because it was a Star Trek game, developers should give you a choice if you want to do it, or just "AI" it up and "roll" on chance to hit.  Felt uncontrollable, but I do not play a lot of space sims.

both of these lead to the point that it felt like the game has all these elements forced in because it is Star Trek.  You need to interact with computers, shoot and fly a space ship.  If you dont like one of those components you are stuck, because you need to want to do them all.  If you are down for all of them, and can remember a plethora of keys, you might have some fun...

If it were not for microtransactions.  I get it is free to play, but so much content is locked behind paywalls and by the time you have what you want, you have spent a lot more money than a 60 dollar title.  Not to mention the microtransactions are confusing for a new player, I have no idea what is good, what I want, and the game just kind of throws it all in your face to figure out.

Lastly, the environments were also pretty bad.  Since its an MMO it has to make large, open environments to fit the amount of people that might be coming through, but hallways felt HUGE, like three stories tall on a space ship that should be 1 story tall, rooms that were mostly empty except for a console or two in the middle.  Just not enough life to it.

Bottom line, if you are a Star Trek Super Fan, and love ground combat, remembering lots of keys, space combat, MMO's and figuring it out for yourself, its a good gamble.  Otherwise, wait for them to make focused games for Star Trek (like a shooter OR space flight simulator...will never happy I know).

review_text:
....This is one of those rare games that stun me, in a bad way. I have no idea how this game sold enough copies to warrant a sequel. I truly did give this a second shot without any prejudice. Thanks for the free weekend, but I genuinely can't even play this for free.

Along with the first game, this is one of the most boring video games I've ever played in my entire life. And I've played A LOT of them.

It's as if they said "What are the most boring parts of linear games? What are the most boring parts of open world games? Let's combine them together!" and started to make the game with this vision. In the most boring setting they could think of. Nothing you haven't seen before in any other game ever made. No flavour. Nothing cool or extraordinary. Like the entire game itself.

The main character has the personality and charisma of a wooden stick. If you don't have a "character", which you don't, it's better to have a silent protagonist. None of the other characters are interesting or charismatic or have anything interesting or cool to say, either.

The dialogue is absolutely banal. Go outside right now, and talk to a total stranger about the weather or something. I can guarantee you, it will be more interesting than any cutscene or dialogue in this game. The writing is so amateurish that they don't even follow the "generic" conventions. Example: A stealth section or even a tutorial section can be used to expose the player to some information about the world. But nope, the guards just talk about their boring everyday lives as you sneak by them. The most amusing part of this game for me was seeing the store page, where it's tagged as "Story Rich". Now THAT, is rich. It's also tagged as "Atmospheric, Realistic, Immersive". None of these adjectives are applicable to this game whatsoever. Though maybe "Realistic" does apply, since the experience of playing this game is close to being as painful, boring and miserable as it must have been in Medieval Europe, in a mental and conceptual sense.

The combat system... Don't even get me started. Just play "Mount & Blade", "Chivalry" or "MORDHAU" to see how a proper medieval 1st person melee combat system is done. Kingdom Come feels like playing "Simon Says" compared to those games. And the rest of the game isn't interesting enough to warrant going "whatever, let's just play as an archer." and ignoring it.

All in all, I invite anyone who's a fan of this game to... play more video games. "Kingdom Come" does not fill any hole within any library of video games, unless there are enthusiasts of experiencing boring medieval life through the lens of a buffoon who's bereft of any personality and charm, while playing the most excruciatingly tedious parts of every RPG ever made.

review_text:
I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

review_text:
Game is fine. But it is a letdown in many ways.

Difficulty: Easy. very easy. Controls are lenient. You can easily miss jumps and go wrong ways and still hold combos. Died a couple times to weird game situations (not bugs).
The music is good. Not great like the Jet Set Radio games. But they would get stuck in my head and they were nice. The Hideki Naganuma are actually the only ones I don't care for. The music is more tame in multiple ways, less punk, more mainstream. Less exciting, more chill.
Game has many mechanics added to it that would be great to see in the previous games. No complaints there really. Maybe just that they make one so powerful that there is not much risk/excitement when playing.
Basically all the characters are super lame. The one I can think of is cool in a sensei kind of way, not a punk kind of way.
The levels are entirely forgettable. Every stage is walk around, spray some graffiti, then do some menial tutorials disguised as competing with other crews. The level design in terms of riding around and doing cool lines, felt lame to me. It feels like there are big obvious lines that you take, nothing really on the side.
The story is down to earth in this game relative to the zaniness of the Jet Set Radio games. But the zaniness meshed well with the punk nature of the Jet Set Radio Games. With this game, the combination of down to earth + lame characters + being not punk, doesn't work, and the story feels both flat and faux.
The "genre" now has skateboards and BMX which is cool, but it exposes one of the most egregious sins of this game: there are not many tricks. Even worse, characters do not have unique tricks! This may sound unimportant, but in Jet Set Radio Future, spamming the trick buttons looked nice and felt nice. In this game, the tricks are kind of cool, but there are only the few tricks that you are stuck with, and get old quickly. One used to be able to play a different character to change things up. Not so here.
The only thing that differentiates characters is which annoying voice you choose to hear. No stats, and as told above, the tricks don't change.

If this game added more tricks, tricks per character, and added a fun post-game, this game would be good enough for me to recommend. But it feels like a lame story that gave me no emotion and left me with no post game to play with.
If one didn't play the Jet Set Radio games, this game will be amusing, but nothing special nor impactful. But it is a moist version of the Jet Set Radio games, and feels incomplete/rushed out. You should play Jet Set Radio Future instead. Jet Set Radio is cool, but it is pretty old and janky.

review_text:
8/10

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun is a really solid stealth game with a fair amount of tactical/strategy elements, and I really enjoyed playing it for a few weeks on my Steam Deck. Where most stealth games use more of a first-person or a third-person view and concentrate on a single character or maybe a pair of characters, Shadow Tactics takes a larger isometric view of the map and uses squads of 2-5 characters with varying special abilties. I really enjoyed that this large-scale vision allows you plan an approach towards your mission goals, especially in conjunction with its planning/execution system. Shadow Tactics allows you to plan and set up moves to be executed at the same time, so that a character who is in disguise and talking to a pair of guards can stab one guard while a second character sneaks up and stabs the other guard, while a third character throws a shuriken at the guard on a rooftop who might see the other two getting ganked. This really enables a lot of skillful tactical planning and execution, presenting you with both difficult challenges to figure out how to approach, and a reasonably wide variety of skills to try to resolve those challenges. 

The game's story wasn't anything special, but I did enjoy the presentation, especially the animated scenes between each mission. There was one particular scene when the entire squad is reunited that I thought was particularly impactful, aided by how the scene physically unfolds. I would've been interested to see some gameplay mechanics that maybe tied into how you decided to accomplish each mission, perhaps making your decisions a bit more impactful in subsequent missions. Absent any such impacts, I just played the whole game as a full-on murder machine, making sure none of my foes lived through any mission. There was one particular vignette that occurred during the mission at an invaded village that I went far out of my way to try to prevent from happening, and I was pretty disappointed that the game didn't support my heroic intervention. Adding some minor elements like this could've really helped elevate the game, to add "small stories" to the game's larger narrative. 

Shadow Tactics was a fairly difficult game, even on "Normal" difficulty mode, which did make it a little grind-y at times. Overall though, I think its a really good addition to both the stealth and the tactical strategy genres. The core gameplay loop of watching, planning, and trying to pull off your plan works really well, especially because the game generally makes it very easy to try again (at least on Normal difficulty) if something goes wrong. I've always enjoyed the watch/plan/execute cycle in other stealth/assassination games, but the squad-based strategy element really elevated the gameplay here. If you enjoy either of the stealth or strategy genres, I think you'll find Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun to be worth your while, especially if you're playing on the Steam Deck.

I've had this game in my library for years. I bought it because everyone says that it is SO GOOD, so I wanted to give it a try.

- PC version also didn't get the updates that the Switch and mobile versions have. They are much nicer looking than the PC version.
- Controls feel clunky. 
- Icons occasionally don't relate to the action you're taking.
- With the resolution being so small it could be hard to see memories to find.

Once I got the game actually working I found it pretty dull. The characters all felt the same throughout their lives. The kids felt too old and the older versions felt too young. River may have two medical conditions but they never name them, so it confused me about why her having autism (I assume) was so terrible. 

Once I made it to the end, some things became clear but then the 'contractual agreement' of Neil and Eva pretty much ruined everything for me. I didn't feel sad, I didn't cry, I was mostly just bored.

review_text:
1 hour in or justabout and i can already see why this game scored poorly. Why is the text for items Gray????, why do your attacks have priority when you hit enemies first? Why the hell are there long ass corridors, ladders, and other such things that you can't go through faster when there is literally no threat around you? The animations and models look nice but when paired with baffling gameplay decisions its really hard to recomend this to anyone.

Another annoyance/issue, the inventory spaces are so low and the fabricators to sell stuff are so far apart from each other you either need to backtrack for the extra money or abandon good sellable loot.

After finishing the game: My final thoughts are basically as listed above. With the following caveat: this game has potential. I would like to see a follow up, but they need to address the problems listed above and they need to either make bosses beatable without guns or just add items to throw at the boss available during the boss fights. The first boss fight on the Tram was especially annoying because if you don't have any ammo, you can't get any mid fight and anytime you attempt to melee you get auto countered and quickly die from that. Atop that there is nothing to throw at the boss for ranged hits and you can't grip it at all. The devs noticed this issue with the boss fights after this but never addressed it for the Tram boss fight. Simple changes to boss mechanics would have saved players so much trouble.

Update: a couple more hours in. Only by Chapter 4 do you get more inventory space (double in fact) at which point you also have more Fabricators to sell stuff at so the loot situation is borked to all heck. At least so far. The Upgrade system and weapon unlock system is also absurd. To unlock new weapons like the skunk gun you need to find the hidden schematics (HIDDEN SCHEMATICS EMPHASIS ON HIDDEN) and bring them to a fabricator. This takes 1 inventory space and when you are forced to drop stuff to possibly get a better gun you will immediately hate the loot system. A simple fix would have been to increase the carry capacity earlier on, however the devs never decided to do this. The game isn't harder by having a smaller inventory, just more frustrating. Anytime you are punished by playing well and using less resources in battle due to arbitrary restrictions like inventory. You actively de-incentivize players from enjoying your game.

First off, I think you should know that this is indeed a fun game, but technical issues have to be fixed for it to be worth imo.
This is essentially Helldivers but in First Person (even though technically Helldivers is inspired by the Starship Trooper movies, kinda funny since Sony also has part of production and distribution rights of the Starship Troopers :P)
The game as of now is pretty fun but it is plagued by a lot of graphical issues (most likely since its UE 5). 
Any sort of Upscaling methods other than Unreal's engine based one tends to cause an issue where the screen occupies the top left quadrant while the other 3 sections have extended lines in them. This fixes itself sometimes and the other times its gives you a flashing screen like situation since it keeps going back and forth from normal to this.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3348852135

Other than that, the base performance of the game is also kinda bad, with frame rates dropping to as low as 26 on Low 1080p settings when you get into the action (playing on the RTX 3060 6GB version). With the minimum specs required being a GTX 970 you'd expect better optimisation (I understand that the game just came out of early access so I'm just stating these as issues that will most likely be fixed)

Currently, the price is kinda close to that of Helldivers 2 (in my region atleast) so when you compare it that way, HD2 seems like the better choice, but you can't get a FPS experience in HD2. 

Recommended, if you currently have a decently powerful system.
Else I'd suggest you to wait for a while. This game has potential, as long as the devs keep supporting it and people who play MP Co-op FPS games stick with it.
I would like to give a neutral recommendation lol but since that is not possible we'll go with a No.. for now.

review_text:
This games wishes for you to suffer. I am not talking about a difficult game where you can master, mess up, and even get a bad ending; this is a game that was made for you to loathe it while playing it.

Now, on the surface, this sounds fun. After all, having the odds stacked against you and legitimately having a chance to lose is awesome. I love difficult games. However, this game is not difficult; it's a knowledge check.

If you do not wish to be spoiled, do not hover over these. However, I consider these the bare minimum you'll need to play the game and not want to shoot yourself. 

[spoiler] Hoard food, the game time speeds up. Literally, it speeds up. If you do not hoard food, you are going to starve and it's not even funny. The game moves twice as fast towards the ending. Even traveling takes multiple hours of in game time. You will not have time to get a lot of food unless you do it early. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Do the antibiotic questline for the panacea or Rubin will die no matter what. This is stupid, and simply a knowledge check from you. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Hoard fingernails, do not use them early in the game. The cost will rise from one fingernail per fast travel to two. You will need a bunch of them in the late game to have a chance at good time management. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] As stated earlier, time does move faster, and it's a lot faster. Account for that in any way. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] You can get herbs by going to the south east of the map past the steppe to the steppe village. Do this in the early days or you will have a bad time. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Hoard shmowders early, do not waste them, the little girl with a bob hair cut can trade shmowders on top of the dead item shop. Trade with these people as often as you can. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Honestly, even hoarding shmowders is only if you care enough to save the people in this game. Unlike Pathologic Classic, there is no real penalty for letting people die; you do not need to save anyone. I think that was a horrible decision since you're literally a plague doctor and it added natural difficulty in the first game, but fuck me amirite? [/spoiler]

These mechanics should not be a thing in the game. Multiplayer.

Can't recommend buying it, just not a lot here for the price, coming in at close to $40 in AUS
Will occasionally fire it up on my steam deck as it's perfect for it, but aside from that?
Rooftops and Alleys will be collecting digital dust in my library.

I saw the trailer for this game awhile ago and i saw a few videos on it and it looked like it would be fun, ohh 
boy was i wrong....
 
STEALTH:

The stealth is annoying to deal with, trying to be sneaky and somehow get spotted by someone that saw me take down an enemy from 100+ meters away (or what ever it is in the game) I could understand if it was a sniper that saw me, but no it was a normal grunt that had a small window of sight on me take down the enemy and instantly alerts the map and die because of how little health u have. 

UPGRADES:

The upgrades u can get are neat some of them are really helpful, like thermal vision, auto marking enemies that are nearby (mask upgrade) and some others. However the other skills that u can get are kinda bland, u cant have all the skills on, u have to choose a certain skill trees. So u cant have 3 special ammo slots u can only have 2 or u can only have certain skills on depending on what skills u have active.

GAMEPLAY:

The gameplay is similar to Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 with some changes like the"high tech" mask you get. The weapons are alright as far as customization and attachments. The gun play was a bit annoying because there would be times where i would shoot someone in the head 2-3 times and they wouldn't die (wasn't a heavy btw) instead they alert the rest of the map that they were taking fire.

STORY:

The Story is very short like the 3rd game (less then 6 hours) there are only 6 "contract missions" with main targets, challenges and collectables to complete that will give that contract a percent complete. The only reason it took me 12 some hours to beat the game it because I would keep getting spotted and i would either die or I would restart from the checkpoint manually. If u want to go back through and 100% everything i would estimate it would take a total 15-20ish hours to fully 100% the game, which i normally do if i enjoyed the game but since i didn't enjoy it Im not going to do that.

Overall and Price:

Overall I would rate the game a 5/10 for all the said things above and for the price of $30 I don't really think this game is worth it maybe if it was one sale for $15 then maybe. I am going to try for a refund for this game if possible.

review_text:
"Scorn," with its striking blend of biomechanical horror and enigmatic puzzles, leaves an indelible mark on the gaming landscape. Its foray into a world inspired by the likes of H.R. Giger presents a compelling, if at times polarizing, experience giving the same feelings I had playing 'I have no voice and I must scream"

Pros:
- Aesthetic and Art Direction: The game's visual presentation is a masterclass in horror and biomechanical design, Though very phallic it is both grotesque and captivating. 
- Puzzles: Offering a challenging yet rewarding experience, the puzzles in "Scorn" are a highlight. They require a blend of logical thinking and environmental interaction, and while few and far between it's a delight when they happen.
-Atmosphere and Sound Design: Beyond its visual horror, "Scorn" excels in it's sound and music design really making everything feel so unnerving like the world it pulls you in.

Cons:
- Combat Mechanics: Combat in "Scorn" often feels clunky and out of place like something they added after but never fully fleshed out... pun intended.
- Save System and Checkpoints: The game's approach to saving and checkpoints is bad. You never truly know when it's saved so you can quit and checkpoint seem to be awkwardly back, so you are stuck watching cutscenes over and over.
- Narrative Clarity and Direction: While "Scorn"tries to tell it's story through the environment it in my opinion found itself falling a little flat (especially in the beginning) and not truly telling a story as strong as I think it could.

"Scorn" navigates the thin line between a masterpiece of horror and a test of patience. It's an unforgettable journey through a beautifully grotesque world, albeit one that might occasionally scorn its travellers with gameplay and technical blemishes. I give it 7/10 suspiciously shaped keys into suspiciously shaped keyhole.

review_text:
Editing this review: Upon loading this game up, the morning after posting my review, I've found that roughly 10 hours of progress did not save, and I have gone from near the end of the game, to right back to the middle of it. I had initially reviewed this game as having very few bugs, none of which were game breaking. I now cannot recommend the game as is, due to having literally lost nearly 50% of my progress in the main story. Buyers beware, until this gets patched, you may lose save data, and lots of it.

------(Original review below)--------

I haven't finished the story mode yet but this game is so much fun omg. It really does carry on the legacy of Jet Set Radio, and it's doing it well :)

The gameplay just flows, the soundtrack is amazing, the character designs are cool, many of the map designs are very reminiscent of the games that clearly inspired this one, and the characters are pretty cool, both in terms of their designs, and their interactions, since Bomb Rush Cyberfunk actually seems to have a proper, coherent, story... something that would likely have never been possible if this game was published by Sega lol.

One thing that I absolutely do not support, whether this game's funky af or not, is paywalling characters on release. Day 1 DLC is bullshit, whether you're selling me the spiritual successor to JSRF or not, and it's dirty to have even tried it in the first place. If you want to sell DLC, sell DLC, don't separate part of a finished product on release and try to sell it back to me as an additional purchase. $40 USD is a good price for a game, but you're not about to tell me that you couldn't have included these in the game, come on.

If there was a neutral option of some kind, where I could say, "Yes, but no." for this game, I absolutely would. I don't agree with the DLC, and I don't think it would be a good idea to support the practice from any developer, including Team Reptile. The game is super fun, but I really dislike that one aspect of it. Were it not for that, this game would be an immediate 10/10 from me :)

--(This part is no longer accurate, as of the day after having posted my review)-- Bomb Rush Cyberfunk has been a relatively bug free experience for me so far, almost none for 99% of my playthrough. I have encountered a few bugs so far, including one that seemingly disabled the in-game phone camera and the ability to view pics that you've taken, as well as another, separate, bug that would briefly flash a dialogue box between scenes in a couple of cutscenes, but that's really nothing super game breaking.

Honestly, if you like JSR or JSRF, you'll love this game. If you like the character and art designs of either game, or of Lethal League, you'll love this game. If you enjoy skating games, or platformers, you'll love this game. 

Bomb Rush Cyberfunk has so much love that's been put into it, and this is something that's very clear, everywhere you look in this beautiful, cel shaded, world, and with a bombastic, funky, soundtrack to boot. Beyond the scummy implementation of DLC on release, I would say this is a game worth playing, even at full (non-discounted) price.

review_text:
This game is like [b]Rocket League meets golfing.[/b] The concept is much more fun in comparison to its competitor, IMO. However, the game isn't without its flaws. I put 8 hours into this game so here are some of my thoughts.

[b]Pros:[/b]

➤ As I already mentioned, the concept is pretty unique, fun and addictive
➤ The mechanics are easy to learn but hard to master, also they are somewhat more complex than in Rocket League, making the game all that much more interesting
➤ Varied vehicle customazation
➤ A lot of active and passive skills you can equip
➤ Great amount of maps
➤ Active updates
➤ Free battle pass
➤ Decent achievements worth grinding for
➤ In-game mission which keep you coming back

[b]Neither:[/b]

➤ The playerbase is small, you tend to play with the same people over and over again, most of the matches therefore are filled with half bots but the queue times are short, meaning you don't need to wait usually more than a minute
➤ In the first hour you kinda get to know everything about this game but you can always improve when it comes down to your skills (for some it gets repetitive real quick)

[b]Cons:[/b]

➤ There are a very few game modes you can choose from (solo = time trial, more players/bots = casual + ranked)
➤ Uncertain future, due to the small playerbase, I can see the game dying in the near future. Most likely, I see the game going free-to-play (the fact, the game was already bundled just makes my theory all that more plausible)
➤ No voice chat (it doesn't matter since there are no teammodes, still it would be a nice thing to have and let those, who don't want it, simply mute it in the settings)

[b]To sum it up,[/b] it's worth giving this game a try. After all, the game is still in early access. I had the chance of trying a demo during Steam's next fest and it was, hands down, one of the best games I tried. Maybe wait for a bit. 

I have my [b]doubts[/b] about the future of this game as I said above and even though the game seems to be getting updated regularly, it's mostly new maps and cosmetics, there doesn't seem to have been any new gamemodes or any groundbreaking updates since the game was released to the public.

My son got this game for from his uncle, so we installed it on his computer and he started playing. By the end of the week he had 12 hours on this game. This was horrible for me, as it was already hard for me to find ways to spend time with my son, as he is always out with his friends or just watching YouTube. So i decided to make a Steam account and get this game to see if I could maybe play alongside him. I loaded into the game and started playing but I was stuck on what you where supposed to do. I asked my Son for help and he let me borrow his controller. Me and my son then played in turns and I loved it as it was the best time I had spent with my Son since my wife had died. This game has ever since brought me and my son closer again and now we actually spend time together outside the house together as well. This game reminded me that there's fun to be had in everything, and it has brought both me and my son many happy memories.

review_text:
I wish we had a 1-5 star rating system instead of a simple yes or no recommendation.  I hate your needing to fully recommend it or fully condemn a game with no middle ground.  It isn’t that simple.  This game has some really good parts, but to me, the bad parts are pretty significant hurdles to get over.

The aiming system on the sniper rifle is just awful and a significant step backwards from this games previous iteration. It’s very clunky and nearly impossible to use accurately at times.  The way Ghost Warrior 3 did it was way better.  Different isn’t always better.

To me, and this is a huge flaw, I hate that you are forced to use full automatic when using your assault rifle.  I’m a former Marine.  On only the rarest of occasions would you ever use this fire select mode as it’s inaccurate and a great waste of the limited ammunition you are provided.  Single shot is way better.  It’s way more accurate.  It’s way less wasteful and it’s less noisy.  A surgical one shot kill is almost always going to be better than spraying and praying.  This is the only first person shooter I’ve ever played that doesn’t offer you a fire select mode.  I realize that this is more of a Hitman, slow and stealthy shooter and not an aggressive run and gun FPS, but there will always be players that want to play a little less stealthy and use their assault rifle more often.  These rifles, like their real world counterparts, should have a fire mode selection option and the ability to equip a silencer like the Ghost Recon series games do.

Lastly, one of the biggest negatives of all is the aggravating game save.  Saves are few and very far between.  You can be over an hour of slow painstaking maneuvering into the mission and have to leave for some reason (say for dinner) and nothing gets saved and you maddeningly have to start the whole mission over from the beginning.  We need way more frequent saves.  Nobody want to go all the way back to a very long mission and start from scratch.  It’s rage inducing.

On a positive note though, the graphics in the Kolchak Harbor campaign are simply stunning.  They’re mind blowing visually.  Some of the other locations are very elaborate and very well done.  I found myself ignoring the mission objectives at times and just looking around to take it all in.  I loved the water at Kolchak Harbor.

Because of the flaws at this time, I can’t recommend this game just yet, certainly not at full price.  If you can get it on sale,  then go ahead and buy it as it does have potential and I’m hoping the developer will address these issues in time.

The flaws I listed could easily be fixed and when they get addressed, I will give this game a enthusiastic  “yes” recommendation.

The UI is based upon a small-screened platform, trying to hide everything is collapsed menus and scrollbars. The scrollbars cannot be grabbed, and flicking the mouse does not keep it sliding at all. So, enjoy your literal 50 clicks to get down the troop window and 5 clicks to rotate through all your resources you have. The collapsable menus hide as little as 5 buttons, making many of them pointless if the developers allowed for the UI to be scaled down.

Enjoy your ads.

Of course, many of the useful units are locked behind the pay-currency of "Nanopods." In the gameplay of F2P to Premium, an analogy would be that of apples to rockets, respectively, not apples to oranges in many other games. F2P can build up resources, but you'll never be able to defend yourself within reason, so your position as F2P continues to fight against you in multiple ways.

If you enjoy this type of game, don't play this game in particular. Find anything else.

review_text:
Cronos is a game that wears its inspirations on its sleeve. From stomping downed enemies and ammo boxes, to collecting statues to solve a puzzle-locked door, it is undeniably clear where BLOOBER got many of the their ideas from. With such perfect examples of Survival-Horror shooters as Dead Space and Resident Evil 4, Cronos could have ended up as one of two things, a pale imitation, or a heartfelt and passionate love letter. 
In my opinion, it is very much the latter. 

To me, Cronos feels completely and utterly original. 
The story is plenty good to keep your attention, with a few semi-predictable twists to spice things up.
The combat, although familiar, is done very well, and while the variety of weapons offer little more than another way to shoot an enemy in the face, each gun is truly fun to discover, upgrade, and use. 
Last but not least, the sound design is truly something special. If Cronos where a living thing, the score would be the pulsing heart, pumping life into every encounter with dark synth melodies and bass-lines. 

When it comes to the familiar ground being tread by Cronos, the whole is undeniably greater than the sum of its parts. 

9/10

review_text:
This is more a comment to self, than a review to others. At the time of writing it has "Very Positive" rating on steam.

For myself, I wanted to understand whether I want to invest time to master "very steep learning curve" that the game boasts or not. I played a bit and I also read a lot of reviews, visited the discord and the game wiki and reddit.

My conclusion was to pass it up. Here is why:

* It seems that this is a game where you inevitably fail. The goal is to survive some predetermined number of years in a number of villages, however the corruption mechanics makes sure you cannot do that forever, and sooner or later your painstakingly created villages are lost. This is not bad per se, it's just I personally dislike this type of setup
* The "steep learning curve" is mostly because game does not tell you what does what. E.g. What buildings do what, etc, there are some disparate hint windows, that help, but they are not enough. There is no good game manual, no good wiki and no good in-game reference.
* Notification system does not let you easily locate where something happened
* Font is too small if you do not have perfect eyesight. You can scale HUD, but the default option is "RECOMMENDED" so I'm worried that if I scale it, the UI won't fit, or that it will leave less useful space on screen than required for the game to be playable. review_text:
Overall, I enjoyed playing through Hiveswap Act 2: the art style was pleasing, the soundtrack was great and had several gems, the writing was on point and the story, while admittedly a bit on the boring side, was still something I enjoyed following. There are a LOT of different item and character interactions, a good amount of which brought a smile to my face as I was exploring the hellhole full of violence, death and segregation that is Alternia.

But the game has its flaws. It is too buggy for a game we've waited three years for, and I already had the same qualm for the previous game in the series. For example, I've had a handful of objects making me walk around the area for a good five seconds for no apparent reason upon inspecting them (the only one I can remember right now is the barnacle in the cave). In addition, it felt like the overall quality of the game's animated sequences had decreased quite a bit compared to Act 1's, which was especially noticeable during certain cutscenes.

What I found most annoying about this game though is how much backtracking the game makes you do towards the latter half of the story: while the things you did in-between the endless area switching you had to do were fine (pretty entertaining at times, too), the endless walking, door-opening, walking, door-opening, walking, escalator-using cycle made the story feel like it dragged on and on. That is a real shame, because I think I would have enjoyed this part of the story a lot more if it were not for the absurd amount of backtracking.

However, Act 2's saving grace is definitely the characters and their interactions with Joey and Xefros. Characters like Marvus, Tyzias and Elwurd made me feel like this whole ordeal was worth it - I have no doubt I wouldn't have bothered to finish the game if it didn't have such fun and interesting characters. I'd say this all culminated during the [strike]Phoenix Wright[/strike] legislaceration segment, which I thought was great fun and helped the characters shine. There are a few bad eggs here and there (Zebruh), but all in all, I really enjoyed getting to spend more time with the characters I got to meet in the Friendsim series.

Was this game worth the three years of waiting? No! The game felt way too short and buggy for it to be the case; if it had come out in Spring 2018, its initial release date, I wouldn't feel nearly as conflicted about it as I do now. Do I think this is still a good game? Well it sure has its flaws, but its upsides outweigh them just enough for me to be able to say Act 2 is at least a nice experience, at least in my opinion. I will absolutely lose my shit if Act 3 takes another 5 years to get released, though.

review_text:
I honestly do not know how to feel about this game. I struggled for a bit on how to sum up how I felt. I needed to sleep overnight to really gather my feelings about it. It’s also hard to say exactly my thoughts in depth about the game without spoiling it, and I refuse to add spoilers into my reviews. For a game that is primarily story-based, I’ll attempt to do my best.

To the Moon is a visual novel made in the format of a cheap RPG Maker game. The artwork, I have to be honest here, doesn’t really look that good. It’s bland, cheap-looking, and doesn’t do enough to distinguish itself from other RPG Maker games. If I showed you this game without telling you what it was, you would simply think it was more RPG Maker shovelware. I won’t harp on this too much, though, because I think that it is absolutely possible to create art even in the form of something that looks cheap or indistinguishable from other games in the same engine. However, it is noticeable, which is why I bring it up. The music in To the Moon is stunning and beautiful. The main piano motif they use for River is fantastic. It’s moving, and really helps weave this emphasis into the game’s somber scenes, and it is a song that becomes synonymous with her. That seems to be by design, so good on them for that. 

The issue with To the Moon is the writing.

I was stunned when I learned that this game only has one writer when the credits rolled. Genuinely shocked. While playing through the entirety of To the Moon, it felt like two writers were clashing against one another’s styles. It’s as if they both wanted to tell different stories. The tone constantly shoots itself in the foot. The cause of this are the game’s two main protags, Eva & Watts. Without spoiling too much, their job is to essentially explore the memories of patients to grant them a last wish that they can experience in their mind during their final days. There’s more to it than that, but that’s the gist of it. Much of the game’s plot involves these two trying to help a man named John, who is on his deathbed, to reach his wish to go to the moon by viewing and altering his memories. This isn’t a big spoiler, this is information you receive within the first 20-30 minutes or so, let me live.

The problem is that Eva and Watts are terrible characters. Both of them show no empathy or sympathy for the events they’re viewing in John’s head, even when the events are depressingly sad. One could argue that they’ve seen many memories like this in the heads of other patients, and maybe that’s fair, but they don’t really show that in their personalities or display behavior that would point to that. Their dialogue is, and I don’t like using this word but it's apt here - cringe. Eva and Watts constantly behave like children for characters who are supposed to be in their late 20s or early 30s. They make needless pop culture references, and the game derails its own pacing at times simply to make unfunny bits involving them, such as one where Watts spends hours drinking at a bar with John in one of his memories. Humor is subjective, and you can argue they’re supposed to be the comic relief of the story. Sure. These are your protagonists though, in a game that is trying to deliver a message that’s really powerful and moving, but you have two morons who are essentially Jessie & James from Pokemon in terms of being goofy. Eva says things like “What the cucumber?” which is cringy in its own right, but even more so when you consider that characters in this game swear freely anyway, albeit the exact words being censored. Watts ridiculously references different media such as Street Fighter, Marvel, Dragon Ball and Doctor Who. (Huh, guess where the names John and River came from?) What is the point of writing these two like this? What, did you think the story was too ****ing dark or something? It’s not that dark, I’ll tell you that much. All of this quirky dialogue is off-putting, and takes you out of the experience. With all these depressing events they’re viewing, Eva & Watts come across as ***holes and childish for the way they react a majority of the time. 

Funnily enough, in some weird moment of self-awareness, Eva scolds Watts at one point for being a moron and says she’s “trying to get into this.” Me too! If you’d like another piece of dialogue from the game as an example of the writing, here’s an actual quote I noted because I was simply so baffled that I was reading it. Watts says early on, “Because we always succeed, because we’re awesome.” Ughhh.

It all really angers me - because on the other hand, To the Moon’s story around John and River is actually a narrative I want to love. There’s something here that is actually saddening to view. To the Moon has events that invoke something beautiful. Something meaningful, something remarkable, something special. Yet the writer insisted on butchering this beauty with amateur, piss-poor bottom of the barrel protagonists - with written dialogue that feels like it was written and forged in the Nine Hells of Ao3, by a 13 year-old girl with a Tumblr blog who’s never written in her life.

What’s worse is that To the Moon’s tragic story features a tale about a mental health condition that is worth telling. I won’t spoil what this condition is since it’s pretty important to the plot, but I know some people who would love to hear that they’re being represented in a game. All this quirky dialogue from Eva & Watts makes it feel like that the writer isn’t taking this condition seriously. It feels insulting, and that genuinely makes me upset and frustrated with the game’s narrative. Hence why I was shocked the game only had one writer. Why? Why would you do this? Why would you butcher and lobotomize your own narrative like this? You had something beautiful here, something meaningful that could really mean a lot to certain people, and it is simply utterly wasted.

I think an important and underrated facet of games is tone. It’s what allows a game like Devil May Cry or Bayonetta to coexist in a genre with Dark Souls, and in turn with The Witcher, or etc. If you can nail your game’s tone, then everything built around becomes woven together, like a perfect silk cloth. Not everything has to be a despair-ridden romp, that’s not what I’m saying. What I am saying is that your game falls apart when it has an inconsistent tone. To the Moon’s poorly conceived dialogue provides nothing of value towards forming its tone, and ultimately has a very inconsistent one throughout due to this. What an example to hear what I mean? It’s like if you sat down to watch an artistically beautiful  film like Forrest Gump, but you had someone right next to you on the couch the whole time cracking jokes and roasting moments of the film as if they were a Red Letter Media wannabe. That’s what it’s like.

I apologize if it seems like I’m harping on these two protags, but this is a visual novel. The most important parts of a visual novel are the narrative and dialogue. So when the dialogue gets unwoven by being so poorly-written, the tone of the game collapses. And when the tone of the game collapses, then so too does the house of cards the narrative stands upon. I don’t really recall a time where I’ve been this disappointed in a game’s narrative. It makes me sad because there’s something here with potential. It genuinely made me begin to tear up at times for certain scenes, albeit right before I was sobered back to reality by the rest of the writing. 

I’m also not sure why this is rated so highly either? Perhaps if you’re only a teenager or never experienced a proper narrative in your lifetime of “muh cozy games”, sure, maybe. I’m already in my seat and cozy, thank you. I want my games to give me something that’s worth my time, and To the Moon is simply not that. I do not recommend this game, even on sale, because I think there are better ways to waste 4 hours. Drive to Chick-fil-a or something instead, I dunno.

review_text:
Oof, this is rough.

The game has really pretty pixel art, visually Lost Ruins is great, but on the gameplay side it's just not fun.
Your attacks are slow and even the largest weapons barely have enough reach to hit an enemy before they are able to get our their *much* faster attacks.

Also almost every enemy in this game will apply some sort of debuff onto you, like bleed or poison damage, which can last up to 30 seconds for certain enemies, dealing 1 damage per second, when that's more than your total HP.
But hey, there's a ton of consumables that let you heal a tiny bit and remove such status effects.
That however means you constantly have to go in and out of your inventory, looking for the right consumable to get rid of effects every time you get hit by an enemy.
And again, enemies get much quicker attack animations than you, so the chance of getting hit isn't exactly low.

And what do you get for defeating enemies?
Well since there's no XP system or anything like that, if you're lucky they may drop another consumable...
Sometimes, but only rarely will enemies drop some coins you can use to buy equipment at vendors.
But prices are super high and the amount of gold dropped by enemies is tiny.
Like a piece of equipment may cost you like 150G, but every 5 or so enemies you may get 5 gold to drop.

To keep it short, gameplay isn't fun at all.

Sadly, the story and characters are just as bad.
It's already weird enough to see all these girls running around in japanese schoolgirl outfits in a dark fantasy setting, but the story revolving around summoning girls from another world for some sacrifice is just extremely threadbare.
The main character, merely named "Heroine" is as milquetoast as they get.
She never has a single interesting thing to say in dialogue nor does she react to things like characters getting straight up killed in front of her.
There's a small handful of other characters here, mainly they're the bosses, but their writing is just as terrible.

It's such a shame, since the they really seemed to have put a lot of work in the pixel art for Lost Ruins, but everything beside the visuals, this is terrible.

Wouldn't recommend this at all sadly.

review_text:
Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is everything you want in a Jet Radio spiritual successor: dripping with style, an interesting world, smooth controls, and an eargasmic soundtrack. Yes, everything you'd want... except a satisfying gameplay loop.

The problem isn't that that Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is not an arcadey, race the clock, high-scoring graffiti-em-up; it'd be fine if it kept the stylish trappings of its inspiration but went a different way with the core mechanics and challenge. It feels like the game left out the game entirely.

Most charitably, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk's core game is a 3D Platformer Collectathon, but instead of collecting Power Moons or Jiggies the game is figuring out how to reach the tagging spots scattered throughout the level, as well as the occasional music track, costume, or graffiti style. It also throws in the occasional "trick combo scoring" challenge and boss fight to mix it up, but neither of those are particularly interesting, for reasons I'll explain. It's all just a bit... boring.

Tricks and Combos and Scoring: This is the closest the game gets to a clever mechanic - you rack up combo multiplier by stringing elements together (specifically: wall runs, ramps, and sharp corners), with each unique element only counting once. If you're not on an element, you have a limited time to manual to a new one or the combo ends, encouraging you to scout the stage for a line that combos as much new stuff as possible. 

Unfortunately, the game faceplants this mechanic in two ways. First, it quickly teaches a mechanic that lets you manual infinitely, eliminating the challenge of finding a tight line through the stage. Second, there's no downside to repeating an element, just no new multiplier. In almost every challenge, it's enough to hit a 10x-20x multiplier from rail corners and then just grind a single loop forever while mashing buttons so you don't risk losing combo. It would have been much stronger if the game focused on stringing as many elements (including graffitti spots, which are hardly rewarded!) in a combo without repeat, as the stages are clearly designed for lines like that!

Combat: Boost into things and kick them. If it's a machine, kick it and graffiti it. There's a fun mechanic where you can tag a cop the moment you deal the killing blow to it, but the window is very small and there's no reward for doing it. If the game forced you to tag police to defeat them it would have been unique and interesting, but here it's just a silly nod.

Besides, outside of the four or so (very short) boss fights, the police element is pointless. In the Jet Radio games, the police presence got worse as the stage wore on, and they could interrupt your tags, requiring you to frantically put enough distance between you and them to get your tag in before they could catch you, then book it under the gun of the clock. In Bomb Rush Cyberfunk, there's no stage timer and no risk of cops interrupting your work, making them just kind of annoying when they spawn. And the mechanic is rendered entirely pointless by the fact that you can clear all police presence by touching a bathroom, so the mechanic might as well not have been included at all during free stage exploration.

Characters: In the Jet Radio games, different characters had different stats like health and graffiti combo length that affected scoring and strategy. In Bomb Rush Cyberfunk, they all... look different. It feels like a mechanic introduced just because the Jet Radio games had them, and not because it adds anything.

In conclusion, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is an homage to everything you remember about the Jet Radio games, minus the _game_. While I did enjoy my time with it just for the style alone, I honestly can't recommend it to anyone - there's not enough interesting gameplay here to attract anyone not familiar with its inspiration, and for fans of the inspiration the game feels like a shell of what it's inspired by. If I could give it a thumbs-middle, I might, but not at $40.
