review_text:
Here is my review for To the Moon:

First off, gameplay is basic and standard RPG maker. You walk around and press the button to interact. That's it. You don't do any fighting (but there was a joke of a fight at the start of the game). And you are usually locked within a room or two with one or two interactive items. Ironically, gameplay is not the focus of this game.

Story, that's what this game is all about. It could have simply been a story or a visual novel and the experience would've likely been the same. You play as two scientists who assist dying old folks. These elderly have regrets from their life and you provide them with solace. You do so by jumping into their memories and seeing them play through. An aged old man was once a middle aged man living his life, who was once a spry young lad with a glimmer of hope in his eyes. You then rewrite those memories to rewrite the future. Of course, this is all in the dying person's head, but their last experiences will be that of achieving their goals and finding peace. In this case you are helping an old man reach the moon. It tells the story of his life, his wife, disease, and past trauma. I won't go too much into it, as that would take too long. The game also includes DLC mini-episodes about the two scientists you play as well as their science company. This also sets up the sequels. The writing is quite strong and makes me want to see how the story plays out.

Overall, I was going into this game expecting a sorrowful story. However; I am relieved it was much more more touching. Either way the eyes did water up.

review_text:
I do not recommend buying this game at full price - I got it for 2 dollars though, and if that is still the price when you see it, then by all means, drop two bucks. That being said, this game is a mess.

I like the idea - I REALLY like the idea - but the execution is mediocre at best. Run around a mansion as a 7 year old and murder everyone in various ways. Sounds like a blast! I didn't even care that it was all scripted, and that there was little to no creativity allowed. What I cared about was the wacky bugs and confusing as hell missions. I had to look at the wiki in order to figure out what to do in the last half of the game, and I regularly play the Sherlock Holmes games, so I'm no stranger to adventure/puzzle games. But there is very little guiding your way. An intial mark on the map shows you your target, but after that, nothing. No markers showing important objects or following your target or anything. You can get a couple "gifts" that give you hints, but unfortunately my game bugged out and failed to register my "chores" so I couldn't get past the Ouiji board (which only hints at an important item to obtain, not what to do). Need to kill one of the maids? Clearly the thing to do is...break the washing machine by dropping an iron into it, thus making her...take a shower? Of course! Need to kill the driver? Well break that washing machine with the iron again to lure out the mechanic (because to hell with washing clothes!), then...find a mix tape so he can turn around and listen to it, allowing you to get some paint thinner and a rag to knock him out with? Masterful! There are also plenty of zero purpose items in the game. Books and bottles can be picked up, but serve no purpose. You can't even throw them to distract NPCs away from locations. Light switches can be flicked on and off, leading one to believe that there is a "stealth" aspect of the game Nope...in the one section where you can do it, darkness has no meaning - mom will find you whether you are standing in pitch black or right under the light bulb. There is a section of stealth gameplay later in the game where darkness actually matters...but you take out the power to the mansion, thus rendering the switches useless anyway!

The powers are cool, but you rarely get to use them. Telekenesis is your go to, followed by mind control. You can mind control a few of the people in the mansion, but unless they have some scripted interaction in that particular "chapter", you can't do anything with them. Later in the game, you get some offensive spells...but unless you choose the "Action" ending (oh yes, that is a thing), you will use the fireball spell twice and the combustion spell - your last spell, btw - once. Yep, one time. The only truly useful spell that doesn't require a scripted event is memory erase, where if you are caught doing something, you can make them forget (but only 6 times a chapter). 

And don't even get me started on the bugs. I have witnessed: an NPC walking into a closed door, effectively locking it for me. A chore not registering as complete (taking out the garbage), thus failing to allow me to continue that line of "side quests". Dropping that iron into the washer didn't work a few times. Dropping a hair dryer into a tub didn't work because it got stuck behind it, and was out of "range" of telekenesis. Entries in my journal not registering, leaving me with zero clues on how to continue. And many more minor annoyances (glitching through walls, glitching through each other, falling through the floor once, getting stuck in the courtyard on a very small "hill"). The voice sync is awful, the voice acting is...not terrible, but not good either. If what they do with their faces could be called "expressions" or "emotions" then those are awful too. Many of these could of probably been fixed, but clearly the developer did not see a reason to. 

Overall, the game is a mess, but it is certainly worth the two dollars I paid for it. I love the idea, and I would like to see more from the developer (although I'm told the sequel to this is even worse), but please polish it up, give a bit more creativity, and let us use our damn spells! If there isn't a sale on, avoid this one. If there is, anywhere from 1 to 5 bucks...go ahead and give it a whirl.

review_text:
THE COMBAT IN THE GAME IS BAD. Let's start off with that. The idea behind parrying your opponents moves and attacking opposite to their guard is cool. However, it often seems that where you swing doesn't even matter because the AI will block it seemingly at random, This makes parrying attacks the best style for sword fighting and even then the hits that connect seem random, and the parry icon doesn't always seem to appear when an enemy is attacking. Using the mouse to look around and be the way to decide where your hits go sucks bc I'll often find that it will just pull my focus off the person i want to hit and to a different enemy. The no indication for enemy health I can live with ig, but it makes combat feel really odd and unimpressive. like I've hit this dude 5 times in the head and it doesn't even seem like he's weaker or bleeding. 

POTION MAKING AND SIMILAR CRAFTING IS NOT THAT FUN. Finding herbs in the wild without really any way to tell them apart from the generic greenery other than remembering what it looks like is certainly an interesting game design choice. I personally thought it was fine and shops and dead bodies generally had the herbs i need for normal potions. But WOW actually making them is so unfun, the recipe book seems to always be just out of character sight so you can't just glance over to it to see what's on the pages, you have to move menus over to it whenever you forget a step. It's better to just write the instructions down in an actual notebook. It also just takes too much time, I don't want to be peeping for a quest for a solid 15 minutes trying to find the nearest patch of herbs just to run another 5 minutes to an alchemy station and spend another 10 minutes crafting all the potions because there isn't an instant menu for it once you've made a certain amount. 

THE BASE LAYOUT FOR CONTROLS IS WEIRD. The movement and weapon swapping buttons are perfectly fine, but the speech menus for NPCs is really bizarre. I mean why is shift+Q+# normal responses, but shift+alt+# is a different speech option, but effectively does the same thing as before.Why are they different controls, I don't understand it, the both say responses when a person talks to you. Also, if you just walk up to someone and press E it just doesn't talk to some NPCs as if they don't acknowledge your existence, but some will pop you into a conversation line. X for call horse and hold+x calls dog is fine, but why when i crouch does it do neither but instead distracts an enemy (sometimes).

UNFUN GAME-PLAY LOOP. I didn't enjoy the game-play loop overall. Needing potions to save unless I'm leaving the game is the dumbest thing in a video game ever. If it was sleeping or something or resting I can understand because it is a game that's pretty realistic, but why give me the option in the pause menu to save if it requires an in-game item to do it anyway. AND I HAVE TO BREW MORE POTIONS TO DO IT. The running is really slow, or it at least feels like it compared to riding a horse, and having to fully stop on the horse to have a different set of key-binds for controls is also just draconian. The slow movement while carrying LITERALLY ANY OBJECT is excruciating, like how bad would it be if i could run with that sack of wheat or dead body or at least move at normal speed. (ps LET ME USE MY HEALING POTIONS IN COMBAT, I DIDNT CRAFT THEM JUST TO DIE IN TWO HITS FROM A GUY WITH A SHIELD WHO STILL SEEMS TO RUN FASTER THAN ME... thank you)

RANDOM HUD QUIRKS. The inventory menu is weird too, like there are 8 tabs that all have information that it should be on maybe 3 or 4 tabs. Why are my player stats divided between 3 tabs when there is already a scroll bar on the tabs anyway. Why when I click or hover over an item does it not describe the item with a pop-out, but I instead need to click a side of the screen that shifts the camera over away from my inventory to tell me about the item then I need to click back into the inventory to see my full list. Why does my proficiency in a skill seem to not do anything when interacting with NPCs unless I choose the option they like. Why do I have 3 pieces of armor all in the same category but they all go on different slots. Why do i need a separate helmet to wear the helmet I want? Why do my bandages have durability that's separate from each-other but consumed on use?

Overall I would rate the game a 5/10. The story is really good, the NPCs have fun dialogue and a lot of it. The random quest adjacent NPC interactions are fun, like beating up a mail carrier who lot a letter so he doesn't get whipped is a cool side tangent. The introduction and cinematic scenes so far in the game are good as well. The scenery and environment is interesting and there are plenty of hidden locations to find. HOWEVER, ultimately a game is only as good as it's game-play and Kingdom Come: II just does not have it. The melee fighting is clunky and seemingly random, the crafting of basic items is atrocious, sneaking is not enjoyable and offers no real extra benefit vs just killing the enemy and stealing their stuff. The quests that seem like they should take place in one location have you running across the map to find someone only to run all the way back just to say you found them.

TL:DR If you are a story driven gamer this game will probably be fun for you, if you spend your time only with NPCs and foraging. If you are looking for a fun action packed exploration based RPG, go somewhere else you will be putting new holes in your monitor from getting frustrated at random groups of bandits that clap you back to 3 towns over because your attacks won't land.

As the core concept is the same for both games, I will cover both [i]Left 4 Dead[/i] (released November, 2008) and it's sequel, [i]Left 4 Dead 2[/i] as a single game. The core plot is the same for both games: You and three other players have to survive the zombie apocalypse and reach the end goal. Along the way, you pick up guns and ammo, explosives, and first aid. All four of you have to survive to the end, or be overwhelmed by the zombie horde. Got it? Go play.

In the past ten years, the gaming landscape is littered with multi-player games that have launched, had their moment in their sun, then the players go on to another game, and soon the game publishers shut down the servers. Yet, when you look at the gaming numbers for the [i]Left 4 Dead[/i] series, with 25K peak players for [i]Left 4 Dead 2[/i] in the week of this posting (and 1,062 for [i]Left 4 Dead[/i]) according to [url=http://markholtz.info/steamdb]SteamDB[/url]. It's easy to see why. The graphics, although slightly dated, still hold up in modern computers. The core gaming mechanics are easy to pick up within a few games. I particularly liked the horror motif, especially since it feels like you are part of a survival horror movie that runs around 60-90 minutes. I also like that you and three other players have to cooperate with each other, although there are some alternative gaming modes as well. The second game is open to mods.... wide open to mods. And, it is compatible across multiple platforms. 

Yet, when I am looking at this game, I cannot feel but annoyance at Valve as a game developer. The last game released by Valve was five years ago with [i]DOTA 2[/i]. The [i]Left 4 Dead[/i] games are overdue for a third release, but none is coming. We won't even speak of [i]Half Life 3[/i]. 

Would I recommend the games? Yes, but with qualifications.

The sequel, [i]Left 4 Dead 2[/i] is [b]HIGHLY RECOMMENDED[/b]. Not only is it an improved game from the original, but all of the missions from the first game have been transferred to the sequel as well. The online player base is larger as well, plus support for more playing modes and there is a GeForce Experience profile. The game got highly discounted during the last Steam Summer sale as well, thus it's worth waiting for a sale.

The original, [i]Left 4 Dead[/i], on the other hand, is [b]NOT RECOMMENDED[/b]. All of the missions from the original game has been ported to the sequel, and the sequel is better supported and has a bigger online population. Save the money.

review_text:
As a lifelong Trek fan, it pains me to see something from this franchise so full of potential yet so devoid of realization.

While I do agree with other reviewers that this isn't exactly the "perfect" Star Trek game (with a balance of exploration, combat, diplomacy, discovery, etc.), I can appreciate what the devs tried to do with this particular vision; and it could have been something... otherworldly... had it not ended up pretty much stagnating.

STO could be an amazing, beautiful game. For the first few years, I enjoyed the presentation, stories and the flow of combat. Of particular note and commendation is the fact that bringing as many original actors from the Trek universe into the game as they could has given it a particular charm that could not otherwise be achieved - it really does make an infinite difference in how the stories are received, and I would not have enjoyed each initial foray anywhere near as much without those iconic presences.

I had enjoyed it so much, initially, that I decided to buy the lifetime subscription. Despite it being easily the most expensive game content I've ever purchased, I did so with the intention of supporting the devs in this project to hopefully make it better. That is not what the money from the lifetime subscription goes to.

The big problem with this title in my opinion is not the mechanics, the (mostly unaddressed / unrepaired) bugs, or the lack of "perfect" Trek balance. The problem is the lack of new content. The only result of spending real cash on a lifetime sub is the devs putting all their effort into new ships to spend MORE real cash on, and little to no actual content. When one looks at any other MMO and the amount of content produced yearly, this one falls incredibly short. I'd be okay with a lack of original actor voices if it meant some decent, sizeable content produced regularly; it wouldn't be as good, but... at least it'd be something. All players get now is event after event of the same few TFO missions endlessly recycled. Why would _anyone_ want to pay huge amounts of cash for ships just to do the same 3 or 4 events over and over again? The devs need to give us reason to WANT to buy new ships and do stuff, and running TFO  for the 16,000,000th time is not gonna cut it AFAIC.

There is also the issue of the "legendary" ships kinda breaking the game for those who have not spent even more money to get them, as they are (from a balance perspective) broken and severely overpowered. This is a much lesser issue, however, and could be remedied by separating legendary and non-legendary players in all content.

For those who might question my review with the sizeable amount of hours sunk into this title... I loved it at first, but now only keep playing every so often to try for the "free" ships offered by event campaigns to feel like I'm getting something - anything - out of my investment into this game.

Best advice I can offer, given STO's current state: play it free, do all the stories and enjoy the actual content that exists, and then consider walking away. As fun as STO can be - and as much untapped potential as it has - "endgame" STO feels like an empty, windowless room, a couple thousand choices of chairs to hoist one's backside upon, and the same 4 songs on endless repeat. Nobody's spending a Saturday evening in a pub like that, y'know?

review_text:
If you love rouge-likes and Dwarf Fortress, this game is up your alley, however I have some caveats and some things I love (I'll start with the caveats).

The Caveats:

1. The UI is extremely small and cloistered with no way to pause and examine things if you're eyes aren't great or to enlarge text if you need it. On top of that, when mobs are in your town it's almost impossible to select them or sometimes even see them amongst all the other things around them including the buildings that are being attacked or the resources they contain (mainly when trying to pick up and move the mob to a less destructive location). When trying to defend my town there's been times where I have to either sit back and watch the destruction because I can't intervene, hoping that it isn't too severe, or just destroy my save and start from scratch because there's no way to recover after a certain amount of setback.
2. The help text and general information surrounding what different game elements and mechanics behave is not robust. It's hard to know what choices to make for defending your territory when it comes to tower upgrades or walls. The wall help text says that it won't be attacked unless mobs have no other way around, but I've routinely had monsters destroy parts of my tower maze walls even with three tile paths perfectly open but a longer path. I love the idea of building a tower defense type pathing structure, but if the walls are vulnerable in an unpredictable way, it isn't a viable path to building.
3. Lastly, the different resistance types for monsters requires you to build a lot of different tower types despite having a fairly low building count ceiling that requires a lot other resources that require other buildings. It's hard to have the perfect mix of towers when you need a lot of support structures and citizens while also trying to build out lighting structures to keep the corruption at bay. It feels to me like threading a needle every time with very little room for improvisation or creativity in terms of what I build, when I build it, and if I built it effectively enough. I've had some games where I can already see that I'm not going to make it even though it's only 5 or 6 days in. It would be nice to have some flexibility in terms of how to get to a successful, defensible build without having to rush the initial building and resource gathering.

The Things I Love:

1. Things ain't easy. Again, like Dwarf Fortress, you get no help if you mess up, but once you learn some of the meta you can make it happen. The balance isn't perfect, such as how much the corruption ramps up when you finally manage to get it to a point where it should be eliminated, but it will put up a fight which I actually appreciate. I want a challenge and not some predictable meta where you just follow some wiki and always win.
2. Getting your essence level up feels incredible and really helps you out, but it takes the right amount of time, Sure, you're a god, and yo've got powers, but you've got to make sure that your faith level is raising or you've got nothing. It's fun trying to raise the essence storage level, and once you do it's smooth sailing for a while but it's never a breaking game mechanic. In fact, if you rely on it too much you'll ruin your chances to survive the later stages of the pressed for space corruption.
3. I'd love a few more storage spaces, or storage spaces that can hold more (or maybe a building that can create crates and barrels to help store more things) but over all I love the mix of clearly important buildings (harvesting, housing, food, defense) with minutiae (trash collecting, dog houses, rangers, lightning rods, magic stuff). It's got a great balance between stopping monsters from attacking and managing a town.
4. I like the blood moon and the trashy slime elements. It's just nice to know that no matter how much you handle the obvious enemy—the corruption—you're never safe. You're _never safe_.

Anyway, I wish the game didn't make me feel so rushed to immediately strike out space wise against the corruption and I wish I had more UI clarity so I can see what is happening and react to it. Additionally, besides the text size and information help, controlling time a bit to slow it down or speed it up would be super helpful. I think being able to drop time down to half and quarter time as well as being able to pause the game and interact with the game would be a huge win with a small amount of change.

I love this game! I'll keep playing it even if I just rage quite it before I wrote this. It has a lot of heart and it's well put together, I highly suggest it, but don't come in here expecting a walk in the park. It's meant to be a bit complex and challenging. As we've learned in Dwarf Fortress: "Losing is fun!" so be prepared to suffer, hate it, love it, and then find yourself jumping back in because you _refuse to leave it like that_.

review_text:
Definitely one of my favorite otome/ dating-sim games out there!
It focuses a lot on the historical setting which does not make it a quick and easy read at times, but nonetheless it is very enjoyable! 

Pros: 
- Lots of different routes and likeable characters 
- I promise you there is a character for anyone to date here
- even "insignificant" choices can give you a different storyline 
- beautiful art
- amazing voiceacting
- story doesn't rush into the romance/ slowburn mostly
- samurais
- has some very funny moments in it I will not forget
- the way the story is written the (main) characters feel genuine and not one dimensional, even if you are not "dating" them
- you actually learn a bit of history
- depending on the route, it can get quite emotional 
- the fantasy elements of the story seem fitting in most of the routes
- hot samurais
- ridiculously dramatic scenes are less cringe and more fun than you would expect from an otome game
- you can date samurais dammit

cons: 
- not too much of a con but in the beginning, a lot of backround info and history details are thrown at you; whenever I didn't really focus on reading it properly it was very difficult to understand why anything is happening further in the story
- some routes are really [b] slow [/b] burn
- MC can be quite the vegetable at the most frustrating parts 
- the dialog options you can choose sometimes don't really give you an idea of what MC is going to say next, it can leave you frustrated at times
- in certain routes the fantasy elements can get a bit too "twillight" for my taste (strangely dramatic and awkward), but it's actually quite bearable 

I would still highly recommend the game for anyone looking for a good story-based dating game. The pros definitely outweigh the cons

review_text: I don't have enough good things to say about this game. I got it on a whim while it was on sale but it's 100% worth buying at full price (if that's in your budget). Challenging enough to keep me engaged, but not so difficult that I wanted to quit. And you can make it more difficult for yourself if you want, by playing on Difficult mode or trying to achieve some of the (very hard imho) optional objectives. The story is emotionally engaging, and the characters feel real (to the point that I got annoyed with some of them like I would real people lol). Each character has strengths and weaknesses, which influence how you can use them on each level. Every action has a consequence - if I set a trap *here* it will affect *this* set of guards, but how will the nearby civilians react? The art style is really attractive, the voice acting is top notch, and the soundtrack is phenomenal - the combination really transports you to the game's world. I played through the original game twice, the second time incorporating the Aiko's Choice expansion (which takes place in the middle of the original game), and I might dabble in a third playthrough one of these days, once my game backlog is a little better. If you like the challenge of strategizing an entire mission and overcoming all obstacles in your path, this game is for you!

Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts is nothing short of a masterpiece, an instant classic crafted by the brilliant minds at CI Games that seamlessly blends gritty realism with a tantalizing touch of fantasy. From the moment you step into the boots of the enigmatic sniper, you’re thrust into a world that feels both authentic and exhilaratingly larger-than-life. CI Games has truly outdone themselves, delivering a title that elevates the sniper genre to new heights with its impeccable design and captivating gameplay.
The realism is striking—every shot requires precision, patience, and a keen understanding of your environment. Wind speed, distance, and bullet drop aren’t just mechanics; they’re immersive elements that make you feel like a true marksman stalking the shadows. The attention to detail in the weapon handling and the sprawling, beautifully rendered Siberian landscapes is jaw-dropping, grounding the experience in a way that few games manage to achieve. It’s as if CI Games studied the art of sniping and translated it into a digital love letter for tactical enthusiasts.
Yet, what sets Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts apart is how it sprinkles in just the right amount of fantasy to keep things thrilling. You’re not just a soldier—you’re a ghost, a near-mythical figure weaving through contracts with gadgets and skills that push the boundaries of what’s possible. The ability to tag enemies with high-tech scopes, execute jaw-dropping slow-motion kills, and navigate missions with a freedom that feels almost superhuman adds a layer of excitement that perfectly complements the realism. It’s this fusion that makes every mission feel like a cinematic blockbuster, where you’re both the director and the star.
CI Games has struck gold with this title, proving they’re a studio with a vision that resonates. The pacing is spot-on, the replayability is endless thanks to the contract system, and the satisfaction of nailing a 500-meter headshot is unmatched. Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts isn’t just a game—it’s a testament to how a developer can take a niche concept and turn it into a timeless gem. If you’re looking for a title that balances the raw tension of real-world sniping with the escapist thrill of a fantastical adventure, this is it. An absolute triumph!

review_text:
Game is decent but pretty far removed from the traditional fast-action metroidvania. This is more of a survival game - you have very limited resources, enemies do a lot of damage, movement is clunky and attacking is slow. You have to be very deliberate with your actions or you'll find yourself dead very quickly. Your character really doesn't grow in power that much over the course of the game, it's more about what items you find and how you put them together to support the playstyle you're trying to achieve.

Something unique about this game is that it has environmental interactions. You can light oil on fire, freeze water to stand on it, etc. You can set these up yourself too using consumables to make puddles of oil for example, then light it with a fire spell and burn all the enemies in the area.

Personally it's not really my thing, I prefer games with tight movement and quick attacks. I did finish it though so it must be doing something right. The art is very nice, it's entirely sprite based but with modern lighting and rotation/scaling. The drawn character portraits are high quality. The story is pretty meh, but when has a metroidvania had a good story? You're here for the gameplay and if you like a more methodical type of game then this is one you should definitely try out.

.hack//G.U. Possibly a great game series with lovable characters, great game-play, a deep world and a nearly never ending amount of lore to read. On the other hand though it could be a game brought down upon by its horrible port. As you can tell by my rating, I highly discourage most people playing this game through this particular avenue. 

I have to say for a first timers introduction to the game series the game itself wasn't that bad. I did have to keep in mind it was originally a single player JPRG from 2006 on the PS2 while it plays as an MMO. I have no qualms with the game itself other than the voice acting and dialogue can be very cheesy at times but it's nothing that you can't help but love. All my hate for this game and the reason I don't recommend the game is mainly because of the port itself. Constant crashes, lost textures and other inconveniences that make the game unfun. 

My experience with the game was as follows: I load up the game for the first time and while the tutorial may not be the most interesting it did at least lure me into their world. After the tutorial and seeing the cut scene onslaught and got back into the game I was mid combat and everything froze except the music. "Interesting," I thought to myself while spamming every button on my controller for a sign of life. I had to reset the tutorial but after skipping cut scenes it didn't take more than 6 minutes and lost nothing of importance so I didn't mind as much. My next time was after the tutorial and I was able to do what I wanted so I went into a random area map and everything ran great; I beat all the monsters in the area, opened all the chests, got as many surprise attacks as I could and got the S rank for the area! Hooray I thought, an armor I can use to replace the one I currently use and continue forward. 

As I run to the save point I couldn't continue on further when talking to the save point. I lost my save data again. In the span of 2 hours I crashed twice. I checked my computer and it wasn't related to my computer at all. I started over for my 3rd time, annoyed but finished everything I did in 30 mins but lost the perfect in that random area. I go to save and continue my journey. It wasn't until where I get to town 2 does the game where it all goes to shit. I was missing textures from the game. Atoli, Silabus and I were missing their faces, buildings were missing glass panes, stairs were missing steps, the game started chugging at this point which hadn't happened to this point yet. 

My frustration set in at this point and looked it up, nothing other than people complaining of constant crashing. I let out a deep sigh and uninstall and reinstall but not before going to get my save data on the off chance steam doesn't save it. I wait my 3 hours for the 40 gigs to finish and with excitement I load the game back up. Everything seemed right and I go to select Vol. 1. "New Game" was the only option on my screen. I sighed but thanked I saved my save file. I close the game, make a copy of my save files and put them in the correct directory. I load the game back up and I see the option "New Game" but not continue nor load game. With a deep sigh I still had my saves copied so I started the tutorial, skipped cut scenes and everything is worse, the texture missing was worsened, I crash at the tutorial now and worst of all even after saving and replacing my save files on top of the newly made saves I had no save to load up when the game was done starting up.

TL;DR: I enjoyed the game itself and its cheesy 2000s ps2 dialogue and none of my issues stem with the game itself it all comes from the port. I'll be purchasing the game on PS4 and playing it that way and restarting the game a possible 4th/5th time just because the game couldn't hold itself stable for 5 minutes. Please, buy it on the PS shop or whatever alternative there is.

If you prefer controller and you have a console, you're better off going that route. (They probably have a remaster that actually works.)

There were two key problems that killed this for me: 

[b]Disappearing Subtitles[/b]
Early on, you'll find that the subtitles will appear just briefly before fading out. But [b]only[/b] if you're playing with a controller. And, seriously, how does that work?

[b]Broken Telekinesis[/b]
A short way in, you get a Telekinesis ability, which you can use to both retrieve and throw things. But the button to drop the item in front of you is the same button that uses an EVE hypo. Basically, you're forced to play with a handicap.

[b]Try the Remaster[/b]
I can only guess what other problems pop up, because these issues were enough for me to say screw it and play the remaster. It's no secret that that's got a whole host of its own problems, but it worked for me. Just save often.

review_text:
After 4-5 hours and completing several missions, Shadow Tactics feels more like a rigid puzzle game than the creative stealth experience I was hoping for. Coming from games like Hitman and Dishonored where you have multiple approaches and can experiment with different solutions, this felt surprisingly limiting.

Every guard is watched by others, creating tedious chains where you must clear entire sections just to eliminate one target. Despite large maps, there's typically only one viable path forward.


The game is well-crafted and polished, but it becomes monotonous quickly. Each area feels like solving the same puzzle: figure out the correct elimination sequence, execute it perfectly, repeat. If you enjoy pure logic puzzles with a stealth theme, you might love this. If you're looking for the emergent gameplay and creative problem-solving of games like Hitman, you'll likely find it frustrating.

review_text:
+ Decent combat, pretty environments, and phenomenal character customization.

Everything else, though, is bad.

- Horrible UI, offensive inventory management, "lootboxes" everywhere, a practically non-functioning market board, a completely meaningless early-game, kinda wonky movement, and story/character writing that unironically gave me a headache. 
- Could never figure out if the game was designed for KB/M or for controller. Sub-palette actions suck on controller, but menu navigation is putrid on KB/M.
- I suspect that the "real" game begins after the story, after finishing up all the main tasks, but enough core stuff here is so unacceptably broken that I don't see myself enjoying that "real" game anyways.

If you have grown used to the comforts of other AAA MMOs, this will be a painful experience for you. It is as if the developers have not spent an iota of effort into learning from other titles in the genre. It would also seem that public sentiment among even the dedicated playerbase is fairly poor - there is apparently a lack of content and meaningful rewards at endgame.

Pass on this one. There are plenty of other games with just as good combat/graphics/character customization that don't suffer nearly as many of mind-boggling systems issues.

review_text:
I wanted to love this game so much.

And at first, I did. My first few hours in the game were pretty nice, but certain issues became apparent with more playtime. The love and work the Devs put in are clear to see, and I'm sure lots of people will have a great time with this. But for me many of the features that set Plum Grove apart also harm it in the end.

The generational gameplay loop, the fact that NPCs can marry, die, etc. It made you think the town and world would feel alive, but that's what killed it in my opinion. The NPC interaction is so shallow and lifeless, so meaningless ultimately. As an old timer of the farm/life sim genre, I know you rarely get novel-level character development, but this was so much less than even what Harvest Moon had on the SNES. 

The NPC weddings that come and go throughout the seasons feel like nothing more than a game of random ''pair the spares'' since no one really has any relationships with each other. No rival events, no dialogue hinting at who they might be interested in. It all feels so pointless, that not even the deaths shake you that much, most of them you never really even know by name anyway.

Even your own marriage is a dull affair. Again no relationship events, no special dialogue, nothing. All the NPCs are basically just randomly generated sims meant to keep the wheelwork of the generations going. In essence, in order to have a game where infinite generations were possible it made none of them matter. 

I could add that the economy is sort of broken besides. As crops are almost so worthless I nearly stopped growing them apart from a few to eat. But I realize that could get sorted out with tweaking and such.

review_text:
I may be the minority here with this take, but I genuinely didn't enjoy the game as much as I hoped. 

It's such an unoriginal, uninspiring gameplay design. This game takes the ideas of Dead Space & RE4 and makes them horrendous.

It's the same copypaste survival-action formula from every modern RE title ever.
The only difference being how terribly implemented it is.

Significantly worse inventory system.
Awful balancing.
Limited "upgrade" system.
Boring and overused enemies.
Clunky movement & combat.
An overused trope of body morphing.. done terribly.

The inventory system racks my brain. I cannot fathom why you'd want such a frustrating system in your game.
Imagine needing to collect a progression item and having no room for it. Why not have a quest-item inventory like every other game in this genre does? I'm sure people are just jumping for joy having to use up their spare meds / ammo in order to free up ONE slot to move on with the game. I feel bad for those that have to back track through everything just to clear 1-2 slots for quest-progression items. Speaking of, why is it that the main weapon of the game is a singular pistol that can change forms, but takes up a slot for each form? You're just making the already-terrible inventory system worse by default with this decision. 

I can't tell if this is a chronic skill-issue on my part, or the RNG is absolutely horrendous. Anytime I break open a yellow-tape box (yes, those stupid things are littered in this game too), I get.. absolutely nothing! That's right, nothing! Break open 3-4 crates and receive completely nothing in return. No ammo, no meds, nothing. When I DO on the off-chance actually get SOMETHING from the crates, it's just energy.. and the smallest amount possible at that (energy is this game's "currency" for the shop). Due to the poor distribution of supplies, I find myself being LUCKY to have 10 bullets to use at any given time. If you're not using the charge shot ability on the pistol at all times, you're literally wasting ammo. 

Upgrading your suit & weapons is as bare bones as it can get. Nothing gives you a special skill, ability, or perk. It is quite simply "number go up" and that's it. Wanna upgrade the duration of burning enemies? Spend a core to make it burn from 1 second, to 1.33 seconds! Wow!!

The enemies are so overused & limited it hurts. I dunno why they do the Dead Space method of "Black skin = strong." Somehow a darker version of the same enemy just has more health. Not only that, but why the worst kinda of enemies? Why slugging pus-balls? Why Spitters? Why wall-attached enemies that just trigger QTE events constantly? These aren't fun, they're annoying. Couple this with the jank movement and you've got boring, clunky combat. I can't lie, I had more fun running up to them & slugging a mean right hook and stomping them than actually trying to shoot. I wish melee was actually usable because the animations are clean. I assumed it was supposed to be a replacement for the utter drought of ammunition, but a loading tip says "Don't rely on your fists, only a last resort." TL;DR melee does absolutely no damage, and no.. you can't upgrade your melee strength / force whatsoever. Which begs the question; why even add the ability to melee, knowing it does nothing and you can't upgrade it? Especially considering the vast majority of enemies spit acid puddles everywhere forbidding you from getting within 20 feet of them. 

All in all, I expected better. It takes existing ideas from other popular titles and.. that's it. It doesn't expand upon any of them, nor does it explore anything deeper than face value. It genuinely just doesn't feel original, new, or fun.


Summarized:
As someone who lives for the horror genre, this doesn't do it justice for me. I wasn't scared a single time, I never felt engrossed in the atmosphere, and to top it all off--I just couldn't care. The game gives you no reason to give an inkling of thought or consideration towards anyone or anything--leading you to have no interest in seeing the results. Final verdict? It's... mediocre. Average. Mid. Generic. "Okay." It's a game, that's really all I can say. Not great, not terrible. Get it on sale.

Look, this point this game is fairly casual for an MMO. I pick it up again every few years and play through the new content (usually relearning the whole game because I forgot how it works in the extended time away) until I get bored and put it on the shelf for another few years.

Yes, its "free." Yes, it can be grindy. Yes, There is so many different systems that trying to keep everything running can seem like you log in just to refresh duty missions ans such. BUT. And here is a good but: It's fun and totally gives players the ability to get into only as much as they care too.

Be the casual, only log on for play with friend times. Be a solo and play it like a single player game. Grind away at events and get a ton of free premium crap (It is grindy to get stuff, but if you are enjoying playing the game a bunch, you tend to just earn stuff as a matter of course). Or, be super sweaty and min/max the heck out of your Epic Gear that you spend untold hours shooting Borg drones to get.

This game is 15 years old, and they are still adding new content. Where they used to have to chart their own narrative course due to a dearth of Star Trek; the newer content does a decent job of incorporating storylines from the new shows into the existing STO cannon.  

Why do I keep coming back, I have fun. When I don't on the shelf it goes, ready to reimerge in few years again

This game will bag the GOTY I'm sure of it (if not in TGA then maybe in other awards).

Personally I find this game extremely immersive (the graphics alone carries this game's immersion and it doesn't even support RT), the story/writing is great from start to finish, the combat have been simplified (lore-wise because Henry is much more experienced now compared to the previous game), and the game is surprisingly well-optimized. Funny enough I played around 10+ hours just by playing/collecting dice (for some reason it's just so much fun). It took me 70+ hours to finish Trosky/the first map alone (there are two maps), and I spent the rest of my end-game hours robbing Kuttenberg/the second map (if you're not robbing then you're playing the game the hard way). 

My complaints in the game are mostly in the Kuttenberg area, it is larger but felt more empty than Trosky, perhaps due to how it's designed as it is largely empty fields 
whereas the Trosky is smaller but more dense. The Kuttenberg area also lack interiors especially in the city (I recommend playing the first game for comparison), and also missing church interiors which I wish they added in the final DLC (there are alot in the second map, and they only added one where the DLC takes place).

Great game regardless and despite the minor criticisms it is still worthy of GOTY.

I have been playing these games for quite awhile. Though mostly on my phone as I have the app downloaded there as well. There are only 5 games for this Steam version and one you HAVE to pay $6.99 to unlock (so 4 are included as is) which I don't like. What should have been done is a "let me play anyway and wait" instead of forcing the premium upload. Covenant is free in the app. In the mobile version, you have access to a lot more and for some reason they have achievements for the ones not on the app currently (unless they become visible when you pay $6.99) so did they want you to use the mobile app and transfer achievements? 

I have given them money by buying stars and keys so I am not 100% opposed, but I am using this app purely for achievements from the mobile version so I am annoyed that I can no longer get achievements for the remaining games. 

Here is how this game works in general: 

1. You start out with 2 keys. 

2. Each chapter requires 1 key to unlock to download and play

3. When you run out of keys, you wait 3 hours for one key or 6 hours for both! Not the worst and you can watch ads to take 30 minutes off the timer.. though they do eventually stop you... best to do this when you are on Chapter 6. 

4. Most stories have 8 chapters, though one game (that I count) and most of the games brought over from the standalone apps before they prioritized this app have 10 chapters!

If you fully refuse to buy anything even slightly adjacent or related to microtransactions than you can on average beat 1 story per day depending on when you start it, how smart you are, how clueless you are at noticing hidden things to pick up and how late you stay up or how much time you have for this kind of thing. Which isn't all that horrible. I did buy a few of the stars for skips (cause I use a guide cause I am a proud dumbass who is dumb as fuck) and keys! 

I found the stories engaging for what this was, and I have downloaded all of the apps I can. Even the first game they worked on! I love these. The art is fantastic. I even enjoyed the music loops that they play (Pirate's Treasure had the worst one but it was good white noise) and wish these developers introduced a music player so that we can listen to completed background music. Or release it to youtube... Many people might not agree, but I wish it was an option.

Tried for a refund, but it was over the 2 hr limit, beacuse i kept thinking "it might get better, il give it a chance, the reviews are great!". So now im stuck with this. 
Its just overall not enjoyable, even for an early accsess.

-deep inhale before rant begins- : 
The Ai is horrible, they just run around aimlessly, or all follow the same pathing in a neat line, OOR shoot at you from over half the map away.

The gunplay is not fun, it feels slow, and the damage on range dropoff is ugh.From oneshoting to 1 dmg.(buuh health bars in shooting games..)

Theres not much of a story feel in this "RPG" game(suppose that may change in later stages of the game)

The "roguelite" element is nonexistent as the bonues are so minor i bearly notice.(and they slow the game down even more.. dont need the animation of the choices everytime.)

The spells are underwhelming.

The level design is boring, as is are "missions". 
The map feels mostly empty and pointless, as you run around looking for foes. anything interesting is noted on the minimap, which btw.. minmap? why? 
Bonus points for not having invisible walls hindering movement, but taking it right back for areas that have rocks and ledges that you just fall through. The movment is pretty free, so we'r gonna go wallclimbing^^

The scaleing is off, like, the skulls on the ground are huuuge, the stake from the stake gun shoots treetrunk sized stakes somehow(i can accept that its "magic" i guess..), but, they get stopped by the leaves of a small bush.. 
The player char looks huge in the art and cinematic but most enemies tower over you.

Doublejump, but fall dmg?


 The only semi enjoyable elements was the theme( but that quickly wore off), and weapon progression.
(Tough i unlocked most weapon types in just a few hrs) 

It's just overall meh. and i dont see how they could fix it without a major rework.

Suggestions for improvement:

Better Ai, or moveset for the differant enemy types.

I'd like to see a meele weapon rather than the weak punches as an option. With a system for blocking/parring attacks, it would make the flow of combat feel better.

inviormental things to play around, maybe make spells create effects etc (tho with the bad AI atm that would make things, sooo easy)

Less bulletproof bushes etc.

Fasttravel when in camp/base

the weapons and damage system, bleah.. if i aim a holy revolver at a unholy creatures head and shoot it, having the -1- dmg float up is just so lame.. dmg reduction at range sure, but rather than just makeing it 1dmg, do something with spread, travletime/bulletdrop and have it atleast be somewhat effective.

I'd personally probably prefer puzzles that are a tad more logically challenging, however the easiness of the puzzles in pleasantly relaxing.

review_text:
[h2]TL;DR[/h2]
[b]A lyric body horror, with top tier visual and audio design.[/b]

[h3]Positives[/h3]
[olist]
[*] H. R. Giger's fever dream. Every shape, every creature, every pulse oozes macabre body horror brutalism.
[*] Audio design is absolutely top notch:
[list]
[*] Both in audio effects of everything from the player characters body to various gizmos small and large and
[*] the music, which is used sparingly to great effect as an exclamation mark on scenes of import.
[/list]
[*] Level design is excellent. One can clearly read from the design language and be led through the hopeless halls of civilization fallen.
[*] Ominous set pieces anchor the player on several places. Each of these is done within gameplay by clever use of architecture.
[*] Tool design (including health and ammo stations) is marvelous. Not sure whether I would like to shake the designers hands or hide from them in terror. Well done.
[*] Puzzle construction is fresh with every turn throwing you something new. There is little to no recycling.
[*] Creature design of "the parasite" needs to receive a special nod. Delicious.
[/olist]

[h3]Neutral[/h3]
[olist]
[*] While logically sound, I found the first tool a bit underwhelming.
[*] Not sure whether I like the inclusion of combat or not. Sure the tools at the players disposal are meaty and visceral, but it gives the player a chance to fight back, which to some extent devalues the predatory nature of the environment.
[/olist]

[h3]Negatives[/h3]
[olist]
[*] The final resolution is unsatisfying. There is a bit of deus ex machina going on with a key element of the conclusion (and honestly throughout the story). I would have loved the player character to make a few steps into a place that would turn out to be even worse than the environs they were trying to get away from.
[*] Color desaturation. I would have loved a bit more contrasts at "the citadel" and in several other places. Muting all color and popping a few reds and greens would have done a lot of good to underline certain scenes.
[/olist]

review_text:
Verdict: don't buy. Reasoning: see below vvvvv

[b] The Positives [/b]
The atmosphere is probably the best part of this game. The entire game takes place in an ungodly biomechanical hell that always seems to have a new level of "what in the god damn?" to throw at you. This along with the surprisingly well put together animation leads to a pretty unique experience all things considered. This however, is where the positives end.

[b] The Negatives [/b]
Scorn isn't actually a game, it is an interactive walking simulator. Despite being given the "Puzzle" tag, this game has only one actual puzzle in it. It also only has one non-linear decision in it. Both of these come within the first act of the game, meaning you experience the most "Game" Scorn has to offer within the first 20 minutes. While there is shooting in this game, it's completely unnecessary since you can run past the majority of encounters. Even if you did want to fight, there's no point since the gun mechanics are incredibly janky and unsatisfying. Towards the end, I found myself more annoyed by Scorn than entertained or amazed. 

[b] Conclusion [/b]
In conclusion, if Scorn was a $15 game, I wouldn't be too disappointed. But since it's an outrageous $40 for what is a literal walking simulator with a highly misleading steam store page description, I am indeed very disappointed. If you have absolutely nothing better to do and enjoy this kind of horror experience, then this game is certainly worth your time. But for $40? it'll never be worth your money.

review_text:
Guilty feeling from playing this game way over outweighs the fun. It's kind of weird killing one guy playing this game feels way worse than killing thousands of enemies playing FPS games. I guess it's because i don't feel obliged to kill my family just because the demon tells me so. You have to follow the exact direction that the devil wants you to do and that makes me feel like a slave not a son of the devil. There are certain things you can do but there's not much freedom living in a fancy castle because the game only focuses on killing the family.  Its like getting chores done that you don't understand why you have to do it anyways.
Graphics and controls are pretty bad even considering the time the game came out. The kid is ugly, the parents are ugly, the demon is ugly.... Sometimes it even glitches. Controls feel a bit janky all the time. I don't feel like I'm controlling the character sometimes. 
It might be still a nice game for horror movie "Omen" fans but I felt disgusted pretty much all the time playing this game. I think there had been steady amount of fans playing this game because there are a sequel and even a third one. It's sad because i get that the content and idea might be appealing to people for being unique but the game doesn't elaborate any farther even worsening it by bad graphics and controls.

그래픽과 컨트롤은 만들어진 떄 고려해도 별로다. 주인공 못생겼고 부모도 못생겼고 악마도 못생겼다..그리고 가끔 그래픽 렉도 생긴다. 컨트롤은 많이 구려서 내가 캐릭터를 컨트롤하는 느낌이 별로 나지않는 수준이다.

review_text:
In the current state of this game, i would not recommend this game, even at £25 GBP
The game has a variety of game breaking bugs, which for me has running the whole play experience for me all together until they are fixed.

Normal ground AI can spot you from what seems like miles away when they get alerted, even if you are in a position that wouldn't normally get you spotted (confirmed to even happen on the easiest difficulty). 

 In some areas of the contract missions, the AI don't stay spotted, They get un spotted almost instantly if you look away for a split second. 

Ai even on the easy difficulty have practically laser like accuracy from more then 300m using AKs. 

Quick save reload spawns are ridiculous to the point an actual save option NEEDS to be implemented. You'd kill a bounty target, after a while and loot them because it somewhat forces you to do them when you enter the area, you will enter a new part of the level, and if you don't hit the correct trigger point on the map, it will reload you all the way back before you kill the bounty target. 

Unlike old sniper ghost warrior games (Such as 3 for an example) had a red dot to tell you where your bullet would go on normal and easy difficulty. In this game its a white line which doesn't stay in the scope and takes a few seconds while breathing in to appear again, and its hard to line up a shot on someone with a white line IN A WHITE COLOUR CONTRAST GAME. 

The bipod attachment, like SGW3 is still broken where it doesnt allow you to pivot the gun lower then about a 20 degree angle, being basically a useless attachment (You could do better trying to snipe people with throwing knifes then trying to kill someone with a bipod)  

On the good side:
The graphics are very good. 

Missions although tedious are very good and have replay-abilty factor with the fact you can do the challenges the mission has set (e.g  Assassinate "Person" without triggering the alarm to get extra money) if you didnt do it on your first run.

Game story and plot seems very immersive (Sadly only on mission 3 due to the bugs)

Game gore is much more present in this as in the last game, all guns now blow peoples heads off clean, with the heavy sniper bullet guns (Like 338 and 50 cals) which can tear arms and legs off.

Edit: 21/12/2019 
I found out the reason the enemys get unspotted was the fact they're signal jammers (lol my bad)

review_text:
Feels more like John Carpenter's Escape From New York than most superhero movies or traditional comicbook plots. If you've seen most superhero games or films you know that's probably for the best, but the plot itself is still pretty dumb. Batman has zero charisma, so why he even has lines I don't know. He sounds like a moron.

There's one important caveat I need to mention since nobody ever criticizes this game's combat, and judging from the forums, blindly defend this game no matter what. Spamming the counter attack button can wipe out a crowd of seven guys without suffering any damage to yourself. You don't even have to face them to counter, rendering the first few hours a complete joke. 

The worst part of the game is that the melee combat system also has an annoying auto-targeting system which means you aren't guaranteed to hit the person you're aiming at. There are moments you will be confused as you fly across the screen to hit someone you didn't see, sapping all the joy or sense of accomplishment out of the game. Of all the games that copied this fighting system, THEY ALL DID IT BETTER. Button prompts in the middle of fight just gets old after a couple hours. To simply hit a guy on the ground you need a special combo move, just to clutter combat up even further. Later you'll have to remember about twenty individual buttons/combinations just to progress. 

The combat in this game is garbage but the controls are just as bad, a bad port from consoles. Because sprint, climb, and roll are all one key, you'll often do random moves you weren't intending or be twirling around a wall when you want to climb over it, kind of like in Assassin's Creed. The controls and gadget selector are all clunky and overly complicated, requiring you to hold down multiple buttons just to do one simple task. Why? 

The game has decent stealth, but the platforming is drudgery and boss fights can be pretty laborious bs. I've tried playing this three times to see if I was missing something, and each time I hate it more as I see more of its flaws.

As a lover of the film I feel obligated to say that this game has indeed so far lived up to its objectives of replicating the movie's feel of a last stand against the bug menace. I was an early believer and bought the game in Early Access in 2023, 
There are a few issues that I feel are keeping back the game from its true potential:
-Overall difficulty through all game modes has seen a dramatic decrease, during Open Beta chances of success on an ARC Mission, the games most involved mode, were at roughly 30 percent, a slow uphill slog that was rather difficult without team communication, since the full release I have not yet lost an ARC Mission unless the team is toatally AWOL, I feel like the attraction of this game was overcoming the challenging yet fair game play of fighting against a severely outnumbering hive mind
-As an Early Access player I would have very much liked to have been able to keep my trooper's classes and unlocks at the position they were at before release, this isnt a PVP game so I feel like the 60 hours I sunk into the game would not have been lost having to grind every trooper back up to full unlocks
-Matchmaking is currently a crap shoot as friends attempt to enter a game with frequent receive error messages, yet I continue on to the game, and when I leave so I can join my friends the game will always automatically make me join the game I just left, not good
+I truly do enjoy this game and feel it was 20 USD well spent, I just wish the developers would realize that everyone doesn't want to make it back, We want an uphill battle that we'll only win if the team is halfway competent. See you on the bounce troopers

review_text:
If you're looking at this game while its on a deep discount, it's actually a recommend. I'm giving a not recommended based on the retail price. 

The story for the main game is alright, though rather short and honestly nothing ground breaking. If you're not going to play the game 5 or 6 times on NG+ for all the achievements I imagine you'll get 10-14 hours out of the base game. The DLC adds another mission but without spoiling anything I could do without that part of the story. 

If you do replay the game multiple times I don't really see much of a point outside of the achievements, honestly. As long as you loot all the enemies in your initial play through you'll almost have everything upgraded. The final upgrades are just an extra weapon ability that causes the weapon to use more ammo, for example. There are other modes added in DLC as well so I guess if you like that kind of thing maybe you'll get more out of it.

The combat is rather strange... to dodge you need to hold down a or d (or the joystick if using a controller) when the enemy goes to attack. It's somewhat fun for a little while but when there are multiple enemies it can get rather annoying. There isn't a perfect timing for dodge, you just have to be holding the key when the enemy swings. Bonelab is a fourth game made by SLZ and the successor to Boneworks. So you might think it's going to be better from his older brother but in reality Bonelab is simply a “Boneworks Director Cut” or “Boneworks: Lab DLC”. I have no idea why this game is released as a standalone title but if I had to guess it would be that they wanted to grab cash from a meta store and to do so the game had to be playable on their devices. by doing so you can feel that some aspects of the game were simplified. Despite all of that Bonelab is still a fun experience but if we include only few life improvements, new reskinned NPC and short story line [if we can call it that way it was more like a tutorial/showcase of new “abilitys” and what bonelab engine can do, with a lore for fans to dig around] then you will start to ask yourself why was’t that simply added to boneworks as a DLC? Another aspect i should mention is that the bonelab is mostly a mod support focus, If bonelab had failed to attract the attention of modders the game would end up differently.

[strike]—-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[/strike]
Things that are worst in Bonelab then in Boneworks

-Legs physics: you know something went wrong when simply standing on a stairs makes your character slowly slide down. Now apply this on other surfaces like a pipe or other element used in parkour and you will have a frustrating experience. and legs works weird when after climb from the edge you try to stand on a prop 

-Hands physics: the amount of times when my hands got stuck inside a prop were too common, grabbing pipes makes your hands partially sucks in them. there is also a weird mechanic that makes your hands glue to your stomach so when inspecting something it's getting weirdly close to you body

- Gun handling: some guns angle are off , aiming straight down is a prue pain, sometimes your character lose grip of your gun when enemy are too close to you 



Things that i have mix feeling 

- Maps: every map feels like it was submitted in an online competition with set rules. I bet if you modded an unofficial map to storyline nobody would notice on his first playthrough. some maps are grate and other lacking in details it really dependent on a person who worked on them 

-Storyline: SLZ has a specific way of telling the story but the biggest disappointment was the length of it. I finish the storyline in 14h that include searching every corner of map, climbing every tall object there is,  playing every minigame in a hub, unlocking most of the collectables. It was fun but short lasted 

- Scoreboard/challenges: whats its the point of it if not only it doesn’t track correctly your time but also because of the nature of bonelab you can easily cheat your way

Things that are better in Bonelab
- Climbing: now you can grab the end of a floor making it much easier to pull yourself up and just in general climbing is more fun

-Slow motion: before it was impossible to move and slow time at the same moment now they added toggle mechanism

- Drop magazine: small detail but really important 

- Melee combat: i avoided melee in boneworks but here it was super fun 

- You keep your inventory on level transition 

- You can shot/break open capsules it's such a improvements for people that want to unlock everything in a legit way (people who played boneworks will know the pain) 

- Spawn gun menu is much better and the nimbus now have a noclip 

Why did i give it a negative review well because the whole experience felt like a tech demo a showcase of cut content. Just image if you played Boneworks and Bonelab you don’t feel any significant different but at least Boneworks had a solid reason to be like that they tried  to push vr experience to a new level when a bonelab is just a cut content mess with some improvements that should have been in both games not worth to be standalone title and the price tag

review_text:
BONELAB is one of the single worst VR experiences I've ever had the displeasure of suffering through. It is a step back from BONEWORKS in every way, shape, and form imaginable. BONEWORKS had problems, but despite its numerous issues, it was a well-designed and enjoyable campaign experience with a neat sandbox to go along with it. BONELAB barely has a campaign - what's there is maybe one or two hours long, everything else is sandbox content.
The campaign itself is a confusing mess of uninspired levels meant to introduce the poorly implemented avatar switching system. One of them was literally just a walking sim that forced you to use a tiny avatar with stubby legs to trudge across a lunar landscape - except you can complete the level within two minutes by stepping on two jump pads and pressing a button. The level that follows is a kart racer - which forces you to use an avatar who's too weak to use the tiny steering wheel with one hand, and on top of that, the kart spins out constantly if you apply too much steering angle - which seems to be any more than five degrees in either direction. The "heavy" avatar, which should enable a fun strength power fantasy, is instead a chore to use, since the avatar's hands don't match up with the position of your IRL hands, totally ruining any muscle memory or immersion you may have had.
The climbing physics are also godawful - there's no way to force yourself up and over a ledge, you instead have to mash yourself against it and pray the game lets you on top of it. Furthermore, a majority of avatars are too weak to actually lift themselves up onto an object, adding to the needless irritation.
Movement is floaty and awkward at times. Jumping is awkward most of the time. Climbing is, as mentioned, awful.
Melee combat lacks any and all impact. When I wind up and deliver a huge punch to an enemy while using the "heavy" avatar, I expect the blow to knock him flat on his back, if not fold him like tissue paper or even send him flying. Instead, they just kind of stumble and fall over.
Gunplay is... It's alright. Pretty hard to screw that up, but given how poor of a showing Stress Level Zero put out here, I wouldn't be surprised.

If you want to shoot things, play H3VR
If you want to use melee, play Blade and Sorcery
If you want a moddable sandbox, play BONEWORKS

BONELAB is a failure of a video game and Stress Level Zero should be ashamed of themselves for ever producing it.

review_text:
Where Winds Meet has great potential, but, sadly, its atrocious localization ruins the experience — and that alone is enough to make me drop the game.

Still, let's start with the positives:
- WWM is gorgeous. I was drawn in by the Chinese aesthetics and wasn’t disappointed. Honestly, just walking around to enjoy the scenery and architecture is a good enough reason to download it.
- Performance is quite solid for the picture you get.
- The combat system is pretty fun and fluid, with a wide variety of weapons and skills to experiment with.
- It’s free, and the monetization is cosmetics-only.

Now for the glaring issue. Most of the English translation was done by AI, and it seems no one bothered to edit any of it. I don’t care much about the voice acting, since you can just switch to Chinese, which is handled fairly well. But if I’m playing a large, story-driven game set in a foreign country, with tons of dialogue and lore, the text has to be of decent quality. Right now, it’s nowhere close. To make matters worse, subtitles are not properly formatted and often poorly synchronized, giving you about a second to read two lines of text. With English not being my native language, you can imagine how frustrating all that becomes.

Some minor issues:
- Progression and menus are convoluted. There’s just way too much unnecessary stuff.
- Even with upscalers turned off, there’s ghosting around the character whenever the camera moves.
- Ubisoft-esque open world activities and collectibles, many of which feel shallow.
- The NPC AI-chatbot system is extremely primitive. Even if you try to roleplay and take it seriously, it breaks too easily.

I’d be happy to give WWM another shot, but only after major improvements to the localization.

review_text:
At least it's cheap. IMSCARED is a meta-horror game where the experience involves your entire computer system, and not just the application itself. It's a bit difficult to start up its tools, as it relies on having a desktop folder to place information for the puzzles into, but the rest of its creepy effects on your computer seem to work reliably. It seems alright at first, and kind of reminds me of the atmosphere of games like Ghoul's Forest, due to the ominous darkness in the game, but I don't think it provides a satisfying or believable setting in its visual design. The graphics aren't just bad, they're terribly done, to the point that it's really hard to read things, or to even figure out what some of the things your looking at even are. If it was a "real" game, even as an experiment, it's likely that someone would have put more work into its visuals, as even old computer games never looked this bad. 

[h1] What I Enjoyed [/h1]
[list]
[*][b]IMSCARED is sometimes frightening[/b]. Before you're aware of what's going on, and when you're entering into new challenges, the atmosphere is sufficiently effective and the scares are shocking, even if you can anticipate when they will appear. It may look like garbage a lot of the time, but the startle from seeing some of its monsters lunge at you was able to scare me several times. Unfortunately, the narrative, locations, and general events of the game are not particularly scary or inventive for a horror genre. The crashing built into the game to convince you that it's "glitched" or "broken" isn't frightening at all, and is so heavy-handed and common it becomes irritating.
[*]The puzzles are often good. There's a few real doozies hidden in this game, and the mechanics of how it works with its computer folder, text documents, and the like can be really fun. Unfortunately, the game is largely a collectathon built around keys, and it can be mystifying what one is expected to do, or where to go--even with the hints provided by the game files. 
[*]The sound quality is fitting for the visual and gameplay direction. The sounds the monsters make, as well as the tone of footsteps, items, and the like is immersive. 
[/list]

[h1]What I Disliked[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]The gameplay is awful[/b]! There was never an old game that controlled like this one does, with full movement in any direction and quick spinning of where you are facing. As a result, this is one of the main things that makes the game feel so fake. It's obvious it was made in 2012 and not in the 80s or 90s, and couldn't possibly be haunted or broken, but was designed that way. As I said, the game is just built on collecting objects, and there's basically nothing to do but press E at relevant points, and crouch just so you can pick stuff up. The rest of the game is a walking simulator where you constantly have to restart because it does a fake-crash every thirty seconds anytime something scary happens. It's like a story that doesn't know how to continue after it has reached the climax, and I don't know if it's worse that the game keeps doing the same crash over and over, or if it would just reset me to a checkpoint. I'm leaning to the crashing, since it takes more time and is so unimaginative you begin to just expect it. Worst of all, you have to collect all of the achievements to complete the game, which essentially requires using a walkthrough, even if it gives you shortcuts for getting close to the ending. 
[*]The atmosphere of having a "game" with the entire computer and not just the application is executed poorly. I enjoy it when a puzzle requires you to do pseudo-programming by changing values in the text boxes, or take hints from files, but the youtube videos that play are awful, annoying, and fake. The programmer's voice is obnoxious, and his idea of scary is childish. And I can't get over how annoying it that it wants to pretend to crash constantly. It was cool when Undertale or Doki Doki Literature Club tried this, as it was done with subtlety and some sense of taste, rather than being something the creator had to rely on because there was NOTHING else interesting or appealing about his video game. 
[*]The story is bad. It's a boring plot that makes no sense and asks for arbitrary emotional reactions that would not coincide with its themes, and its written badly. Perhaps it's the translation, but if the developer knows English, he should have been able to find something satisfying in the localization. It doesn't have to be the Divine Comedy, but the game honestly feels like it was written by a person with one digit IQ. 
[*]It's full of boring segments like a hedgemaze or a freezer that just serve to artifically lengthen a game that's likely too short to even be released. The gameplay puzzles in these sections also don't work well, and between the headache from puzzling about abstract ways to continue, from having to stare at the awful graphics and listen to the grating sounds, it's hard to find any reason to even continue.
[/list]

I almost feel like I should have been paid for playing this, and it's worth two dollars at most. I'm saying that as a person who literally won't even pick up small change if it's less than a dollar. Skip it, and don't fall for any sort of hype on this game. Pretty much all horror games are like this, and there's a lot better without the gimmicks.

Before buying this game, I was a hockey fan but only casually. I had no idea what I was getting into. I knew so little that I edited my starting database to give myself a better team, and thought up some players I was vaguely familiar with. My defensive pairings included Ristolainen, Nurse, and Dumba... I was the Pittsburgh Penguins. Christian Dvorak was my 3rd line centre, and Auston Matthews was my 4th line centre. I was clueless.

Several seasons and failures later, I now have a near-encyclopedic knowledge of hockey just by absorbing what's in the game. I'm not sure how I feel about this, but it got me way more into hockey than I already was.

This spreadsheet simulator has me making spreadsheets outside of the game and learning features in Excel I didn't know existed. This game has thoroughly obliterated my life.

10/10, one of the best, most engaging and life-ruining games I've ever played.

Get the TBL and ECK rosters and facepacks immediately after installing, they're on the workshop. TBL is a frozen season-start roster, ECK evolves with the season.

Have fun, and enjoy becoming a savant who can tell exactly when the opposition's 4th line left winger who has no goals is about to score his first goal of the season, against you, because you've used the exact tactic you can see them lining up for as they go for the face-off.

Rooftops & Alleys: The Parkour Game’s ethos is perfectly described by its own subtitle. This is quite simply, “The Parkour Game.” For decades, we’ve had many big-budget open-world titles implementing freerunning into their exploration, like Assassin’s Creed or Dying Light. Parkour in these games feels satisfying, but the controls are simplified as it’s just another tool in games with very broad focuses. When you get a game more holistically focused on parkour, such as Mirror’s Edge, it’s usually an extremely fast-paced experience that wraps up after a few hours.

Rooftops & Alleys breaks these trends by focusing on an elaborate freerunning system whilst also providing total player freedom. Whether you want swift, efficient movement or ridiculously elaborate displays of style, Rooftops & Alleys has you covered.

But how much can an excellent parkour system carry a full game? Well, if it’s fun enough, I’d say it absolutely can, but Rooftops & Alleys stumbles just often enough to make enjoying the game a constant battle. Despite an excellent core, issues across its movement systems and empty levels always seemed to limit its potential. How much these issues will bother you will come down to personal experience. When Rooftops & Alleys is at its best, it’s an amazing experience. Unfortunately, it’s rarely at its best.

So, honestly, I feel torn on this game. It has some really fun bones, some really cool base systems, but nothing feels like it works together. Everything feels like it has a rough edge. Inventory management ends up being clunky, dropping down from ledges is positively disorienting, and sometimes grabbing something seems to grab something entirely unrelated simply because the game decided that was the more "relevant" option. It's also somewhat threadbare on content.

Performance is [i]rough[/i], even on my decently beefy machine (64 GB DDR4, AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, RTX 2080 Super). If there's more than a few recently-dead zombies, I get enough frames dropped to be motionsick.

I almost feel bad not recommending this, because it's fun. It's enjoyable. But I feel like $40 is too much of an ask for it in this state. I'm not upset I bought it, I am a little upset that I bought it for the full price. If you see it on sale, I'd say pick it up. Even still, if you think you'll enjoy it, you probably will, but just be aware of what you're getting into.
