EDIT 7/31/2025: As of the most recent update, Webgrave, I cannot recommend this game to anyone with arachnophobia. The new zone has given me the most severe reaction to spiders in a game that I have had in years. Which is a huge shame, since I love this game, and the rest of the system and game changes they have made have been awesome. But the new zone Velmore, which serves as a mid way point through the game, is unplayable to me because of the design choices. 

A very unique Action FPS blending together a mix of Destiny and Doom-like combat that has a very fun end result. Each of the weapons you can unlock has unique perks that dramatically change how they play, and the overall gunfeel of them is great.

The core gameplay is a novel pve Extraction + roguelite loop where you portal into an area, explore, and fight large groups of enemies to clear out the map. Each group that you kill grants you a boon that buffs and augments your build in different ways. Only played for about 9 hours, but I know for a fact that this is something I'm gonna spend a large amount of time in.
Not only is the story and general atmosphere incredibly interesting, having to survive in the world of Pathologic is incredibly engaging and extremely fun. The close-range combat is not my favorite part, but successfully getting a hit in on an enemy and taking their stuff means that I'm willing to take it for how it is.
On another note, the trading system is incredibly simple, but I've never seen any other game do it quite like this. Store-owners are the only NPCs that take money, and they're locked inside their establishment, while regular people roam the streets. Vendors are pretty scarce on the map, and you have an extremely limited amount of time to do things during the day, so you don't wanna make huge detours unless it's necessary. Regular civilians will trade in items, and every one of them has their own preferences, so while in my current playthrough I have a bit of money, I'm barely managing to get by on the slim amounts of food and healing items I can obtain.
What little jank there is I am able to look over due to the immense amount of enjoyment I've already gotten out of it.
The atmosphere and story go hand-in-hand, and both are unlike any other game I've played before. I tried the first game, and found it to be far too difficult and complicated for me to actually get into. This, however, I am more than able to get into. The music is tinny and weird, the way characters act and talk is bizarre, and I've realized that I become extremely nervous and greedy when playing it. 
A good example of this is that I was originally hoarding money for a particularly expensive item, but recently I decided not to buy it. So if I'm not in need of the money for the expensive item, why am I still insistent on hoarding it? I need food and various other things to keep me alive, but I'm still looking to make a profit when it's not that important. I should just buy food and supplies, but I'm not. 
On another note, due to an early rep-hit, I'm now constantly looking over my shoulder and worried about someone chasing me even though my reputation is positive everywhere. The enemies that only appear at night are not helping my paranoia.
It's so good at what it does that it makes me fall back on self-destructive and neurotic tendencies in-game. Hopefully the devs keep making stuff, 'cause they're extremely talented and I want to see more of whatever ideas they come up with. 10/10.

review_text:
This was one of two or three games I actually expected to be good this year. Felt like Boneworks DLC. I held off on writing a review but since finishing it on my second session I have not once felt the "urge" to come back to it.

Shorter, more linear and less interesting campaign. Zero innovation besides the 'avatar switching' with 3 of the 6 avatars being completely redundant ("Strong", Light and Short). It's not a bad game, but I don't know if it's worth recommending if you've played Boneworks. When I saw the medieval setting teased in the intro I just wanted to go and play whatever game THAT was, not what I ended up slogging through for ~6 hours. You end up returning to that area later on but it's a LOT smaller and all the enemies just use their fists even though there are guns and melee weapons lying around everywhere (also enemies cannot use melee weapons in this game, and there is only one enemy type that can use guns; the same copy+pasted hologram enemy from Boneworks).

No new guns except a pump action and semi-auto shotugn, which modders added into Boneworks yonks ago (in fact the devs said they would add shotguns into Boneworks but obviously that never happened). Unless you want to count reskins of course. Good to see the same M4, MP5K etc copy+pasted into this game. On one hand, I want devs to keep content from previous games if the sequel is in the same engine, however I expect to see something NEW when playing a game sold as brand new rather than just picking up the same weapons to kill the same enemies in the same environments.

There are no new enemies except a short, fragile 'turret' type thing which  does a lot of damage but goes down in a couple shots. Only shows up in the last 2(?) levels. They also remodeled/reskinned a couple enemies from the first game. The blue zombie type enemies are not present in the campaign but are in the other modes, so there is very little variety when playing.

You've probably already read stuff about the Moonbase and 'Pillar' levels, though these criticisms pale in comparison to the other issues I feel the game has.

This game's only saving grace is ironically what probably made it such an underwhelming experience; massive marketing (externally and in-game, integrated into the canon story of the game lol) focused on modding and player made content - would've been no problem in my opinion if the initial offering wasn't so sparse and shallow. Hopefully players can add campaigns and new game modes to extend the longevity of the game as it currently does nothing better than its competitors; 

Blade and Sorcery wins melee and stealth, 
Hellsplit and Grimlord win 'dark'/difficult combat, 
H3VR and Contractors win firearms,
Hard bullet wins 'brutal' sandbox gameplay...

...not to mention the janky impact physics and amateur sounds that abound this game. Main draw of this game is structured levels so without that sort of content there is no real draw as long as there are other games with 'endless' modes that feel better to play.

But the worst of all is that the music in this game is somehow worse than Boneworks. Boneworks has one of the best OSTs in gaming, undoubtedly the best of any VR game. The main theme is subtly included in a few tracks here but otherwise the entire soundtrack in Bonelab is forgettable, and for some reason they decided to include strange, almost slurred vocals in one of the songs. Maybe my problem is that I am not a hipster but this was a total L and took me out of the game (the 'game' being walking around the HUB and being forced to try random minigames before being able to continue playing the walking simulator-esque campaign.

Finally, the game is unbelievably easy, almost as easy as Boneworks. The most trouble one would have in this game is climbing, as the legs sometimes go all wack and twist 90 degrees to the side or get stuck in ladder rungs. Maybe it was a few one-offs for me, so in general the climbing and movement was very similar to Boneworks so the muscle memory carried over. Most enemies die in one or two headshots and the enemies are typically few and far between, and you have a Borderlands-style 'last chance' if you die where you can revive yourself by getting a kill. I also detest the ammo system in this game just as I did in Boneworks; you have a total pool of ammo that carries over between levels, and you don't lose ammo in magazines if you throw them away so there is little care for ammo management. This means you use very little ammo in combat and will always be able to top up your mag without worrying about 'wasting' ammo. The weird thing about this is that the system had a use in Boneworks as ammo was a currency used to buy things (like weapons or developer tools) from vending machines, which are completely absent in this game. I wish they went with a different system, perhaps like having an ammo limit or needing to put ammo physically on your body a la H3VR/etc.

Anyway, rant over. While this review was mostly negative, the game is good, but not the revolutionary experience they advertised it as. The whole ending felt very on-the-nose, and there is even a Discord link to a modding server at the end for those looking to get into modding. There is a bit of polish compared to the prequel and they added one or two cool new things but this just seems like a modding platform - a double edged sword that I love and hate. Modded games last longer and the experience of tailoring your mod list is great, but there is a niggling feeling at the back of my head suggesting that developers use this as an excuse to underdevelop their game as players will just fix it later (Bethesda moment). Not sure if SLZ are like that, so far it seems not, but my main takeaway from this game was that it's an okay if underwhelming experience with massive potential for future improvement. Maybe in a year we will see videos titled "Bonelab is GREAT if you don't play the campaign..." or "This mod makes Bonelab worth playing again" or "This epic mod FIXES Bonelab".

tl:dr $50 for a $20 DLC, watch this space

review_text:
I got this on a 75% sale ($6.50 CAD) and I feel like I barely got my money's worth. There's a lot of great concepts but a lot of dull ones as well. The core of this game is great, the art, sounds, sprites, concept, core mechanics, but everything around it stymies its depth: 

Everything that you control is based around one resource. Which in theory I like, since you're always considering this balancing act between army size, food, and modifiers, but the problem is how detrimental starvation is and how strong the modifiers are. In reality, the balancing act is knowing how small to keep your army so that you can maximise upgrades until you get near the end and you inflate it quickly.

A lot of the upgrades are the same across unit types, so the more unique upgrades feel few and far between, and those upgrades are what let you play around with builds more, and upgrades aren't very common. Without the more unique upgrades you are more restricted to how you build your army, since there's only one real form of consistent healing and there's only one real form of consistent tank.

The unique room encounters are whatever and are mostly designed quite similarly, you bring something, you get either money or an upgrade for one specific unit type. The unique prompt at the start of every floor feels more like a test in how much you've played the game, you can guess the first option pretty consistently to avoid a penalty, but if you want the benefit you kind of just have to look it up, which isn't exactly fun.

Pretty disappointed with how half-baked this game is. At just under 6 hours, I've done most of what this game has to offer. Which is exceptionally bad for a roguelike, which, by definition should have a high degree of replayability.

Review: Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun is a brilliant example of how a game can focus on one core idea and execute it to perfection. It’s a strategy masterpiece that rewards patience, planning, and precision. Every level is a puzzle waiting to be solved, and every character you command feels essential to the bigger picture.

Pros:

Deep Strategy Gameplay: Every mission demands clever thinking, timing, and coordination. It’s the kind of game that makes you feel smart when your plan works.

Beautiful Graphics & Design: The art style captures feudal Japan in stunning detail, with vibrant environments that are both gorgeous and functional.

Variety in Levels: Each stage feels different and forces you to adapt your strategy—no two missions play the same.

Interesting Characters: Every character has unique abilities, and the synergy between them adds endless tactical depth.

For Strategy Lovers: If you enjoy games that focus on precision and problem-solving, this is pure genius in its own right.

Polished & Refined: Everything feels carefully designed, from the UI to the level layouts, giving the game a sense of quality rarely seen in its niche.

Cons:

High Difficulty: This isn’t a casual game—mistakes are punished, and trial-and-error is part of the experience.

Niche Appeal: Players looking for fast action might find the methodical pace too slow.

Final Thoughts

Shadow Tactics is a shining gem in the strategy genre. It doesn’t try to be everything—it picks a lane and masters it. For fans of stealth tactics and smart problem-solving, this is one of the best experiences you can play.

In a world full of games that try to do too much, Shadow Tactics reminds us that sometimes less is more—and when done right, it’s genius.

I would not recommend this game, even at sale price.

There must be something wrong with me as this game has rave reviews and it falls in the category of the exact type of game I like. I loved RimWorld, I'm a huge fan of population simulators like Tropico and Anno so this isn't my first rodeo.

This game, quite simply, doesn't work. It's not that it has a high learning curve, again, I've played Rimworld. It's just that it doesn't work well, at all.

You can assign workers to a building and they, just, won't do anything. Ever. For days. The "produce until no storage is available" function does not work. You cannot possibly convince me otherwise, it's just broken. So I'm guessing all the people who enjoy this game manually set values or tell it to disregard storage. Having an in game feature that seems incredibly important just, not work, is not really my idea of good game development.

The game encourages you to build building quickly, based on the in-game hints, they expect you to have a bow tower before the first night fall. This requires a bowyer, a lumber shack, a lumber mill, a crystal gathering station, etc. etc. It's not reasonable. You will be spreading your 11 man population so like 1 person is at each station.

This brings me to my next point, Population. This game doesn't like it, they don't want you to have any. You're going to be sitting on your hands waiting for something to happen because you simply don't have the personnel to accomplish anything. This became such an absolute roadblock I had to look it up online and the suggestions recommended un-tasking everyone in your village so they could socialize with one another and mate.

That has got to be the laziest and stupidest game design I have ever heard of.

I am just amiss at how this game has amazing ratings. Maybe if you slog through the broken and tedious beginning, getting attacked every night and spending half of your time rebuilding your structures because there is no feasible way to establish a defense early on, maybe then it starts to get interesting.

I don't have the patience for such a lazy approach when there are much better options out there. If you're looking for a unique, complex and procedurally generated survival game, save yourself the headache and buy Rimworld. Even Dawn of Man was a more enjoyable experience than this, and that one is fairly shallow.

review_text:
This is an excerpt from another review, it's all you need to read.

"The pricing is truly truly truly outrageous. Oh ho ho yeah. $30 for ONE ship. $5.50 for a costume. $12.50 to make your ship's bridge look like the Enterprise-D. Everything is just a little more expensive than you would expect.

Fans on the forums will tell you, "Yeah, but you can just grind and buy the stuff for free." This is true. You absolutely can work to get the items for free. However, the time investment is hardly worth it.

The system is complicated. Try to follow me.

Tier 6 ships (the highest tier, I believe) cost 3000 zen. 3000 zen costs $30. You can earn dilithium ore in-game by completing daily missions and repeating "Task Force Operations". (Which are equivalent to dungeons in most mmos.) You can refine up to 8000 dilithium ore per day. The refined version can be exchanged for zen. However, the exchange rate is roughly 500 dilithium for 1 zen.

So to obtain a $30 ship for "free", you would need nearly 1.5 million units of refined ore. At a rate of 8k per day, this requires around 180 days.

Assuming you login and gain the 8k every single day. Which is estimated to take a little under 4 hours. That's 720 hours of your life you are never getting back. For a $30 ship. That's like working for $0.04 per hour. No way I'm doing that! That's not even remotely reasonable." -Jackie Daytona

review_text:
Okay I think its time to revisit this, for reference I haven't played in probably around 2 months minus one time I logged in to pay a friend back who lent me N-Meseta. but lets get into it shall we? Oh Boy! (I'm a player who has played since base and always said PSO2 was my WOW, The game I never wanted to quit, NGS is just a worse version. 6000hrs+ on steam more on Xbox from before it was on PC, most in PSO2)

-We got Personal Quarters/ Creative Space back, Win for the social community, huge positive. I have small gripes about the ways to gain GP but there are bigger issues.

-They gave out that free extra storage. Yay! For small victory's.

-Story actually improved in Stia! till the falz boss fight, then it got cringe when the power of friendship stuff, not anything like idk character development... and the story since has basically been fetch quests with cut scenes so I tuned out.

-Access to selling on the auction house is pay walled to P2P players minus a once a month 3 day pass you "can" earn through the free track of the mission pass.

-They overvalue the premium and the proof is the 500SG price tag on auto dismantle compared to the other "premium features." (100sg "premium battle pass" and 300sg "material storage" which also auto deposits any crafting materials you pick up.) (you get the premium battle pass for free and auto dismantle if you buy premium with real money monthly, like a sub fee.)

-Events are still (mostly) copy and paste versions of one another, But the sonic collab one with the race was good, but it feels like they are trying to shove combat into every LTQ. Race LTQ! Boss battle at the end!? Quiz LTQ! Boss battle at the end!? why not just have the quiz's be quiz's then make a alternative boss battle LTQ? why does everything need combat? (maybe just me.)

-SG is still a constant issue for F2P (mostly.), if you plan to be F2P know your gonna have a bad time with SG if you are playing for Phashion.

-Trading is still absent 2 and a half years later which most of the community has been asking for back due to a continuing to inflate market and a small portion of the community loves to defend the removal of, why is that bad? because gifting items and them getting sniped by randoms who want to sell them for profit is annoying. In the words of many other MMO players "Allowing others to negatively impact another players gameplay experience without consent is just bad game design."

-They heavily nerfed drop rates of items in events. specifically ticket during the new years event i could farm 15+ tickets in roughly 1-2hrs. current events? sometimes i have went days of grinding 2-3hrs without a single ticket.

-Still missing a lot of content such as Casino, leader boards which give out SG every week, PVP, multiple ways to earn Shop passes. ETC. (though there are a few leader boards but some don't give out SG.)

-Classes balance is terrible, no more spreed sheet balancing please? BUT pay walled respec is gone small Win. 

-PSO2 base was not available to the PS community in global but NGS is. Yet some Players like to say if NGS could get more exposure, it would grow and solve lots of the games issues, but fact is that now PS which could not play PSO2 (in global) now has access to it and yet the numbers are still shrinking not growing. (wonder why. *looks at people claiming this.*)

-Why have I stopped playing the game? because I see no signs of it getting better and every time I try talk about it with new people I get either, A: a good convo about there own Dislikes, likes. Or the more commonly B: people tell me "don't like it. go play something else!" (in a less polite way.) So I am. I'm done repeatedly posting my feedback on the discord to try to fix the issues me and my friends had. As well as the feedback of other players who I think have really good ideas of how to solve major issues the game has, that get passed over week after week for things that are very minor and fix nothing in the long run... (trading being a major example.)

RANT WARNING INCOMING.

1.Players talking about how its not fair to compare NGS to PSO2? 
   A. PSO2 and NGS are quite literally connected! as you can switch between them without ever going to the menu.
   B. NGS is quite literally a squeal to PSO2! would you say you can't judge Avengers endgame by Avengers: age of ultron? or how about Dragon age 2 by Dragon age origins?
   C. Your character directly transfers from PSO2 to NGS! items and all skins, looks, everything. except certain currency's.
   D. Development time, some love to remind me that PSO2 took 7 years to make. Yes that's true, but the thing and they love to leave out is, it didn't take 7 years for PSO2 to be good.

It is not unreasonable to compare NGS to PSO2. lets get into the next rant, shall we?

2.NGS is not meant to replace or be PSO2.
anyone remember the announcement trailer for NGS? apparently not. Let me remind you of some quotes in the reveal trailer "In 2021, PSO2 will soar to new heights, and be reborn. NEW Genesis Phantasy Star Online 2." different trailer same channel "The next generation of PSO2 has arrived." Please tell me how is anyone able to say NGS is not the replacement for PSO2? when in the official trailer for NGS these Quotes are plain as day?! don't believe me? go to SEGAs OFFICAL youtube scroll to the bottom and find the "[4K] Latest Phantasy Star Online 2 New Genesis Follow-Up Video" and watch it because some people can't seem to remember what SEGA themselves marketed NGS as. A sequel to PSO2, which means NGS should be and rightfully expected to be a upgraded PSO2!

3.The community is too toxic? Ok lets look into what is most commonly being talked about in this way. "Players criticising the game without constructive feedback." Or as they like to say "Hating on it without suggesting ways to make it better." is it really necessary for several thousand players to say "drop rates are bad." to all be required to then follow it up with "buff the drop rates by roughly blank% because blank."? to not be called toxic? or is that ridiculous? Oh to specific? Ok, how about "all events feel like copy and pasted versions of one another."? do you need every last player to say there idea of what a good event would be? 
where should they get the ideas then? I find it hard to believe you can't find a few ideas among the community, or look at what other MMOs do? like you know? most MMO devs say they do?...

End

Why post this review 2 months after you stopped playing? Because every time I started writing it in a word doc i would rant endlessly about it till I was way over the steam character limit and would spend hours removing parts to try make it fit only to give up... This time I didn't, simple as that.

Lets end this the same way I did the first time because for me it still rings true.
I could have recommended you play PSO2 back when it was at its prime and I would be comfortable you would enjoy it with some guidance. But NGS? I can say you "might" enjoy it for a month or less, but will more then likely get bored after that, I can't recommend it because there are better alternatives that will respect your time more. Ultimately the only things that make this game arguably better then others is, its a MMO with action combat and Phashion better then pretty much any other MMO I know of. but the Fashion is 90% pay walled through AC scratch tickets minus what you can afford on the overpriced market and the action combat does not have enough interesting end game content to actually challenge you... The story? well stia was ok everything else not so much.

"Its not as bad as ___." is not a excuse to recommend any game to others, recommendations should be because you can say "I Like this game, it is a good game. The concept is brilliant! Sadly the pace of the gameplay is too erratic to hold my interest. 

Long periods of point-and-click style play happen between tasks/murders which vary in difficulty, seemingly at random. Generally in games keystage challenges become exponentially more difficult, but in my (short) exploration of this one it seems  one task can be virtually impossible to complete followed by a task which is ludicrously simple. 

It is challenging, in some instances overly so; actions expected of the player can be very obscure with no hints, once you've finally figured out what you have to do it can then be a feat of superhuman dexterity to complete your mission... creaing a  serious anticlimax. It is frustrating and slightly tedious in alternating intervals. This is not helped by the fact the game mechanics appear to struggle with a controller, there are a great many graphics glitches, odd bouts of lag, and reloading from a checkpoint takes a very long time. 

Perhaps the game is just older and I am being unfair. It is also possible that I'm just not suited to this type of puzzle solving as, to be candid, this game very quickly felt like a chore rather than a joy which is a pity because, as I said, the concept is awesome.

review_text:
I've had a pretty good time playing this game. It's aged remarkably well for a game with 30 years just around the corner. The Director is still one of the most advanced systems I've ever seen in a video game. However, it has an unintended consequence: it forces you to play very fast, and this can break immersion. If you are afraid of the zombies in even the slightest you will fail repeatedly and your resources will dwindle. So, the best solution is to not be afraid - and you are greatly rewarded for this. Once you learn the zombies really aren't as threatening as they sound, the game just gets very easy. Speaking of sound, this game is full of amazing sounds. Terrifying, unsettling sounds. There were so many moments were I was huddled in a corner looking for the source of some foreign rumbling just to realize it was another Common Infected sound I hadn't heard yet. The music is incredible and so crucial to the gameplay, a big part of why it has left such an impression on so many players (the other part being that it is just well written music). Another great thing about this game is that it's actually very well balanced. For the most part, nothing ever feels unfair or insurmountable. Unless your teammates make it so, which brings me to my next point: the bots.

The bots are just stupid. Unbearably stupid. They don't understand how to avoid witches to the point that if you are forced to pass one, she is guaranteed to be startled after you pass her. Their target priority is generally awful. They have a logical hierarchy (Bosses, Special Infected, Common Infected), but don't react to live or fluid situations well. They struggle greatly to navigate the environment well, are often in the worst possible place at all times and Smokers. Oh, my god Smokers. For some reason, these boneheads can only conceive of shoving the grabbed player to break the Smoker's tongue. They won't shoot it, won't shoot it's tongue, and certainly won't react to anything attacking you while you are grabbed. They just mindlessly walk at you until they can get into melee range the majority of the time. It's insufferable. They refuse to heal when they need to, refuse to accept no for answer when healing isn't needed, and just don't pick up items under any circumstances and wouldn't use them if they fell from the sky into their pockets anyway. That said, they actually do have incredible aim and will take out anything it seems aside from a Tank or Witch in seconds, sometimes before you can even react. 

Audio design is great, the game is stylish and intuitive, the levels are unique and interesting, the enemies are awesome and fun. This game packs a lot into such a small box. The only reason I don't recommend it is because there isn't much to experience beyond the singleplayer campaigns. I couldn't figure out how to mod this game, so that part may be on me, but the servers are dead. The few people still playing it are not very fun to play with, either speedrunning levels in seconds with the expectation that you will keep up, or just doing... nothing. Like nothing. At all. Wandering aimlessly. But you won't have to worry about that, because odds are when you are logged on, you won't find any lobbies anyway. 

The reason for this is because the game is just obsolete. Everything in Left 4 Dead is in Left 4 Dead 2. Every survivor, weapon, campaign, mode, and more plus a ton of mods. Even if you're looking for a purist experience, Left 4 Dead 2 has modes where you that filter out all of the new content and you can tailor the experience in unique ways with the countless workshop mods. There's no reason to spend the money on this game. There wouldn't even be a justification for the storage space if it were free.

I mean none of this as criticism of the game. Obviously, Left 4 Dead was not made with a sequel in mind, and what the devs have done in Left 4 Dead 2 is worthy of praise, not critique, but that does mean that is the reality for this game.

review_text:
Damn, this is a weird review to write.

During the first 3 hours playing the game, I really wondered why the reviews are only on mixed. I thought that this was such a great game; how could you dislike it. After a few more hours, I now can understand it. So I try to explain what actually happened. 

This game is like one of the most beautiful hikes you ever did. The problem being that your feet are fully covered in blisters. While the story, graphics and especially the level design are all fantastic, the actual gameplay is one of the worst one I have ever experienced. I played the game on maximum security difficulty, mainly with the melee weapon. If you play on a different difficulty or a different game mode in general, this could differ a lot from my playthrough. 

From the 10-12 hours estimated playtime, a good half just consists of fighting enemies. And the fights are what totally kills the game for me. In the beginning, it is quite okay to just press "A" and "D" to dodge enemy attacks to strike back at them. But this is pretty much all that is happening when encountering enemies. Its nearly the same thing every second room. Enemies run to you -> Fight -> "A" -> "D" -> "A" -> 3xLeft Click -> Repeat the dodge. There are some opportunities to kill the enemies a lot faster with environmental hazards or by stealthing, which isnt really fantastic but at least it is something different. No fight in this game is difficult, it just takes its time. That issue is even getting worse when enemies got a special feature about 1/4 into the game that "require" to shoot a special part of them. This could have been interesting if it wasnt for the "feature" that autolocked on enemy limbs and makes it really weird for you to aim at the special parts (You cannot turn this off). The gameplay is just so repetitive and boring that it manages to kill the vibe of the game. 

The atmosphere would be there because the graphics are top-notch, the sounds are neat, and the design overall is nothing but fantastic. But because of the actual gameplay, you will never feel a sense of dread or horror. My best comparison would be "Deadly premonition" where the game just got a combat mechanic the last second before release.

Okay aside from the rambling about gameplay, I really love some things about the game. The graphic- and level-designers really understood what they were doing. Also, even though the story was not the craziest idea ever, I enjoyed it. Especially because of the great actors playing the main characters. These were the reasons I didnt quit the game early on, and also the reason why the game is so infuriating. If it were not for the gameplay, I would have loved this game.

BUT if you manage to play the DLC "Final Transmission", everything from my review changes! Just kidding, the fighting even has a stronger focus here. Still the DLC concludes the base game with an expanded ending, which I liked a lot.

So my conclusion is: You might enjoy this game if you play it on a different difficulty or gamemode (I havent checked those out) and you can ignore the lack of proper gameplay. From the perspective of my own playthrough, I unfortunately cannot recommend it, though.

review_text:
To put it simply - Scorn is an interesting artistic experience, but an atrocious game to play.
[h1] The good[/h1]
[list]
    [*] This game replicates Giger rather well - everything is disturbingly organic, however if you are underaged or from a puritan family - welp, this isn’t a style for you, as everything has a rather specific… shape.
    [*] Great visuals. While you are in the meaty halls - it is not that obvious, but sometimes the game gives you really nice sceneries.
   [*] Good atmosphere. This is a dead decaying world and you can feel it.
[/list]

[h1] The bad [/h1]
[list]
    [*] Absolutely horrible combat. The enemies are unpleasant to fight as your character moves sluggish and most of the enemies have a ranged attack. They also take too long to deal with. When you get your guns - they take too many bullets from a really limited ammo pool. When you have only a melee tool - well, running into a ranged enemy, making 2 strikes that may or may not kill an enemy, and having to recover the stamina (biotech, in case you forgot) of your tool for 5 seconds mid fight is just a terrible design decision. And unlike the games with good gunplay, Scorn presents its combat more like a puzzle: if you find an ammo refill be prepared to use 90% of said refill on the enemies that will spawn the second you take it, and don’t you dare to miss! The combat is so bad that most of it I wished that Scorn was just a walking sim .
    [*] The puzzles. They aren’t hard, but every single animation takes WAY too long. In fact some of the puzzles have solutions that are obvious in under a minute, but to implement this solution you can waste 10 or more minutes.
    [*] Map layouts/location design. You know how in games you are used to exploring every branching path? And how you are used to finding ammo, collectables or lore in those branches? Forget it, because in Scorn any attempt to go out of your way will be punished by a dead end and a slow way back. This game doesn't have any exploration and even punishes you for attempting to explore. 
    [*] Story. There is none. You can guess the overall events, but it is all left to the player to make sense of the game. And there aren't many things that you can make a story from here - it is just a sightseeing trip but your tour guide is an elitist with a smug face who just offers you to “figure it out” (but in reality he just doesn't have a story to tell).
    [*] The price is too much, both in terms of quality of gameplay, and in terms of quantity. I fully completed the game in 4 hours even though I took my time and didn’t rush.
[/list]
As a conclusion I would rather recommend watching this game on youtube instead of playing it and, god forbid, buying it.

review_text:
Witchfire is a difficult, extraction FPS where you enter an area, defeat groups of enemies and complete other objectives, generated and scripted, alike. I also emphasise the difficulty in that you are required to experiment with the range of abilities and weapons that slowly build as you play, on top of the harsh gameplay and punishment you receive if you die. Furthermore, the game also tests you to take risks to progress, especially through the Gnosis system. So while the objectives and experimentation make each experience fresh and replayable; the difficulty and risk-taking can deter some players.

I can comfortably say, going by the dev. team's updates and the game itself, that this is a game that is at least worth trying, because it certainly looks like The Astronauts are putting in the effort to trying to make a game with the game itself being the focus. Once getting my bearings and learning how the game works, I felt very accomplished and rewarded after taking that leap in trying a Vault, defeating a boss, or advancing to the next Gnosis level.

The narrative and world is simple but very immersive. The detail in the levels, characters and items, and the lore are very rich in detail and presentation. There's not much that I can say is being taken for granted here. Even the UI and menus feel alive. This is also complemented by a gameplay style that, even though it definitely takes influences by a lot of other well-established titles and genres, is still trying to do its own thing and being fun while at it.

The price is still a little on the steep side, I can at least rest assured that the developers here are trying to make it worth it. I say give it a try and stick to it.

review_text:
A game with plenty of potential for fun, I mean, it's STARSHIP TROOPERS.
The game did an amazing job capturing all the humour and bloody zaniness of the movies, it has base-building, objectives that are (usually) relatively easy to achieve, and so much of it is fulfilling and viscerally pleasing, very immersive.

There's only a couple of problems that keep me from recommending this game:
1. Troll Players. In almost every match I played after the first couple of months, many of the people building bases actively work to make it impossible to defend or otherwise make the mission significantly more difficult. I spend almost as much time disassembling problematic structure placement so I can actually make a defensible position as I do shooting bugs.

2. Weapon Progression. At least as of the last time I played it, pretty much every weapon except the basic starter assault rifle and the heavy gun of the tank-class felt worthless. Using a sniper rifle was almost completely ineffective because it takes longer to kill the same warrior/worker bugs with the sniper than it does with the Mk. 1 rifle, for example. 

3. A Toxic Community. Again, perhaps it's evened out and changed, but I doubt it. In line with Troll Players, if you complain or comment about pretty much literally anything that could easily be resolved with a simple tweak or a buff to equipment in the forums, you're more likely to find yourself buried under various versions of "Get Good, lol noob" than receive any actual  vindication that your idea might have merit.

4. Sudden Extreme Difficulty. Because of the Randomly Generated Nature of the mission maps and objectives, there have been multiple occasions where a completion of the mission has been actively impossible, especially with the extraction phases. Having to run through a slavering and unending horde of bugs across the entire map, for example, sometimes with less time to do so than it actually takes to physically make that journey.

All in all, it's a wonderful game, but at least for me I don't see any reason to keep playing it. Grab a full server's worth of friends and have a blast, great for community game nights, etc, but as a predominantly solo player it's a toxic and unpleasant experience.

review_text:
As a massive fan of the Just Cause series, I really wanted to like this game, but it thwarted my every attempt.

I'm assuming that you've played Just Cause 3 if you're reading this review and that you're trying to figure out if you'll like this game too. The short answer is no, you won't. On the other hand, if you're reading this and you haven't played Just Cause 3, then what are you doing? Go buy it on some $1 bundle deal, it's insane how cheap you can get it these days. Then you can come back and read this review.

Right, now that we're just down to the Just Cause 3 players, let's talk about expectations. Whatever the original Just Cause did, Just Cause 2 improved upon. The map was a massive improvement, the combat was an improvement, there are more easter eggs, more vehicles, and a much nicer quest system with well implemented factions among other things. Given that the original Just Cause released to PlayStation 2 among other consoles in 2006, Just Cause 2 arriving in 2010 was the first truly modern game in the series.

In December 2015, we got Just Cause 3. Avalanche Studios did a lot in that 5 year gap, improving on every system that was available in Just Cause 2, adding whole new mechanics and upgrades for the grappling hook to enable a whole new world of possibility. The beauty of the world was, and still is, staggering, as is its scale. Everywhere you went there was either something to see or do. The challenges were actually challenging, and the arcadey gameplay was actually fun.

I'm not normally the sort to enjoy hunting all the collectibles, getting all the achievements, completing all the time trials, or even competing on leaderboards with my steam friends for the in-game challenges. Yet I found myself doing that with Just Cause 3 just because it was such a fun game, and all those mechanics were integrated seamlessly. It was a fantastic addition to the Just Cause series and remains the best Just Cause game by far.

All of this context is necessary because if there was to be a Just Cause 4 (and there is), there needed to be a good reason for it. What might they improve upon in the next iteration? How did they plan to top Just Cause 3, releasing only 3 years after it? (Only 2 years if you count the time only after all the DLC content for JC3 had dropped)

It's a question with an easy answer. They changed the engine to something marginally different, they added over 400 challenges, turning them into a boring chore, they removed the vibrancy and colour from the game, opting to split the land into 4 environmental regions, and they made the most common/important mission type (liberations) dependent on an awful protect-the-idiot-ai system. Just Cause has never been a combat sim, it thrived on chaos and a bit of silliness. 

All that is to say, Just Cause 4 wasn't even remotely as much fun to play. Along with the engine changes, a lot of stuff just feels wrong too. Look, if you've played Just Cause 3 to death and you REALLY want more Just Cause, then fine. Grab a whiskey and sit down to to play Just Cause 4 with greatly lowered expectations. Grab the Danger Rising DLC so you at least have a hoverboard.

review_text: This is one of the better mmorpgs I've played. Best part first, it's FREE! You can spend money on perks but it's not necessary to play and be competitive. Combat is fun and intuitive. There are a dozen or so classes (fighter, gunner, mage, etc.) and they all have their own unique techniques and roles to play. A full weapon and armor upgrading system. The community is fun and supportive for the most part. If you like customizing your characters looks, this one is a 10. There's literally thousands of options. Their "Creative Space" property building simulator is one of the best I've seen. Especially or FREE! You can build a castle, an amusement park, or Malibu Barbies dream house. Again, thousands of options. Graphics and performance are also solid, I've had the occasional dropped connection but nothing worth taking points over. Especially considering it's FREE! They seem to have seasonal and weekly events that cycle regularly. There's plenty to do. On the downside, the side quests can be a little directionless. They'll ask you to go gather something and not give you much to go on. You can find yourself running around aimlessly looking for a certain ration or mineral. It's biggest flaw is that the story missions aren't co-op. It's a large game, in playtime and hard drive space. The basic version is about 90 GB, the full version is almost 140 GB. Don't worry, both versions are FREE! That's a pretty good deal. I've gotten 160+ hours of entertainment at the time of this review for FREE! What do you have to lose trying it out?. In closing I'd like to say that the only reason I'm even writing this review is the server is under maintenance. Otherwise I'd be playing. I'm giving this one two ratings. Because it's FREE!, I give it a 9 of 10. If I'd had to pay for it, it would be a 7 of 10. Hope this helps.

review_text:
Save Your Money! Not Worth $40!

I'll start with the complements to get them out of the way. HR Griger inspiration is phenomenally executed. The ambience and world-building is top notch. 

But that's all the complements this game is worth.

Kickstarter and trailers promised a horror game. Early trailers showed the use of guns with a hint that, just because there are guns, doesn't make it an action game.

However, the enemies in this game move quick, sometimes quicker than you. They have long-ranged projectiles and very good aim. You cannot out run their attacks if you were already close - you will get hit. Your best bet is to cheese the enemies by running in circles around the level, if any loops are available, or get behind something. You will have a close-range "weapon" that has 2 hits before a lengthy cooldown. You cannot help but GET CLOSE to kill these enemies. And there will be more than you ought to deal with for a game that wants to deny its title of being a "non-action" game.

Yeah there's not a lot of action alright - not a lot I can fucking DO about some of these enemies except get killed and hope that RNG is better next time. Most of the time I had to run away and wait for enemies to just leave as they crawl back into the environment. Later, I get better weapons but health and ammo is slim. The issues with slower movement and enemies having long-range projectiles still existed but was better. 

Then, you meet a bigger, faster, tougher enemy that requires use of your "magnum" gun. You HAVE to kill it. Good luck figuring out when to save your bullets. You're going to die.

Speaking of "figuring out when" to conserve resources and dying, later in the end-game, there is a game mechanic that requires you to take damage over time to solve a puzzle.

Let me say that again: THERE IS A GAME MECHANIC THAT REQUIRES YOU TO LOSE HEALTH OVER TIME TO SOLVE PUZZLES.

Tie that into the conservation design of this game and you have a recipe for screwing over your players and calling it "good game design". I almost forgot. You take health damage during cutscenes animations too. I hope you weren't finally making progress at 1 HP.

I did NOT have fun playing this game. Scorn is not horrifying either. It's just gross and violent. I can get most of the same feeling I had playing scorn in a Mortal Kombat finisher. 

Scorn is also filled with cryptic and boring puzzles. People have compared it to Myst which I can say is very accurate except you die a lot and unfairly as I've already expressed in detail. 

There's no strategy to this game. The "game design" formula is as follows:
1. conserve ammo
2. kill the big guys
3. find keys
4. keep walking
5. (late game) have plenty of health because you WILL lose it during puzzles

I cannot in good consciousness suggest anyone spend their own money on this game. Not at $40. If it wasn't for the triple-A graphics I'd throw this in the "indie game" bin for anywhere $10-$20 which is worth the entertainment value Scorn provides.

The ending is a let down too. And there's no replayability either. I solved my puzzles. I spent hours patiently finding my way through hoping to find something about this game that I liked. I served my nickel and did my time.

In short, I'd call this game a huge dissapointment for horror fans like me who waited years since it was first announced on kickstarter. I wish I could get a refund.

review_text:
I played this game and finished it, got the good ending.  It was ok.  If there was a "Meh - Sideways Thumb" that's what this game would be:

PROS:
 - Kinda fun combat
 - Some of the art is well done
 - Game map is well done
 - There seems to be a bunch of new game+ / other modes
 - Lots of spell and weapon options

CONS:
 - I encountered several crashes, but I lost several hours of playtime because of the crashes.  I played around with my settings and that went away.
 - NOT A METROIDVANIA - There are no skill unlocks, or real need to backtrack.  For the most part each zone could be a standalone level.
 -  Combat and exploration are very slow, even the fastest weapon takes about 1 full second to swing.  Running jumping, are all slow.  The jumps are always full height, instead of being based on how long the button was held.  The platforming is extremely simple.  Most of the puzzles are very simple, the remaining ones just rely on you knowing which random spell to cast.
 - Uneven difficulty.  The first few hours are VERY tough, but once you start getting some items that can give healing it becomes very easy.
 - Art style is very cringey - Every character is a cute anime girl, there are multiple bosses where you have to beat up on the breasts.  It's 2023, there is hentai one search away, you don't need to make a softcore game.

If you really like the anime vibe, and aren't looking for anything too deep, you may like it.  If you're a fan of good metroidvanias, and are hoping for more.  Keep looking.

review_text:
Understand something: This game is hard. It's frustratingly hard. It's not bad. But it is strictly for fans of the genre. It is absolutely not for people interested in trying something new. If you are easily frustrated, and not already a fan of real time stealth (think Commandos and Desperados for examples), this is not the game for you. Don't waste your time and money like I did. Try the demo.

Why is this a negative recommendation if I've already said it's not a bad game? Because I cannot know if you are already a fan of the real-time stealth genre, and this game is quite literally not for anyone else, except perhaps a masochist. Look, some people like running headlong into a wall over and over again. Some people like the challenge of being absolutely frustrated constantly until they "git gud," beat one tiny obstacle, and then have to start the whole process over again at the next one. If that's you, great. Have fun. It's not me. This game isn't made for me. It's probably not made for you, either. Hence the negative recommendation.

I'm not trying to insult the people this game was made for - you have your tastes, and this game was designed for them. Have fun. I'm trying to provide a small public service. I'd have appreciated a warning that this game is a massive exercise in frustration for anyone but the subset of people who have already mastered real-time stealth puzzle-solving and who like save-die-repeat trial and error gameplay. I should have tried the demo. I didn't. That's on me.

TLDR: It's a good game in a genre for very specific people, and literally no one else. Try the demo to find out if you're one of them. If you're not, save your money.

review_text:
To The Moon, developed using RPG Maker, may not boast cutting edge graphics or elaborate gameplay mechanics, but it delivers something far more enduring: a deeply emotional narrative interwoven with philosophical depth and introspective storytelling.

The game follows two doctors, Neil Watts and Eva Rosalene, who work for a company that grants dying patients their last wish by altering their memories. Their latest client, an elderly man named John, wishes to go to the moon but doesn't know why. The story unfolds as Neil and Eva dive into his memories, moving backwards through his life to uncover the origin of his mysterious desire.

What makes this narrative structure so captivating is its meta layer: we, as players, are essentially watching two characters experience a man's life as if viewing a film. Their commentary serves as both comic relief and philosophical reflection, drawing us deeper into the story. It feels almost like watching your favorite Twitch streamer or YouTuber play through a game except here, the game is someone's life, and the stakes are heartbreakingly real. (But imagine watching your favorite Youtuber or Twitch Streamer playing the game and controlling Neil and Eva who are watching Johns Memories through the Memory Machine. So many layers)

The emotional impact is heightened by the game's masterful duality between romance and realism which is a reccuring theme in the game. At the heart of the narrative is the complex relationship between John and his wife River. These two characters embody the game's central philosophical theme:

John, the dreamer, represents romanticism. His longing to "go to the moon" is not just a literal wish, but a symbol of his search for purpose and transcendence. He's driven by emotion, nostalgia, and the yearning to rewrite a life filled with missed connections and unanswered questions.

River, by contrast, is the anchor of realism. Her actions often seem puzzling or emotionally distant, yet they're grounded in quiet intention and a deep, unspoken understanding of life's limitations. She clings to truth, even when it's painful. Her struggle with her autism spectrum disorder is portrayed with subtlety and respect. River doesn't seek to reshape the past or escape into fantasy; instead, she holds fiercely to moments of sincerity and authenticity.

Their relationship is where the emotional weight of the game truly lies. John wants to change the past so that he can find a sense of fulfillment, but River quietly accepts the imperfect present. This conflict becomes a lens through which the game explores profound philosophical questions: Is it better to remember a comforting lie or a painful truth? Can a rewritten memory give life meaning or does meaning come from how we face reality?

Despite its many strengths, To The Moon is not without flaws. The story, while moving, can at times feel overly sentimental or emotionally manipulative, leaning heavily on tragic tropes to evoke a response. Some plot points especially involving River's condition and John's childhood could have been explored with greater depth and nuance. Additionally, the setting, though charming in its pixel art simplicity, sometimes feels too static or sparse, which can make the world feel a bit underdeveloped compared to the emotional weight it carries. Some of the situations between Eva and Neil can be a little cringeworthy, but at least they break up the serious tone from time to time.

And of course there are also the logical questions that naturally wonder whether it wouldn't somehow be illegal to access the memories of others due to data protection laws or human rights and why a company would specialize in this and conduct research without thoroughly protecting itself from the law and consequences. Yes, there's certainly something to that, but this is a romanticized story and not everything has to make sense. Deal with it, you realist.

That said, these shortcomings are relatively minor when weighed against the game's overall achievement. To The Moon may be humble in presentation, but it reaches emotional heights few big budget titles dare to attempt. It's not just a story about a man who wants to go to the moon, it's a meditation on love, memory, regret, and the quiet power of a life lived.

review_text:
5/10     Plays like and should be a $39.99 game.

Full breakdown

This game has so many great ideas that it refuses to explore more than on a surface level. It's not terrible just so very mediocre and by the numbers. You walk around reading a stack of notes and audio logs left behind by people while also gathering resources. You do one or two smaller enemy encounters to whittle down those resources you just collected. You visit a safe room right before a bigger fight so you can use currency and points to upgrade your equipment. Unfortunately the weapon upgrades don't have branching paths or any interesting bonuses to them, it's the "number goes up" type of a deal.

The game draws heavy inspiration from action focused survival horror games like Dead Space and Resident Evil 4. It however doesn't include fun or useful quality of life features like quickturning or a map. There is no separate inventory for quest items. There were multiple times where I had to backtrack to a safe room to store some items or simply waste some bullets so I could pick up the next mcguffin required to proceed. Inventory is very limited and needs to be upgraded with points for more space.
You only have one gun that transforms between different types so why is it that all the different forms take up one more inventory slot? This resulted in me not experimenting with the different variations simply because there wasn't enough space to carry them around.

You can charge your weapons up for more damage but this causes the crosshair to start shaking around violently while the enemy is barreling towards you. This adds a nice risk&reward mechanic that forces you to risk getting hit by the enemy. Character movement is deliberately slow and slightly clunky. Enemies are rather slow so it balances out decently enough.

Enemies aren't very interesting. It's the very trope biomass that deforms people into hideous monstrosities. This type of body horror loses all scare factor when used too much. Almost every area is just goopy flesh walls so it trivializes the horrid nature of the sickness that wiped out the world.

Game includes minor environmental puzzles where you have to route electricity by shooting spikes into a wall. I wish you could charge up these spikes so you could use them to stun enemies during combat or to create electrical traps during fights. The spikes are used on puzzles only and nothing else.
You can also rewind time at certain points of the game. Usually this means uncollapsing a structure so you can walk forward. It also allows you to rewind exploded barrels so you can reuse them during combat. This makes some enemy encounters trivially easy.
There is also gravity defying platforming similar to Dead Space remake but those are at very set points and usually just a way to get the player across longer distances. The gravity shenanigans aren't used in any interesting way, simply to get player across floating platforms in a boring void. Towards the end of the game there is a glimpse of what could have been when you get to fight upside down against some enemies.

The enemies themselves can merge with dead bodies becoming more powerful but this was rarely an issue. It did put nice pressure on the player during some of the early fights in the game when guns aren't as powerful and ammo is scarce. Later on this whole thing is trivialized by your powerful guns and the abundance of explosive canisters in nearly every big arena you fight in. You can also reuse the explosive canisters by rewinding time to reconstruct them.

WHOEVER WAS IN CHARGE OF APPROVING THE FOLLOWING ENEMY DESIGNS NEEDS TO BE PUT IN THE NAUGHTY CORNER! It is as if they tried to take the worst types of enemies from other games. Exploding acid blisters that are hidden behind corners or on walls. They can be shot to pop them or triggered by going near them for a second and running away. They spew acid on the floor forcing you to wait for a moment before proceeding. There are also tiny crawling explosive acid enemies that crawl towards you, explode if you get too close and jump at you exploding at contact. Worst ones are the wall enemies that quickly grab you forcing you to complete a quick time event to break free. Very often they are placed in very cheap spots or trigger when you pick up resources from a certain spot. Did they not listen to any of the playtesters since I can't fathom anyone enjoying these miserable time wasting traps.

The game has a poor balance between resource gathering and combat. There is too much snooping around for ammo and not enough situations to use said ammo. Whenever the game showed me a hallucination of a massive enemy horde I was ecstatic "FINALLY A BIG FIGHT!" only to make all the enemies vanish.

Boss fights early on are alright and those types become standard enemies later as is typical. Closer to the end of the game there are two boss fights almost back to back and both are such annoying ordeals to slog through. Acid spitting one liner repeating flesh totem with wall blisters that need to be popped and a teleporting bastard that has nearly unavoidable attacks. The final boss has two cutscenes right before you encounter him and thankfully you can skip those.

The performance of the game was all over the place. Lots of moments where it was stuttering and dropping FPS. I haven't tried the game on the Steam Deck yet but I'm very sceptical about them getting it Verified when it runs this poorly on a gaming PC on medium graphics (with DLSS on ultra performance setting).

I would recommend picking this up from a 50-75% sale if you're really thirsty for some third person shooting. Just don't expect to do that much shooting.

review_text:
At this time I do not recommend this game, and it's for a good reason, trust me. The biggest being there's a lot of gameplay and mechanic issues that haven't been addressed or fixed since release, and no info on when they will be fixed.

Also keep in mind I didn't play the story mode yet, only arena mode so far. I play with the Valve Index.

Before I even review the game, I'd like to say I believe this could have been a really cool DLC of Boneworks. I believe this didn't need to be it's own game and could have just made an update to Boneworks. This game is literally an improved version of Boneworks, nothing really life changing. VERY little is really new about the game. Sure, there's some new gimmics, but it's the same game.

First off, I've played 179 hours of Boneworks as of typing this review. I'd play it mainly for the arena mode. I'd put on my favorite music, and just vibe. Sure, there'd be some slowdown, there are days I wish they'd fix some things, but it works.

As for this game, they broke a lot of what I enjoyed about Boneworks. The gun play is broken, guns don't like to stay in one place and move on their own, and the horrendous addition of forced virtual stock. Yes, there's a virtual stock, no you can't turn it off. Some times it works great, reloading the shotgun SOME TIMES feels good. Other times I look down and the weapon I'm holding is completely upside down. Tracking seems to break more often in this game than any other, I genuinely thought it was my headset, but I tried this game on another headset and had the same issues.

Things I actually liked so far:
- Arena mode is looking good, but you run out of ammo VERY quickly. There's only a VERY small amount of new weapons in the game, so not much changed since Boneworks. I very much look forward to custom arena areas.
- FPS remains pretty steady, not as much lag as the first game.

Biggest issues:
- Guns don't work like they should: As mentioned above, guns would randomly shake and pop out of your hands, turn upside down, or you just can't grip them. As someone with nearly 200 hours in Boneworks, I know how the game works and it's genuinely annoying.
- Forced virtual weapon stock: For those who don't know what it is, it's game mechanic that mimics the way you would put the stock of a gun to your shoulder. 99% of ALL games allow you to toggle this on and off, but this game has no option to turn it off, so guns with stocks will feel VERY different than they should.
- I don't care what anyone in the forums say, starting your VR game with the player literally hanging themselves is NOT a selling point and isn't going to help with sales. I have no earthly idea why this is a forced LITERALLY the FIRST thing you do in the game. My advice is to just have a platform in front of the player, they step on it and they are transported to that exact same scene but their arms and legs are bound to something while it's set on fire. GOING THROUGH THE ACTUAL PROCESS OF HANGING YOURSELF ISN'T NEEDED OR ASKED FOR IN VR.

Until they update all the issues others and myself have outlined about the game, I cannot recommend this yet. Stick with Boneworks. For now, I'll leave this review as it is.

The combat was also quite good, at least to me. I could see how someone would dislike it but at the bare minimum it is "Passable."

I also take back my "not annoying" comment because apparently he can Superman lunge about 20ft and track you regardless of what direction you strafe... Skill issue? maybe, but outside of that one singular thing, the game is still amazing. And as bold as it sounds, its probably one of my new favorite horror games due to its uniqueness. If you are a fan of Deadspace or even RE games for that matter, give it a shot. 8.5/10

review_text:
This is one of my "Greatest games ever, do not ever play it" recommendations. Ask me about it and I'll rant and rave about it for hours.

Some posts that hit harder after playing:

"If the characters suffer, you've got ok drama. If the reader suffers, you've got better drama. If the artist suffers, you've got art. If all 3 suffer, you've got typical Russian literature."
"In Russia, Game Plays You."

I went in entirely blind to this game - no videos or review guides. I thought I was getting some Bioshock style weird action game, with some stealth mechanics of a looter shooter. What I got was something that inspired genuine horror and fear without the traditional jumpscare. If possible and if you want the challenge, go into this game blind - without spoilers, know that you may need to restart once or twice once you get the hang of things.

This game was a dream, a collection of hardcore mechanics so artfully disjointed and then sewn together. It's a genuinely unique horror game: It does not have jumpscares or traditional stealth or an Andrew Ryan / Fontaine, because there's no time for it. Things are happening, Green Doctor Needs Food Badly, and resources are delectably rare. Despite all the brutally hardcore typical survival bars you gotta keep up, time is the most valuable resource, and on my first playthrough, dread started eating at me like a plague until it (ALMOST) consumed me entirely. Like XCOM or the early days of an SMT hardcore game, the odds are stacked against you, and it will be entirely unfair - especially if you're going in blind discovering the various ways the game will play you. Like those games, it's a challenge that seems insurmountable - unless you know the Lines.

This game is art. Nowhere else do you feel the intense pain and suffering of being thrust upon the role of Artemy Burakh. You wander the town, both in fear of being instant-killed in the night losing hours of progress, and in constant fear of the ever-ticking clock. You'll scavenge and barter desperately, attempting to make split minute decisions that will alter the course and lives of many - where murder and survival are both excusable and morally accepted, even from someone who vowed to never cause harm. Play it on the intended difficulty, and go in blind for some pristine hardcore suffering (at least on your first try before looking up tips). Like a Souls game, the uncompomising gameplay difficulty is a story in its own right, which weaves together a connection between the inputs you make, the brutal inventory choices you are forced to make, and Artemy's excellently aggressive dialogue choices. Like a good piece of media, I'm left with so many questions, so much regret, so much inspiration. Truly, one of my favorite games of this year, and I played and loved Sekiro and AW2.

Side rant, I love being insulted by a character and then shouting that they don't know the Lines like I do (things I definitely shouted while streaming before seeing that was a dialogue option), or being told shitty orders by a pawn and the chat line is just a hearty "Piss Off." A reflection of my own soul.

Dread will consume you entirely. Only those who know the Lines can mend it.
Thanks, Pathologic.
I mean, you know... Fuck you, but... Thanks.

review_text:
Who is this for: fans of souls-like shooters like Returnal and Remnant, but want that top-tier tight gunfeel from Destiny 2. 

Visuals: Grimdark, dark fantasy, occult and gothic. Atmosphere is part Bloodborne, part Infinity Blade. Environments span from the remains of a castle atop battleworn ground to a dark tower overlooking a coastline hiding secrets to be discovered, and the violent tension is everywhere.

Gameplay: You explore, shoot and cast spells across several sandbox levels. You choose to push on and potentially die, losing all your resources to level up, or you run away to fight another day, level up and get back into the fight smarter and stronger.

Gunfeel, gunplay, and gun sound are top-tier and among the core foundations the game is built on. With every weapon allowing you to master its mini gameplay loop, for a more powerful output.

Enemies are a challenge, without being impossible. Often easily overcome with a mix of remembering their timing and moveset, and you optimising your build for DPS. Boss fights are pretty epic… but that’s for you to discover.

Sound design: Immersive. The foreboding music, the haunting drone of the winds, the chimes that make the back of your neck stand like Spidey-sense - could be a boon, could be a curse. The sound of pitter-patter of feet and the scream and growls of the occult around every corner. 

And then all hell breaks loose. 

Summary: This all coalesces into second-to-second tension, minute-to-minute action, hour-to-hour anticipation. You will die. And you will return, every single time, always, for one... more... round. 

Can't wait for 1.0. Where they actually flesh out the story.

review_text:
[h1] Cronos: The New Dawn is a technical disaster [/h1]

After spending over an hour tweaking settings, I came to the conclusion that this game is simply unplayable for me. GPU memory usage is constantly maxed out at 100%, causing the game to run out of VRAM and throttle nonstop. Frame rates swing wildly — jumping up to 80 FPS, then dropping to as low as 20 in an instant. Traveling between areas causes constant stuttering, even after shaders have supposedly finished compiling. No matter what settings I use, performance remains awful across the board.

It’s a shame, because the game itself looks genuinely interesting. However, some design choices completely kill immersion. Having to press a button just to jump or squeeze through tight spaces feels clunky. The bright yellow paint marking breakable crates look ridiculous and break the atmosphere. And for some reason, the flashlight turns on and off automatically — you can’t control it yourself. It even flickers to “warn” you of nearby danger. Hard to believe this is the same studio behind last year’s Silent Hill 2 Remake.

It’s clear that Cronos: The New Dawn takes a lot of inspiration from Dead Space, and I’ve heard the story is actually really good. Unfortunately, the technical performance is so bad that I can’t even experience it properly. Until the developers fix these issues, I can’t recommend this game in its current state.

review_text:
I love this game. The team dynamic is fun, there are very few "go it alone" play options, especially on harder difficulties, so you really need to coordinate with other players. It's decently challenging, even for veteran crews. The game is innovative with its carnage system (bug corpses don't despawn but become part of the landscape and bugs can use them as ramps to get to you, like the movie). The play style is fun with classes that have cool features and perks that help them stand out.

The major limitation is performance. I have a decent system and still get periodic rubber banding and lag ... so I opt to play classes with splash damage so it matters a bit less. If you play the smaller map modes it seems to be better. The performance will improve over time, every update is mostly optimizations at this point, and it has improved significantly since the 1.0 launch. But there's nothing more infuriating than thinking you're out of a horde just to lag and snap back to the middle of it :D

Overall I have no complaints about this game other than performance, and that's improving steadily with each update.

review_text:
Scorn is a totally unique game that is not for everyone. The environmental storytelling is incredible, the art is jaw-dropping and intricate, the grotesque scenes are picturesque and uncomfortably beautiful. There are many things I would describe as gut-wrenching and disgusting, but as someone who has played countless horror games, I found that to pull me in to the experience even more. I enjoyed the puzzles and figuring out where to go quite a lot. The game does not give a shit about holding your hand as there is no dialog, no hints, you have to pay attention to detail and find your way through this dismal, broken world. I totally loved that about this game. Each level is DENSE and very complex to digest. There's so much to get a grip on in each area, and it feels as if every nook and cranny has been lovingly crafted by a team of fine artists. The gore is abhorrent, the body horror had me reeling and leaning away from the screen. The monstrosities that loom over you in this bleak world are ominous and vaguely sad. Everything drips in the classic art style I've come to understand from East European game developers- a collective consciousness utopia inevitably ending in disaster that is a staple in portraying communist authoritarianism. Games like Stalker, Darkwood and several others also feature this theme, and Scorn portrays it with aplomb. I highly, highly recommend this to fans of other East European sci-fi and horror, you'll likely fall in love with it immediately. 

That being said, the combat is definitely the biggest detractor to the fun I had in this game. The clunky movement and gunplay forced several restarts to some relatively easy to kill enemies, and before you get the shotgun(?), the pistol(?) is very underwhelming. As a horror game with puzzles, it's a fantastic experience and I had a lot of things to reflect on after finishing each chapter about what I had just seen. As a horror game with combat, it's more stiff than the original Silent Hill or Resident Evil in terms of movement. You fire slow, you run slow, you reload slow, and enemies have an unusually good chance of hitting you with attacks, in particular the enemies that look sort of like chickens. The final boss also had an annoying habit of firing 3 grenades but 4 explosions would happen, which killed me multiple times. I was not frustrated by the austerity of the world or puzzles, I was only frustrated by the handful of enemies and the fact that I couldn't quicksave to skip the cutscenes that have to play before each encounter.
