review_text:
★☆☆☆☆ – The Callisto Protocol: A $160 Million Tech Demo That Forgot to Be a Game

I usually don’t write negative reviews, but The Callisto Protocol deserves every bit of criticism it gets. This game is a complete mess, a beautiful, shiny, soulless husk of what could have been a great horror experience. I’m glad I paid $6 from a third-party site, because this isn’t even worth $10, let alone the $60–$70 it launched at.

🎨 Graphics: The Only Redeeming Quality
Yes, the game looks absolutely stunning. The lighting, reflections, character models, chef’s kiss. If you're buying this as a graphical benchmark, sure, it’ll impress your eyeballs.

But the moment you pick up a controller, it all goes downhill.

🎮 Combat: Repetitive, Clunky, and Boring
The melee system is laughable. You just dodge left-right-left and mash attack. Every fight feels exactly the same.

Gunplay? Feels like an afterthought. Barely any weapon variety, and aiming is sluggish.

Enemy variety is awful. You'll fight the same handful of enemies over and over with slightly different skins.

At some point I stopped being scared and just got annoyed.

🧠 Story: Generic Sci-Fi Mush
Warden Cole is a one-note villain with some dollar-store "eugenics" ideology.

The plot is a copy-paste of better horror games, but with zero emotional investment.

Jacob Lee, the main character, is boring. I kept waiting for a character arc or twist that never came.

Even the big “twists” are predictable : "evil corporation," "experiment gone wrong," etc. It’s like they wrote the plot in a weekend.

🧬 Enemy Design & Horror: Weak
This is supposed to be a horror game, but there’s no tension.

Jump scares are predictable.

No resource management, no puzzles, no psychological horror. Just linear corridors and recycled enemy ambushes.

The only fear I had was whether I’d have to sit through another mindless combat section.

🧠 Artificial Intelligence? More like Artificial Dumbness
Enemy AI is just “run at player.”

Level design is strictly A to B, no exploration, no branching paths.

It’s not scary. It’s not smart. It’s not fun.

🧠 Final Verdict:
The Callisto Protocol is a $160 million cinematic tech demo disguised as a horror game. It has incredible visuals... and nothing else. No gameplay innovation, no scares, no replayability. Just a shallow, sluggish, and repetitive experience wearing a very expensive coat of paint.

If you find this on sale for $5 and want to see pretty lighting effects while you mash the dodge button for 8 hours, go for it. Otherwise? Skip it. Or better yet, just play Dead Space Remake — everything Callisto tried to be, and more.

review_text:
I'll keep this as short as possible;

One of my favourite anime show is Rurouni Kenshin (or Samurai X as I've learned what it's called in the west). For some reason I kept thinking about the show frequently while I was playing the game. The era which the game takes place, music, story,...basically everything was perfect in my opinion. I guess it gave me similar vibes?

The game is amazingly as historically accurate as it can be. Well, obviously it is not but you learn a lot about the last years of Edo/Tokugawa period and how Meiji Period came to the scene. Information regarding to the historical figures (all of the LI's basically) are also accurate -of course not regarding the ones related to the story. 

You have 12 LI's to choose from. While the prologue of the story is the same for every route, every LI's story is remarkably different from the other. There is a main story going on and it too is mainly the same but it goes a bit differently in each route. It's like LI's are the different players in this story and you see the big picture from their and MC's perspective. The main event is there and you play a different role and although some things change, main thing doesn't. (Yeah, it may not make much sense but I don't know how to explain it better) 

Don't expect heavy & steamy love scenes. The romance is quite light all over. It is not a bad thing though, in fact, it was quite refreshing to play a game where everyone doesn't try to get into each others pants.

Each route has a good, bad and unrequited love ending. Also each chapter before the last one has an ending which is "game over" You have to see ALL to unlock all achievements so check how to "skip read" lol. 

The MC is the one of best among the otome games I've played. She is not a total pushover or naive girl you usually see in these type of games. She is not very strong (the reason is explained a bit in Edo Blossoms) or particularly clever but she is not annoyingly dumb which is a huge plus for me. She doesn't fall for the LI's because "they made her heart flutter with the smoulder" You can relate to her a bit at least. 

CG's, character designs and soundtrack are very good. 

Additional info: There are several Hakuoki anime shows & movies. I haven't watched them so I cannot sat which order you should watch or which one to watch. But one thing I know is that Hijikata Toshiro is the canon LI in those. It kind of makes sense even in the games when you think about it.

To sum up; probably the best otome I've ever played to this date (if I said "the best" for another, well it has been replaced with Hakuoki series) If you like otome games, this one and Edo Blossoms is definitely a "must play" for you.

review_text:
An absolute failure of a game from start to finish, I loved JC2 and enjoyed JC3 almost as much, but this game is just terrible and *consistently frustrating*.

All the mechanics we loved in the series, the destruction of bases to liberate territory, being able to mix in a bit of stealth with the run and gun, having a viable loadout for several types of missions, all that has been replaced with what I can only assume is the product of a Square-approved design committee who all hated fun.

My first two hours in this game was a comedy of broken gameplay, with me rage alt+f4'ing this monstrosity three separate times, along with two crashes to desktop.

For some reason, the menus are hard coded to the most arbitrary keys, with no real help, so when the game tried to show me the big complex menu for grapple tools and then crashed me halfway through the mission, I was stuck on coming back in since the menu for doing that got re-locked after the checkpoint.

Then you spend a half hour messing around getting supply and grapple stuff set up, and realize that even when getting a weapon resupply that there is no extra ammo with it, meaning that I end up setting all 3 pilots to the same item and dropping 3 so I can get stocked up.

The stunts and side quests are 100% garbage, the ones that aren't broken are just "find a vehicle and drive through this ring" and a lot of them are pretty broken, the driving and airsuit controls are horrid and feels like piloting an ocean liner that suddenly jerks about when the input has been held long enough.

Nearly every mission has either a trailing component where you watch an NPC stand at a console until the bar is full, you killing enormous waves of brain dead enemies until the bar runs out, or will throw a stupid timer which makes a boring fetch quest into a fury-inducing frustration festival where you just grapple through huge swarms of enemies because if you actually fight the enemies then you'll run out of time and fail the mission.

You'll get randomly annihilated by five attack choppers spawning instantly above you, having fighter jets kill every helicopter you touch within a minute of takeoff, or my favorite was a rally race down a mountain with checkpoints spaced out so poorly I had to backtrack each one and then the last point had an invisible wall which sent my shitty buggy into the water and failed the mission.

The enemies are useless, they'll shoot at you from six feet away and miss on foot, but will throw grenades perfectly from hundreds of feet away and will instantly see you pepper you with laser-perfect heavy weapons fire if they are in a vehicle, and as soon as Rico fires a weapon, literally dozens of troops and vehicles will spawn all around you, usually in a way that lets them crash into your car and send you off a cliff during the timed mission.

I left the game running overnight but I've got about 15 hours of real play time in, which has been a chore that I was enduring hoping that the game would get better, but it actually gets worse thanks to the ungodly heat levels, stupid allies who fail to do their parts of scripted missions leading to failures, random glitches and bugs, and a complete lack of compelling gameplay loop that made the prior games favorites of mine.

I got it on super sale at 95% off and I still think it was too much, I'm adding in some mods to let me burn through the game faster without all the horseshit, but it's only out of spite and not in the expectation that I'll actually have much fun doing so.

review_text:
Oh boy do I have things to talk about this game. This is a long one btw, but i assure you, if you're debating wether to buy this or not, this review will probably answer you. I usually don't write reviews but this felt like such a waste of time and money that I just had to do it. How this has a 90% steam review score is beyond me.
I played on hard (veteran difficulty i guess?) but as far as i know, after playing boss mode, the only thing that changes is damage/hp numbers. The game ends up being hard because of bad game design, not because of real difficulty.
Let's start with the good, which isn't much, because the bad is where it gets real.

[hr][/hr]
[list]
[h1]The good:[/h1]
[*]The art is amazing. Very nice pixel art style, very good backgrounds with a big BUT(T) which will come on the next section.
[*] Also some bosses/enemies designs are very good. The Yuki Onna was really pretty, for example. But this is an exception and not the usual.
[*]Good animations itself, with a big but as well.
[*]Cringe writing. Why is it good? Well, it made me laugh, so that's good i guess?
[/list]

[hr][/hr]
[list]
[h1]The bad:[/h1]
[*]Your character doesn't react properly to stuff, as in, sometimes her expression doesn't quite match what is happening or to what she's saying. Also whenever she's talking i just wanna skip the dialogue, it just sucks, no way to talk around it.
[*]Rolling is useless, too much end lag, so you'll end up 1 - not being able to counter the enemy or 2 - be hit by other attack. Just jump or move back so... Yeah. The animation is pretty, but it's just useless 9/10 times.
[*]As i said, pretty graphics, BUT, they don't mix together. You have a dark and broody world with anime girls and jiggly booba EVERYWHERE. I thought it would be only the Slime Girls but... Nope. There IS kind of a reason as to why everything is a girl but is it justified? Is the jiggle physics justified? No. No it's not.
[*]Predictable story. The idea of souls being summoned (isekai much?) wasn't bad itself but the twist and ending was very predictable, like, an hour in i already knew what was gonna happen. Come on, i played bloodstained, it was the same twist but this managed to be more predictable than it.
[*]90% of weapons are useless. If you try to attack with a weapon that isn't very fast, the enemy will attack first, even if you try to plan around both animations. Didn't know this was a turn based RPG with ATB gauges. Also freezing and then attacking with a heavy weapon doesn't work because of 2 points: 1 - Freezing is VERY short. 2 - The animation for the spell is too long, while the heavy weapon takes too long to use. Mix both and the enemy is already attacking before you can smash it. How to use heavy weapons? Invisibility. Yep, only way.
[*]90% of spells are useless as well. Freezing? Worthless. Fireball? Situational, as it can hurt you as well.
[*]This isn't a metroidvania. You won't get the usual abilities upgrade which open up new paths and new areas. You won't backtrack unless you want 100%. There's an entire quest line (which leads to the true ending, which i figured the moment i got it so i played this thing only once, thank God) where you can't open a single golden treasure chest so the only backtracking you'll do is going after them.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]
[list]
[h1]Extra: The ugly:[/h1]
[*]The game is EXTREMELY horny. For no reason at all. I get why every enemy is girl based but WHY SO HORNY? I don't mind a little bit of fan service here and there but... Damn. It gets embarassing. I was streaming this and just got second hand embarassment out of it. Why an extra equipment slot IS A STRIPED PANTY??? Was it supposed to be quirky and funny? Because i'm not laughing. Not anymore, at least, i chuckled a little but started thinking "oh that's bad" soon after.
[*]Forgettable OST. Most metroidvania advertised games have at least one song that will stuck with you but not this one, no no.
[*]Level design itself was whatever. Tight jumps for the sake of being tight and making you waste time if you fail.
[*]This is more of a nitpick but there's little variation in enemy sounds.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

SO, to finally end this review: Was it fun? "Should i buy it" you're probably asking.
No and also no. It was fun for the first half an hour or so, and i can't recommend 30 min of fun for a 4h long game.

[b]My final rating for this game is: Booba/10
Thank you for reading[/b]

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun — Precision, Strategy, and Stealth

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun isn’t just a tactics game; it’s a thrilling test of planning, timing, and cunning. From war-torn villages to heavily guarded fortresses, every mission is packed with enemies, traps, and opportunities to outsmart your opponents.

Gameplay is methodical, tense, and deeply rewarding. Each character has unique abilities that change how you approach every encounter, and careful coordination, stealth, and timing turn each mission into a satisfying puzzle. One wrong move can be fatal, making success feel earned and exhilarating. Boss encounters and heavily fortified areas require strategy, observation, and adaptability.

Exploration and preparation are just as important as execution. Scouting enemy positions, setting traps, and planning routes encourage careful thought and experimentation. Hidden objectives, collectibles, and alternate paths reward thoroughness and creativity.

The story and setting add depth and atmosphere. Shadow Tactics immerses players in a richly detailed Edo-period Japan, with memorable characters and tense, cinematic sequences that make each mission feel purposeful and engaging.

Visually, the game is stunning. Detailed environments, clear tactical layouts, and expressive animations make every stealth maneuver and attack satisfying to execute. Coupled with a dramatic, atmospheric soundtrack, every sneak, strike, and escape is heightened and memorable.

[h3]Final Verdict:[/h3]
Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun is a tense, rewarding strategy experience that combines precise planning, stealth, and clever execution. Challenging, satisfying, and endlessly engaging, it’s a must-play for fans of tactical gameplay.

review_text:
I think this was an amazing game,heck, I even went for the new game plus to get the true ending, which is rare for me.
I bought it randomly, in fact I didn't think I'd like it.
The ambiance is decent, the music is great, the gameplay is fun yet tense.
This game succeeds in doing something that many horror games don't : give you weapons and still make you feel limited. Your inventory management makes that despite having guns, you need to handle ammo with care, you can't pick it all up,sometimes you need to get rid of some stuff and do without.
Play with the environment, etc.
There's been a few jumpscares, and usually I don't like it, but these jumpscares had more of a psychological impact than "boohoo I scared you".
On my first run I was actually really tense through most of the game, even on NG+ I still got scared a few times.
Although I'd say it's more of a survival game with horror ambiance than a survival horror and a lot of the horror was psychological, which is great.
When a horror game makes you paranoid, it means it works.
The story is actually what amazed me the most, it's one of the rare games that involve time travel and don't mess it up.
Voice acting was decent, gameplay was fluid.
Your character isn't too slow or too rapid, it's mostly exploring,shooting, thinking, a few puzzles, etc.
It keeps it's difficulty and horror aspect without doing 2 of the things I hate in horror games : Cheap instant kills and annoying QTE (the only ones are when you get caught by specific enemies but you can easily free yourself).
I definitively recommend the game, like, I think I like it more than Resident Evil 4 Remake, which I adored.
Also I love the fact that cats can be found and saved, and that you can pet them.

review_text:
This game was almost great! I gave it a good 20 hours before I realized how absolutely frustrating and unrewarding this game is. I got the hype at first, fun design and progression system I didn't mind. Some people will love this game however it's unclear goals on what it wants to be makes this game inherently disappointing. The insane level of irritating grind is not acceptable for what it's trying to do. In a soulslike game you need to plan your route, you need to prepare and you need to think smart. In this game, skill is almost irrelevant when.

-Enemies spawn directly on top of you/behind you out of literally nowhere. Often times ambushing you.
-80% of the weapons and magic is useless compared to others and the only way to actually progress is to find a build you like and not deviate so you can use the INCREDIBLY scant resources given in your first ten whole hours.
-The only way to unlock more character abilities is to literally make the entire game harder (Which doesn't add nuace, just make the enemies tankier and hurt more.)
-When you DO make the game harder just to progress more, it becomes impossible. I have played shooters since I was a child and this is not hard for the sake of triumph and skill, this is hard for the sake of calling itself a "Souls-Like" Game. The ONLY thing this game has in common with Darksouls is the grim setting, and dying A LOT.
-So many of the events are VERY unclear on what you are actually supposed to do. One, tiny, vague sentence doesn't make anything clearer when you're trying just to figure out what to do among swarms of enemies that again, spawn out of nowhere. Oh also don't worry about remembering each event so you can improve, they change constantly so you can never establish a strategy. Just shoot and pray.
-This is a smaller, pettier complaint but WHY IN THE HELL does the trader move every time I respawn. What a dumbfounding idea to force the player to go on a time wasting goose chase just to buy a couple ammo packs.

review_text:
If you are old enough to have played Dead Space 1 when it was released in 2008, you'd distinctly remember how your mind was blown when the atmosphere was sucked out of a room and all sound went with it. Only the muffled vibrations reaching the spacesuit through physical contact were audible. It was eerie and claustrophobic, heightening that sense of being alone in the vacuum of a derelict spaceship. All UI was diegetic - meaning all UI existed in the game world. Planets were mostly fictional and large enough to believably produce a gravity similar to Earth's and so, all locomotion was normal. In other words, what science there was in the science-fiction of Dead Space felt grounded by design. And then there's The Callisto Protocol. 

Callisto, the second largest real moon of Jupiter, only has 12.5% of Earth's gravity. (For context, our Moon has 16.5%). This means that if you walk on Callisto, you would be leaping large distances like the Hulk or John Carter. Callisto has a negligible atmosphere whose pressure is 0.00000075 Pa while Earth's atmosphere exerts 101325 Pa of pressure on the body. One would spontaneously explode without a spacesuit on the surface of Callisto.

Callisto Protocol is a video game in which all this is summarily dismissed. Why Callisto Protocol failed to incorporate at least some science while blatantly attempting a rote copy of Dead Space is puzzling. And this is just one example. Callisto Protocol successfully copies the superficial bits from Dead Space, even adds its own flourishes, but ignores the deep pillars that make Dead Space the masterpiece that it was.

Here's another pillar that was ignored - mystery. In Dead Space, the thing that turns dead bodies into necromorphs is a giant alien monolith called the Marker. Nobody knows who made the Marker, or what the writings on it say, or how it makes people go insane just by being near them. But some people believe it is humanity's destiny to be turned into necromorphs by the Marker, a process they call Unification. They form a religion called Unitology whose goals are to find new Markers to enable this Unification. (Altman be praised!)

Callisto throws out all attempts at mystery and subtext for yet another virus/bacteria, the biophage, that turns humans into zombies. Very boring! [spoiler]That it is an alien virus first found deep under Callisto does not really change anything. In place of a believably wacko religion, there is an Illuminati-like group who release the biophage in the Callisto prison just to see if something useful emerges out of the shit show that can be used to modify humans for deep space travel. That's the protocol in Callisto Protocol. "And what about you, huh? Watching people die for fun? Is that your 'Protocol'?" is a line the player character says to the main baddie.[/spoiler] But, to be fair, there was a strong sense of mystery to the plot until these deflating details were uncovered near the end.

There are some good things about Callisto Protocol too. The melee combat was not half-bad, especially on Hardcore difficulty. Sure, you can dodge easily, and you can keep dodging easily indefinitely but I didn't do that because I wanted to get on with it. 

The stealth sections were lip-biting good. The environments, guns, and enemies were sufficiently varied. Throwing enemies with the GRP (kinesis module) into spikes, grinders, and fans never got old. The surface of Callisto and the subterranean, decrepit colony of the first settlers were spectacularly rendered and memorable. Although severely linear for most of the playtime, there were occasional branching paths that rewarded mild exploration. Overall, just playing the game was not as bad as most reviews made it out to be. However, it only got really interesting to play after exactly halfway through the game when some new environments, weapons, upgrades, and enemies were introduced and some actual plot development showed up. Pacing was not Callisto Protocol's strong suit.

The most terrible thing in Callisto Protocol is the four encounters with the same "two-head" mini-boss in the last three chapters of the game. In some of these fights, if you don't have enough ammo, you must reload an old save and stock up. It is a really bad design and stuck out like a sore thumb even amidst the other flaws in this game.

One very strange thing about the level layouts was that I always felt as though I was travelling down, never up. I couldn't count the number of times the elevators broke down or I fell into a pit and ended up far below the surface. And yet, there was not enough travelling up to compensate. It left me feeling the game world was not correctly architected.

All of this is to say that The Callisto Protocol is a poor man's Dead Space. If you read this review and know what you are getting into, get it on discount, and enjoy a romp on Callisto. Just don't squint at the details and do not play the DLC.

[h1]UPDATE[/h1] - As good as my word, I have revisited my recommendation based on the fact that they did (eventually) fix the index controller issue and the game is actually much more enjoyable as a result. I'm still not impressed with the decision to abandon any kind of campaign and go with grinding the same maps for PVE over and over, but it is pretty slick now and a lot of fun to play with friends. The new Boulevard map is shorter than others but a lot more interesting. The game is still lacking content and longevity IMO but it's fun enough for what I paid. 

===OLD REVIEW===

[h1]INDEX USERS BEWARE[/h1]
This game has serious issues with Index controls - there is no grip toggle option for index and the turn controls are flaky AF unless you use a custom community binding. The discussions pages are full of complaints and requests for help from devs and so far complete silence. The latest update delivered fixes specifically targeted at Quest and PSVR players but completely ignored index. I will remove this and reconsider my recommendation if / when they at least acknowledge the issue but am seriously considering making my case for a refund. 
Apart from that the game is just meh. Quite aside from the very disappointing amount of content, and the focus on mindless grinding the same 5 missions over and over with a really shitty drop rate for mods vs the earlier marketing that suggested a cross between L4D and the division, the game has the exact same janky gunplay as arizona sunshine (actually, having just re-visited Arizona Sunshine, I think it might actually be [i]worse[/i] - at least AS had a decent variety of gun models and feel) .
Is it fun? Sure, with your mates. But that's true of almost any mutliplayer game. It has a lot of promise (you can clearly see the skeleton of the game it was supposed to be before they decided to re-tool it for a wider market) and it could be a truly great game despite its flaws.

review_text:
As the sequel to Arkham Asylum, this game raises the stakes and draws us deeper into Batman’s world. This time, we explore Arkham City, a walled-off section of Gotham where Hugo Strange keeps the city’s most notorious criminals. A mix of new and returning classic villains stands in Batman’s way, each more dangerous than the last.

One of the standout moments for me is the boss fight with Mr. Freeze, which demands every bit of your gameplay skill. It’s tough, but it’s also one of the most rewarding encounters I’ve played. The Mad Hatter side quest is wonderfully surreal, while Zsasz’s detective-style missions are tense and engaging.

A huge highlight is being able to play as Catwoman. Her whip, pouncing attacks, and fluid acrobatics make combat feel fresh and exciting, offering a perfect contrast to Batman’s bulkier fighting style. Along the way, new enemy types push you to adapt and refine your strategies.

Not everything landed perfectly for me. The Riddler’s Challenges didn’t hold the same magic as in Asylum. The tighter, more contained environment in the first game made those puzzles more satisfying to track down. In the sprawl of a larger city, the thrill was harder to replicate.

As of writing, I’ve finished the main story and started Harley Quinn’s Revenge. I can already tell that Arkham City has greater replay value than its predecessor, thanks to its bigger map, hidden quests, and layered challenges.

This is an incredible sequel—one that shows how much care, dedication, and attention went into Batman’s world-building. It’s immersive, addictive in the best way, and proof that superhero games can combine action and storytelling at the highest level.

review_text:
I played We Were Here: The Friendship with a friend, and while I enjoyed it, it’s by far the shortest entry in the series—much shorter than the others, which are already relatively brief experiences.

The graphics are not great, staying consistent with the visuals of previous games in the series, but the artistic direction remains strong. The atmosphere and design make up for the technical shortcomings, creating a charming and engaging world.

The game offers three trials, each focused heavily on cooperation. They’re fun and well-designed, requiring solid communication to solve. The challenges are engaging enough to encourage replayability, especially if you’re aiming to get 100%. My friend and I managed to achieve 12/12 trophies, so we fully completed the game, which added to the satisfaction.

While I liked the experience overall, it’s undeniably too short. The brevity left us wanting more, especially since the core cooperative gameplay is so enjoyable.

We Were Here: The Friendship is a fun and creative co-op game, but its length limits its impact. If you’re a fan of the series, it’s worth playing—but don’t expect it to last long.

review_text:
It pains me to mark this as not recommended, but I am just not feeling it.

The game is visually stunning and I can't name many other games that surpass it in terms of art style. Sadly that's where most of the praises end. Sure it has a fittingly oppressive atmosphere and it provides a niche horror experience, but they really aren't well experienced with gameplay design.

Where the game excels artistically, it falls short with giving the player a fun time alongside it. The combat is geniunely some of the worst I've seen. It's incredibly clunky, sluggish and not rewarding in the slightest. Enemies are more of a chore and annoyance, meant to frustrate the player, than they are a fun and integral part of the game. Honestly, you could've taken them out completely and probably be left with a better, more engaging experience overall. It also doesn't help that you can't tell the recharge on your basic weapon due to the color choice and that same recharge is incredibly slow as is everything else in this game. Not to mention the abhorrent range on that thing. I missed more stuff at near point blank and ended up getting hit back as a result because it's so absurdly short. It also doesn't help that there's little clutter everywhere on the ground that you can easily get stuck on resulting in getting hit more. It only leads to a more frustrating experience. 
And that's not where the shortcomings of the combat end. Switching weapons is also very slow and you can't dodge anything while doing it, so good luck switching to another weapon after running out of ammo mid fight. Also the reloads are slow as hell as is everything else and it's even worse since you can't reload cancel. Once you start reloading, you better believe you're putting every bullet you have into the mag even though you only needed one to finish off the enemy. It also doesn't help that enemies are inconsistent with their health. Sometimes they take 2 shots, sometimes 4. I know it's probably due to the crit spots, but I swear, sometimes I shoot them in the exact same places and they either survive or they just die. This only leads to more unpredictability which can be a detriment to the player and cause more health loss. It really doesn't help that the game is pretty stingy with giving the player healing and that the checkpoints are spaced apart quite a bit.

Apart from that it's also easy to get lost in some of these places. They tend to be quite large, although linear, but most of the areas look the same. Since the game requires quite a bit of backtracking at certain points, you'll be finding yourself blindly searching for where you're supposed to be going. The game doesn't tell the player anything at all. It won't hold your hand and that is completely fine. Sometimes it will leave a better impression if it allows player agency even if it is a linear game, however, it would help if some of the areas weren't so similar looking and maze-like.

The game is also kind of buggy. Sometimes the bullets phase through the enemies, leaving them unaffected. I'm pretty sure the enemies don't have some kind of i-frames, but I could be wrong. Either way it's really annoying missing a shot that clearly hit and then losing precious health because of it. Apart from that, I got stuck in place twice after certain cutscenes for seemingly no reason, resulting in me needing to restart to the latest checkpoint and one time the game didn't allow me to interact with anything even though it was giving me the prompts, leading to another soft lock and reset. It really took away from the overall experience, especially since these bugs were really only a waste of time.

(minor spoilers for the ending) The game is very ambiguous with its story. It doesn't tell you much and only poses more questions than it answers, but it definitely ends with a very negative ending that could be unsatisfying for some, especially because of what you have to go through only to end the game with it. I could bet everyone (myself included) were expecting something very grandiose, but were left disappointed with such a cruel outcome.

Overall, the game has tons of potential, but is too clunky and unsatisfying to play as is. I really do care about it, hence why I'm writing this much. I hope that the developers improve upon the annoyances of this game in their possible future titles and combine such an astounding visual style with good gameplay to form an extremely palatable horror experience.

Most information was given out in conversations and the background wasn't decorated as well and the world didn't feel as alive as it did in act one. 

The puzzles were tedious , they usually made you just walk up and down talking to different people and not a lot of problem solving nor the inventory or ablities used much (save a few exceptions). Joey was pretty much useless this game and was just there for banter and exposition

review_text:
While there are plenty of enjoyable moments, The Callisto Protocol does just enough to engage you to see the main story through, while simultaneously making you question why you are doing so.

To it's credit, it does manage to have a wider array of environments than I expected, and the melee combat can be fun, but the rest of the game is bogged down with long reused animations for many doors/chests, crawl/slide through this vent/crevice slowly, button mash QTE prompts, poor enemy variety and a bunch of other tropes that other games ditched a few years ago.

Also worth noting that the last 1/3 of the game rapidly scrubbed all of the goodwill that the game had built up until that point, stealth killing the blind enemies got boring after the 3rd one, so it was a real eye roll when the next hour or two of the game was just that over and over again. And don't even get me started on the two headed monster (iykyk).

tldr; It's not as bad as some made it out to be, but I wouldn't even think about touching this at full price.

review_text:
Witchfire is a game that I think has a lot of fun mechanics...in small, SMALL doses.

The developer says they believe it's "Fairly priced" but it's more like a demo in it's current state. $40 is a lot to ask for what is essentially a handful of stages with no variance. It bills itself as an extraction roguelike. It has little to no features of either.

Weapons are pre-set, and upgradable, and the overall core mechanics are fine, but the roguelike elements rear their heads at the very start of the run and pretty much never again. The upgrades are limited in quantity and the effects they provide tend to be very similar or unimpressive.

One thing I WILL praise the game for is it's graphics, sound design, and atmosphere. But that only lasts so long for a game based on doing the same thing over and over. A vista may be beautiful, a cavern haunting...but only the first handful of times you see it. After that, it becomes just another PNG. Just another hole.  And once you've seen the handful of events on a stage, it's done. There's not enough content to draw me back. The leveling system is soulsborne to it's core, and that is both a blessing and a curse. Each level feels like a slog, each run, a promise of miniscule progress.

The best I can say is that you should get it....on sale. $30, maybe. $20, absolutely. Because as a one-time experience, Witchfire can be a lot of fun. As a Roguelike? As an "Extraction shooter"? It's "OK". That's it. Just "OK."

review_text:
This has the makings of a cool game but it just isn't fun yet. People are saying it's like Rocket League x Golf With Your Friends, but it misses an important thing that those two games have in common: player interaction. GWYF is about playing in small groups and then accidentally (on purpose) trolling each other by colliding your balls. RL is about close-knit teamplay and direct competition: you're playing with some people (possibly friends) against some other people (possibly also friends, since you can set up custom games). In Turbo Golf Racing you can't collide with other players' cars or balls, like TrackMania, so the only player interaction is with the one "homing missle" weapon, which you don't pick up that frequently, there's no interesting gameplay around, and it just slows someone down by a few seconds. There's also no custom games, you can just join a party with friends to get into the same match.

Obviously full player-on-player collision would lead to a lot of trolling, with troll players not even playing their own ball and just knocking opponents off the map, but even ball-to-ball collision would be more interaction and make that kind of trolling a lot harder; and a custom game mode where you can turn on collisions would allow you to get the GWYF trolling experience with your party without ruining the public games. After that I'd like to see more gameplay options explored to allow more player interaction and competition.

Finally, the car's movement and controls just don't feel as fluid and controllable as RL, particularly the double-jump flipping. Right now, I think the silly game modes they keep putting as short-term events in RL are much more fun than this, but I do have high hopes that this game will find its fun in the next six months to a year.

review_text:
Lucius is a great concept, with a well written story and a good voice-actor for the narrator.

The gameplay is very linear, the "pick every object you see and then find out how and where to use them" gameplay. If you explore and pick EVERYTHING right away (when it's not yet needed) you make the game much easier and faster. If you wait until the items are needed before picking them up some parts of the game will become slow and frustrating.

You don't ever leave the house (except for the gardens). There's only one way to execute every kill, and you have to find out what it is (no physics involved like in HITMAN). Also, when the game progresses you unlock new skills, but you can't use them unless you are meant to for that specific kill (you can't go around burning people with your fireball skill). So the feeling you get is as if the story was already written and you only had to recreate exactly what had happened, instead of making your own story.

Conclusion: Good concept, execution could be better, but still fun (mostly). Buy if it's on sale.

review_text:
An awesome small parkour game that is basically everything I wanted for years now. If you are one of the maybe 5 people to share my experience of playing every small game involving parkour or even stuff like parkour mods in GTA San Andreas, this is finally the game to finally deliver on the Parkour Sandbox experience. If you ever played Free Running, it is a more refined and fun focused version of that game.
Don't expect a grand story mode or tons of singleplayer content, there are very beautiful maps with varied environments and challenges, after which you find your own lines to run either for speed or for trick score. That or just be like me and try to land one ridiculous gap trick for an hour. Multiplayer is also quick, easy and good! I especially like the tag mode.

I got the game early in its development and I am glad that the solo dev delivered on all his promises and is also going beyond with his post launch support.

The Soundtrack is also fantastic and has been stuck in my head! Great Tracks that I instantly recognize and mentally connect to the game.

I couldn't even ask for much more if I tried, besides maybe more tricks? I was spoiled by all the combinations you could do with Free Runnings Trick buffer system that allowed for deep lists of moves, R&A is already pretty much maximizing it's available buttons so I'm not disappointed if more Tricks won't happen.


A fun product in early access, a finished product outside of early access in a reasonable time, this is one of the great examples of Indie Early Access done right. The final asking price is also fair, I got a solid discount as an Early Access player but i'd gladly pay the full asking price again and I wish the best to the dev. Hope you continue with more games of this quality even if it leaves the realm of parkour!

There's a lot of non-canon fun in this Star Trek universe; Crossovers at a level that puts most comics to shame, extending stories and plots from various series to sometimes extreme levels. It does give players something to chew through, plenty of things to do, although most the more peaceful missions mostly just running about and using NPCs or scanning rather than needing reading and nerding.

Missions are mostly combat, and that's where things go stale for me. It first ramps up a bit around L30 when you hit Captain, and you learn certain enemies can pin your ship and have instakill missile volleys (yes, I tried rotating shield frequencies and harmonics, but was still pinned. Not a fix, apparently.)
Fights start to drag on longer, with a whole lot more clicking, ability use, moving your ship, switching to shoot torpedoes or fighters, then remembering to click on the enemy again so you actually fire. More and more clicking.

I do like that they get to experiment with the story and universes, there are some of the series cast giving their voices to the game, and there are a few other mechanics to learn and invest time in.
These are not the core of the game though, eventually everything just circles back to combat, so play is mostly going to be based around it: Death by clicking.

I still think Tape to Tape has huge potential with the art, the music, and the concept but right now it needs some serious balancing, and a bit of polishing before it can become great.

review_text:
After a rough ride (starting as a F2P, losing a publisher, mostly switching to a paid single/multiplayer game), Relic Hunters has been released from EA. And it's almost great. Almost. It's held by a small number of design decisions ranging from annoying to catastrophic.

Pros:
The 6 characters feel pretty unique and most are fun to use. The skill trees are interesting enough that there are plausible routes to good build diversity, too.

Art style and direction is good.

The gunplay (you know, the main thing in the game) is actually good and fun. It's a looter shooter, and the looting and the shooting both have their high points. Weapons feel different, and definitely play into build variety.

The exploration missions are pretty great - it's fun to wander around, and most bosses feel different and have fun mechanics to interact with.

The animated movies are pretty good!

Cons:
It's a looter shooter with the single worst inventory management system I've ever seen. The small inventory is shared by every character. If one character equips a piece of gear, all have to carry it around. This is idiotic. There is a stash, but it's literally pointless.

The majority of the missions are not exploration. 80% of them are some version of "keep the bad guys out of this small circle." Sometimes the circle moves, sometimes you clear one circle and have to go to another. They all suck. It's a terrible mechanic, and it's literally most of what you do in the game.

Charge skills/jumping. Initially, these feel cool and fun to play with, but given that in almost every encounter enemies will be able to interrupt your skill charge up and your jump (making you fall straight down and waste the skill), these become annoying and a detriment, so you don't use them.

Falling off an edge - you take a little damage and you respawn pretty quick, but you keep a little momentum from when you fell. Meaning, sometimes you just keep respawning and falling over and over. It doesn't work well.

Grinding. The F2P bones of it are still obvious, and it's the bad parts of F2P. Did you love rep grinding in WoW Classic to get those items you need? No? Screw you, it's in here anyway. I hope you like territory control (*insert Xzibit meme*).

Mid - the plot and writing. It... exists.

TLDR; it's a pretty good game that's almost great. Almost. Except for some design decisions, some of which are fixable (enemy interrupts), some of which aren't (the F2P bones).

cons it's a looter shooter with the single worst inventory management system i've ever seen. the small inventory is shared by every character. if one character equips a piece of gear, all have to carry it around. this is idiotic. there is a stash, but it's literally pointless. the majority of the missions are not exploration. 80 of them are some version of keep the bad guys out of this small circle. sometimes the circle moves, sometimes you clear one circle and have to go to another. they all suck. it's a terrible mechanic, and it's literally most of what you do in the game. charge skills jumping. initially, these feel cool and fun to play with, but given that in almost every encounter enemies will be able to interrupt your skill charge up and your jump making you fall straight down and waste the skill , these become annoying and a detriment, so you don't use them. falling off an edge - you take a little damage and you respawn pretty quick, but you keep a little momentum from when you fell. meaning, sometimes you just keep respawning and falling over and over. it doesn't work well. grinding. the f2p bones of it are still obvious, and it's the bad parts of f2p. did you love rep grinding in wow classic to get those items you need? no? screw you, it's in here anyway. i hope you like territory control insert xzibit meme . mid - the plot and writing. it... exists. tldr it's a pretty good game that's almost great. almost. except for some design decisions, some of which are fixable enemy interrupts , some of which aren't the f2p bones .

review_text:
Having played many versions of this game from the English translated JP version for years, all the way to the global release, I "would" say that this game is worth your time to enjoy, unfortunately I can't say that today with a straight face since the release of New Genesis.

My overall opinions of this game has changed drastically over the years so I'll try to keep this brief from memory.

The global version of base game has had 10 years of content from the JP version shoved into 1 year making the game undoubtedly one of the best experiences you could have. Game play was very addicting, the world was a spectacle, though the story while not the greatest, it is definitely not the worst, just justifiable.

This all changed ever since the literal announcement of New Genesis was coming, right as the global version of base game had just launched, making some people outright quit the game and said "we'll wait for THAT to release"

Now, I understand that the JP release of base game was not the greatest either. If memory serves as I type this, the JP version was dripped fed very minimal of content that either had to do with story, game play changes, or new classes over the 10 years it was around.

Ever heard the saying, [b]"Those who don't know history are destined to repeat it"[/b]? Well, history is repeating itself yet again for New Genesis. 
1. Story is potentially the worst over base.
2. Game play while potentially better than base game, overstays it's welcome with how bare-bones the combat is compared.
3. Classes are just shells of their former selves, if not worse.
4. [Extra] While the "Open World" you explore is indeed very graphically beautiful.. that's its, it looks nice, there's nothing substantial to look for at all but "materials" I guess.

Anyway, I have many more opinions about NGS, be it a little bit positive but mostly negative.

At the end of the day, NGS is just a bigger empty shell of it's former self... and I miss the old days.

review_text:
Witchfire Webgrave Update

The game is now in a great place, even from what the devs are saying (for Q1 2026 1.0 and how the game now is almost mostly about more content) and Steam/Reddit agrees the game feels excellent to play and very polished. I said it before, but if you miss Destiny being Destiny - here's a witch-themed Destiny that replicates that signature of Destiny-Bungie-Halo like gun and movement feel. It's excellent, also because it's not just trying to be Slavic-Witcher-like Destiny, but also just having strong progression and game loop. It's just fun, the enemies are fun, the guns and upgrades are fun. Not to sound like a broken record, but it's all just fun. There's a nice mix of moods too, from more Slavic-Nordic elements to some Inquisition-style Spanish influence and a lot of western vibes straight from Hunt: Showdown.

There are not many games I would recommend in early access (like No Rest for The Wicked) because they feel too amazing to play (and have almost no bugs), but this is one of them. Early 2026 is not far off, but if you get in now - you have almost the final version. After 60h (20h of this new update), I'm level 81, so more-or-less late-mid/early-late game.

The roguelite.
The random run roguelite element is well integrated into the game design, allowing you to further customise your build per run. As with many great roguelites (like Hades), you can upgrade your character and gain access to more control over the random skills by choosing tier prefs (a bit like gods' trinkets in Hades for getting more types of certain boons). You can pick between beefing up your guns (like dash reload or bullet refunds on crits, etc.), your magic, or your life. It makes for a fun random skill system that can make each run different even when using the same core gear.

The extraction.
I feel that this is where many people hesitate, as extraction shooters are usually a bit more hardcore. While Witchfire is an extraction shooter, it is also a single-player game. Most extraction shooters feel more intense as you know other players are out there and may wait for you at the extraction. With Witchfire, that's not the case. The game has systems to keep tension high (like extraction portals guarded by enemies or calamities that work as a timer for you to not grind one map too long) - it's never as stressful as in a multiplayer game and works great within the lore of the world for you to get in, fight the evil witch's minions, and make your way out.

Some tips if you start:
- Level up your guns, they can have game-changing mechanics, so even if you don't love the gun on level 1 - by level 3/3 it may be amazing and super fun to use.
- Mix status elementals, the game allows you to mix more elementals than just obvious ones like Fire and Ice. All elementals mix - so a decay and lightning can produce more lightning, or a fire with lightning can produce a more rapid burn. Don't be afraid to mix - you don't need to (you can) just focus on one elemental.
- Experiment with your gear - one ring or a totem can change the way you play. One of my favorite rings is one that freezes enemies when they melee you and you dash - makes (all enemies, but especially) elites much easier as all enemies in this game have a melee attack and it can be a pressure off if you can freeze a stronger enemy to strike back or just reposition. They melee - you dash - they freeze - you crit-hit. It's poetry. Or how about electric shocks every time you dash after hitting an enemy?

With the Webgrave update - Witchfire is one of the best FPS games on the market, it's fun - has very satisfying combat and gunplay and just works. Oh yeah - it's also great on Steam Deck - had to add that hahah.

review_text:
I've played a number from MMO's from LotRo, ESO, Rift, and SWO and yet none has kept me logging in daily quite like STO has. And the weird thing is that I am not a huge Trekkie either, or should I say I wasn't a huge trekkie before I started. LotR and ES have both had me investing far more time in the past in other games and delving into their lore, but I started playing STO about 3 years ago simply because I started rewatching next generation. 

Star Trek Online is very easy to play in bitesize chunks because of the episodic nature of the chapters and missions, and honestly it is done in a way that no other MMO I have played has ever beaten. In games like LotrO and ESO I found myself logging in after a week away or an extended absence and simply having no idea which quests I was doing or why and so would generally drop them all and start picking up random quests until I found a common story thread to follow. It's not a major issue, but it is a bit jarring when going back to a game after a break. With STO though, the chapters just seem to be more neatly wrapped up and easier to digest and there is a very definite order where you just follow one by one when it comes to the main story. There are other world missions that you pick up on the way too, but are generally repeatable which means they don't tend to affect the main story much. I don't know why but STO just feels neater when it comes to storytelling, and it really helps you not feel overwhelmed. 

The devs also keep constant mini events running where you can earn ships, upgrades and in game items on pretty much a monthly basis which in my view also makes it one of the most generous MMO's I have played. Most games give a daily reward for free, but its usually a one use consumable or something you never would have bought anyway. In this game, the ships alone are worth logging in for the events as each one can be claimed on every character and every ship has a unique trait or sometimes equipment that can help you experiment with builds. I see a lot of "STO is pay to win" but in my experience that just isn't true. They are more than generous with free stuff and they have regular sales on the in game store. Most of what people cry about the cost of seems to be things like rare ships too, which just seems to me like a huge FOMO that they themselves need to either cough up or get over. You can absolutely play this game without investing much at all, as I played f2p for quite a while before starting to spend money on it. 

As well as the in game rewards and freebies, there are regular update giveways on sites like intel, alienware and Steel series and these giveaways tend to have something that ties into the latest game update. For example a recent update was all about the borg and so the giveaways had borg consoles and borg ground weapons that you could claim. What is more every single time they do these giveaways, every one contains a pack that gives you bank and inventory space which means that there is another thing you don't necessarily have to buy in game. These sites always have their own unique updates too giving away different items, and so at each update you get to claim 2-4 different ones and so that is 2-4 different bank and inventory packs. Again, in my opinion just another showing of how overly generous the game actually is. 

There are also in game work arounds to some of the paid content, for example one thing people buy is "cross faction flying" but this can be unlocked for free just by levelling a Klingon KDF character to max level. Once your klingon is max level, every character on the account can fly whatever ship they like so again saves you money after a little time investment. 

As for levelling too, I find this to be one of the easiest games to level characters in personally. I have something like 8 max level characters and most of them I haven't really played that much. They have been levelled mainly through events, random TFO's (group missions) and solo patrols. This wasn't for any other reason than because I wanted different characters of different races to be able to jump in and play when I felt like it and have access to similar skills across them. 

Quite honestly, even as a someone who is fairly new to star trek I can say that this game gives you a lot to log in for and a lot of content to play. It also got me interested in watching other star trek shows such as Deep Space 9 and TOS, neither of which ever interested me before. The fact that the game hires many of the voice actors to reprise their roles got me wanting to know more about them and so it kindled a bit of a star trek deep dive and in turn made me appreciate the whole fandom a lot more. 

My final thought is simply that if you are on the fence about trying this game, just try it. I was and I did, and I haven't looked back.

review_text:
[Gifted by a friend]

No matter what I accomplish in my life, I regret that I cannot say I came up with the single greatest title for a video game ever: "Bomb Rush Cyberfunk."

A triumph! This was my introduction to the gang/graffiti/parkour platformer genre and what a way to start! So no, for reference, I have not played the *Jet Set Radio* games yet, so I can't compare this obvious spiritual successor to those. But man, what a ride!

I've had my eye on Team Reptile since *Lethal League* - a superb unique fighting/sports game. Throw in Hideki Naganuma's music and I had to play this. And yes, even if you only play for the soundtrack it might be worth your time. A compilation of electronic funk songs from an eclectic array of composers that makes the entire game just one solid continuous vibe. Add addictive platforming and tricking gameplay with collectathon elements, a genuinely perfect cel-shaded artstyle, and tight controls and the game really does exceed the sum of its relatively small development team.

If I had to nitpick, there were a few frustrating segments - particularly any time combat is involved. Combat never feels as tight or responsive as the skate controls and bosses are relatively simple and uninspired. That's really all the negatives I have for it, though.

World building and narrative were shockingly...uh...present? I don't know why I wasn't expecting much of a story, but there is one here. It's not the best story ever, but it's solid enough and even tries to pull off some ambitious twists and turns that mostly work. Rival gangs are unique and honestly hilarious. The game introduces a deeper story and better side missions, which help to flesh out the experience, making it feel more substantial than Just Cause 3. However, despite its improvements, Just Cause 4 still falls short of offering the depth and lasting impact that a truly life-changing game can provide. It remains, at its core, a fun but ultimately shallow experience, one that doesn’t provide the emotional or intellectual challenge that makes a game memorable in the long run.

Dark Souls 2 is a transformative experience that reshapes the way you approach both games and life. Its world is meticulously designed, every combat encounter demands mastery and precision, and its cryptic storytelling invites deep exploration and introspection. Unlike the chaotic spectacle of Just Cause, Dark Souls 2 offers a profound, deliberate challenge that rewards patience, skill, and perseverance. Playing Dark Souls 2 isn’t just about beating a game; it’s about personal growth, learning from failure, and overcoming seemingly insurmountable obstacles. Dark Souls 2 is the best thing to ever exist in gaming, a life-changing journey that will stay with you long after you've finished it, elevating your understanding of what games can truly offer.

which I haven't gotten into much due to having nobody to play it with, but it's good to have it in case.

Personally, I find this game to be very calming even in intense moments due to its excelent music,
the story is quite simplem I have managed to finish the game within first 20 hours in about 8 standings 
(2.5 hr each) I feel it really helped me distract myself when really needed, especially in July of 2025 when my grandfather passed away, surprisingly it gave me space to really think about things, to figure out what happens now from this point. 

I can certainly see myself revisitting it, to complete all of those achievements I missed, and experiment more.

The novelty of the gameplay wears off after hitting 8-10h mark. I am aware that there are plenty of things to 'unlock' still - but as it stands I feel the game needs just bit more fine tuning and content for in between stages when you're working towards next goal. Only thing that seems to change is the enemy difficulty as you progress, everything else remains the same and is rather easy and simple.

So in short, this is a great game, but needs a bit more agency why you should continue playing after novelty period wears off. 

I'll check it out again after 1.0

review_text:
****THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS ****
--
I can’t believe I’ve never written a review for this game after all these years. I’ve played countless JRPGs and MMOs over the decades, but this little gem remains my favorite video game of all time.

It was originally gifted to me by my ex-boyfriend. As a huge Cloud and Tifa shipper from the OG Final Fantasy VII, he thought I’d fall in love with Johnny and River’s story: two childhood sweethearts bound by memories, loss, and love.

Johnny and River’s journey is a powerful reminder to cherish the ones we love while facing the memories we often bury. It also shines a compassionate light on neurodivergence and the barriers it can create in understanding and connection. Everything about this story from the writing, the pacing, the emotions is breathtaking, compelling, and absolutely award-worthy.

The music, though, is what truly elevates it. When my beloved dog passed away, this soundtrack was playing softly in the background.

Even as I write this, I’m crying. The themes of memory, love, and letting go feel more relevant than ever as we inch closer to the kind of technology this game imagined ; technology that might one day let us revisit our most precious memories in our final moments or achieve the dreams we couldn't reach during our gifted time.

The creator deserves recognition as one of the most emotionally intelligent storytellers of our time.

review_text:
Wish this could co-exist alongside Helldivers without the constant comparisons, but alas, that's not going to happen. This is a different game from Helldivers, where that is a small strike force sent behind enemy lines, and can be extremely frustrating depending on the difficult you select and the materials you're trying to collect - this game has you join an expeditionary force of 16 other players to take down the bugs. Both titles have a hectic extraction run at the end of the mission, although I prefer the Starship Troopers model here. 

Starship Troopers Extermination is a blast, the update adding persistent corpses has made the game play quite a bit different as well. There are ample classes and loadout options to keep players occupied with the play style they want. XP and unlocks are tied to gameplay, not item collection and difficulty, which instantly makes it better than Helldivers IMO. 

It could use a few more maps and it's difficult not to admire the weather effects that Helldivers offers, but the number of possible players and base defense gameplay is where this game really shines.

Join a squad, drop into the war, build a base, destroy the bugs, get out... I'm doing my part.

review_text:
died to a bug, stepped onto some instakill area at the ocean border, got back, picked up my things, then wanted to do what I originally wanted when I died, died again to some nonsense situation where the map lied to me (I thought I was at a place I had visited before, because of the chest symbol, but it lead me straight into a dozen mobs), then died again by some BS thing before I could pick up the 70k witchfire I had dropped and I am done with this game.

it's not bad, just a little bit empty and the Unreal 4 look is just so ancient at this point... it's another game with no real colors, everything's under 2 dozen layers of grey-brown color scheme and mist everywhere. FoV isn't doing anything. No NPCs, no animals, all lifeless. tiny maps. Hyper grind but you still can lose things you worked for for over an hour. 

fyi: I started the game with "Saint", i.e. lvl 1 and the game is not difficult. this is not about difficulty. it is about taking away something I've worked for.

none of these things would have been worth a downvote individually, but I can't play games any more that think it's a virtue to undo almost 2h of my time. just stop it.
let me pick up my corpses. I basically never died in the game, until that bug killed me and I got more frustrated and played less careful, because I felt I was already wasting my time. if a player is at such a point, deleting all progress someone made in the last hours is a surefire way to get them to leave the game for good and give it a bad rating.

there's so many weird decisions in this game: like that picking up things need a long press of E... this is for dialogue games that want to make sure that you don't accidentally click a button and bork your quest-line. NOT FOR ACTION GAMES.

the magic is fantastic, but I never use it. because every time I want to use it, I think to myself: it takes 30 minutes to get off cooldown, so why waste it?
having such insane cooldowns with the most fun aspect in the game is laughably self-defeating. every time I actually decide to use magic, I almost immediately get into a situation where I really needed it and can't use it.

there is so many things that could improve this, like a big mana bar that VISIBLY fills up, albeit slowly, mana potions or the devs potentially deciding that it's ok to just let you use the fun stuff when I can headshot things from a distance. why the ban on letting me freeze things often?

but all of this would not be a reason to rate it down... but losing so much time and so many items I had collected... tons of letters and crosses and such... subjectively speaking, I may as well restart the game. that's how it feels, as ridiculous as it sounds.
it makes not much sense, but that's how I feel and I have no interest in starting over. any time investment into an old looking UE4 title with mechanics that spit on my time investment with BS "now your stuff is gone" mechanics is just a waste

I won't return the game (I basically never do) because this can be fixed. but as Zero Sievert and so many other games have shown, devs have some weird stuff stuck in their heads sometimes and won't budge on it.
(in Zero Sievert it was the minimum damage range that killed the game for me... an AR can't hit anything that's 10m away and do no damage to it? (and also nothing that's too far away :D) sure buddy...)

dev: if you pick up an item, even if that item is just converted to gold, NEVER have to be taken away. anything dropped should stay there and be pickupable. no deadline. 
this isn't about difficulty. it's about frustration.

I played Wukong and beat the blue mega child-like boss after trying for 2h, as the very first thing I did in the game. I beat Yellow Loong too (the hardest boss). I have nothing against difficulty.

but it just does something to my enjoyment when loot that drops despawns (instant down vote for any modern game that does that) or if I can permanently lose items or currency I worked for.

review_text:
I decided to give it another try. The biggest issue - it is a mix of base/city builder and tower defense but building towers ( and other buildings but that doesn't matter that much) doesn't feel snappy - it always takes ages ages even when you have resources, assigned maximum  workers to builders slots and are building only few things at time. Workers are probably wasting time on building repairs. Extreme weather conditions like hail or meteor shower usually don't destroy anything but just waste time of builders.
Lacks basic QoL features - hard to say where all the workers are, zoom-out is limited, workers love to repair enemy roads if they are placed in corruption free ares. Worker death message disappear very slowly obscuring middle of screen but there is no option to jump to place where it happened. Same for announcement log - no way to visit the building that was completed/destroyed.
This is not a clicker but still a waiting game - wait for more resources, place building, repeat - you know the drill. And 3x speed slows down to x2 or less with 70+ villagers.
Adding trash to game was crazy idea and wall-e golems don't change that - the game tiles are very small and now we have 5 types of trash that looks like just some items/resources and litter every fragment of map.

---old version review below---
I like particle effects, storm spell and available tower/turret choice. And that is pretty much all that is good about it. 
After hour or two there isn't much to do other than placing another turret, shack or farm. Monsters aren't very agressive or dangerous, in 10 hours I lost only 20-30 villagers i 4-5 buildings (in Survival mode). Interface isn't great, the side menus: profession assigment and building selection are biggest offenders. I know building upgrades and limits are common in tower defence games but here they give me the "mobile P2W" vibe.
The game is still under active development so I hope it gets better in future, the idea looked great on paper.

review_text:
I've only played traditional or whatever the normal mode is. Overall it's a decent game that seems to tie together a lot of elements from other similar games, making an attempt at covering a lot of aspects from those games that I enjoy.

Issues thus far. Game is EA, so obviously there are going to be issues. The dev is super responsive, my problem is that from some of his responses, some changes haven't come even though he commented about them a year ago. For example, if you accidentally dismantle a building, there's no obvious way to stop this. Researching it shows a comment from the dev stating this function is planned for InDev 18, the game is now on InDev 28.

This really ties into another issue, it's a combination of the game having a small playerbase and the dev probably being indie, there's no updated wiki to look up the game in its current state. The wiki link on the game's official site gives you a WIP page. Trying to look up information on the game leads to posts that span years, making it unreliable on whether or not it's still relevant.

I also have a pretty big issue with the way your buildable area expands. Your walls cut off your "sphere of influence" and you can't build beyond your them. This forces you to tear down walls in order to release your "SOI" in order to build beyond it. This makes it a huge pain in the ass to expand. It's constant leapfrogging your sphere to expand and it gets rather repetitive.

As a final note, props to the dev for being super responsive. This however, leads to another con for me. The dev has indicated some game decisions that I don't really agree with.

For example, I'm in my second game on traditional, it took me some time figuring out how to get things going in my first attempt so I abandoned it after 20ish minutes to restart. My 2nd and current game started a bit hairy, but now I control like 40% of the map and it's just a slow grind at this point. I realize that I'm playing the easiest mode in probably an easy mapset, my issue is that I don't really feel like doing it all over again because of the time investment to build from the ground up again.

I know the dev has made responses as to speeding up the game, my problem is with his responses. The dev has indicated that he wants to add a spell to the game as a temporary buff to your villagers speed instead of just adding a game speed option. My problem with this is that a speed buff is pretty much irrelevant to the issue game speed, they're two entirely different things and the fact that the dev thought this was a response makes me doubt his decision making and the future of the game.

The lack of a game speed option is pretty much deterring me from wanting to try any other maps. Sure, it might be harder and the challenge might be a bit more interesting, but there's just too much sitting and waiting for your villagers to get anything done. Especially when you do get strong enough and start having to expand your base.

I'm 9.5 hours into the game and pretty much finished with it in my opinion. I got it on sale so I guess I got my money's worth, I'd recommend the game for a quick play, but for the type of game it is, that relies on replayability, I think it still needs a lot of work which might never come, so I can't really recommend it.

review_text: The first time I played BioShock, I thought, “Oh cool, an underwater shooter with superpowers and art deco vibes!” By the time I finished it, I was asking everyone “Would you kindly?” and questioning the illusion of free will in my daily life. So, you know, it escalated quickly. Let’s talk about the intro. You crash into the ocean, swim to a mysterious lighthouse, take a bathysphere ride down into the sea, and BAM—Rapture. An underwater city full of philosophical graffiti, broken dreams, and vending machines that scream at you. It’s stunning. It’s terrifying. It’s also completely abandoned except for the homicidal maniacs and giant men in vintage diving suits stomping around with power drills. Vacation destination of the year. The combat? A chaotic ballet of guns, fire hands, and “oh no I accidentally electrocuted myself again.” Plasmids let you do everything from shooting bees out of your arms to mind-controlling enemies, which raises questions that science should never answer. And the Big Daddies? They’re like boss fights combined with emotional damage. You want to fight them. You also kind of want to hug them. (You shouldn't.) But let’s be honest: you're here for the story. The atmosphere. The vibes. This game doesn’t just pull the rug out from under you—it tears out the floorboards, drops you into a moral philosophy class, and then politely hands you a wrench. And just when you think you’re getting the hang of it—BOOM. Plot twist so good it made me question if I was being mind-controlled by my microwave the whole time. Also, shoutout to the audio diaries. I learned more about failed utopias, corporate betrayal, and what happens when you mix unchecked ambition with genetic tampering than I did in any history class.

review_text:
*SIGH* Another potentially good game, completely killed by horrible development designs. This game is a huge let down for me. Not because it's a complete pile of rubbish, but because what it does well, it does incredibly well.

COMBAT. Combat in this game is probably the most satisfying hand to hand combat that I've ever experienced. You feel like you are in an action movie, the movement is smooth and intuitive. But fighting against opponents with guns is a real fun killer. You have the batclaw, which can be upgraded to disarm the gunmen that you experience. However, even after upgrading it to do so, you still can't disarm the gunmen until the third or fourth attempt. By that time, it's already too late. The reason being is that you never fight one opponent with a gun. It's either all people with melee weapons (FUN) or all gunmen (NOT FUN), which will mow you down extremely quickly. If the batclaw actually worked then it wouldn't be a problem and you could overcome this obstacle with skill. You are totally Batman in a movie, except when it comes to gunmen. The bat boomerang or even a claw being shot at the gun of an opponent isn't enough to disarm them. Even beating them to a pulp won't cause them to drop their guns. *SMH*

PHONE CALLS: There are side missions given to you by phone from ringing payphones. You have a certain amount of time to get to the next payphone and answer it, otherwise you fail. The problem is that most of the phones are guarded by several enemies who will fight you and not allow you to answer the phone. If you play perfectly, and get to the phone, you will have about 15 seconds at most to answer the phone. This isn't a problem if you are psychic and know ahead of time where the phone call will send you to answer the next phone. You just clear out the enemies ahead of time and then answer the phone that you are being sent to. But if you lack clairvoyance, you can't possibly take out the enemies and answer the phone in time. Seriously, who thought that this was a good idea?

RIDDLER MISSIONS. The real riddle is actually finding where to go for the mission. You will see a marker on your mini map telling you where to go, you head there, and there is nothing visible. You use your detective vision, which has every high tech gadget that you can think of,. Predator vision, plus every kind of gadget from a James Bond movie. This thing helps you see EVERYTHING through out the game. But not on the Riddler missions. Nope. Even when you have a paper thin wall, you can't see it. This makes absolutely no sense at all because seeing destructible walls is literally one of the powers you gain from using detective vision. Smooth brain 500 IQ decision there.

Finally the pacing of this game is just killed by needless obfuscation of what you are supposed to be doing. You can have your progress blocked in an area by trying to figure out how to get from point A to B. That's fine. I don't mind having to solve a puzzle. I get it that this game isn't a mindless beat em up game. Cool. But when you scan every room with your detective ability and can't see what you are supposed to do to shut down a steam valve, or have to watch a Youtube video to realize that you needed to slide under a door that's got a 3 inch gap between it and the ground all of the fun just turns to frustration. Make a slide under the door gap look....actually....possible so that a player would naturally think to try that. 

Only a few hours into the game, I've been to Youtube 3 times to figure out WTF I'm supposed to be doing. Instead of feeling like Batman in a Batman movie thinking: "What would Batman do?" I feel like I'm a rat, trapped in some game devs maze thinking: "What obscure corner did this dev hid a button behind that makes no sense at all?" This is why modern games suck. There is an amazing game here. The feel of Arkham city, the voice acting, the combat. It's all right there to be grabbed and ran with. To be enjoyed and leave you feeling satisfied...only to be plucked from your grasp by some stupid road block so that a game dev can turn a 15 hour gaming experience into a 20 hour gaming experience while you bash your head against the wall thinking: "How did it come to this? It's not rocket surgery. Just let my abilities work. Just let puzzles make sense!"
