Really solid addition to Sniper Ghost Warrior series. Compared to Sniper Ghost Warrior 3, this game does many things better.

Graphics looks great, clean. Performance - smooth as butter. Controls and movement are fluid and fairly responsive. Sound design and voice acting good too. Your mission commander sounds just like Vega from Doom games ^^

The first missions is probably the hardest, because you don't have a powerful sniper and no skills unlocked. Once you earn more money and tokens for completing quite hard challenges - the game opens up. You have many different ways to deal with your enemies. BUT the problem is - once they spot you (only 1 miss! or they find a body), the whole area instantly  knows where you are and every single enemy is alerted of your presence, even though they are like 500m away from that location. it's like all of them are connected like a hive mind ^^. This is the biggest problem with the game overall. You have no room for error if you want to be the silent killer. But playing as a sniper Rambo is an option, so yeah, there is that.

Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 with its vast open world maps didn't have such a big problem (but it still had enemies with eyes on their backs). 

There are some annoying bugs, like some objective progress resetting after a reload or enemies getting stuck in animation. 

Really hard to notice enemy snipers if you don't have a skill which unveils their line of sight.

I remember playing Delta Force 20+ years ago. You basically shoot at pixeIs from far far away haha. Can't imagine how incredible this game would have looked back then with this gameplay and graphics. Probably an instant masterpiece. 

Sniper Contracts has 5 semi-big maps with good replayability if you choose to complete all challenges. Some of them are really hard. 

Good game. I enjoyed it.

Under the hood, there have been some major changes to the game. It's still a work in progress, but it is already an improvement over EHM 2007. Once things have been tweaked further, I think it will be a big improvement over EHM 2007. It already makes a difference having customisable start dates (great for retro rosters) and having up-to-date rules and league structures. review_text:
Fun game, but has some very annoying sides too. 
Things that should be fixed or adapted in my opinion (This is after 150+hrs, so some of them might just be an issue with my playstyle):


* Trash at this point is little more than an annoyance which doesn't really contribute anything to the game apart from adding another aspect that needs to be managed. You can make walls with trashy cubes, but that's about all you can do with it while you are forced to waste around 4 building slots on it early on already. Along with this, everything made with trash lowers the appeal of the area it's built on, so all this system does is force the player to deal with trash for no other reason than dealing with trash.


* Food production is slow as hell, i've tried pretty much every set-up suggested on steam forums and on other pages i could find, have it close to a lake, have a purifier next to it, have a bottler, however nothing seems to work for me (if i'm doing anything wrong please let me know). Also, Farms are supposed to be self-sufficient, currently the farmers take food from the map > plant it in farm > harvest > go back to taking food from the map. 
While it should be, Take food from map > plant seeds in farm > harvest > take seeds from harvest > replant in farm > repeat. There is no reason why they have to farm from the map once again once they have a farm up and running.

Same goes for meat collection in clucker coops and animal pens, the rate at which animals get brought in and the rate at which meat is produced is a fraction of what is needed, this is especially the case when you play on custom and play around with the nomads spawnrate.


* The learning curve is steep, but in the wrong places. This game has a lot of features that aren't new, therefore everyone with a bit of experience in comparable games wouldn't take too long familiarizing themselves with the options, interface and gameplay. The steep learning curve that's mentioned applies to certain gameplay mechanics that do not get mentioned in the tips, so even if you follow the tips to the letter you will still have to google for most parts that will actually confuse you.


* Some jobs benefit a lot from extra population while some don't seem to benefit at all. If you up the amounts of lumberjacks and miners you will see a large increase in work speed, the same goes for builders. However if you look at farmers or stonecutters and the lumbermill there doesn't seem to be a change in speed whatsoever after adding more population (even after googling and following advice).


* Priorities don't really get prioritized, when you prioritize a job as number 1 in the queue, if your workers don't have materials they will just go further down the queue, which is fine, but occasionally it goes on for so long that that building you needed to have ASAP is still not done after multiple days.


* The game is really really slow, with no way to make it go faster apart from using the fast forward option in the game, and even with it on the highest setting it is still really slow. This doesnt really make it a very suitable if you just want to play a game in your downtime.


* Upgrades are still a bit lacking, everything has 3 upgrades after placing it down (With some exceptions like fountains) and if i'm honest, that's too little for how i'd personally like to play. At the end i'd like to have a utopia running off of just 1 or 2 gathering buildings because the upgrades are getting so strong.


* You play the role of god and the population recognizes your godly acts (citizens stand and watch with questionmarks popping up when they see one of your powers). However, there is no religion or anything comparable in the game. Which makes the whole "god" setting redundant and without purpose, much like the trash.

It seems that Sniper Ghost Warrior's looking for its identity after going full Far Cry with the third game. This time the foundation is much more simple - smaller maps with multiple contracts to fulfill where it's up to the players what and when they do.
With nearly two hours played I've finished the first map,on the highest difficulty and have done some testing. And this is what I think so far:
-First of all,the AI. Picking the highest difficulty the game says that the enemies are wiser and more vigilant,but unfortunately they are dumb as a brick and blind as a mole. The most important thing about the sniper's experience is the challenge,a requirement of being stealthy, under threat of being mown down or captured by overwhelming enemy forces,but SGW Contracts lacks that feeling. You can go full Call of Duty here,on the highest difficulty and it won't really be much of a challenge.
-Plenty of bugs and glitches. 2 bugs killed me in the very first minutes of gameplay.
-Shooting with anything except for a sniper rifle feels dull and lacks any feeling of impact.
-Graphics are mediocre - the terrain's geometry and textures are poor quality,but the devs quite successfully mask it under a thick layer of additional effects.
-If you know what you're doing, most of contracts can be finished in merely seconds,but not for the first time.
-All the objects have multiple entrances and exits,allowing for different approach.

review_text:
Three years after the release of Act 1, the change in writers has made itself quite apparent in Act 2. Gone are the charming flavor texts that sprouted from almost every background element to inspect or trying to get your trusty pidgeon to interact with a piano, and here to stay is a minimal amount of text that says "that won't work" and nothing for human out of water Joey to say about the intriguing designs of the characters around her that weren't introduced in Troll Call. What remains of Hiveswap is a rather lifeless journey through a series of beautifully crafted dioramas of lovingly animated trolls that all have increasingly bizarre yet charming personalities; what's clear with Act 2 is a devotion to character writing, as is common with post-Act 7 Homestuck content, with little effort placed into actual world building. As fun as the characters are, there is little of their characterization from their appearances in Friendsim, so long time fans might be displeased to see this. Many of these characters also end up being not but set pieces of little relevance, which is disappointing given a couple of the trolls' potential connections to future villains. 
Much of the narrative of the game is also quite pointless to Joey and Xefros' endgame goal. A lot of the game could've been cut and nothing would've changed; the entirety of the first third where the two explore Charun and Zebede's hives (both characters cut for time) could've been cut as the only plot-relevant content occurs once they reach the train station. The narrative itself grinds to a halt for an Ace Attorney parody that is also completely irrelevant to the main narrative. [spoiler]The only plot relevant thing occurs when Xefros and Joey and Xefros manage to hi-jack the train, only for the train to be blown up and potentially killing everyone on board, making the entirety of Act 2's plot beats completely irrelevant. The ending also comes across as simple shock value which is the standard Homestuck faire, but even that old trick is becoming rather old.[/spoiler] 
More than anything, the game comes across as wasted potential, and it's all the more frustrating that players will have to wait another three years to see the conclusion to such a disappointing cliffhanger. 
Also again, a game that only added its credits earlier than anticipated due to backlash for even removing them in the first place doesn't deserve your money.

Overall, I was left feeling disappointed and would not recommend it to others.

review_text:
Pathologic 2 is a pretty alright game. It's not fun, though - which, realistically, is part of the point in the experience. However, I personally find the features irritating rather than interesting. To begin with...

Survival Meters. The survival meters are implemented better than many other games, because rather than being strange, obligatory things that you are forced to take care of in situations that seem random or outright ridiculous, it makes sense that your character, under the duress of a plague and running around all day, would likely need a lot of food, water, and rest. However, they're still the irritating, fast-rising meters that take a lot away from my enjoyment of the game. Maybe it's a personal taste issue, but in almost every game with these garish meters, they rarely make any logical sense with how fast they rise, how much you have to eat just to be "fine", ect. I know that part of the game's story is about coping with starvation, dehydration, lacking money, and simply getting sick; but, honestly? I feel like it's more of an excuse for poor game design.

The game's story and "mood" are interesting, if a bit...over-bearing. I have this problem with some games and media, especially recently - there is simply an overbearing feeling of total dread and pointlessness. Again this could simply be my preferences, but I don't think any story is all that interesting when it's simply a conga line of trauma, death, and despair. Even if it ends with a light at the end of the tunnel, at that point I couldn't care less because the entire journey felt useless.

The way that the game is set up to purposefully stress you so you have to run/walk across the city every five minutes becomes more of an exercise in patience than anything, at a certain point I stopped caring about many of the things to do because the game seems to want to make a point about how you can't save everyone, you can't do everything, you can't always be the good guy, and other very critical (if realistic) viewpoints. That's all well and good, but, I just can't bring myself to *care* about the messages when the game makes it possible to do many of those things, but only if you're willing to tear your hair out and min-max.

The saving system is...annoying. I never personally liked saving systems where you had to run up to some random object just to smack it and sprint the other way, especially in an open-world game. I can abide it in certain games because it feels less intrusive, but not here, personally.

The infection system isn't really...interesting? It feels, again, as if it's more simply designed to be obtuse and frustrating to deal with; which, if it was, fair enough! However, given that it's another one the imperfect "survival bars", it simply makes me roll my eyes and reload a save because the game cheekily decides to spawn a cloud of death directly in front of me, or randomly chooses to have opening a random door give me sickness. Obviously that might be the point, but, it again feels like an excuse.

All in all, the entire game seems like it's *fine*, but I can't help but not want to really play it anymore. It's not because I don't think I can, or because it's not fun (it's not necessarily supposed to be fun), but the entire experience feels empty to me. Sure, the story and characters are well written, but when everything surrounding them feels so jagged and awkward to handle on top of having mechanics that kick you in the teeth repeatedly, I just don't think it's worth playing - the experience reminds me that I have actual work to do and honestly, promises that it's probably a better idea to do that instead. Discussing, maybe watching? Perhaps. Playing? I'd rather pass.

it feels, again, as if it's more simply designed to be obtuse and frustrating to deal with which, if it was, fair enough! however, given that it's another one the imperfect survival bars , it simply makes me roll my eyes and reload a save because the game cheekily decides to spawn a cloud of death directly in front of me, or randomly chooses to have opening a random door give me sickness. obviously that might be the point, but, it again feels like an excuse. all in all, the entire game seems like it's fine , but i can't help but not want to really play it anymore. it's not because i don't think i can, or because it's not fun it's not necessarily supposed to be fun , but the entire experience feels empty to me. sure, the story and characters are well written, but when everything surrounding them feels so jagged and awkward to handle on top of having mechanics that kick you in the teeth repeatedly, i just don't think it's worth playing - the experience reminds me that i have actual work to do and honestly, promises that it's probably a better idea to do that instead. discussing, maybe watching? perhaps. playing? i'd rather pass.

To be frank, I bought this game on a whim after seeing that it dropped its Webgrave update, and that it was on sale. I figured that, if anything, this game will help me waste a few hours.

Honestly? Some of the best 35 hours that I have spent.

Witchfire is a FPS Roguelite Extraction Shooter where you shoot, dash, slide, and punch your ways through the vile manifestations of the Witch. Every "match" has you spawning into your selected map where you roam around trying to uncover "Manifestations" that power up your player until you're strong enough to face the map boss. 

As you improve your character you'll unlock new weapons, spells, and magical items that will help to further flesh out your character. He can also be leveled up through harvesting Witchfire. Progression is straightforward, and a little bit grindy as you need to farm both Mysterium pages and complete weapon challenges unique to each gun/spell/equipment. Thankfully these challenges are very straightforward as they require you to A) Kill/Hex things with used equipment, and B) Use guns new feature you just unlocked! It's very organic!

That being said: there are optimization issues with the new map. While I was able to run the game on ultra settings for most of playtime, I was forced to notch it down to medium settings when entering the aforementioned map. Seriously, I got less than 10fps + stuttering on a 3080 rig. 

I've 100% the game. I reached level 100, all equipment is maxed out, and I have completed all end game trials/dungeons. This is a rare Steam early access W.

I’ve been spending a lot of my free time in this game now. Time that I normally would have been putting into EVE Online but given that they’re not doing anything to let gamers opt out of PvP I’ve given them up for dead. The very idea of putting yourself at risk every time you go to mine some ore or go play a mission is just a dumb model for gaming, pure and simple. Especially when mining ore is (in a word) boring. The fact that they’re just sitting on that problem led me on a search for some other game to play that was worthy of my time.

I’ll be up front – EVE had pretty much put me off MMOs. I figured that the only people who got value out of them were the little nobodies who spent their entire lives on the game ganking other players just for the fun of it. Ruining other people’s experiences just to enhance their own self-esteem.

That said, I’d had STO in my library and never tried it before. I tried it. So much closer to what I wanted from an MMO experience. Certainly not the sociopath incubating zero trust environment of EVE. More of an immersive experience rooted in the ST universe.

Starting out was tough, but then every MMO is tough until you get your head around all the complexity that they’ve added and how it all works and fits together. Inside a month I was at the top of the level tree (Fleet Admiral 65) and having a ball. I’ve now pretty much played out all the episodes (yeah, episodes. Each looks like a mission but tells a story) for all the arcs that are out there and I sit and do task force operations (PvE Co-Op team missions) to stay in the game and wait for more content to come out in the form of events. That’s the real point of it being an MMO – they keep creating new content for it.

That content includes voice acting by actual ST character actors who appear in the story arcs as they’re developed. You get to see new takes on what various characters are doing or have done, and you get to see them all integrated in some fashion with a current timeline, usually through temporal operations and the like, but they’re there and that is the most important thing. The developers are making this world as immersive as they can by adding characters you can relate to and interact with, at least in the context of mission delivery.

It’s mostly single or co-op team play but they do release some PvP content for those who want to do that. The important thing is that the PvP is opt in, not (can’t) opt-out or any other model. Like all good co-op systems, you have the chance to respawn (so you’re not putting your stuff at risk) which makes sense in a ST environment – all your stuff can essentially be replicated again, right? But, it also makes sense because you only earn ships through certain events and the rank system. Every other ship you’re going to own, you’re going to buy. Either through resources in-game, or with Zen, which is effectively in-game cash that you’ve paid for with real world currency. Who wants to pay $30 US for a ship only to have some griefer blow it up 30 seconds after you leave spacedock? No-one would support that so in effect, the ships you either earn or buy are better thought of as ship templates.

The social aspect of it is minimal, or at least it was for me because I was actively looking to avoid it. If knowing about the social model is important to you, go read reviews written by Gen Ys or Millenials. They know about that kind of thing.

I did however join a fleet because my toon kept getting fleet join requests that I had to go out of my way to decline. In the end one came through with an interesting name that I could relate to so I accepted. That’s the last I’ve heard of any of them, or of anyone else wanting me to join them. That said, it turns out the fleet gives you some minor boosts in the game and you can contribute to fleet assets like colonies and starbases that you can visit (and use to certain levels) in the game.

Generally speaking, I have to say that it is an enjoyable experience that can be a little overly complex in my opinion, but I can live with that. Every large scale game that has been around long enough has complexity built in simply because of the organic nature of keeping itself relevant in a sea of changing wants and needs from an evolving player base.

What I find much harder to live with is the interface. It’s bad.

[b]BAD.[/b]

It doesn’t suck; sitting next to a bickering couple in a movie theatre sucks. This interface licks the slime off the scrotum of a three-weeks-dead llama carcass. If I was still teaching interface design and one of my second years put this in front of me, I’d not only fail them but I’d be looking for ways to get them kicked out of the uni for fear a future employer might ask ‘where is it you said you studied?’

Buttons keep jumping from the lower right corner of the screen to the lower centre, and then flipping back. They mask what’s going on in the fight when they’re centre. In TFOs, you can sometimes have to click a button on the lower right, then the centre, then in the lower left just to claim a single item. During combat, no less. The stacking of objects on the lower left push the current buttons up, so you can think you’re passing on something you don’t want only to find you’ve just passed up that one item you’ve been looking for because it took the place of the other one in the stack. There’s no ‘take all’ or ‘claim all’ buttons on any of the interfaces for combat, research, missions, et al. The inventory [i]sometimes[/i] stacks items of the same type, with no logic I can see as to why. Claiming on duty officer missions requires you to keep changing your mouse location because the claim button will be at a different height depending on the length of the mission name. At least they stack; research and admiralty systems force you to go to each slot, which again moves as the empty slots are thinner than the full ones (and by different sizes). Searching is either non-existent or a joke.

Cryptic - get your interface design team to actually play the game. Put it in their employment contracts that they have to play the game for at least 8hrs per week, and I’m not talking about opening the inventory once every 15 mins so the idle checkers don’t trip. Play the game and interact with all parts of it that require you to interact with a different interface. If they can’t see what’s wrong after a month of that; sack them. They’re not doing you any favours.

Another point that I want to make here is that there is a gambling element to this game and you need to consider that before you buy into it. They give away lock boxes, but you have to buy the keys. For actual money (via Zen). Each key opens a box with a chance of an epic prize of a great ship, but a lot more [i]not[/i]-epic prizes. Arguably, there should be gambler warnings on the purchase of things like master keys. They’ve certainly got public announcements when someone wins an epic prize. If you have a gambling addiction, this is not your game.

One other area that needs a [b]LOT[/b] more attention is starship internals. Currently they’re great but you can’t really do anything there. I’ve got a massive captain’s cabin that allows me to do precisely nothing inside it. I can’t even sit in the chairs. I can’t put my toon to sleep in the bed. I can’t interact with it. Hell, the cabin itself (to scale) is bigger than my house. I’d love to be able to do things in it.

If gambling doesn’t phase you, if you can live with one of the worst interface disasters I’ve ever seen, and if you love star trek and can except that you’ll never see a light sabre in the game because of cross-over concerns (but let’s face it – a phaser sabre; [b]phabre[/b] if you will – would be an AWESOME addition, and given most scientists think that a plasma energy sword is more realistic than a laser sword, the Romulans should have this SO covered; again I digress), then you need to give this a try.

review_text:
I have to say this is a terrible game.  The concept is good and it could have been a lot of fun, but the pay to win aspect ruins it.  Anything you pay money for is about 4 times better than standard units and buildings.  I'm not exaggerating.  Buildings cost about £3 each and you need probably 40 of them.  You can build the standard ones but you will never match someone who pays.  PvP is a joke, there seems to be some balancing but quality always beats quantity.

I brought the starter back for £2.99 and a special pack that gave me two units that could one shot everything I went against until level 11.  Without these units it would have taken much longer and I'm sure I would have dumped the game.

To sum up:  The story is OK and I'm interested in where it's going but there are many better games out there so don't waste your time.

review_text:
Turbo Golf Racing: A Fun, Fast-Paced Twist on Rocket League

Turbo Golf Racing delivers a thrilling, high-octane experience, merging the exhilarating world of golf with the fast-paced action of arcade racing. Think of it as Rocket League’s little brother with a golfing twist, and while it’s an enjoyable ride, it doesn’t quite capture the same magic that makes Rocket League an all-time classic.

Gameplay Mechanics: In Turbo Golf Racing, players control customizable vehicles equipped with a giant golf club to hit oversized balls into the goal—except this time, it’s not just about power shots. You’re racing through courses, battling rivals, and using power-ups to outmaneuver opponents while trying to get your ball into the hole first. The gameplay is fast-paced and feels like a delightful fusion of kart racing and golf, with enough chaos to keep you engaged.

Compared to Rocket League, Turbo Golf Racing keeps a similar sense of fluid, arcade-style action but shifts the primary focus from car control to the skill of hitting the ball with accuracy and timing. While Rocket League thrives on the deep mastery of aerial control and strategic positioning, Turbo Golf Racing focuses more on rapid, accessible gameplay with a slight learning curve. This makes it easier to jump into, but it might not have the same long-term depth that players love in Rocket League’s competitive scene.

Graphics and Aesthetic: Visually, Turbo Golf Racing leans into a vibrant, cartoonish aesthetic. The bright colors and whimsical environments give the game a fun, approachable feel. You’re racing through wild and imaginative golf courses with various environments—from tropical beaches to futuristic cities. It’s visually pleasing, but it doesn’t quite match the polished, almost photorealistic feel of Rocket League, which has an impressively immersive arena vibe that elevates the overall experience.

Customization: Both games offer extensive vehicle customization, but Turbo Golf Racing gives you more freedom with your car’s design. From skins to wheels to even the golf clubs used for hitting the ball, there’s plenty to personalize. Rocket League, on the other hand, excels in making customizations feel meaningful and integrated into the competitive experience with specific items that appeal to players’ skill and status.

Competitive Scene: Here’s where the comparison feels a bit uneven. Rocket League has built a massive competitive community over the years, with esports tournaments, professional leagues, and a deep tactical element that makes it a serious game for the pros. Turbo Golf Racing is more casual, focusing on fun and fast matches rather than deep strategy and positioning. While it has the potential for competitive play, it currently lacks the same level of seriousness and depth that Rocket League players crave.

Fun Factor: The real strength of Turbo Golf Racing lies in its fun factor. It’s easy to pick up and play, offering a more casual and less intense experience compared to Rocket League. If you’re looking for a lighthearted, fast-paced title to enjoy with friends, Turbo Golf Racing does its job brilliantly. However, it doesn’t quite have the same addictive quality that keeps Rocket League players coming back for more. Rocket League’s blend of skill, tactics, and team play keeps it fresh year after year, whereas Turbo Golf Racing feels more like a great way to kill time than a game that will develop a massive competitive scene of its own.

Conclusion: In the end, Turbo Golf Racing is a delightful, arcade-style racing experience with a unique twist on golf. It’s a fun game that will undoubtedly entertain, especially for players looking for a casual and enjoyable racing experience. However, if you’re comparing it directly to Rocket League, Turbo Golf Racing may feel a bit like a simplified version of its more polished and competitive counterpart. While it has its own charm and potential, it doesn’t yet have the same level of depth or esports appeal that Rocket League has so masterfully cultivated over the years.

Thank God for subtitles or else I wouldn't have known anyone was even talking. I decided to return it and wait for it to cook. There seemed like promise somewhere in there, but lord was the launch bad. Plus, they were charging for kill animations locked behind DLC and that was disgusting. SDS will forever be trash developers in my mind for that. But we are here to discuss the game.

Time passed and Humble Choice told me it was time to play it again. I'm glad to see that all of those experience destroying bugs were fixed, but why is everything blurry!? It's like they turned up motion blur to "crack head mode" and there's no setting to turn it off. I used to wear glasses before I had eye surgery, and this game looks like my vision used to. Which is disappointing, because as an original Dead Space fan, not that trash ass de-make, I wanted this game to be amazing! Which it could be, but why are they seemingly doing little extra things that make no sense to make this experience awful? I like the combat system... I guess there's that. review_text:
I love this game. At the start of development it seemed like a great way to look at an escalating defense game. Honestly just needed to work a bit more on late game and add more enemies, possibly change them or add some more elements to them. It is not fun worrying about if my people are getting their back scratched correctly. I am defending them from death on the other side of thin wall. At any moment an earthquake could take out everything these little people built, and I protect, away with the help of the hoards of monsters outside.

Pros: It is a difficult base building game where you have to defend against increasingly harder to kill enemies. There are specialized towers to help you with this that each have their purpose. You can build nearly anywhere and eventually create a happy nook of salvation until eventually time takes your kingdom into ruins. You have to care and provide for your people so they can survive and proliferate. There is a bit of a learning curve, but your bonuses carry over to the next run.

Cons: The direction the game is currently headed is not focusing on the death on the outside of your little shelter, it is currently focused on making the game a little bit of nitpicking and making sure your people get their back scratched the correct direction. The game is already difficult with the 100% random events that can end your run at any moment but you will have to worry about their trash, and toiletries. The first addition to this was the need for social interaction, this honestly makes sense in an apocalyptic scenario, some simple words go a long way. In reality you have to worry about little tidbits to survive such as those, but we don't have fire elementals, wraiths, or zombies attempting to tear down everything we love.

Simply put, this is a difficult game because your people will complain and let themselves die in a world where death is honestly next door.

review_text:
Quick and simple: 9/10, far improved from what it used to be. 

Complicated answer:
If you were turned off from GTTOD in the past, due to jank, lack of progression, or a artstyle that didn't have much direction, but were really into the concepts at play, well have I got news for you. The game is in the best state it's ever been in, with quickplay (a simpler, clear a floor, move on mode with no progression saving) and the main gamemode being fleshed out (finally), I can confidently recommend this game now. The kinks have been (mostly) ironed out, it's better optimized, and the visuals are so much better.

Gameplay/Movement:
The gameplay is smooth and fluid, and immensely satisfying, and entirely skill based, even with maxed out grenade launcher, if you get too cocky, you'll get killed quick. With the most recent updates, having overhauled blessings and curses, along with adding clothing for additional effects, you can build classes, everything from a, one hit wonder, doing insane damage, but with no health, or a juggernaut that heals on every kill, with classes often slipping into different types, depending on what weapons/equipment you have, or your skill level.

Maps/Levels:
The maps in this game are linear, you have a set path, and you follow it till the end, where you go on to the next map. The entire game is like playing the TF|2 gauntlet mode, but if the enemies fought back. Speeding through the levels is addicting, get faster and faster times, as you progress and become more skilled, it's like a neon-gun filled acid trip, and I love it. (I swear I can stop anytime I want).

Visuals/Design:
(somewhat) recently the shaders got a overhaul, drastically improving FPS, and looks. And it certainly looks. You'd have to be blind not to see this game. It's like if you took the neon-dipped aesthetics of Hotline Miami, the weapons and enemies of Halo and DOOM, the movement of TitanFall2 and put them into a blender with just a hint of some "snow" and essence roguelite, you'd get GTTOD.

Mods:
The game is moddable via the steam workshop. Not much there now, but what's there is some good stuff, you can add/change music, weapons, and more, and I'm sure we'll see some of those "other" mods as the game gets more popular.

P.S: Thanks Andrew for your hard work, if you see this, you've probly made the best movement game on the market right now, and I'm grateful to you for fueling my speed addiction (i can stop anytime i want)

review_text:
Scorn is a visually stunning masterpiece that transports players into a terrifying world. While Steam doesn't offer a [i]'neutral'[/i] recommendation, I find myself leaning towards a positive review, albeit with some significant caveats

[b]In short[/b] - Scorn is a short experience, clocking in just at 3-4 hours for most players, though thorough explorers may find more to uncover. Despite its flaws in combat and navigation, game's unparalleled visual design and atmospheric immersion make it a worthwhile journey for those who appreciate artistic vision in gaming. But If you can push through the frustrating elements, you'll find a hauntingly beautiful world that lingers in your mind long after finishing the game. Now to a more expanded version:

[h3]Visuals and Atmosphere:[/h3]
Scorn's greatest triumph lies in its breathtaking aesthetic. Drawing heavy inspiration from the works of H.R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński, the game transports players into a living, breathing biomechanical nightmare. Every environment is a little showpiece of unsettling design, making the simple act of exploration a reward in itself. And haunting soundtrack complements the visuals perfectly, maintaining a consistent atmosphere of unease and wonder while giving some chills

[h3]Gameplay:[/h3]
To me personally game presents itself more as an interactive [i]art piece[/i] than a traditional video game. Puzzle-solving forms the core of the experience, with some genuinely intriguing challenges. However, frequent backtracking can make progression feel tedious at times. Combat is the weakest point of the game. Scarce ammunition, frustrating enemy design and clunky movement combine to create encounters that often feel more irritating than tense

[h3]Accessibility and Story:[/h3]
Scorn takes a bold approach by offering [i]no hand-holding[/i] whatsoever. There are no quest markers, no dialogue, and no narrative elements whatsoever. While this adds to the game's mysterious atmosphere, it also can lead to confusion and frustration for some players. Raising such questions as [i]'Am I going the right way?'[/i], [i]'Where am I?'[/i] or [i]'What's the point of all this?'[/i]
The story, or lack thereof, is told entirely through environmental storytelling and symbolism. And it may leave many players feeling lost or unsatisfied

[h3]Thematic Depth:[/h3]
For those willing to dig deeper, Scorn offers a wealth of philosophical and esoteric themes to ponder. References to ascension, various religions and even Freudian psychology are woven throughout the experience in the last quarter of the game. However, it's worth noting that much of the game's lore is only fully explored in the accompanying [b]ARTBOOK[/b], which may disappoint those hoping for more in-game revelations, with also having a need to purchase it in the first place! (I mean just look at the price!)

Recommended for: Art enthusiasts, fans of atmospheric horror, and those who enjoy piecing together abstract narratives.
Approach with caution if: You prefer clear storytelling, user-friendly game design, or action-oriented gameplay 

And remember [b][u]There is a very fine line between loving life and being greedy for it [/u] [/b]

review_text:
Although this game presents itself very well and has had an overwhelmingly positive reception, I must beg to disagree. Let's start with what I liked about this game: The soundtrack. Oh my God, is it amazing! It's one of the most perfect OST-Game combinations I've ever seen! It simply ties in perfectly with the game, as if the story and the song were but one thing. Also, the story up until Act 2 is simply superb. I honestly had myself close to crying more than a few times and it deeply touched me multiple times.

But, that, as they say, is that. Nothing else good, to be honest. The graphical design is neither good nor bad, it's simply a matter of personal choice (one with which I agree). The controls/interactivity is, simply put, godawful. You get stuck on random parts of the scenery ALL THE GODDAMN TIME and the mouse control simply doesn't work for movement. The gameplay is awfully repetitive and gets annoying quite quickly and even though some might argue that 'gameplay isn't the point of this game, story is!' that isn't an excuse for a lack of interesting gameplay. The lack of multiple endings and the puzzle solving of interacting with the mementos is, in all seriousness, a letdown.

And finally we arrive at what let me down the most: the story. Now, as I said earlier, I absolutely LOVED the story up untill the second act. What happened after that, you might ask. Well, what happened was they completely and utterly thrashed a lovely and sad, but heartwarming story. Spoilers ahead. [spoiler]Throughout the first two acts we get to see how John and River got to know eachother, fall in love, get married, the troubles and whatnot they went through. Then we find out about Joey (what, to be honest, was more than expected at this point in the game) and the reason why John wants to go to the moon. All fine and dandy still. But then... They somehow manage to change his memories and make him [i]happier[/i] memories. The thing is, how is that a good message? All they ever did was present him with a comfortable lie which, although comfortable, is still A LIE. Instead of an inspiring story teaching us how life, no matter how troubling at times, is happy in itself and that we should all struggle to learn to enjoy our life as it is... We get a 'you done wrong, your life sucks because of some bad choices made for you when you were very young and you should be sad about it'... Which completely ruined the experience for me. Honestly, I was playing this game from beggining to end straight, without a single pause and right after the emotional crescendo which was the revelation at the carnival, we get this absolutely mindblowing idea that 'a comfortable lie is better than the truth'.[/spoiler]  I honestly wish the game had had a different ending. For me, it was a completely waste of time and emotions. [spoiler]Why should you ever feel sad at all? Simply construct a comfortable lie for yourself and everything will be fine![/spoiler]

That's only my opinion, of course, but sadly I cannot agree with this game, despite the hype.

As quite a lot of people have mentioned, Bioshock has not aged well. The games does work on Windows 7 64 bit (the os I ran it on) but I had to do a bit of tweaking to get it stable, for instance, I had to run it in Dx9 mode. With Vsync on the game suffers from frequent slowdowns and stutter (with i5 3570k and hd7950) and if you have the mouse sensitivity on low, the in game menus are near impossible to navigate. Turning off Vsync will alleviate these problems but you will get a lot of screen tearing.

The game itself is an interesting idea but suffers from a poor user interface, the environments all look pretty much the same and the objectives are mostly 'kill something and collect items from corpse'. This involves lots of random searching for enemies in the hope they might hold the item you need. You can also 'hack' certain things in the game (security systems, vending machines etc) but the hacking game is so annoying that I didnt bother for the entire game, I just used the auto hacking tool.

Overall, the game was fairly enjoyable in spite of all the flaws, this was helped by the interesting story and freaky characters. If you can put up with all the flaws I am sure you will get some enjoyment out of this but as a full price release I cannot recommend it.

Pretty solid game, there's a campaign that you play through to learn the ropes and unlock all of the characters to use in multiplayer, but obviously the multiplayer is where you're expected to spend most of your time.

The multiplayer is a completely COOP experience, no PVP. There's a basic coop mode where you run through a normal mission with a party of 4, but there's 5 parties in each mission, so you have 20 players total, but each party is sent to their own section of the map which overlaps during certain points, so it's kind of cool because at first you're doing objectives with just your party and as you progress you temporarily combine parties to complete even bigger objectives and then ultimately all parties join up at the end to fight the end boss.

There's also a raid boss mode where you just go straight into the big boss battle with 20 players and just try and take down the big boys.

Aside from that there's something called free roam which I haven't spent too much time on, but it is a good way to just grind resources and learn a character without feeling like you need to focus on completing objectives.

The game is just really fun, I haven't watched the anime or played any of the previous games, so I cannot comment on that aspect, but the loop is fun and the different playstyles linked to the various different character archetypes is really fun.

review_text:
While Scorn provides a stunning visual and audio feast, its gameplay, storytelling, and amount of content leave me decidedly against recommending this game to all but the most hardcore alien-horror enthusiast. 

Scorn is a first-person horror/puzzler set on an alien factory world straight out of the nightmares of H.R Giger and Riddley Scott.  You explore post-apocalyptic bio-mechanical labyrinths of flesh, chitin, and bones where the race of the planet was experimenting with bioengineering to outpace a devastating infection/biological weapon ravaging their people (my own theory because the game does not provide firm lore). The art style is the game’s selling point. I got through the game to see the whole thing. At some points I was struggling with the gameplay loop and combat, but I pushed through because of the detailed and creative world that Scorn presents. I cannot stress this enough; it is a good-looking game! 

However, there is a lot to dislike. First, I dislike how the story is told and its world is presented. The worldbuilding is completely absent. It presents you with the gorgeous and engrossing world but tells you absolutely nothing about it, aside from what you can glean from small details that leave you with more questions than answers. The game could have added needed length and reason to explore by feeding the player lore to make for a satisfying world and an engrossing story. Along with worldbuilding, the story telling is absent. Aside from moving to the next area of the labyrinth, you have no idea why you are doing what you are doing until the end of the game. What meager story elements contained in the game are even told in a confusing way, with the intro cutscene telling a part of the story that should have been told after act 2. I should not have to go back and play the game’s intro again to put some pieces together. 

Next the gameplay loop leaves something to be desired. The gameplay loop looks something like this: You wander this gorgeous labyrinth, soaking in the sights and sounds. You come upon an interactable alien device. If you can interact with it, great, you solve its puzzle and gain a way to move forward somehow. If you cannot interact with it, you make a mental note about where it is and then you move on. Enemies dot the map from act 2 on. You either run away from them or suffer through the game’s terrible combat. That’s pretty much it. I would have liked for it to have been punctuated by story telling elements or dialogue or something to diversify the loop. 

The game’s combat is bad. I feel like the game cannot decide if combat is important or not. There are various enemies, there are boss fights.  But there is not enough ammo or health to engage in regular combat. I get it, its not a shooter. Then why is combat so prevalent? It hard to describe why the combat is so bad. Its slow moving and its weapons are not fun or satisfying. For example, the first weapon you get basically gently slaps a target 2 feet in front of you. Even the most basic enemy takes more than one hit. The first two hits happen one after another, but if you want to shoot again, you must wait 5-7 seconds, which gives the enemy time to hit you because you are at point blank range. You will lose health on most combat encounters.

All in all, I loved its atmosphere and art, but just wished it gave you more than it did. Its 6-7 hour playtime was a bit short. Its worth a buy on a major sale for lovers of alien horror who don’t mind mediocre gameplay to get a great visual experience.

review_text:
It's an emotional story with a few comedy bits. That's pretty much it, there needn't be a game around it.

The only player input is controls and solving puzzles. The controls are janky, floaty, and uncalibrated, I couldn't decide which input method was worse: keyboard, keyboard + mouse, or controller; the various obstacles blended in with the terrain (like bushes and flowers on grass) don't make navigating any easier, and I overall was annoyed with moving the character around. The puzzles (appearing only in the first act) are identical and serve no meaningful purpose; they are purely a mechanical obstacle with no creativity or thought behind it.

There is no exploration gameplay whatsoever, which makes me wondering what was the purpose of granting the player control over character navigation - it merely wastes time, and, as mentioned earlier, is annoying on its own. In other "walking simulator" games like Life is Strange series you are rewarded for exploration with extra lore bits, collectibles, or easter eggs, this game has none of that. There are no choices to be made either, which essentially makes this game a movie where you must constantly click buttons to show you the next scene. This is perhaps the only game I've played that is better experienced through a let's play in any case imaginable. Not only does it save you the trouble of pushing buttons and makes it an actual movie, it also saves you money.

The music is non-intrusive and rather pleasant. That's about everything I've noticed about the soundtrack.

The third act of the story pretty much ruined it for me. It made very little sense and made me genuinely angry, both from a character development perspective (hey, Eva) and technical accuracy (the entire NASA sequence). I've enjoyed the first two acts (except for the puzzles), particularly the banter between the two protagonists and their early character development, but the culmination and the ending went into an entirely different direction than I had anticipated. Playing the mini episodes changed nothing, it's the same exact thing there - the story takes a drastic turn and forces the player to suffer through it with no relief in the end.

Overall, it's an alright novel with a decent idea that for some reason was turned into a poorly made game.

review_text: No game, upon its completion, has made me feel as disappointed and as enraged as To The Moon. What was supposed to be an emotional journey through an old man's memories to fulfill his final wish turned out to be a horribly offensive and inconsistent story that isn't subtle about its hatred. There isn't much gameplay, but I didn't mind that as the focus of the game is supposed to be on the story. The tone is all over the place. It aims to be a heartbreaking game, but the constant unfunny commentary from the two main characters (one of whom makes blatantly sexist remarks to his partner throughout the game) ruins any tension the game would otherwise build. This is one of very few games that features an autistic character (the game never directly tells you she's autistic, but it's heavily implied), but she is treated as a soulless husk whose abilities and limitations are wildly inconsistent. Every other character treats her as a problem to be solved, so it wasn't surprising to find out the developers have donated to Autism Speaks which is considered by autistic people to be a hate group. This game boasts its representation of neurodivergent minds but strips its character of her autonomy and turns her into an animal to be studied and ogled, and these are dangerous stereotypes that real autistic people already have to fight. I don't think any real autistic person was involved in the making of this game. I really wanted to like To The Moon, and the glowing recommendations and reviews I saw made me think that I would, but its disgusting sexism and autistic rep make me hate this one. I won't be recommending it to anyone, and I will be trying to remove it from my memory.

review_text:
Honestly.... I can't say I did not enjoy playing it, but this is game... phew. This game is a mess

It's extremely, painfully clearly unpolished. Like they tried to meet some imaginary deadline. I'll try to explain my best.

[b] Firstly, the plot/the gameplay [/b]
The part of the game prior to the train is visibly lacking momentum and has problems with pacing.
Spoilers ahead I guess, but honestly it's not much.
You go from one station, to the mountain, to the cave, to the Zebede's hive, to another station in the span of 10 minutes (maybe a bit more if you get stuck on simplistic puzzles). That part feels weirdly lonely, and honestly it's obvious what's wrong if you rewatch the trailer that was posted back at the end of October: there's no Charun! For some freakin reason they cut out Charun (and most likely Zebede too) from the game just a month before release? Without them the cave and Zebede's hive feel just wrong. It feels like they wouldn've been such an important piece of the plot, and they were just ditched. I'm lost on this

The train is okay. Not really great in terms of puzzles (except the engine car), and it forces you to do A LOT of walking from one end to another, which got just a bit old at the end. The courtroom part dragged on forever, and instead of being the cornerstone of Act 2 (which what I presume Pumpkins were hoping for), it was just.. kind of a slog? Like, it's such a sudden change of pace, I personally wasn't prepared to play Act Attorney at all.

[b] Da writing [/b]
Personally, while the writing was plentiful: like, damn, this was more a visual novel than a puzzle game, but I guess I wouldn't mind if the writing was.. better? Honestly, I can't tell it's bad, because it's really not, but something felt off to me. It just didn't hit me like it did in Act 1. But you get to interact with the trollcall cast and receive some worldbuilding titbits, which is appreciated. But still, I felt like the writing was more cut-and-dried. Funky item interactions were stripped down in favor of more general responses, and there were a lot LESS stuff to click on in general. 

[b] Now, the art [/b]
I must say, the backgrounds are still beatiful, just like in Act 1, whoever was responsible for the art really did their best, it felt almost immersive. Unofrtunately, this amazing artwork is just that - a background. Again, you can't interact with a lot of stuff. 
The thing I have gripe the most with are transitions. Transitions from one place to another really killed the pace, because there simply were none. For exmaple, when you get yourself the tickets and decide to board the train, you click on the gate, and with no visual representation whatsoever, appear in the lowblood car. Like, Act 1 had all those beautiful transitions (even the smallest stuff like Joey using the green cube thingy in Dammek's hive), which really set the mood, whereas in Act 2.. you get none of that. The most we see is one frame of an explosion and clunky game over screens. It's as if they didn't have the time to make all of it

[b] Now, the music. [/b]
Well, ugh, there really weren't a lot of it. At least, this is what it felt like to me. Like, I think that variations playing in different cars slapped for sure, but I can't remember a single other track from Act 2. I really would like to mention a video, which James Roach posted a long time ago on youtube (which is now deleted??), where he showed variating themes for trolls of different castes. They were supposed to play when you'd TALK to a troll, but, obviously, we didn't get that at the end, sadly. 
Additionally, I'd like to point out the laziest reuse of a track from the Act 1 (the "Old secret" one), in the closing scene. Personally, it felt like it didn't fit the scene at all, and honestly I'm just surprised they couldn't write another track. 


My overall play time was almost 10 hours, which is a lot more than Act 1, but at least the third of that time must've been spent in the teal car, which isn't a good sign. 


Overall, I honestly believe that we have gotten a half-baked game made in 2 or 3 months. I heard this is somehow the fault of viz, but if this is true, it's the second time What Pumpkins have been played by some other company, and at this point I don't know what to make of it.
 I don't really regret spending my money (that's not my problem with it). Rather, I feel like the second installment of the game I was anticipating for a long time kind of disappointed me. I really got a lot more enjoyment out of replaying Act 1 like 3 times to get all the achievements, to hang out in all the different locations and see all the writing. with which that game filled to the brim. This... this is just heartbreaking, honestly. I'm really scared of what will come next. If it will come at all.

name: Just Cause 4 Reloaded

review_text:
Great game! Reviewed it on my gaming channel and went in depth, but the cliff notes are that I really enjoyed it. Has 1 or 2 flaws here and there, mostly the clunkiness of the controls in certain aspects. I think that's what the developers were going for though, to feel like you're not in complete control of your body/responsive, which goes in line with the story (not going to spoil it here). But overall a mysterious/captivating game that doesn't hold you by the hand and leaves it to your interpretation of what's going on. It instills a gutteral, visceral reaction in you from the moment you start playing the game, with the haunting hallways and corrupted gore all over the place, like an infection taking over a long forgotten civilization. I recommend it if you want to jump into something new and lose your self for a few hours. Not a long game and is pretty straightforward, which is refreshing every now and then. I give it a 9/10 personally, with the dings on it being the aforementioned clunky controls. If you'd like to see snippets from my review, here's my channel and feel free to take a look if its a game you'd be interested in. SPOILER WARNINGS though.

review_text:
Do I recommend this game? Yes and no.
This is a "litrpg game". It is set in a massive game world, but only shows you the very narrow path of the protagonist through that. Everything is very pre-meditated and it fulfills almost all tropes of a litrpg story, but without the isekai element. 
Gameplay is solid, but only that. It is somewhat stale, and at times frustrating.
Most NPCs are very rigid, grating or overplayed. There is an undeniable charm to this, but it has to be what you are looking for.
And sure, the story moment when the character finally unlocks their new secret skills and what not is impressive, but with the game hinting at there being a choice as to what you can unlock, and the story dictating a certain path, this kinda just ended in frustration for me.

Are you okay with being shown a world that looks extremely open, but funnels you down a narrow path?
Are you okay with llusion of choice being executed badly, but still there, meaning you often think you can make a decision, but really just have to take what the game gives you?
Are you okay with NPC companions that are walking tropes with a "but" thrown in?

If you can firmly answer "Yes" to all three of these, and are looking for decently nice JRPG in a litrpg world, then I can highly recommend this game.
If even one of your answers to these questions is a "No", then I firmly advise against this game.

review_text:
I really wanted to try and like this, but I just can't. I don't understand all of the positive reviews on here saying how great the story is, and how fun the combat is. I found myself BEGGING for a skip dialog button, because I cannot STAND how slow the voice acting is. It is intentionally delayed and fragmented into sentences that make me want to rip my ears off. I want to try and enjoy the story, but I end up skipping half of the cutscenes because of the whiny, boring dialog. 

The combat boils down to A A A A A A. . . A A A A A  RB A, A A A A A A , RB A, AAAAAAAAA. I actually fell asleep at one point at my desk. 

The HAND HOLDING! My god. Here's your objective. Better not forget your objective. Go to the marker for the objective. I'll bet I need X of this objective. I should buy X of this item for this objective. 

The pacing is just, bizarre and annoying. You finish a quest, then it forces you to log out of the world to check your mail, only to log back into the world, to do another 15 minute quest. Then you must log back out of the world, so you can check that mail, or forum post, or whatever, then log back in to progress the story. I'm sorry bout after the 15th time of this, I'm over it. 

The world looks like garbage. The landscapes are uninspired. You run copy pastes of the same dungeons and/or fields over and over and over again that consist of the same exact tile sets. I feel like I'm playing a PS1 game. 

Just don't waste your time. Unless you REALLY like the tropey anime stuff with shitty voice acting, boring combat, and mundane, repetitive "quests", find a different game. I know I am.

I finished the main story, overall its a good story, especially if you are a SAO fan, character interactions is interesting, the new system in the story is really cool, the story had a good pace and many memorable moments.

I really love how the enemy and friends of kirito interacts with each other. Such a treat i hope there will be many characters to come.

Gameplay wise its a good action rpg not on level as GBFR tho, still clunky on some ways especially the camera. But its still good.
Coop overall is fun they implement a system where we must level up to unlock our skill, i havent been grinding much, its pretty much still alive, i can find matches without waiting, i play on Asia server its not that laggy, iam playing from SEA.
For characters, there is 21 free character from the enemy and friends of kirito, they all have unique move set.

Overall the game is not worth the price if you're just buying it for the gameplay, but if youre a SAO fan that watches all of the anime and movies you will love the story and characters.

The grind is for equipment i haven't do much but seeing there is cosmetics that we can get freely i will do it from now on since i finished the story. I hope this game can be alive longer than GBFR it has potential hope bandai will give it a good update.

For some reason your first chicken coop, ranger hall, animal pen and kitchen can keep you going for a long while, up to 100 pop. The market is an option but it seems like there's only a limited amount you can import into your city. Now, without this problem there are no problems ... and that's a problem. The enemies are slow and attack one at a time. They need to group up and attack as a unit. Once you have the corruption contained, a few towers and a few golem spawns you're pretty well protected. They could attack any one of my towns with 10x the amount of forces that they are using and it wouldn't matter. I should be far more worried about the monster attacks than running out of food when I have so much invested in food production. I can't tell if its a glitch in the game mechanics but I've spent a lot of time on it and can not figure out why a hand full of buildings can feed 100 people and five times that many can't seem to feed more than 170. For $15 I feel like I got my money's worth (knowing me I probably bought it on sale) however after playing so much I have to say that after the first excitement of getting a city going the game is pretty boring. I guess I could just wait until the monsters get harder but the thought of that doesn't seem appealing.

review_text:
A decent 3D point and click adventure game if gotten on sale. There's an entertaining B movie horror plot to play out here, the passion of the developers showing in the melodramatic build ups and loving focus on the kill shots. It's just a shame the gameplay built around this is threadbare.

Lucius stars the unambiguously evil Antichrist, a six year old boy awakening to his calling of murdering those around him to fuel his new power. The entire game takes place inside the spacious family mansion as your father's senatorial campaign begins to collapse due to the strange murders at his home, the world's most incompetent police vaguely consider doing something about it and all the staff stay on well past the point of good sense. Classic camp. It's an entertaining one and done almost all the way through.

You're guided to your murder of the day and explore the mansion to pick up things for the occasional clever kill. You wander around, it's a big place, the mansion has a lot of heart even if it's not the best level design. Lots of good set pieces never used for the entire game like the library/billiards room. Sometimes you get a healthy amount of tips and are pointed in a good direction, there's a set of optional little chores you can do to get presents that'll help you. One gives a vague hint for the chapter, the other highlights interactables and should be an infinite use base ability for this kind of game. It's fun to run around and explore the mansion... for a time. Realizing that every drawer in the game can be opened but only one has anything deflates the map design a bit. The murders themselves are simple puzzles and ideally between the music box, in-game hints and spending some time on observation you can piece together what you're supposed to do. If not you wander around aimlessly growing bored. This is definitely a title where playing with a guide might save you headaches, or at least giving each stage a fair go for 15-30 minutes and looking up the answer as last resort. Lucius can devolve to pixel hunting and nothing highlights easily, especially with the dodgy power targeting.

There's strictly one correct way to do everything in the game and that undermines the appeal of the sandbox. You get powers though they're either far too limited in what they do or are used so liberally they undermine the creative puzzle-solving. One particularly good stage is framing somebody for your crimes while also providing enough emotional shock to make them a sobbing wreck, allowing you to mind control them to suicide. Good set up, good execution, fun premise, practical addition to the story, love it. Another is filler: you place a loaded gun next to somebody and mind control them to kill themselves. Considering Lucius can fire the gun himself that's not a clever murder, it's a regular one with extra steps. Combustion can only be used at very specific plot mandated points, Memory Wipe is just a get out of mistakes free card instead of an actual thing for setting up ironic suicides. Why not have a scenario where I can make somebody forget what they're doing like mixing medication or cooking with something volatile and make them double dose it? Mind Control people to start fights with one another and sneak in an escalating murder tool? Start small fires? Alternative kills could justify a second playthrough.

Lucius is decent. It has heart. I think the charming cheesiness of the story carries it but at the end of the day this game could've gone a bit further. The only really bad bits are the combat and the almost complete absence of the stealth mechanics. If you get seen, memory wipe. If you're in a stealth section, redo it and pray it ends soon. There aren't any actual threats for most of the game and perhaps the police and priests should've been an acting roaming danger, escalating at each new third of the game. 

And for the record it's not 20 hours of game, definitely not 40 hours of game. Nice try, achievements. There's no reason to replay it since the paths are so strict. As it is Lucius is a really nice $2 game. It's almost worth the $10 asking price but I recommend you get Lucius on sale for a decent 3-4+ hours of macabre fun.

and done almost all the way through. you're guided to your murder of the day and explore the mansion to pick up things for the occasional clever kill. you wander around, it's a big place, the mansion be an infinite use base ability for this kind of game. it's fun to run around and explore the mansion... for a time. realizing that every drawer in the game can be opened but only one has anything deflates the map design a bit. the murders themselves are simple puzzles and ideally between the music box, in-game hints and spending some time on observation you can piece together what you're second playthrough. lucius is decent. it has heart. i think the charming cheesiness of the story carries it but at the end of the day this game could've gone a bit further. the only really bad bits review_text:
Among all the great games that sprouted in 2025, this one stands out as a true gem, carefully crafted by a small team, without chasing current trends. Having no expectations whatsoever, I was able to fully enjoy every aspect that shapes its world and the experience within. And for those complaining that it’s too hard: planning and making the careful decisions is all you need to get the most out of the gameplay, regardless of the difficulty.

Before you even launch the game, take a step back: make sure you have enough time, the right conditions, headphones, and the proper mood. There are moments full of tension and combat, but also quieter stages when everything slows down and you can truly appreciate the sound details that build the entire atmosphere. It’s also worth taking a moment to admire the beautifully modelled environments.

The game’s linearity still allows for partial exploration and secret hunting. Whether you decide to spend some extra time finding additional resources will ultimately define your own difficulty level. Without upgrades, every fight will take longer, consume more ammo, and relying solely on melee attacks can become frustrating. Each encounter is a challenge: sometimes you must trust your intuition, while other times you’ll need to use the environment wisely and plan your approach before the fight even begins.

The story and lore blend nicely with the gameplay, encouraging you to read notes and discover the world through environmental storytelling. It may not be the strongest point of the game, but it’s original and unfolds at a satisfying pace.
Despite a few rough edges, this is still a solid, well-crafted, and complete experience - something that’s becoming increasingly rare these days.

review_text:
I played the 3DS version of Hakuoki years ago, and had my eye on this one and it's sequel, Edo Blossoms, for some time due to there being extra routes for new characters. I was not disappointed.
The new characters are as  well written as the originals, and both their design and backstories fit perfectly with the preexisting characters. The sprites for the originals have been altered slightly, and new content has been added to their routes, so although playing through their individual storylines felt a little nostalgic, it didn't feel as much of a repetition of the 3DS version as I had expected it to. I was excited that they had added Nagakura as a love interest in this game (he wasn't in the 3DS version), and finally being able to play through his route was awesome.
The artwork, from sprites, to CGs, to backgrounds are still stunning, and the soundtrack is as good as I remember, and often fits the events occurring perfectly. The characters are all voiced (excluding the protagonist), and the voice acting is great quality. 
The plot is interesting, and their are plenty of choices to explore some diverse content. Also, there is some amount of historical accuracy for the time period, and an in-game encyclopedia explains terms that may be unfamiliar. The romances don't feel forced, and feel unique to each character.
There are some points where the translations can be a little lacking, whether this is because of a missing word, something repeated, or a phrase that doesn't make sense, but they are easy to ignore. 
The controls seemed a little odd at first, but users can set them to what they like.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who has previously enjoyed otome games, as Hakuoki is one of the best available. This version has only improved upon what was already a great game, so I would also recommend to anyone who had played a previous Hakuoki title.

review_text:
It pains me that I can't recommend this, because I was an absolute shill for Boneworks. Ironically, Bonelab's own predecessor feels so much more like a game than it. The game that was kind of tossed around as a tech demo originally now feels so much less like one than its damn successor.Everything feels like such a downgrade, with gun handling and general physics feeling super jank in comparison to Boneworks, which had its own myriad of issues. It feels like Bonelab amplified these issues. 

But bleeding-edge VR tech jank aside, the actual content is utterly disappointing. The campaign itself can be completed in just a few hours, with more than half of the levels feeling like a showcase for the character-swap (Bodylog) mechanic, which kills replay value because it's so narrowly and linearly designed for specific characters in certain sections. Only in the last few levels does the game open up a little and let you go ham with all of the options that this mechanic has to offer. And then it ends, in such an anticlimactic way. 

It makes you ask for more, and the game's answer? Modding. I genuinely hope I eat my words, but at the time of writing, the modding scene is incredibly lackluster, with the official SDK not receiving an update in a fair while. Basic levels and avatar skins are at your disposal without dipping your toes into fan-authored tools instead. It's still awesome that the fanbase is devoted enough to do this, but it's frustrating that the modding tools for a game that heavily holds itself up with modding potential are so lightweight and barebones at the moment.

The price tag is a killer too. 40 bucks, really? Something like $20-25 (maybe 30??) and we have a deal no problem), but Bonelab charges almost double the price of its predecessor and doesn't offer something more enticing and more content-rich. Yes, the game was advertised primarily as a sandbox rather than a story-heavy experience. But 40 dollars is not a fair deal when the sandbox elements don't really bring much replay value to it. In fact, the more I replay Bonelab, the more I feel frustrated and just miserable at the state of the game. It feels so incomplete, and this isn't even tagged as early access!

I dunno, man. It feels hollow right now, empty and bare. Maybe there was a lot more planned for it? It's like the game was chopped in half, and who knows where the other half is. Maybe after some content updates things will be different? I hope so, but the patches so far that have added content to some of the levels feel sloppy and rushed (thanks for the hardly-avoidable hitscan helicopter on Sprint Bridge ya nerds) like duct-tape solutions, so I dunno at this point. Fingers crossed, right?

I recommend Boneworks instead if you want a longer experience for half the price. For now, personally, Bonelab feels like a minigame-esque experience in a VR industry presently drowning in bite-sized cheap-feeling experiences. YMMV, of course. If anything, wait for a sale and nab this then.

EDIT: Patches have done utterly nothing. Game's less buggy, I guess, but it's still hardly a game. Mods are still just stuck as player skins and that's it. No amount of John Halo skins can redeem this.

review_text:
I'm sure I'm going to get grilled on this review, but I honestly didn't like this game. I finished it because the reviews were so positve and I wanted to see what all the fuss was about. Now I know. It was not worth it. 

Pros:

The story was very thoughtful and original. I haven't heard of any other game, movie, book, etc that explores this last wish memory adjustment concept. It had an unexpected twist 3/4ths through and some feels. A++ for the story. That was the only thing that kept me going. 

The artwork was very well done, colorful, and overall impressive for the format. Personally, I do not like the sprite style. That was a hesitation when I bought the game, but I was willing to give it a shot. Nah, I just don't like it. If you like sprites, you'll love this. 

Music. Yes, the main theme is really nice. Generally the music supported the feels. 

Cons: 

The pacing was dreadfully slow. This game has almost exactly four hours of content. You can speed that up a bit by tapping through all the dialogue, but you can't speed up the ponderously slow panning, animations, walking, etc. Be prepared to spend some time just waiting because you don't have any other choice. 

This was a very story driven experience. The minigames were not needed and were just in the way most of the time. Its not like I got some sort of reward for solving them them faster or more efficiently so what was the point? I have enjoyed good minigames that added to the game experience - these did not. 

The navigation. So bad. I'm talking about just walking around. I shouldn't be blocked by a *small* plant if I'm trying to get across a half acre property. And the entire screen shifting suddenly to track with the player in the center. Because you could only move up/down or left/right, it was so distracting. If I tried to use the mouse to direct teh characters, they would not go farther than about 6 tiles without needing more direction. Why was this? The player controls and navigation were what I hated the most about this game. 

TLDR: 

If you want a sweet boy+girl story, you like sprite animation, or just want a low-impact diversion for a few hours, you may like this game. If you want something challenging or faster paced, this is not for you.

The majority of players will struggle to gain anything in L4D1 that L4D2 wouldn't offer at a higher quality. 

I can only recommend this title for L4D1 Purists who are hoping to take advantage of various exploits and minor tricks that were fixed and altered in L4D2

review_text:
[h2] Style Over Substance [/h2] 

The more times I go back to Bioshock, the more glaring a lot of its faults become to me. 

I'll always appreciate how the game accurately depicts the logical conclusion of an anarcho-capitalistic society, the game gets really full of its own philosophy and intellectual enlightenment yet rarely conveys it into a compelling story or in moment to moment gameplay. 

It does the Half-Life approach of giving you the illusion that you're in charge of your own destiny, while the game design and the NPCs in your head basically guide you on a rail from start to finish, with morality choices and character decisions barely mattering and the game going from fascinating set pieces to basically busywork of deactivating alarms, puzzle minigames and dealing with an ever-increasing number of bullet sponge enemies. 

But we rarely remember this game's faults, shortcomings and questionable decisions. Because none of that really matters when you get lost in the decaying, destroyed remnants of Rapture. It's twisted, it's dark, it's bleak and it's absolutely beautiful. Helps that the game for the most part swaps the scatological yellow and brown of the 7th gen for bluer hues that make the grime and blood and wreckage much more palatable, and the crumbling art deco aesthetic is just so well done. 

It was style over substance back in the day and is even more so now with the power of hindsight and reflection, but man is that style just kind of immaculate.
