review_text:
If I reviewed this on launch my only issue would've been the asking price out the door, but that comes with the assumption that they'd spare no effort in giving you consistent, high-quality content every other week or so to dip your fingers into and work towards at no extra cost.

Well that was true up to the high-quality part, I'll just list what they did wrong since the game launched, what mistakes made it worse and what they honestly should have done.

First of all the cosmetics are, most of the time, recolours or reused from previous games of SAO. That's just really dumb, while free for the most part you can ignore that until the "free pass" gives literal recolours with minor modifications as the main reward with maybe an accessory. Note that these passes give two 'actual' cosmetics, I'm not counting profile elements here, over the span of a 4 week period. That's it.

Granted, they release these packages with cosmetics in them, often themed after characters or events and while some are also reused or simple- they're unique and cool and sometimes coming with an in-game effect changing their ultimate skill animation for example. Unfortunately not only do these take 3 months a piece to even come out, they're not a part of said "free" pass. You have to either earn ONE ticket per 4 WEEK season, or pay some extra to get what you want. Do remember this game was full price on entry, plus the DLC characters all costing a lot individually.

Props where they're due, there's a lot of cosmetics by now but they're still bland or just don't work in most cases since you can't change the colours at all, since the idea of making alternate colours a separate costume exists you likely have dozens of dead in the water options that exist just to make you look stupid.

Secondly, the gameplay is actually pretty strong at first, every character is unique in function, achieve different roles, better at different things. They made each option meaningful even when they're in the same class. The animations are also some of the best we've seen in SAO's history taking their personalities and skill sets into account:

Kirito maintains his position with large sweeping movements that flow into each other, he maintains a torrent of hits naturally and it feels really nice to chain attack after attack. Leafa's kendo is shown through strong singular strikes, with robust form and deliberate strikes and gains speed/strength while airborne which is a nice metaphor to her character. Strea, one of the DLC cast- who has basically zero references outside her original game which more or less used general animations all the time, has incredible weight to her attacks, letting her sword guide her along for the ride- with nods to her in-lore abilities as an MHCP in Aincrad that sells her as a powerhouse.

That's all well n' good, all that effort is well placed and it shows genuine care but unfortunately the same 4 skills get old, and the only thing allowing them to change is barely unlockable and with the rate of updates it basically NEVER means your favourite character is getting any new variations or content towards their kit.

Speaking of, Equipment. It's the main means of farming in the game. Your player rank controls what equips are dropped, higher it is, higher the level you do, the higher the equip rank. They come in multiple rarities and you can dismantle them to upgrade equipment up to +10: which is the short version. Legendary equipment however gives bonus abilities tailored to the character's weapon which is cool, it don't change much but is definitely the most exciting part. This sucked originally but they actually added a means to inherit abilities into new equipment so honestly fair to them. Sadly however until you reach max rank all of that is dead in the water so you're saving all of what you get until it's worthwhile to upgrade them and dismantle your old stuff. It's pretty inoffensive, but a lot more can be done, such as weapon accessories, or even effects you can earn for "prestige", they haven't though.

Thirdly and probably the worst part if you read anything about the game is the player count. Now believe me when I say this game had 15,000 players PLUS going by PC numbers alone from its launch and beta test, that's cool- just hop in, find 19 other guys and let the good times roll. Unfortunately, remember I mentioned player rank? Yeah so that dictates what level of content you can do and forgive me not checking this but there's like 20 or so different individual levels, from rank 1 to 150. All of which have separate queues. This included with the boss raid modes which also have like 5 to pick from for different queues.
Not enough? Well, region is a thing too. On EU? good luck. Switch to Asia and worsen your connection significantly for a room 'cause at this current time, playing at any other hour that isn't peak for Asian players is a certified infinite 1/20 players found.
Credit again, the netcode is actually really solid in your own region, surprisingly so. Unfortunately it took like 2 months before I had to switch indefinitely to even get games at my rank.

That raises another issue by the way, newer players will never find games due to the abhorrent splits to the point that the day 1 crossplay means nothing. They can't rank up and do the missions where players are since there's no one to reach the minimum necessary. Higher rank players can answer SOS requests to join in which is nice but it's just a bandaid on a much larger issue.

So you might ask, where did all the players go?

Well aside the combination of reasons I just mentioned, it's because that while the content for cosmetics and your literal REASON TO COME BACK didn't exist, they add like no new stages or bosses at all. Since launch we've had 2 bosses that are actually new. The others were just existing models repurposed, and the other "new" one was a tutorial enemy that wasn't already a boss because I kid you not it had two moves for the sake of the tutorial but nothing else so it wouldn't function otherwise.

Story mode is okay, as in the story, the gameplay is horrendous it's just walking around doing single player stuff in a co-op experience- I liked the new characters and setting and it's really cool to see everyone interact who normally wouldn't. Naturally that was the main draw for me since I love this series a lot.

Solutions:

But yeah to fix the game it's actually pretty easy, first of all they make it free cause the player base is cooked, second they add 4 cosmetics to the pass where 1 is a recolour or whatever the hell they want and 3 of them are actually given time and care, also two tickets per season not one. Third is they unify the queues entirely, it's not that simple but there should be no more than three, split it three ways, and let the players who queued up VOTE ON A MAP RATHER THAN LISTING ALL OF THEM AT ONCE. Hell, make it two a day and cycle, anything to make it more streamlined. Same for bosses, three ways, cycle them as they already do. Fourth, every MONTH at minimum just add either a new boss or map to select from, ideally both- then remove one from rotation until the next season, that way you don't miss out on the cosmetics they drop.

And lastly, every month, as a last bonus, choose at least two characters who gets a different preset of skills. Make ONE skill different entirely that you can swap out, and all three originals (minus the ultimate since those are changed with costumes) can be given different secondary effects that you earn with rank like how legendary equipment effects already work. This would spice up people's mains a lot and keep it fresh.

Sorry for the essay but I can't recommend the game in this state, it has genuinely great aspects and potential with an awful live-service support system, every PR post is just a "fight this boss but purple for an ugly hat" and it's sad. I love SAO and fans will love the character presentation, but this game isn't worth it.

I'd still recommend the game if abstract horror interests you. It's priced well and you can finish it in one sitting. It's also hard to not have a soft spot for this game, being a pillar of the indie horror scene back then.

review_text:
8 Bucks for a hit of nostalgia? Yes, please.
.Hack//SIGN was the first anime I got SERIOUSLY into back before the before times. Then I followed it up with the first 4 games after the series ended. Then I found and watched .Hack//ROOTS (and the other quirky bracelet spin-off, but that one was kind of weird).

I was aware of this game's existence, but I never really followed it up. Just never cared to.
Then I see it's 85% off? 8 bucks? I spend that much on breakfast some times! Why wouldn't I buy it?

Anyway, the old world-building ways are back. Lots and LOTS of reading. I think in the first two and a half hours I've put into the game, maybe 15 minutes of it were playing through the tutorial.

Then you get CTDed (not ACTUALLY a CTD, but an In Game CTD) and there's just READING and READING and READING.
I'm one of these people who gets twitchy if I see a 'NEW!' tag on an element, so I have to go through and clear everything until there are no more new tags.

But it was also interesting, and a neat way to sort of immerse the player into the world that exists between the real world, where you are now, reading this weird review, and the one in the video game. You know, 'ZA WARULDO!' There's a lot of lore and stuff in those news articles and 'forum posts' that I imagine people familiar with the story of the entire .Hack//CANON will read and start to wonder 'Okay, so... what the f*** is gonna happen when $#!+ gets f***y with all of this stuff they're talking about?'

I know I am.

Whelp. Back to it.

review_text:
Can't recommend it yet. Let's run through it. 

The game is fun, but a bit obnoxiously harsh on occasion that really just takes the piss out of you and those pisstakers are where I'll be focusing.

Clunky, I believe you need 1.5x-2x the BASE stamina you get now if you want to be the dashing dastard witch hunter the game wants you to be. Still don't know how regaining focus works, don't care until I come across something I need focus for. 

AI is a little bad, especially for the Swordsman enemy. For being a decently HPed lunge enemy they sure like to run around and not do a whole lot until they do a lunge around a corner and clip you. 
Most automatic guns feel absolutely awful. No wonder humanity is losing the witch war we are using paintball guns. 


Another thing is that when you first get a weapon, the flavor text lies to you. It tells you what it WILL do, not what it does after you spend about 40 minutes with it to level it and actually get the weapon mechanics. There are some basic errors here that severely hinder this game. I do not recommend this game as it stands, and I am even further negative than I was to begin with.

Largest issue, in my opinion, is the Calamity system. It just sucks, its bad, its dumb. Kicks you when you are down as taking damage directly correlates to you having less HP/healing. Oh, you triggered the ice mine a guy you took down 10 seconds ago? Hope you were finished up because the Calamity is coming and your run is done either way. Rewards are pitiful for interrupting the event for it being normally end running. The ritual site seems to spawn as far away from you as possible, and from at least my experience, in the most heavily populated area on the map. Right now, about 10 hours in, I have not found a way to reduce the calamity counter. I do believe clearing mob areas (the ones that result in a witchfire shard) should reduce the counter, and if not that clearing more dangerous areas/rituals should reduce it instead. 
EDIT: I still maintain what I said about the calamity, however at higher levels the calamity is more absolutely obnoxious than anything else. It destroys the flow of the game and can be triggered in areas, like boss arenas, where you cannot counter it. I assume that will be changed as it SUCKS but for now it makes the game strictly worse.

Spells really dont feel good either. I am not a fan of any damage spell so far, I find the CC much more valuable but that is neither here nor there. Also along that line, give me a more visible sign that spells are off cooldown. They current UI is far too minimal for those. Tie them to the crosshair or something.

Edit: This game hates you and wants you to know it. There are several mechanics for objectives further in that will require a replay or two. Flying Ship calamity, right? Hide from it's broadside, right, maybe dash from building to building so you avoid its shots? No. In fact, it shoots homing balls of darkness that are so accurate at patrolling they can hunt you down through the bowels of a castle. After countering it, it is an absolute push over but still doesn't really make sense. Stick your face out during its barrage pass to hit a weakspot or turn around the...shoot the cannonballs? What? If you have anything but a rifle, you just lose as the damage drop off will ensure you can't actually hit the weakpoint of the ship well. The counter for the ship is moronic and boils down to 'shoot the shinies' instead of actually dealing with the giant piss big ship. Should have made it a floating priest or something instead those balls of shadow would make a lot more sense than from a SHIP. Endless arena that actively damages you? No idea wtf to do, no direction. Had to rely on a guide. You just die the first time which yeah its a roguelike but with enough skill and PROPER direction you should be able to burn through objectives after understanding the mechanics on a fundamental level.

Another thing is that when you first get a weapon, the flavor text lies to you. It tells you what it WILL do, not what it does. You must spend about 40 minutes with it to level it to get the actual mechanic and so far, the upgrades kinda suck. There are standouts but for the most part I am disappointed to uncover their upgrades. There are some basic errors here that severely hinder this game. I do not recommend this game as it stands, and I am even further negative than I was to begin with.

EDIT after webgrave update. Reset my character to experience the full game. Man, it does not feel great. I don't think I've experienced a game before where I've looked at my guns and went 'damn I wish I had one I liked'. Movement still feels shit, this game has far too complex of systems for its own good. Gnosis is still a crutch the dev team relies on to not balance the game properly.

review_text:
[b]TLDR[/b]:
     This is one of those reviews where a "mixed" rating would be more appropriate. However, since this game is pretty much universally praised, I'm going to be a bit of a contrarian. I did like the game but it left me with a bitter aftertaste that turns a timeless classic into what I would describe as a strong 6/10.

[b]The good[/b]:
     I think the main story is actually really good. I did think I would end up tearing up and even though I didn't, it is still a well written tragedy that pulls at your heart strings... at least for the time. I don't think it holds a candle to some other indie games that have come out since but it's easy to see why it was so acclaimed. The unique way of storytelling, the mystery that keeps you engaged for its, pretty short, runtime and all that wrapped in visuals that still hold up quite well. I've seen some people complain about how slow it is and while I agree that the walking speed could've been faster (or there could've been a run button), I think it lent itself to the story pretty well.

[b]The bad[/b]:
     ...I couldn't say the same for the main characters. The de facto point of view narrators are extremely dislikable and it only gets worse as the game goes on. I can excuse the outdated references and jokes that I simply didn't find funny but even without that they were easily the worst part of the writing which is pretty bad when they also get the most screentime. I get that having comedy relief is a good way to not make the experience feel too depressing but at times it really took me out of it. It's like watching a serious movie with a guy who scrolls through Tik Tok the entire time and keeps making jokes about the movie without actually caring about what's happening in it, and his friend who just as loudly keeps telling him to shut up.

[b]The ugly[/b]:
     Another big problem for me was the ending but I can't really discuss that without getting into spoiler territory so there's your warning:
[spoiler] I think the ending makes sense given the whole premise of artificially changing someones memory to make them think they lived a happy life but it's why I thought the moral of the story would end up being completely different. I can get behind the doctors wanting to fulfill Johnny's wish but after learning the context behind it, this bittersweet finale doesn't have any sweetness to it. The whole reason why he wanted to go to the moon (LAST SPOILER WARNING) was because of River. 
      This would be a fine motivation but the thing is that he already knew River in real life, even got married and stayed with her until death did them part. Johnny didn't know it but the real tragedy of his life wasn't that he didn't fulfill his own ambitions, it's that he forgot all of these memories, which she wanted to remind him of in her own way. With that said, the doctors should've asked Johnny if he actually wants to go through with the wish after actually knowing why he asked for it in the first place. 
     It's honestly hard to say if the artificial life he was given was even a better one, sure he achieved something big but it also cost him a lot of time that in the real world he spent with River. Would he actually want his memory to be changed into a fake fantasy or would he be satisfied with finally understanding why his house was filled with origami, knowing that in his last moments he would finally remember things as they were? Did he even expect that simply making himself believe that he went to the moon would come with these ramifications?
    I don't think he did and personally, I would much rather prefer knowing the painful truth over simply thinking that everything in my life went according to plan. If he thought differently then I would understand but we never get that answer, it was pretty much chosen for him and that just feels... wrong. Wrong in a way that I don't think was intended. [/spoiler]

[b]Conclusion[/b]:
I think this game is good experience for it's time that may not hold up as well as it used to. If you think this is a game for you then I recommend giving it a try as you might end up loving it. As for me, I just can't say I did.

7.5 / 10 

After finishing the first Vol of this 4 part-er, I would lightly recommend this game.
For the most part this game suffers primarily from the fact its from the mid 00s/PS2 era.
I played the first 2 Vols back in the day, and as of the year 2023, it's certainly dated, and plays
more of an interactive Anime, than strictly a Meta game-within-a-game.

If you are looking for a challenge, there really isnt one here. So long as you can juggle with your team there's not much to the combat. The start of the game makes it seem like theres more to it, than the reality.

That being said, I still like the simulated/emulated MMO in these games. Starting back from even the Outbreak/Quarantine games. There is something here that I prefer to the SAO cartoon. Where SAO felt as they just told you about MMO features/ideas/systems,  //.hack both in the Anime and Games has you/the characters interact with XYZ system. (Even if they are limited)

Decent game. If you're into SAO you'll probably like the idea of this game too.

TLDR - Older games with very stripped down, but good mechanics. Feels more like an interactive novel/anime than a straight up game.  4-in-1. Pick it up if it's on sale.

review_text:
I set out to play through this VR rip-off of Left4Dead solo and then replay it online at harder difficulties once I had learned the basics.

Halfway through (3 of the 5 maps), I felt pretty certain that I would end up giving this short and unpolished game a slightly reserved but positive recommendation.

Then, as the zombie count increased, the frames started dropping. Even though sub-90fps in VR can be quite jarring, it's something I've learned to tolerate. But here, it seemed to go hand in hand with nasty glitches. Suddenly, the manual gun reload became super unreliable and inconsistent. The weapon model would start to drift out of position and remain there, something I never experience in any other similar VR FPS games.

I have an Intel 8700K CPU (@4.8ghz) and a RTX 3080 GPU. Regardless of the quality preset, this would happen. I double-checked that there was no thermal throttling going on.

There's potential here, but I cannot recommend it in its current state, and I have no intention of spending more time with it.

review_text:
Maybe it was the bad performance at launch, or maybe it was the over-expectation of people. But for me, I failed to see the mind boggling criticism this game received because it is a decent game. The Callisto Protocol hailed itself as a spiritual successor to Dead Space, and it did well enough in that regard. Here is a linear, immersive experience with an engaging survivalist story - basically a good old-fashioned game where you enjoyed for around 10 hours, then come back for the experience when nostalgia hit after some time has passed.

The gameplay loop is basically Dead Space but heavily focused on melee. Maybe for some people, shooting a gun with different trajectory is less repetitive, but TCP gameplay is as repetitive as any game can get, as it can't be more repetitive than games where criticism have praised to high heaven but had even more repetitive gameplay loop.

This game biggest fault would be its checkpoint system, it would often put you back to a long cutscene, or where you had to spend a lot of time thinking on what to upgrade. And not long after said checkpoint, you ended up picking loots that could have spawn earlier before the checkpoint so you could manage your inventory better. And level design is nowhere as sophisticated as Dead Space, it is more linear and you would spend most time sticking to a straight corridor. These are the only criticism I have for this game. 

It's sad to see how TCP could have done well as a horror franchise and a sequel with many improvements. But with its troubled development, the crazy budget it needed and the hyperbolic criticism it received, this game will be a one timed experience. And the circle of the gaming industry cater to people who prefer loot box multiplayer and short attention span experience coils again.

review_text:
This is an absolutely amazing game so far. I am only in summer of year one, but I can't remember the last time I enjoyed a farming sim this much. There is a longer questline in the game that feels like the main goal, but it has very little impact from a storytelling point of view, especially since I have too few resources to tackle it atm. This is more than made up by the cast of villagers though. It's like your own soap opera. Came to town, got set up, suddenly everyone got married within 1 week, left with like 3 single people in the entire village, first one rejects me, contemplated going lesbian, nevermind people died, married a widower, had to befriend my nemesis for that, found a homeless child that lives with me now, have aspirations to get my daughter into the mayors family so I can commit tax evasion. Bridgerton could never. 

The artstyle is also very cute and the entire atmosphere makes it really feel like I am in the 1700s. You rely on the other villagers and their professions to trade a lot of materials, and once a week there is market day with a whole tradeship coming into port. Livestock can (allegedly) be bred and also butchered for meat, which I have not gotten to but am looking forward to. 

There are also a lot of settings to customize your experience, like toggling aging, sickness, food and tool decay or the fishing minigame which is just good QoL. There are of course a few known bugs, but the devs are amazing with their responses and working on fixes already. 

The only negative things I can say about this game is that SO FAR, there is no way to auto-sort your inventory, and some of the item pricing feels a bit unbalanced, as does the cooking when a meal gives you less food or coin than the seperate ingredients would have given. I would also like for new learned recipes to have the name pop up along with a picture of the item, as I have goldfish brain and could not match some of them to anything on my crafting list. But if that is the extent of my complaints, I think it is safe to recommend this game wholeheartedly.

It seems to be a common theme in reviews to this game that it might move the player to tears.  I didn't find that to be the case, but I might believe that it would bore the player to tears.  I think this might be better rehashed as a simple walk-through interactive story kind of game, because the "game" components are severely lacking.  The basic notion is that you play as one of a pair of scientists brought to a dying man's bedside to install in his mind the memories of having gone to the moon.  It is an interesting premise and in a different medium, I would likely have enjoyed it.  

The way the game unfolds is that you watch a cut-scene providing a bit of story then are left wandering around to find memory-triggering objects.  When you've collected the objects, you bring them to a portal and solve a simple puzzle involving toggling rows and/or columns of an image until the whole image lines up properly.  There is no conflict for the player to resolve, nor is there much interplay between the game elements and the puzzle elements (to be clear, the objects collected and images revealed are often references to parts of the story, but the player's presence is one merely of observation rather than interaction).  

The graphics are very good, however, in a style similar to and quality comparable to some of the best rpg's and overhead hack'n'slash adventures of the 16 bit era.  Dialog is similarly on par with games of that era.  I found it generally too corny but it was definitely true-to-style of 16 bit JRPG translations (I find those generally too corny, as well).  The music is well-done but overdone.  There is solemn piano piece that, while pleasant to listen to a few times, starts to really grate in a depressing way in extended sessions.  

Bottom line:  There's no game to the game.  I appreciate the dev's willingness to take a leap on an experimental concept but it ultimately fell flat for me.  I think perhaps the concept would be more suitaed to a passive medium like film or prose, or that the idea should have been worked to incorporate the player into the story in a way that make's the player's role more integral.  I got about a third the way through the game and never really felt any connection to the story unfolding or to the characters shown.  As a result, I just wasn't enjoying the time I spent playing To the Moon (it felt at least twice as long as the > 2 hours steam reports I played) and as a result, I gave up on it.

This game sucks. Units don't stay where they should, run out front, die, then you lose them forever (yeah, i know it's a rogue like). you beat the room with a few ranged characters... then buy some fresh lvl 1 guys to put the few pieces of equipment you got back from your recently deceased. I've heard there is PVP in this game, i couldn't care less about that. I thought this was finally the PVE only autochess game for me, but no.

review_text:
At 75% off and played it with a big surprise. I liked Callisto Protocol a lot and can't understand the big amount of negative reviews!

It clearly wants to be as Dead Space and yes the gameplay + atmosphere can't hold up to that, but that doesn't mean it's bad. It's still more than solid, a lot of fun, good graphics with an interessting story to tell. Not many games out there within this genre and quality.

Close combat has a huge impact feeling and ranged combat is something limited because the weapons feel more or less all like the same and upgrade options are a pain to collect because of the extremely limited inventory space.
Audio synchronisation is sometimes off (during cutscenes), which points out negative next to the all over good (sound) atmosphere.

Main story was finished after ~ 10h and the story DLC will be next, so for me the playtime is good. I don't like unnecessary stretched games going 20+ hours. All in all, as said, a very welcome positive surprise, a high quality, well done horror/gore sci-fi game.

review_text:
An interesting Metroidvania with survival aspects and rather difficult on the higher difficulties. Item usage is a big part of this game and you don't get increased movement options and abilities like in other metroidvanias, but there are a wide variety of spells and items with different play styles that still makes the game entertaining.

As mentioned in other reviews, the combat is pretty slow and there are no iframes meaning that you get one shot by pretty much every multi-hit attack in the game which can be annoying, but it is fun to plan out which items can best counter different enemy types which is where a lot of the strategy comes in.

One complaint that I do have is that because combat is slow and getting hit once is really punishing, there is no reason to use any melee weapon other than a dagger since it's the only weapon fast enough to reliably get in melee hits and this makes all other melee weapons practically useless which is unfortunate since there are some interesting weapons available that you can't really use. 

Magic is versatile and fun and there are multiple items that allow you to use magic more later on in the game. 

Overall, this is a pretty fun game and I recommend it.

review_text:
Just not the game for me, after putting 10 hours into ultrakill in just two sessions, I started up this game on a new day and barely got in and hour before I just got bored. 

Movement is flashy and fast, but doesn't actually feel good. I feel like I'm on ice all the time, walls barely work, no UI for when I do or don't have my dash anymore, monkey bars just confuse how momentum is supposed to work, and I lose and gain speed seemingly at random. 

The aesthetic was pleasing at first, but when you're trying to shoot enemies and do wallruns like some anime shit, it just makes me feel sick and confused. I haven't experienced vertigo in games after coming from speedrun-esque stuff like Ghostrunner and Solar Ash until I came here. 

I unlocked like three guns and they're all boring. Basic pistol with two firing modes: Useless and auto. The same pistol with one firing mode, auto, the bolt action rifle with a melee attack for some reason, and the laser cannon. 

Enemies just kind of... Pop in with no like, reasonable entrance flare. They just suddenly decide to exist, and immediately start firing at you. I guess you heal through close range damage or picking up some orb after you kill enemies or... I dunno, don't remember seeing any sort of tutorial on that. 

Like, I bought this game hoping for something that I'm going to love like Ultrakill, Ghostrunner, Titanfall and I just feel like I spent fifteen dollars for the Alpha, not Early Access. I'm not refunding, because I want the game to hopefully get support and enthrall me in the future, but if you have a choice between this and another game, I'm going to say hold out on this.

review_text:
DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME! yes, it have OVER A THOUSAND HOURS recorded, and i will continue to play it. but this was a MASSIVE mistake on my part. i regret coming to the "global" version of pso2 nearly every day that i play. but I've now invested too much time and money in this version to switch back to the Japanese game. 

you don't need to read this review. just know that the Japanese version is free, easily accessible, has way more content and is cheaper if you decide to put money into it. AVOID THIS VERSION!!! 

the game itself is... fine, but where it falls apart is the people running this version. tech support alone is bad enough that i'd never recommend this game. if you have any problems with purchasing in game items, or experiencing some sort of bug, you're 100% on your own. the support staff have a totally hands-off policy. they won't compensate you for mistaken purchases, or if you lose something you purchased. even if you can definitively prove that it was an in-game glitch or error that caused it. and this is absolutely a game where something like this is bound to happen to you at some point. 

you're literally better off playing the Japanese version of the game, and using google translate if you encounter an error in game through their support. its a nightmare. 

on top of that, this version of the game is missing a ton of content. everything from clothes, to weapons, to emotes and even story cut-scenes. 

basic items that are available for in-game currency in japan, are only available for cash in this version. and not re-salable on the player market. 

on top of this, in game currency is about 10% more expensive in this version than in the original. so every single thing in game is going to cost more if you decide to play this version. 

another element to consider, is how lazy and downright awful the translation is. honestly, its one of the worst I've encountered on an official product. simple things like characters with themed names, like "tea" and "coffee" have been translated directly without thought to "tia" and "cofy." there is even a main character in pso2 named lisa, laughably translated to "risa" its... quite embarrassing. 

even worse, is basic spelling and grammatical errors through the bulk of the original games' story. and even names, titles, events and places having their names change mid-story. If i hadn't played the original version of this game, i doubt I'd even know what the story was about in this version. 

and it gets even WORSE. the translation is incredibly inconsistent. to a level that affects gameplay and item management. on more than one occasion, a character in game will request an item, and the item actually has a differently translated name than the item requested. its a joke. 

here is an example. the primary nation you'll be fighting for in the episode 5 story, is a kingdom called Cuentia. but if you want to wear some of the outfits worn by the characters in this story, half the time the item will be named "Cuentian" and half the time it will be called "Cuentica" 

there are dozens of clothing outfits where one item is translated a couple letters off, so you'll be unable to find them in the player shop, unless you use an external website and copy/paste the name. since searching for specific items, REQUIRES you to spell the name correctly. to the letter. 

and, the worst of all, in my opinion anyways. is how many things are simply not translated. 100% of the weapons and items in game have NO description. there is no flavor text. they'll simply have a generic "this is a clothing item" description in the info box, which in the Japanese version would be filled with lore details. so you are missing out on a MASSIVE amount of world building by playing this version. its inexcusable. 

one other thing, which I'd just like to mention, is that the character creator in this version is... censored? I'm not sure if this was intentional, or a glitch. but you can't make your character shorter than 152cm. for... no reason i can think of. in the Japanese version, you can make your character as small as 140cm? this doesn't really matter, but its... weird?? 

anyways, a TL;DR to summarize. this entire version of the game seems to be developed by a group of incredibly lazy, incredibly greedy devs who don't care about the playerbase, and simply want to make a quick buck. please don't put your money into this game. go play the Japanese one instead.

I continued my playthrough of the Yakuza franchise, which was highly recommended to me, and I had to try Yakuza 5 Remastered. First of all, I’m quite impressed with the amount of side content, side quests, and random encounters in the game. I even completed nearly 85% of the game on my own, excluding restaurants, mini-games, and similar activities.

I had a lot of fun playing two new characters on the roster, Haruka and Shinada. Now as Kiryu lay in the desolated snow, I fear that I hear the final song is approaching.

review_text:
Playing through the entire Yakuza franchise, and 5 is a new low. I can appreciate the ambition and scope of the game, but it very clearly collapsed under its own weight. Narrative-wise, it is easily the messiest game in the series, somehow surpassing 4's laughably awful story with its exposition, conveniences, and surprise reveals. 

The Kiryu section was entertaining enough that I was hopeful that it would be a better experience overall than 4. Kiryu is still very fun to play and has by far the most options during combat. The story for his chapter was also decently intriguing and was set up pretty well. 

Saejima's section is where it all goes to shit. His gameplay is fun enough, when those charge attack hits land they are incredibly satisfying, but his section is an absolute snoozefest to get through, and I genuinely can't believe people thought it was a good idea to add in a hunting section in the game. Starting from the prison section which goes on far too long, to being forced to play through an imaginary Sapporo, to the mentioned hunting village, it legitimately made me drop the game for a month before I finished it again because it was so exhausting and mindnumbingly boring. 

Akiyama and Haruka's section is incredibly mixed. I actually found myself enjoying Haruka's section and gameplay. The story is no Perfect Blue but it still does a pretty good job making me feel repulsed towards Japan's idol industry. I can definitely see why people would hate it though, I'm sure it's jarring to go from a beat em up game to a rhythm game for the next 5 or so hours. Akiyama's story I don't remember at all, and his gameplay is atrocious. He does pitiful damage, has almost no defensive options, and in general feels incredibly scuffed compared to 4. His final fight where Kanai gangs up on you is just miserable to play through, almost as bad as Tanimura's fight against Munakata in 4. I get that I'm playing Hard mode but I don't see how being knocked around like a pinball by Kanai and his goons are supposed to help me get better at the game. 

Shinada has an interesting story but the way its connected to everyone else is nonsensical and felt like the developers pulled it out of their ass. His gameplay is also incredibly unfun, and using weapons doesn't make it any better. 

The final chapter is just exposition, exposition, exposition. At that point, I genuinely couldn't care less about what was going on, because it was just convenience and contrivances one after another with exposition, exposition, and exposition. Has it sunk in yet? This game in general has the most egregious usage of unskippable cutscenes and dialogue in any of the Yakuza games to date. My E key is probably broken from skipping all the worthless padding and filler for so long. I feel like the story would've been nonsensical even if I didn't start skipping everything, the plans that the characters come up with are so incredibly dumb, like that mastermind reveal ploy where they all fight each other. 

Maybe it's recency bias, but this game is easily the worst in the series, because while 4's story was awful and ruined Saejima's character as a whole with rubber bullets, at least it wasn't this long or this much of a slog (although it was because 4's continuous backstabs from characters reached comedic levels). The only new character I remember from this game is Shigeki Baba, who is admittedly handled well because I found him compelling with his split loyalty. Every other new character I've forgotten already. 

As a whole, I'm just done with the multiple protagonist route with Yakuza and can't wait to just play Kiryu the entire game in 6.

review_text:
You choke out medieval knights and steal their pants for beer money!

I also became alcoholic in this game, who knew it was so realistic.

AUDENTES FORTUNA IUVAT!!!!!

It's like if you took an Elder Scrolls game, removed all the magic or fantastical elements, and replaced them with realism and historical accuracy.

My wife’s boyfriend says it’s like if Project Zomboid was a medieval FPS.

KCDII makes every Bethesda game look like a child’s crayon drawing. It is better in every objective measure from graphics to stability, and it’s better in most of the subjective ways too. They have surpassed Bethesda by a country mile in the 7 years from their start-up release to their second game release. They've surpassed a whole lot of studios who are stuck in the mud, tbh. They deserve ALL the credit. It’s insane for a game of this scale to have so much detail and charm. It has set the standard of modern open world RPGs. God, what a game. 

I love this company. I hope they stay true to their visions and keep making great games. It's incredibly hard to make dynamic choice based, dialogue heavy games with consequences for your actions all inside a living world. And they have achieved it in one of the better looking games that's ever released that runs on all current gen and older gen GPUs. And it's also a cinematic AAA story driven game on top of that. Only Sony first party studios tend to release games in this state, and their games are on-rails for the most part, and designed to run on one bit of hardware. Mind blowing, really. Warhorse. 👏👏👏

This game, to me, is perfect. The stories are amazing, from the smallest interaction or conversation to the side and main quest. Combat, alchemy, SMITHING, all of it is fun. They have taken everything that was cool, and made it 100 times better. I am so f**king happy after playing this and I'm still thoroughly addicted. The music is amazing, world and exploration is breathtaking. I cannot praise it enough. It was so worth the wait, and it's making me so excited for the future. I'm just so damn happy Warhorse made this game. It puts Bethesda (who I love) to shame in so many ways. I played Skyrim often for a decade, I see myself playing this for far longer.

I love so so much about it, I love its commitment to realism and aversion to fantasy (I love fantasy, but the hard commitment to realism is a breath of fresh air). I love the character writing, I love how Hans grows on you like a mold, I love how naive and hopeful and just young Henry is, there’s so many gruff jaded protagonists that having him freak out at the mention of the devil or just blindly believe random sh*t or just refuse to compromise on his morals is so endearing to me. I love the world and systems for stealth and stealing and character schedules, just a pleasure to be in and play around with. But by far my favorite part of the game are the side quests, they’re so unique and fun, the rewards are universally bad but it genuinely doesn’t matter, you just go somewhere and you watch some weird, funny or creepy medieval drama unfold, and it’s different and interesting every time. I also love how your different character stats can also play into it New Vegas style.

I loved how small things in this game had a level of challenge to them.  You have to watch your characters hunger, and at the beginning of the game it's a bit hard to find food without stealing. Your equipment wears down (especially boots), and your character can stink if you don't visit the bathhouse.  I laughed when an enemy found me while I was crouching behind them just because they could smell how bad my character stunk. I also really enjoyed learning about medieval Europe as a lot of it is historically accurate with an in-depth codex’s detailing events, real noblemen, and general things like historical professions and the like. I could never in a million years have imagined that a game this hardcore and slow paced could have as few rough edges as KCD2.

The fact that myself, and seemingly most of the people that are still talking about it online drop 40-60 hours into the game before starting the first real main mission is testament to how well designed, integrated and engaging all of the systems in the game are, which for a game with such a large amount of very in depth systems is a straight up masterstroke of game design. I've played countless open world RPGs and no game has come close to getting me this deeply invested via its gameplay systems alone. Just existing as Henry, building up his stats and gear while also improving my own understanding of the game and combat evokes a feeling I can only compare to the "one more turn" feeling you get from the Civilization games. There is always something to do and a reason for me to want to do it and that feeling seemingly just never stops.

It's a lot like RDR2 for masochists and if Arthur was 15 again. It's not a "fun every minute" kind of game. It's immersive and challenging, and there's a great satisfaction loop as you improve at various things. I think it requires a bit more nuance and preparation than a lot of modern day RPGs, which can be frustrating to people expecting more of a Ghost of Tsushima type game, or a game with fights every 5 minutes. Let's say that where in RDR2 the immersion stuff felt rapidly like a chore here is linked to actual gameplay mechanics and not just for the sake of it. Personally, I think KCD2 does a great job of rewarding the extra effort that it asks of the player.

It's one of those games where the positives far outweigh the negatives. The game can be quite buggy especially in the second map, the story drags on in certain parts (especially those extended sections where you can't explore freely until you complete the quest), pacing is inconsistent, good loot is easy to obtain early game, etc. However, the writing, characters, voice acting, visuals, soundtrack, realism and detail this game has far compensate those issues. In a way it reminds me of The Witcher 3 10 years ago. I put about 100 hours into the game and don't regret a single minute of it. I'm looking forward to a second playthrough in the future, trying different choices and gameplay styles. It's GOTY contender for sure, though Clair Obscur has a strong case to win as well.

I have not felt like this about a video game since crawling out of the prison in Bethesda's Oblivion and discovering a sprawling world rife with adventure and nature. This game is not for everyone, the combat takes patience and finesse, it is a survival sim and you are not the chosen one and you will fail at conversations constantly, but this is a game for me and I'm so thrilled to have played it. I know I'm rambling here but the best comparison to make my point is Larian Studios: Divinity Original Sin 1&2 are some of the best games made for CRPG fans. Baldurs Gate 3 however is a game that creates CRPG fans. Similarly KCD1 was a very good game made for a specific niche of hardcore immersive RPGs. KCD2 I think has the potential to create fans of such games, in a way that I don't think we've seen since Skyrim.

In conclusion, I've never felt more immersed in the Middle Ages. The graphics are stunning, and the level of detail is astonishing. Everything just feels right. Even walking through the forest is so immersive it's breathtaking. This level of detail, combined with the vast possibilities the game offers, makes it an experience you don't want to miss out on! If you’re willing to sit down, take things slow, and just get lost in it, there really is no game that does it better in my opinion. I can wholeheartedly say that if you want to experience an amazing campaign set in a perfectly recreated version of life in 1403 Europe, give it a try you won't regret it. 

10/10 JESUS CHRIST BE PRAISED!

play into it new vegas style. i loved how small things in this game had a level of challenge to them. you have to watch your characters hunger, and at the beginning of the game it's a bit hard to find food without stealing. your equipment wears down especially boots , and your character can stink if you don't visit the bathhouse. i laughed when an enemy found me while i was crouching behind them just because they could smell how bad my character stunk. i also really enjoyed learning about medieval europe as a lot of it is historically accurate with an in-depth codex s detailing events, real noblemen, and general things like historical professions and the like. i could never in a million years have imagined that a game this hardcore and slow paced could have as few rough edges as kcd2. the fact that myself, and seemingly most of the people that are still talking about it online drop 40-60 hours into the game before starting the first real main mission is testament to how well designed, integrated and engaging all of the systems in the game are, which for a game with such a large amount of very in depth systems is a straight up masterstroke of game design. i've played countless open world rpgs and no game has come close to getting me this deeply invested via its gameplay systems alone. just existing as henry, building up his stats and gear while also improving my own understanding of the game and combat evokes a feeling i can only compare to the one more turn feeling you get from the civilization games. there is always something to do and a reason for me to want to do it and that feeling seemingly just never stops. it's a lot like rdr2 for masochists and if arthur was 15 again. it's not a fun every minute kind of game. it's immersive and challenging, and there's a great satisfaction loop as you improve at various things. i think it requires a bit more nuance and preparation than a lot of modern day rpgs, which can be frustrating to people expecting more of a ghost of tsushima type game, or a game with fights every 5 minutes. let's say that where in rdr2 the immersion stuff felt rapidly like a chore here is linked to actual gameplay mechanics and not just for the sake of it. personally, i think kcd2 does a great job of rewarding the extra effort that it asks of the player. it's one of those games where the positives far outweigh the negatives. the game can be quite buggy especially in the second map, the story drags on in certain parts especially those extended sections where you can't explore freely until you complete the quest , pacing is inconsistent, good loot is easy to obtain early game, etc. however, the writing, characters, voice acting, visuals, soundtrack, realism and detail this game has far compensate those issues. in a way it reminds me of the witcher 3 10 years ago. i put about 100 hours into the game and don't regret a single minute of it. i'm looking forward to a second playthrough in the future, trying different choices and gameplay styles. it's goty contender for sure, though clair obscur has a strong case to win as well. i have not felt like this about a video game since crawling out of the prison in bethesda's oblivion and discovering a sprawling world rife with adventure and nature. this game is not for everyone, the combat takes patience and finesse, it is a survival sim and you are not the chosen one and you will fail at conversations constantly, but this is a game for me and i'm so thrilled to have played it. i know i'm rambling here but the best comparison to make my point is larian studios divinity original sin 1 2 are some of the best games made for crpg fans. baldurs gate 3 however is a game that creates crpg fans. similarly kcd1 was a very good game made for a specific niche of hardcore immersive rpgs. kcd2 i think has the potential to create fans of such games, in a way that i don't think we've seen since skyrim. in conclusion, i've never felt more immersed in the middle ages. the graphics are stunning, and the level of detail is astonishing. everything just feels right. even walking through the forest is so immersive it's breathtaking. this level of detail, combined with the vast possibilities the game offers, makes it an experience you don't want to miss out on! if you re willing to sit down, take things slow, and just get lost in it, there really is no game that does it better in my opinion. i can wholeheartedly say that if you want to experience an amazing campaign set in a perfectly recreated version of life in 1403 europe, give it a try you won't regret it. 10 10 jesus christ be praised!

If you liked JC 1-3 and are playing with keyboard+mouse, do not buy (i don't use controller so can't give advice there). Or set a timer so you don't over that 2 hour limit and refund. That was obviously the wrong direction for the devs. They want more button smashing, not less!

There is literally nothing better in this then in JC3, even graphics are similar to 3, it's just more jungle and more UI-crap on the screen that means nothing. So do yourself a favour and pick the Just Cause 3 (last good Just Cause-game) from a discount, put a couple mods in and enjoy much more then you could ever do in this ... game. 

Nothing works like the previous and well working games. Everything was changed and for the worse. In [b]Just Can't 4[/b] they doubled down on the controls so that many of the buttons need two functions, just so they could cram more things in. "Just Cause" and "buttons-galore" are not two things that belong in the same sentence. It's like the devs noticed there is thing called keyboard and they could cram more things into it then previously!

I can imagine the discussion:
Director: I want buttons for everything.
Coders: Everything..?
Director: EVERYTHING!!!
Coders: How about two functions for every button!?
Director: *heavy breathing*

The functions are scattered all around the keyboard with little logic. You need several hours to just learn and memorize the buttons and their functions. As a little example, the control options lists 4 different buttons for "next menu" and "previous menu". Where is that menu? It's button "1" where it previously was in "Tab". And the grab hook? They changed it from "mouse right" because heck, why not! It's only the most used thing in the game! "Right mouse" has now zoom aim. And that "mouse right" has to have two modes, press and hold, just so they could get more things in! And if you happen to have machine gun with a shield, it's a third button for one gun plus the mandatory reload button! And that previously working grab hook, the biggest and funniest thing in Just Cause-games..? There is now half a dozen buttons for it! You apparently can't tighten the tether yourself anymore, it does it automatically. But there is now two buttons for "quick-reel" because that was apparently a priority. Previously used "F" for throwing grenades was changed to the industry standard "Middle Mouse". Why? So they could cram more buttons for that "F"!!!

And all in all, everything that previously nice and neat, is now menus, CONSTANT mayhem (whether you wanted or not) and idiotic controls because .. i don't know. They like it confusing. It's not like nobody wanted to play a fun and casual game like Just Cause. More convenient to take button controls, mix them up in a bag and throw them to table and see how confusing they could make everything. I'm not going to spend hours to just get this game playable in menus and with mods, this game is dead to me. Make the next Just Cause like JC2 or JC3 and i'll consider buying. With big reservations.

review_text:
A cute little meta-horror experience well worth its extremely cheap asking price.

Only a few complaints which weren't enough to ruin the overall experience for me, but your mileage may vary:

- The game can sometimes be a pain to get running properly depending on your system setup. It needs to be able to create a folder on your desktop and place files in there, among other things. In my instance I had to fight with my PC's security and antivirus software for quite a while before I could convince them that the game was harmless.

- The game likes to close itself [i]a lot[/i]. Collected a key item? Closed. Caught by the monster? Closed. Looked at something the wrong way? Closed. Oftentimes closing and restarting the game is required in order to progress or even move between locations. You sometimes have to do this multiple times in the span of just a couple minutes. It can get very tedious.

- There are an unfortunate amount of jumpscares which is a shame considering the atmosphere and environments are otherwise quite good with lots of neat set pieces.

If any of the above doesn't sound like a dealbreaker to you then jump right in and have fun. It's worth a romp. Just mind your ears with all the screaming it'll be doing at you later on.

review_text:
Rise to Ruins has been a delightful surprise in the Early Access scene, offering a refreshing mix of strategy and survival elements. From the moment I started building my first village, I was hooked by the game's ability to balance resource management with the thrill of tower defense.

The game presents a world where corruption spreads, and monsters threaten your villagers, adding a layer of tension to the otherwise peaceful task of building and expanding. The attention to detail in the pixel artstyle is commendable, and the music sets a perfect tone for the atmosphere of the game.

One of the standout features is the villagers themselves, who have distinct needs and behaviors, making the management aspect deeply engaging. The introduction of a lifespan for villagers adds a new layer of strategy, as you must balance their immediate needs with the long-term health of your community.

The tower defense component is challenging and rewarding, with the game cleverly ramping up the difficulty as you progress. The ability to share resources and villagers between multiple villages on the overworld map is a welcome addition that adds to the game's complexity and depth.

While the game is still in Early Access, the developer has shown a commitment to updating and improving the game, which is promising for its future. Rise to Ruins is a gem that offers a lot of bang for your buck, and I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone looking for a game that combines strategy, management, and a touch of retro charm.

review_text:
Lucius is a very interesting game about a 10 year old going on a rampage in his family home. Granted, to actually go on said rampage, you'll need to follow a steam guide (I recommend this one right here: https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=182953522) as there is only one way of killing each target and if you struggle with common sense like I did, you'll need it. Trust me, since the game doesn't really give any hints as to who or how your going to pull off each murder.

The game has you scheme to kill each of the human subjects (mother, maid you name it), spread over 18 chapters, as you progress unlocking Lucius' powers: Telekinesis, mind control, combustion and memory erase given to him by the devil. As well as doing side tasks like cleaning lucius' room, taking out the rubbish, grabbing a buttler a bottle of 1930s champagne and collecting dirty washing for you to sort into seprate baskets, you'll also be collecting Items and weapons that will come in handy for future chapters. 

(If you're an achievement hunter, there are a few housekeeping ones that need you to repeat an action/task multiple times to unlock like: opening cupboards, smashing/dropping items, turning on and off TVs and using Lucius' abilities as you unlock them)

After a while, it does get repetitive, so I would come back to it on and off if you get bored easily. 

Graphically it was OK. I was playing this on a Steam Deck at medium settings, so I know the game is capable of more on better hardware. 

My only main issue with Lucius was the control scheme. On Steam Deck, the game wasn't responding properly with the set buttons, so I had to find a useable layout on Steam Input and then edit it to what I liked as I started the game. It might be helpful if you plan to play on a controller or steam deck. Search for "Playable control scheme for steam deck - Lucius" on the steam input page (It's not perfect but it gets the job done) 

Overall, since I got this game on sale, I would say it was worth it. Mainly because of all the different ways Lucius kills each victim, and although the game's narrative feels uncoincidental to justify each killing, if you haven't played narrative based games in awhile (like me) it's a good game to get started with.

review_text:
TLDR; A game that may be worth keeping an eye on, worth buying for £30 or £40 but requires improvement to become and stay competitive.

It sort of reminds me of early BF4, it has to look like arse (ass for those across the pond) in order to run, plays like arse at times, has it's own bug infestation (ironically), and has a couple of crappy game mechanics; namely the company system (more on this later), yet has a good game design at its core as well as a great sound (bar a couple of bugs) to it, and most importantly massive potential. 

Looks wise, it is decent. Higher resolutions and high settings will cause serious performance issues (even the NASA computer kids on reddit have problems), yet it still looks decent enough (and is immersive enough) on the necessary settings (namely 2560-1440 res, ultra performance balancing, low everything bar medium texture) that it doesn't cause me any major issues for long-term game enjoyment. 

Play wise it works well overall, there are some bugs that may cause a slight freeze (although I suspect it is more performance issues than anything, especially when the flammenwerfer comes out to play), sometimes the sound can bug out when rapid firing HMG emplacements, and there is the occasional crashing to menu/desktop. yet to be fair these are fairly rare (past dozen or so games it crashed once at the end of a performance intensive match). Overall it is great to play, especially due to the seemingly innovative and very fun decision to not despawn bodies and add physics and mass to them, filling a corridor at the end of a 10 wave horde fight is incredibly fun, especially in urban maps.

It's biggest issue by far though is the company system. It's (as others have pointed out) obviously a clone of the helldivers system, the issue is that unless you start your own company (and have 30 mates willing to play it with you at set times) you will likely have problems with it. Either because they (a company) don't want new players (level up is reasonably fast but shouldn't make a difference), are holding a spot for somebody else, can't be bothered to deal with sorting through join requests, or just simply aren't active. Whilst it doesn't stop you from playing, it does look as though there are certain rewards (and possibly a storyline of sorts) that you can't obtain. 

Personally I would have said the best way forwards was to scrap the need for being in a company (have it like Holdfast's and most other games clan/regiment systems (even war thunder has it's squadrons reasonably sorted on issues like this)), and have it so there is an overarching series of grand campaigns (as with Helldivers) you can join, either as a squad (of up to 25 people), regiment (of up to 50), battalion (of up to 100), or a division (up to 200), with the opportunity for larger armies if someone really cares enough to try and herd a playerbase like that (personally I would rather herd cats). Have it so players can either join a group on a more permenant basis or simply play with random squads/groups rather than having to group up. It could be fun to have an overarching campaign where players actions (especially the larger groups) influence the outcome and state of the galaxy as a whole, win or lose like in old (I won't touch the new with a barge-pole) BF2.  

Overall it is a fun game to play, I wouldn't pay more than forty quid, but I suspect (or hope perhaps) that it is going to be a game that sees some very interesting development. Should they go down the line of overarching opt in or out large scale campaigns/events, bug squashing, concept optimisation, and NON-DLC weapons and kit development this has some good potential, so long as the developers don't simply use it as a cash-cow. It seems like a bit of a labour of love (at its core at least) and like I said, is very reminiscent of early BF4 in that it has a rough-ish start but could skyrocket to become a much loved classic, definitely worth watching for now.

*Sigh* smiles at camera and armed commissar stood behind it

I'm doing my part!

review_text:
Sloplab. For a game that is constantly priced higher than its predecessor and most VR games, it really lacks quality. In the base game you get "13" levels, 8 being filler levels. By the time you finish all the filler levels, the game gives you one good level, a "story" level then the game ends. Hell, I remember being audibly confused when I first finished the game due to how short the campaign was. The rest of the non filler levels are very simple in design compared to the "approach every situation how you want to" design that the previous game BOASTED about in its tutorial. This design made the game easy. To explain how easy the game is, the AI is incredibly brain dead. The melee enemies constantly fall over, causing them perform their 30s stand up animation, making them unsatisfying to kill. Additionally, the game gives you guns way too often. In the previous game, at the end of each level there was a field that would delete all your weapons. This would make the game more challenging for you as you had to get creative on how to defend yourself in every level, since you couldn't rely on your previous collection of guns. In Bonelab they save your weapons from level to level, meaning you can save your overpowered weapons to each level and kill everything without a challenge. Finally the avatar system ALSO MAKES THE GAME EASY. If you avatar is slightly strong, then all of your guns will basically have no recoil. If you have an avatar that is somewhat obese then you will basically not die. If you have an avatar who is tall you can basically skip most of the level. Some people may think that this is a creative way of solving the level, but I think its a boring way to cheese through the campaign. 

"But what about the sandbox and mods" if you a good sandbox and mod experience in VR buy Gmod and install the VR mod. What Gmod has did in 2006 is EXTREMELY better than what this game has done with its sandbox and mods. To name a few example, Gmod has a better objects menu, more tools, better tools (ex:making welds invisible), the ability to save your scene, a PROPER PHYSICS GUN, ragdolls (you don't need to kill NPC), a lower barrier to entry, base game multiplayer, better base game campaign (Half-Life 2) and this is for the user side. I am personally not a moder, but what I've SEEN, the SDK that Gmod has allows for more creativity and complexity for mod makers. If you want a quality VR game, please consider other games, If you want a VR sandbox, PLEASE consider Gmod with the VR mod installed.

review_text:
The Story was very boring. The main "Villain" appeared like, 2 times. I literally can't even remember his name there wasn't like any fun way to kill him either, he dies in a cutscene. 
In just cause 1 you jump out of a plane and put a bomb on Mendoza as you're both free falling 
In just cause 2 you fight Baby Panai on 3 nuclear missiles having a gunfight while also disarming them 
In just cause 3 Di Ravello appears several times in cutscenes, theres all this propaganda of him and you have a fight in a volcano against a high tech gunship with a gold paint on it in a volcano and you actually have the option to shoot him or to not shoot him in which he kills himself.
And here the dude like, dies in his private jet.

Then the Heat System which is gone. In the all the other games you have heat and you would have different tier of units come after you as more elite troops and vehicles are put against you.
Here theres none instead you just fight the regular recruits, there are all these unique enemy types yet they only appear in missions and honestly I rarely ever saw them which is disappointing. Also I found in just cause 3 that there were like unuiqe enemy types for every vehicle. There was a specific unit for every vehicle. Tanks bikes and helicopters.

The ammo is also a bit of a problem in my opinion, I feel like I could never use most weapons since the enemies that use them are rare and instead of just going of weapon type so if an enemy had a shotgun like the pump action one and I had the automatic one I could just pick up that ammo instead of having to get it from the exact weapon. So I would always just carry like the regular SMG and assault rifle with me. Also I don't understand why Rico wouldn't have a sidearm. In the all the games he has dual wield pistols yet here only 2 weapons. I had some fun with the railgun and if I wanted more ammo I could always just fast travel to the crash site where I could always find plenty of ammo.

The grappling was very interesting however it is very confusing for starters and I also got confused.

The Challenges were extremely disappointing like it wasn't the same anymore. For wingsuit you just have to through like 3 rings in a few seconds, unlike the old one which was very frustrating but thats what made it so cool, always trying to get the max score and pushing yourself to the limit. I mean the gears that Rico could get were very fun. Things like homing grenades and explosives with boosters on them. I feel like Rico really wasn't as powerful as he was in Just cause 3. 

The only cool part was the agency DLC with the hoverboard challenges. You had a challenge for every submarine and 1 very long course which kind of reminded me of the old challenges and at least they brought back the liberation system.

The liberation system is very sad.
There was like this main base in which you had some thing to do and this wasn't very interesting like they are all the same.
I really wouldev like to just destroy all of these massive bases and leave everything destroyed instead of having everything respawn every time. The only reason they are even there was just so you could cause chaos to gain "Squads" to fully take over an area. Destroying the weather control station missions were the only ones I liked honestly.
When I was playing just cause 3 I liked to liberate every base in the island region and then start the missions which would mean I always had an easier time with every mission so the rebels were always there to cover my back and in some missions I could just walk in freely with no one shooting at me.

review_text:
This is going to cover a lot. I dont structure reviews very well so this will be a cluster fu... a mess. Enjoy.

I REALLY did NOT enjoy this game.... I really want to give it a thumbs up anyway because it is a high quality game (great graphics, no bugs etc) and its obvious the developers (small indie team) put their hearts and souls into this; I wish the big triple A studios put as much effort into their titles. It doesnt feel fair to give it a thumbs down just because I didnt have fun playing it, but their overall rating is so high I dont think my down vote is going to ruin their rating :) 


Lets begin...... The game takes place in an "alternate reality" town during a plague, you essentially investigate the cause, try and help people and ultimately try to stop the plague all while trying to keep yourself and a handful of main characters alive throughout. The game is really difficult and I usually enjoy that (especially in survival games) but something about this just annoys the heck out of me and leaves me irritated.  You have to watch your hunger, thirst and monitor your infection level - make sure you dont catch the plague.  Food, medicine and clean water is really hard to get and becomes exponentially more so as the game goes on.  You have to CONSTANTLY ( i am not exaggerating) loot trash cans for trinkets like buttons, yarn, marbles etc and trade with NPCs for scraps of food. There are men, women, and kiddos but there are only a few preset models for each-for example, if you see 5 men in a group, 3 of them will look identical, hopefully that makes sense, I really didnt like this, ANYWAY... On top of always worrying about getting a nut or crumbs of bread to not die of starvation you have to CONSTANTLY worry about gathering enough herbs to craft under powered medicines to keep the main characters alive. You also have to maintain your gear and equipment which degrades INSANELY fast...as the plague progresses certain areas of town will be infected and there will be thugs who will attack you on sight... there are a few different weapons you can get, lets say you have a gun, you shoot a thug 2 times and you not only lost 2 bullets which are EXTREMELY expensive and rare but your revolver now lost 1/4 of its durability.  To repair it? Oh, well on top of all the other items you need but cannot get, you need to try and round up the scrap items to repair your gun/knife etc. 
You can wear special clothing in infected areas to SLOW DOWN the rate you become infected...  you wanna cut through an infected area? throw on your plague boots and take a few dozen steps and see the durability has dropped significantly...wanna repair your clothing? You know the drill, go loot for junk, try and trade with all the npcs who look identical, nobody wants what you have, rinse repeat. All while having a VERY limited inventory.  It is just too much for me personally, I didnt find this fun.  Your character WILL die multiple times but the game goes on, its actually part of the game in a way.... IDK. 

This is a "parellel universe" type situation. Its a world that looks like ours, but there is a "supernatural" force at work and the people use A LOT of lingo and terminology you will not understand and its used so often it got annoying to never understand what exactly is being said to me. Your responses also contain this weird jargon and you will not know what youre saying back to these NPCs.   

The main mission/ point to the game is essentially racing back and forth across a map to a bunch of main characters at different times and talking to them.  Quests are timed so youll never complete them all...  You get a "quest" to go see character 'A', you make your way ( at great cost) to get to this person, they are - and always will be- a stationary NPC. People in the reviews say your choices matter and will have consequences but id like to say this isnt as dramatic as you think it would or should be - in my opinion of course. Your "quests" and "decisions" are STRICTLY dialogue choices. You have a conversation that you wont understand and get more of the strange story and thats about it.  You can try and save certain main characters if they get sick, or let them die, and if certain characters die then youll lose out on some dialogue with certain characters later on but thats my point is its only dialogue..... You go to a character, you talk to them, chose dialogue options, and the convo/quest ends. Based on your dialogue options this will set up certain interactions with other stationary NPCs later on.   You dont go on missions with these characters or anything like that... Its just you talking to stationary NPCs and picking dialogue and inbetween these "interactions" you are scavenging junk to trade for junk to survive. 

I think a large part of the game for people is getting attached to the world and characters? Thats what makes all the different dialogue trees interesting for them, thats why trying to save them is fun and thats why they get so invested? Not sure... but for me its just... shallow. I dont see the magic everyone else sees.  

A thing that appealed to me in reviews  was the decay of a city while the plague takes over, but it wasnt as I thought itd be. The city is made up of a dozen or so separate "sections" or "zones".   The length of the game is 13 in game days, and on a set schedule 2 zones/ sections of the city become "infected" with the plague.  During this time if you walk through either of these 2 zones you will slowly get sick so you avoid these areas and just walk around them. Then after a day or two those 2 areas go into a "after plague" phase where a bunch of thugs wonder the streets but there is no more sickness, then after a day or two the zones recover to normal as 2 different "zones" go into plague mode.  My point is: its not like you slowly notice the sickness spreading throughout the entire city as time goes on and things completely go to hell... its just certain zones at certain times... no matter what, 80% of the city will always be normal. The plague is only in 2 sections at a time basically and it spreads at a scheduled interval.  To me that really breaks immersion.

Id say before buying this game you NEED to watch a lets play on youtube, seriously.  Its hard to explain why I find it "shallow". People will read me saying "shallow" and argue that the lore and story is super deep and theyre right (but its not interesting), im talking about the actual game play. The weird language and lengthy conversations to read (it isnt voiced)  left me mostly wanting to rush through the convo instead of stop to carefully read all this confusing jargon that didnt make sense. 

Its very story driven. VERY.  Maybe too much for me.  The choices and consequences dont seem as dynamic as people made it out to be. the actual game play is just you looting, trading, and constantly starving, always having somewhere you need to be, never having what you need ALL just so you can read a conversation with a stationary NPC.  It just didnt spike my interest. 
Because I never formed bonds with these characters & because I wasnt able to fully dive into the lore or story it made the "struggle" of the game pointless for me.  
I didnt find the looting of items, trading for scraps fun.

I did find out how to cheat tho hehe.  I figureed out how to add items to my inventory, it took forever but it can be done.  Heres the problem, even with cheats the game was a drag.  I gave myself clothing you otherwise cannot get which is the "crow costume" the plague doctors wear (high plague resist), I gave myself what looks like a 98K rifle, a "wehrmacht" helmet and uniform, ammo, ENTIRE fish etc.... so I could travel anywhere and do as I pleased, shoot thugs, stay healthy... but IT WAS STILL a drag because using the rifle a few times left the damned thing broken, the clothing would degrade, id end up hungry five minutes later. Even cheating isnt fun.
