review_text: I previously recommended this game, but after getting into the late areas of this game, I just... I can't fucking do it anymore.  I LOVE Batman.  I love listening to Mark Hamill as the Joker, and Kevin Conroy as Batman.  Their voices are THE voices of those two characters, to me, and probably always will be, so when they get the whole team together again, I love it.  However, the control scheme is horrifically and abysmally unresponsive.  I hate that when you start doing one action, there's NO WAY to cancel it, in order to respond quickly.  Oh, batman is punching a guy on the ground?  Sorry, he can't stop doing that to defend himself!  Nope nope, not possible!  ... Seriously, the way Batman fights comes across as clumsy and r-tarded., in all but the stealth aspects.  I just can't do this anymore.  The boss battles are sheer pain.  Not challenge, just pain, because there's literally no way to get any better at this kind of thing, when it's more a matter of the lack of response to input commands, than it is the skill of the player.  They tried to do too much with too few buttons.  Fuck this shit.

review_text:
I have not finished this game, but I feel like I've played long enough to give an honest review.  Do I like this game? Yes, somewhat. Do I recommend it? No, not really. Long review incoming as to why. I played 100% of this game on the Steam Deck, so that will likely influence some of this.

First off, a couple things I do appreciate about this game is the manual save (seriously, thank you for this one. I HATE sleep to save!!) It does save automatically at midnight so there is an auto-save backup which is nice. I also like the art style. Unfortunately it does mean that doing certain tasks become more difficult, such as using your processing equipment (soap maker, mills, etc). It is incredibly annoying especially with controller to get the character clicking on the correct spot. You run the risk of eating raw fish and making your character sick. The controls really need some work. They are janky on controller. There is also a bunch of settings you can change so make sure to check that to customize to your playstyle!

I think they have a nice idea with this game.  But it really needs more work in my opinion. I would have to agree with other reviews that it still feels very early access, and is missing a lot of things that could really add some interest to the gameplay. I actually bought this game originally over a year ago, and ended up getting a refund because it felt so bare. I repurchased it again a year later because it looked like that had been continuing updates and I want to like this game, but it still feels like it is missing a lot.

Here is where it all goes downhill for me. It is loaded with bugs and glitches. Eventually it started to get on my nerves. Winter is a stuttering mess. There are weird glitches on the ground all over that I couldn't tell if it was supposed to be ice, or that the ground was clipping. I messed with the settings but it made no difference. It is also the most boring season. They really need to add in a greenhouse (preferably), or at least some crops that will grow during winter. A shed would be great as well. You will need processing equipment, but I personally hate filling my house with that stuff, although there is still some there, and the other half is all over my farm. A shed would really help tidy things up for those of us who prefer that. 

 There is very little variation in your day. It's incredibly repetitive. (Winter being the worst). There is NO irrigation. EVER. Eventually when you have them, your children will help water. However, I have noticed multiple times where they will just wander off and not water at all, even though there is full watering cans in the outdoor chest. I always have to check during some point of the day that they have watered. There is also a potion, but it doesn't come cheap. There should be some sort of drip system unlocked eventually. It's also incredibly grindy. You have to make sure you are continually shaking any and all trees you walk past because you need a lot of wood. The mines are a waste of time. It's a long walk to get down the mining spots, and there is I think 4 or 5 spots where you are just clicking 'A' maybe 3 times to get a couple stone and maybe a gem at the lowest spot. That's it. You can however teleport out.

There are no descriptions on your toolbar. If you want to plant a specific seed you will need to open your inventory and check what it is, and either remember what it looks like or move it to a certain spot so you don't plant the wrong one. The seeds are a whole other thing. You have to make sure you are checking multiple people for seeds EVERYDAY, because usually they are only selling maybe a handful to purchase. That is, if you can afford it. The day to day routine is generally take care of your farming business, shake some trees, forage some bushes, maybe talk to a few people (they are pretty flat personality wise, wah wah), and do some fishing. There just aren't enough different activities to change up your day.

Honestly, I could go on with even more paragraphs about stuff that either needs to be fixed or flat out annoyed me. I know it probably sounds like I hate this game. I don't, I think it has potential, but I am not sure if they have anything else planned. As is, I am not sure it is worth it. The consensus I generally see around on different forums is that it is boring. Given that, if you are really interested then I would wait for a sale.

review_text:
This game is ok. 
It's not great. It's not bad, It's ok.

The Good:

You probably are looking through it because you saw the trailer and saw those big bosses with bouncy tits, let's not lie to ourselves. The trailer doesn't betray you. You'll see big bosses with bouncy tits.

Most of the art is okay, sometimes it is even really pretty and quite sexy. The pixel art animations are also dressed with shading from real time light sources and particles and this compensates the non-purist pixel art wonkyness of pixels of different size.

Also from time to time the music is really nice. It's not the best, but it matches the mood of the game really well.

The game is replayable with fresh features on new game+, so even if its quite short, you can play again with a different story and different mechanics.

The Bad:

The game is bland. The story is bland.  The gameplay feels either wonky or annoying. The menues are... a hurdle. This is important because you'll be juggling passive items in the few item slots you have. No double jump and no dash make the controls feel sometimes slow and sometimes unwieldy. There are absolutely killer combinations that are extremely easy to achieve, a few for each zone. This makes some fights against bosses and some entire sections of the map so easy it's boring. There's some sort of environment system, if either you or the enemies touch the ground they might become wet and be further affected by electricity or catch on fire. While I'm impressed with the idea, I've found that I have not enjoyed it much. It felt mostly annoying when it was inconvenient (something that forced you to enter the menu to spend an item to become immune to the floor effects) or boring (entire parts of the map are submerged in water and you can destroy everything with an electricity spell, making these sections pointless)

The metroidvania aspects of the game, for any experimented platform game player will seem too simple. The problem is not that the game is short (it is, but that isn't necessarily a bad thing) the problem is that the exploration is not interesting. I can't really put into words how simple the layout is, but it is amazing how the game can have so much effort put into so many things and the parts that are supposed to be the most important feel so unpolished.

I'll be sincere. I'll only reccomend this game because I want these guys to succeed and make further games. I think they have the potential to do something amazing next. And if you enjoy the genre, you probably will want too, the game has a bit of soul, despite all its flaws.

review_text:
I'm always down for something indie, especially when it leans on the horror or the meta genre. 

[b]IMSCARED[/b], is exactly a combo of both, not only it tries to manipulate you, but also your computer. This oldschool-esque video game does well in evoking a sense of dread, paranoia, and a sad haunting atmosphere. In my opinion, pixelated horror games are often the scariest to me than those with realistic graphics, so this hits the spot. It's scary that I got a lot of chills, even if I'm replaying for achievements, it still does not fail to startle and unsettle me. Really cool stuff.

This is, if not, one of the first ever video games involving fourth wall breaking, and for such a short game, it's pretty underrated, yet good! Really showing how simple graphics are enough to immerse in a setting. 

Nonetheless, if you like games such as OneShot, Undertale, and or The Witch's House because of the unbelievable lot of jumpscares it has prepared, then you should definitely give this a chance. But I must warn you to be careful, [b]because it's waiting for you to play, one more time.[/b]




---
[Also, shoutout to Kubz Scouts aka Papi Jay, helping me in times I was stuck for too long.]

review_text:
Being a fan of Dungeon Keeper and resource-gathering and structure-building games like Startopia, let's just say I really wanted to love this game. I don't even like it.

There's just not much game here. All buildings seem to be lackluster and blatantly 2-tier right up front. Little is hidden. Want wood? Lumber jack or advanced lumberjack. Want stone? mason or advanced Mason. The buildings are rather bland and show little innovation or setting/theme.

Basically you set your people to work by painting resource gathering areas on trees, stone, etc. Then you construct buildings to process these resources so you can make a defense tower or two and some magic makers.

You have a set of spells, once again all presented up front with little in the way of unlocking or earning their acquisition. Fireball for killing. Healing aura for ... healing. You can guess the rest. You've seen them in just about every other god-game.

My point is, re-hashing all the tired old god-game concepts from the 90's to now in a cute little pixel style doesn't show much originality and doesn't necessarily make the game fun. Grinding through several hours of this in attempt to enjoy it I finally realized, this simply is not a fun game yet. 

I hope, sincerely, to update this review later upon release, praising it for it's clever spell set, tiered growth and scaling, intense combat mechanics creative buildings, hearty and lore-filled setting and my attachment to the characters I'm leading. Right now it just has none of these features.

review_text:
Hello Human, here are some notes to help you on your journey of the DEAD BY DAYLIGHT experience:

- Lots of crossovers, allowing you to play as cool characters from many horror universes

- Game naturally creates chaotic scenarios with all the combinations of perks and addons in play (sometimes for good, sometimes for ill)

- Heavy DLC policy, requiring you to purchase characters. Not as important on the survivor side (since the survivors are essentially cosmetic changes), but on the killer side you are much more limited since they have unique powers you are missing out on. Not as expensive as other games with this same model but still not great practice

- Very poor progression, takes a long time to unlock people. Bloodpoints and Bloodweb system is basically just a waste of time that pulls you out of just playing the game (different currency then the one you use to get characters). Get stuck in scenarios where you want to play a character for their abilities/looks but also want to get other characters just for their associated perks. Further made worse by shrine of secrets being very unforgiving (can't just buy perks, need to get them for a high price from a random weekly rotation of 4/200+ perks) and uses the same currency (Iridescent shards) to buy characters, further complicating the process.

- Game controls are not bad but are strange sometimes (they try to keep it only 2 buttons no matter the cost, even if it means creating these weird cycle mode abilities rather then just have it be 3 separate buttons) (seems to be done to simplify controller, at the expense of keyboard). Not a terribly degrading thing just a bit weird to get used to.

- Quite buggy, some characters are in weird broken states for extended periods of time. For instance, one character named the houndmaster has a dog that follows them. There is about a 10%? chance that using your ability to send the dog out just does nothing, this bug has existed for a very long time considering how impactful it is.

- Design wise is in this weird limbo state where it isn't optimal for either causal nor competitive ways of playing. A good example of this is with map design. Many maps are slightly unoptimal to play more competitively since the RNG makes them not always spawn the same, preventing 100% optimization for cool map-knowledge plays. On the other hand, the way that the RNG is implemented is not very interesting (mostly a reshuffling of generic tiles) so casually it feels essentially like the same map. This basically causes a local minima where neither side is completely satisfied. This philosophy extends onto character design, perk design, and base kit design with particular playstyles.

- Adding onto design philosophy, it is also counter-intuitive and punishing in strange ways. On survivor, you have no ability to see your teammates, see your teammates' perks, or communicate to them via text or voice chat in game. This creates a very large disparity between coordinated teams using discord versus uncoordinated teams, further exacerbated by the difference between coordinated perk and add-on usage versus uncoordinated. The game is obscuring information preventing you from working with your team in the team-based game. On killer, the most logical way to win a 1v4 scenario is to remove one person from the equation as fast as possible (known as tunneling) so that it simplifies the game-state in your favor. It makes then the most sense that on survivor that you need to spread out damage across your team so that no one dies too early. The way that it is currently implemented is in such a manner where tunneling isn't really fun to do or go against, but is also in a state where the game is sort of balanced around it. You are punished for killing in the killing game as a killer. It's not impossible for the game to be fun on both sides while balancing around tunneling being the norm (Identity V does this quite well), and I don't believe that it is impossible to have a scenario where tunneling is one of multiple strategies that exist, but the way DBD handles it again puts it in a local minima where neither side really has as much fun doing it as alternative playstyles (if they win in a scenario where they spread out hooks, it doesn't offer them any unique advantage and is not as decisive of a victory as if they just tunneled), but there is some game scenarios where there isn't really an alternative other than just lose immediately. TLDR, there exists aspects of the game that are punishing and not clear, some of which create a circumstance where the path to victory is not congruent with the most fun way of playing.

- Development time on these aforementioned problems as well as just balance changes in general is very slow. Some changes that one would think would be a easy net positive QOL can take years to implement for not very clear reasons. 

Overall, this game has very good potential, but is stunted from questionable design decisions and progression. It is enjoyable on occasion, but you basically need to completely dissassociate from 1. Winning/Losing  2.  Progression and 3. Bugs (just laugh at them),  in order to have consistent fun. As you can see I have followed this game for a while, so I had a lot to say about it (I have about +100 hours not on this account), and can say that my Disassociation Techinque is one of the most effective techniques in all of gaming, perfectly employable in this specific scenario to be used to the upmost advantage. Good luck out their in the fog soldier, or just play Identity V which is free and is advantaged in almost all areas except graphics and horror icon crossovers.

If you enjoy star trek and flying around in ships from the series, it is a great game. The graphics are alright for a game as old as it is. The game play is still fun and exciting, especially if you enjoy moving up to more challenging levels. The character customization goes real far. To be frank, further than I have seen most games go. All around, a really fun game. However, I hold this against it:

The game is older, so there are a few bugs, achievements, and missions that are not around anymore. For instance, they removed the foundry section of the game (create a custom mission). Having people create things lets them enjoy the experience at their leisure and expands the story. However, it has been removed with no sight of returning. review_text:
[h1]Don't. Simply Don't.[/h1]

I bought this game during the beta for below 25€ and we did have a lot of fun. That nonwithstanding, the current state of the game post-release is a shame and the developer should be deeply embarrassed for what they force upon their community. 
[hr][/hr]
[h2]The Pros:[/h2]

[h3]Multiplayer fun[/h3]
If you have a couple of friends to play with, rounds can be fun. They are highly repetitive, so don't expect to be challenged mentally, but the classes make sense and are diverse, and with the right type of people it's good for a lot of fun.

[h3]interesting multi-level definition of "success"[/h3]
The lobby is divided in up to 5 4-player squads (though only 16 players fit a map, don't know where this math comes from). A well-oiled squad can achieve objectives without external help, which encourages players to divide their forces, e.g. one squad defends the base while two squads independently of each other go for resources and the remains are afk or something xD

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The cons:[/h2]

[h3]The interface[/h3]
The interface has been designed someone who should ask for a refund of their tuition fee. Menu options are confusing, translations are catastrophically bad, hints - where available, such as the information that you have new weapon options - are inconsistent, don't tell you WHAAT they hint for and are buggy. You can change a squad until you choose a class, but not after. This is not told to you. Your Squad View on the left sometimes only shows 3 members, despite the Squad being full. To check who is in which squad, you need to use the 'very intuitive' key combination "TAB, then z". This is not visible anywhere in the UI. When trying to repair a building, you have around a 50% chance that left click starts the repair action. In one occasion, the game just removed any kind of HUD from my screen, which left me targetting with Iron Sights and ask others to look for my health since I had no health bar. Was kinda fun but definitely not deliberate.

[h3]Stability[/h3]
During our first session post-release we (party of 8) had
- multiple game crashes mid-mission
- 2 game crashes in the Menu
- 1 occasion where the game crashed and wouldn't start again, even after verifying, uninstalling, reinstalling, multiple reboots and essentially deleting everything but the operating system
- one kick due to cheating (no cheats were present)
- multiple kicks because of "Server closed" (the remainder of the team was able to continue playing on that server
- a broken lobby where nobody could join or be invited
- countless Lagspikes where the FPS dropped to <1
- multiple (false?) informations that the company server is currently down

[h3]Features[/h3]
The game has a lot of nice ideas, however they are sometimes implemented in a way so idiotic it beggars belief. 
1.0 introduced a new game mode that supposedly seems to be some kind of multiple-missions thing. I say supposedly because here we get to the juicy bits. In order to play this mode, you appear to have to be part of a so called "company". You have a randomly selected list of 30 companies to join, but you can also create your own. Of course we created our own - only to figure out that YOU CANNOT SEARCH FOR OR INVITE INTO a company!! Also, the suggestion dialog only offers you companies that contain at least 2 members. However since a newly formed company obviously starts with 1 member, there appears to be actually no way for us to join our own company. Whoever designed this and deemed it fit for release seriously should question his or her life's choices.

One of the more interesting features is that enemy corpses don't despawn. Instead they litter the area and eventually allow the enemy to scale walls and overrun your defenses from a vantage point. While this concept is interesting and I have to give it to the devs that they manage all this with relatively neglible impact to performance, it is BUGGY AS HELL. Frequently, you are unable to actually leave or enter a building because countless corpses and alive enemies intersect and form a solid wall. Even with this, spawnpoints are sometimes INSIDE of corpse piles, which leaves you trying to dig yourself out of that pile while enemies can selectively ignore collisions and still attack you. You can clean up the corpses with melee and some explosives. However, this is also somewhat unresponsive and seems to change between updates without any real apparent concept.

[h3]Price[/h3]
The beta was priced at around 25€. However, for release they raised the price to 50€ AND added Skin Packs on top, which brings the total tally to around 90€. This is a ridiculous entry price even for AAA games, let alone for such an unpolished bugfest (pun intended) like this game sadly became.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
This game had high aspirations and a very compelling theme it was set in. The idea is interesting and the core gameplay loop is fun. However, the developers in my opinion completely dropped the ball by overpromising, favoring new features over actually fixing usability bugs or even considering usability in general. Also, the 1.0 tag appears completely random, subjectively I would say the polishing of the game HEAVILY decreased between the last beta and 1.0.

Personally I do not regret having bought that game in Beta, however I [b]strongly[/b] advise anybody who made it until here against spending money on this unfinished, badly thought-through wreck of a game.

Update: I am still playing it but with increasing rage quits. The devs just don't understand how to design a game and I would actually pay to have them never release a game again. What the fuck kind of concept is "oh here you have an endless horde so you will loose, glhf" for a game? Did you watch your playerbase lately? Hardly anybody plays the game anymore but sure, let's focus on punishing the players for minor glitch abuse rather than fixing the plethora of bugs the game STILL has. Oh you are revived? here, let us spawn you INSIDE A BUILDING! Oh you try to complete a mission? too bad, we're not counting it. Oh you are dead? here you can walk around, but not shoot. though you will not be revivable because fuck you. I could rant on for hours. It really beggars believe how badly this game is written. The premise is marvellous, the possibilities endless. And the studio decides to flush it down the drain and adds insult to injury by making this unmitigated bug-desaster harder with ill-conceived modifiers.

I've been playing this game quite a lot on the PS5 and loved it, so I thought I would get the PC version and see what it looks like with the graphics cranked up - good is the answer, although, to be fair, the PS5 version is sweet.

The gunplay is smooth and fun once you get the muscle memory working for you. The environments are well laid out and beautiful, and the various corridors and arenas have been planned with fun horde defence in mind. You can feel the pedigree of Arizona Sunshine 'shining' through in this title.

I have played in co-op mode a couple of times and have played loads in solo. The AI team members are OK on the whole, they do sometimes get in the way, but this is rare and momentary. 

The premise is quite simple, you are a runner and go on various 'runs'. On your way through each run you collect goodies, if you complete the run, you get all of the goodies, if you die, you lose the items but keep the money. The money and guns can be upgraded, broken down or scrapped. For example, if you find a gun with an ammo counter, collect the gun then strip it down when you're back at the hub.

All of this gives a great deal of replayability. The various difficulty levels don't just nerf your guns. They directly alter the feel of each run. Hordes will be larger and more aggressive, and health will be sparse to non-existent, but with this, the rewards are greater. 

I love this game and Arizona Sunshine, the balance between gun realism and fun gameplay is excellent.

review_text:
The problem with Yakuza 5 is the failure of it's penta-narrative. Y4 used a quad-narrative that worked, but only because each character was either directly impacted or entangled in the main narrative elements. Y5 fails because each character is basically doing their own thing unrelated to everyone else, until the last 15 or so minutes of their parts.

	The biggest perpetrators of this are Haruka and Shinada's parts. Saejima is related to the larger plot, but spends a lot of time on irrelevant material. Kiryu's is the only strong chapter that directly builds up the main plotline. Let's delve into that first.

	Kiryu is currently supporting his orphanage financially via taxi driving. Haruka was scouted by a talent agency, and without giving too much away let's just say that Kiryu leaves so that she can follow her ambitions untethered. Kiryu picks up a passenger early on: Dojima, the current chairman of the Tojo clan. We get the setup right away: the current Omi chairman is gravely ill and will pass soon, so the current alliance between them and the Tojo is under threat of dissolution. Dojima is therefore seeking alliances elsewhere. He goes missing soon after.

	Kiryu, as was the case with the other games, doesn't want any part in underworld events. But he's slowly drawn into the fray, and with a resolution and drive that was missing in Y4 (which made his inclusion feel shoe-horned). Kiryu accepts his legendary status and reasons that it can be a force for good to protect those in his life. If the game stayed on Kiryu it would've had a stronger narrative.

	But then we get the narrative switching. Seajima is the first up, and at first it isn't too bad. He's (willingly) serving a 2 year prison sentence, but abruptly denied parole for no apparent reason. Without spoiling a lot, let's just say that an urgent matter comes up with Majima, so we bust out of prison. Once out we patrol Tsukimino (the local city) in search of the local clan leader, who is [i]allegedly[/i] behind the transgressions.

	The problem is that a large chunk of the chapter takes place in this tiny prison yard where you talk to the same 3 people to progress the story. And most of the story deals with Saejma's prison pals and the warden's ethics. It's not that interesting, or related to the larger narrative. When we finally get to a new city, the game rushes towards the end for the character switch.

	Next up is Haruka, who is working at an idol agency and gearing up for a local competition. Where's Daigo? What's happening with Majima? Who cares; you have a handshake event today! I hope you enjoy playing Idolmaster for the following 30 hours! Haruka's part has a character switch to Akiyama halfway in, which ties it back to the main story via an Omi Alliance run talent agency. But this part also sucks because they NERFED THE HELL out of Akiyama's moveset. He's real weak.

	Character switch to Shinada - an ex professional baseball player kicked out of the league for suspected match fixing. He lives life as an impoverished sleaze magazine writer. He begins uncovering the truth of his past as he seeks out the mysterious Nagoya family, whom are allegedly behind his downfall. His motivation being, at first, money from a 'mystery' benefactor (in a bad disguise). The mystery deepens as Shinada finds that the Nagoya family is seemingly nowhere (and everywhere) to be found.

	I think by now the issue I talked about at the start is more clearly laid out now. Completely unrelated storylines that detract from the main narrative. There is a silver lining, which is that Haruka's part is at least conceptually interesting. You dance instead of fight. And Shinada's is a good mystery. But it's completely out of place in the game. Akin to filler material that barely moves the story. Remember, this is about Daigo and the Tojo alliance, so when we connect Haruka and Shinada to the main story it's both silly, confusing, and still inconsequential

	By the ending, Kiryu is the only one with any real motivation for being there. Saejima is there as a Tojo soldier. Fine. Shinada is just helping out, I guess. Akiyama is there to take care of Haruka. And Haruka is dancing in the background at a concert. Which is under jeopardy for no discernible reason other than she is a main character and has to be in the finale. 

	The writing is all over the place. It works for the most part. But you frequently have characters fighting for no reason. Like Shinada's fight in the finale. Shinada is attempting to stop a shooting, but the shooter decides to not go through with it before Shinada arrives. Shinada still fights him because we need a boss fight for Shinada.

	Similarly, Saejima's part has him making up and shaking hands with an ally, only to fight him anyway because...I don't know, actually. There's no reason to fight someone after you've made up. We needed a boss fight to close up the chapter. Speaking of, after the fight Saejima is asked if he wants to know who the mastermind is behind everything and he passes because 'it won't change anything'. Just, really, the best writers behind this product! 

	Oh, and let's not forget this 4-way boss battle towards the end between allies: “we have to draw out the mastermind by killing each other. Whoever survives can end this”. That's not an exaggeration by the way, allies helping each other bring up the possibility of murdering each other in the off chance that the mastermind might decide to show himself (and reveal his nonsensical plot of shooting a girl at a concert? review_text:
I gotta hand it to my fellow countrymen - if there is one feature that SCORN showcases exemplary, it's its atmosphere. Truly foreboding, gloomy, with certain scenes instilling uneasiness and chill running down my spine. The thorough study of Beksiński and Giger is masterfully reflected in the visuals, to the point where I cannot marvel enough at it! Environmental storytelling is also a big plus given the design of each animate creature, protagonist included. The "puzzles" are also pretty logical, if logic and rationale can even be applied to this somber, unwelcoming world Ebb Software had created. For a "walking simulator", SCORN gets my highest praise.

Alas, it stumbles in a couple of other areas which excite both frustration and sorrow. The first one stems from pretty short game time and unrealized potential as far as hostile interactions go (namely, there are only three enemy types you can encounter (four if you count the parasite, which is passive and sort of a MacGuffin), which is overall pretty low). I do understand that the game is not an FPS in a classic sense (and actually like the hopelessness and vulnerability of the main character, scarcity of ammo for each of its 3 projectile-based weapons, and clumsiness in applying lethal force), but more visual splendor reflected in the gruesome-yet-majestic environments would have been a treat. 

The "sorrow" part stems from two reasons - the protracted, arduous development cycle which skyrocketed expectations of fans worldwide only to crash & burn upon finally releasing (mostly due to the said expectations), as well as ludicrous price for what the game offers (got my copy from Humble Choice way back in February 2024, so this point does not apply to me). Similar games at the time didn't go over 30 (The Invincible), and even the newly released Necrophosis (which is considered to be at least inspired by SCORN) is $15 at release!

So why the positive review then, if there clearly are glaring issues with the game? The reasons are both objective and subjective - subjective because this is by far & hands-down the BEST game to come out of Serbia. The person and patriot in me wants Ebb Software to succeed, to continue doing this kind of thing (albeit a bit more restrained in terms of promises and deadlines), because we need more of SCORN! To be a harsh critic of their first foray into building their dream game would be cruel and inappropriate, for the spark of genius is clearly present in SCORN. It needs to be further nurtured so that, eventually, it grows into something truly genre-defining. The objective reason for my positive rating is that the game really delivers on what it sets out to do - it unnerved me, made me feel at awe and (finally) shocked me in its final chapter, and I'll surely pitch it as a topic for discussion amongst my peers for these reasons alone. It just, once more, pains me to see it not being more successful due to questionable pricing and the perceived lack of content.

review_text:
It is really hard to like this game.
On one side, it's a very pretty and intriguing game, but on the other, the performance is bad, the combat is slow and repetitive, and the resource scarcity is punishing, to the point it makes it hard to win a scenario if you miss just a few shots.

Bloober team did an excellent job with the feel of the game, a lot of people saying the game is "clunky" but it really just feels like classic re4 with strafing instead of tank controls. The character designs are cool, the world and worldbuilding are fantastic, and the sound effects are like candy to the ear.

But to me the big issue is the combat. For something so slowly paced, there should be more options in the way you handle combat encounters. So far, half of the encounters are pretty resource demanding, revolving around shooting nearby explosives or trying to land as many charged headshots as possible. You could shoot them in the legs and stomp on them, but they can still hit you if not stunned, so there's not much reason to do that unless it's a one-on-one encounter. 

And the resource pay off is taxing, even if I do everything perfectly, It will result in missing a good chunk of ammo and not nearly getting enough back for another encounter. And there are moments in the game where there are two scenarios back to back, which is just draining.

The next big thing that annoys me is resource crafting - it was dumb in re4r, so why do it in this game? You never get enough to craft until you've fully explored an area, and for what? Five more bullets? 2 SHOTGUN SHELLS? A light medpen that I find EVERYWHERE!? The crafting system is redundant, there is no thinking behind it, I never have the moment where I need to consider what I should craft first before going into anything, since you rarely ever get enough chemicals anyway. 

Lastly the flame charge. It should not even be a resource since you get a technically "infinite" amount of them. It seriously should be just a recharging ability, that would punish you if you chose the wrong spot to use it, and would take some time to get back. It's very gimmicky and doesn't feel like an actual mechanic, save for the harder combat scenarios.

Underneath all of that the game is still pretty enjoyable, but I wouldn't recommend it. To me it's just a slower, more tedious iteration of dead space, without the cool dismemberment stuff.

I've got lots of good things to say about Rise to Ruins:
- The graphics are cute 
- The game is challenging
- Its an excellent city builder and a good take on the god genre
- The tower defence aspects keep the game moving
- There is a nice difficulty curve to work your way through

All in all really enjoy playing this game. The dev has been putting out updates for a long time and its definitely been worth the price!!

Suggestions for the next updates:
- larger map size (it can feel too restrictive sometimes)
- Maybe some monolithic structures that give a bonus to your current map and a small bonus to other maps in the world, they'd cost a lot to build, it'd be a great endgame task
- Animal training, would unlock mounts and pack mules for your gathers
- Maybe some sort of magic training for villagers that could be cool

Message to the dev: Make some DLC for the game or an expansion pack or something, people will pay for extra content if its there and decent.

review_text: I want to love this game. The combat is fun, when it works, the landscape and world are amazing. The characters are all interesting and I actually enjoy all the stealth and thief mechanics. BUT, the games reliance on "realism" is where it loses me. I can get behind the combat system being "realistic" but when you claim to have a game founded on realistic everything then continually put the player character in situations that are unrealistic and only an unrealistic RPG character could win them, then you've just made your game hard for the sake of being hard. I'm not against a challenging game or challenging mechanics but hard for the sake of hard is like hot sauce that's insanely hot but tastes horrible. There's no point, there's no coming out on the other side like "man i finally did it". You don't feel accomplishment in this game, only a sigh of relief that "insert next mechanic, or 1 v 20 fight is over". It would be different if your character was the standard RPG character, the second coming of Achilles or whatever, but you're not and that would normally be fine but not here. If you're gonna do realism, do it all the way. If you like RPG's, don't buy this game.

[list]
[*] boring
[*] repetetive
[*] oftentimes cringeworthy in the moments it tried to be funny (in other words all the time)
[*] lacking in the storytelling
[*] predictable
[*] a real pain to navigate through

And finally the soundtrack which I also struggle with because of its repetitiveness (they even joke about it IN the game) and generally poor production quality. They also might want to consider hiring a professional singer for their next title. This is definitely amongst the worse games I paid for. I'm aware that a lot of people disagree with me but I think it's important for potential buyers of this game to hear diverse opinions about it.

------ Below is my review for the game one day prior to release-----

C'mon you dumb apes, you wanna stick together?
Apes together strong, remember your training and you will live to see the magic school-bus again!

Would you like to know more?
Sign up today and you too can have warriors commit their 1-hit kill charge attack burrowing right underneath your feet, see Grenadiers levitate at will, watch bombardiers launch themselves into high orbit, and be targeted by gunner bugs from inside rocks and pre-made building alike?
Have you ever thought 'if you look after your bunker your bunker will look after you'? WELL THINK AGAIN our build tool matches your ping! Never have a dull moment as you repair your bunker in 2 second intervals. 

Have you ever wanted to co-ordinate main and side objectives as if you are the threat!?
Me too! If you know how to make comms reliable inject that solution right into my bug brain. Am I speaking local, or global? Push to talk or toggle voice activated? These terms mean nothing to the bugs that infest YOUR VERY OWN PERSONAL COMPUTER.

Once you overcome these challenges be prepared for the mutators to provide all the drama and action during the Arc Slam. That is if you are lucky enough not to have the ambush (and its always ambush) occur 4 seconds prior to the slam as this magnificent feat of Federation equipment scares the bugs back into their burrows when fired up (IT'S AFRAID).
Hope you have a deck of cards to match that helmet decal as we are going to have to occupy ourselves somehow during those long buggless slams on Agni Prime. All bugs can and will be attracted to but ignore gates and are unable to pass or attack these structures. 
Turns out that a dumb bug is just as good as a dead bug. 

BUT FEAR NOT TROOPER, for after every single slam comes the extraction and now that your trigger finger has rusted in place it would be the worst time for a thousand bug horde to appear. So naturally that's what happens.
Be prepared for the mission to be saved by one lone ranger/sniper entering the dropship and refusing to provide cover fire for his squad mates. That is, if the vessel of Federation glory doesn't reject that trooper for cowardice and ejects them upon re-orbit.

REMEMBER A TECHNICAL WIN IS STILL A WIN (for the federation; citizenship may be applied posthumously).

All jokes aside this is a fun game, that has a good community but frustrates the ever living hell out of it's most loyal playerbase due to bugs that have persisted and even returned through many updates. The gun system is fun and engaging, the class system is diverse yet winnable with any combination of classes as long as the team works together.
There is a significant learning curve, and the meta isn't always the best course of action. 
My advice to new players is to stick with at least one other member of your squad for survival, experiment with buildings freely, and ASK QUESTIONS.

I would recommend this game as long as you STOP HONEYCOMBING THE BASE I CAN'T GET OUT SAVE ME RICO! RIC-NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO

They have finally decided to send monthly updates on what they are working on but it was evident we needed that in Early Access, another rush job where we are waiting for another patch to fix.

Like so many early access games before it it got rushed for release and the lessons meant to be learnt before release happen after release.

If the servers stay up and if the spawn system works its a good game, but it's not worth the price tag in it's current state.

review_text:
Quick version: Amazing and fun game... with one con IMO.

---->>>The con: no Demonic Revolver<<<---- :(:( I can't do a full load out of hand cannons :(:(

Pros:
-The weapons feel sharp,sound good and look great, with perks that combo well with different spells. Giving you lots of choices for play styles.

-Mysteries. The devs did a great job at leaving things vague enough that you have to figure things out, but not to an annoying level where you miss out on something and have to go look up guides to figure it out. Making it fun to work though finding things, opening up secrets and learning what everything does.

-Leveling: Early game leveling is rewarding and you will feel the satisfying effects of it from zero up to about lvl 200. After that the effects are less noticeable.

-Difficulty: Once again, the Devs did a great job at giving the player control over the options of difficulty. By separating skill leveling from world difficulty, the player get to choose when they want things to become harder. Harder difficulty is rewarded by faster leveling,new secrets, new gear and spells.

-Death: Like the world difficulty leveling, the devs give the player options here. Instead of punishing you completely for, oh I don't, jumping off the map backwards because of a jump scare that's trying to chop your face off and dying from the fall, you have the chance to go back in after respawn and retrieve the witchfire, gold and keys you lost, but other items you will keep regardless, so even on death you don't feel horrible. But it doesn't end there. There is also the option for high risk (dying and loosing it all completly), high reward (double the witchfire gains for drastic leveling), but it is all up to the player to decide. Or the options that let you safeguard all the witchfire gain on death and only loosing keys and gold. Lots of ways to play it.

-Enemies: There is a large variation of enemies and attacks to keep each area unique. The art style and details or very well done. 

-Maps: Each map is very different from each other and have their own excellent detailed ambience. 

-Bosses: Each boss is unique and fits really well into the map they're apart of. Each one is more fun to fight, then they are a "horrible challenge to dread". But I've no idea what giant tentacled horror awaits in the Labyrinth and technically they're all mini-bosses and the coming witch is ultimate boss.

10/10 Highly recommend

review_text:
So, another remaster, still with the old engine, but noticeably better graphics than before, an almost-usable UI (although the map is still [i]entirely[/i] underwhelming), and more, like shops taking on-line orders now, [i]LOL[/i]. You travel (and eat, drink, and, of course fight) across quite a few (fictional) parts of Japan, playing multiple characters, most of which you've probably seen before, but one of them has grown up quite a bit and sports entirely different abilities. You might guess this would be foreshadowing the 'jobs' mechanics of later episodes, but, no, it's just a collection of minigames, mostly rhythm-based. But don't worry (except about the really weird ones, 'Running Girl', [i]cough[/i]): even if you're not cut out for those, it should be... fun, actually!

Story-wise, there's a [i]lot[/i] to like, with less intrusive cutscenes than before (you can fast-forward most of the time and not just skip) and a bit more "show" than "tell", which is great, despite lore-dumps and "go talk to X then talk to Y, then talk to X again" loops definitely still being a thing. There's [i]tons[/i] to do, and even if you initially don't intend to, you may still need to travel back and forth a bit to get to a point where you're ready for the finale (it can seem like a but of a drag, but just finish the initial training master arcs in each city, gather lots of high-potency energy drinks, and you'll be fine). 

The way all the various storylines come together in the end is [i]very[/i] well done, moving even, and more than compensate for the bits that don't make all that much sense. And there's still plenty to explore after the main story concludes (as you can defer the nonessential side jobs until then), but whether you'll actually want to do that mostly depends on your tolerance for the dated environment. Despite that, easily one of the better entries in the series!

review_text:
Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a standalone expansion developed by Ubisoft Montreal. Built on the mechanics of Far Cry 3, it transforms the tropical shooter into a neon-soaked 1980s action parody. It’s a self-contained experience that celebrates and mocks the era’s sci-fi clichés with style and humor.

Gameplay retains the core Far Cry formula: open-ended combat, stealth takedowns, and light progression. Players control Sergeant Rex “Power” Colt, a cyber commando sent to eliminate a rogue army on a retro-futuristic island. The structure mirrors Far Cry 3’s sandbox but compresses it into a smaller, more focused world.

Combat is fast, chaotic, and exaggerated. Enemies burst into neon sparks, explosions light up the horizon, and every weapon feels overpowered in the best way. The bow, shotgun, and laser rifle offer satisfying variety, while takedowns remain fluid and rewarding. Stealth is still viable, but the tone encourages loud, destructive play.

Visually, Blood Dragon is striking. The world glows with neon lighting, purple skies, and scan-line effects that emulate VHS-era aesthetics. The interface and HUD pulse with retro energy, and every visual choice supports the parody theme without breaking functionality.

The soundtrack by Power Glove is essential to the experience. Heavy synth beats and rhythmic basslines perfectly capture the feel of 1980s action cinema. Combined with intentionally over-the-top dialogue and one-liners, the game nails its comedic tone without overstaying its welcome.

The campaign lasts around six hours, balancing exploration and set-piece missions. Side activities like base captures and collectibles add replay value, but the pacing keeps the experience tight. The simplified progression system ensures constant power growth without grinding.

Overall, Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a focused, stylish reinvention of the Far Cry formula. It turns familiar mechanics into a celebration of retro absurdity—fun, fast, and self-aware. It’s short but perfectly tuned for what it aims to be: a neon homage to 80s action that never takes itself seriously and never stops being entertaining.

review_text:
Amazing Survival Horror. Absolutely gripping environments and well crafted encounters with enemies that made my whole experience full of wonder and fear from start to finish.

There is definitely inspiration from Dead Space, but it's so much more than that. The game really rewards you for being careful and good with your inventory management. The encounters are difficult, but can a lot of times be strategically thought out before you begin due to most of them having environmental interactions that you can use to even the odds.

Horror is well done. Not too horrifying that you can't take a step, but not cheap either where everything just feels like a stupid jumpscare. Great balance between action and horror as well.

Atmosphere is top notch. All areas and cutscenes are masterfully designed and always in sync with an incredible soundtrack that elevates the experience and always manages to out do itself as you play through the game.

Exploration to find resources, secrets and lore was always extremely rewarding. Even if you don't find something directly useful, you would at least get more insight on what's happening in the world.

Story, voice acting and characters are also some of the best. It really made you want to understand, read and listen to everything and try to piece everything together. World building is top notch.

My two complaints would be the lack of a dodge or good enough control over your movement to sometimes avoid what seem to be very simple or predictable attacks by enemies and the weapon variety is not the best. There is a good amount of weapons, but a few of them feel too useless to be even considered as a viable weapon in my opinion or just an unnecessary alternate version of a weapon you already have.

Absolute cinema.

review_text:
You can kill people.

Ah yes, "Help me my stepsister gave me an STD!" - The Game

I decided I wanted to marry an NPC who was already married, so I bided my time until her husband had an "accident" and then I swooped in like the scumbag I am.

The devs were not kidding when they said that the game is cozy with consequences!

On my latest play through I'm almost at the end of my first generation, and I'm quite satisfied with it. All the mechanics I was interested in (illnesses that kill villagers, a harsher economy, the generational gameplay) met my expectations and satisfied me. I married the evil looking carpenter and got blessed with an evil son, an angel son, and a completely apathetic daughter (that will be my heir). Now the two sons are married, the evil one has become a dad, and I love meeting them around the village and gifting their spouses with nice things so that I can be a good mother-in-law. But I was pretty upset almost no one showed up at my husband's funeral; I know he was an evil drunkard, but he had his sweet moments. And he liked to gift me horrible wallpapers for our home.

Oh! And I have a coop exclusively built for my legacy of geese named Goostarion. Goostarion deserves the best.

What surprised me the most of this game was how attached I managed to get to villagers with a very faint personality. Usually I don't care much about NPC’s, even when well written, but with Echoes it was the opposite. I married the drunkard bad boy of the village, I insult the witch and the teacher's daughter every time I see them just because I don't like their faces. And today the old trapper who lived in the wood died, and I really liked him (such an adorable old man), so I went to his funeral and used the crying animation to convey all of my sadness. Maybe because they don't have a deep personality, I can make my own and be more free to see them as I want. 

They might not tell you lines and lines of texts about their life, but that didn't prevent me from loving or hating them and coming up with my own backstories for them. I was sad when Rowland the blacksmith died, because I traded with him almost daily, and he apprenticed my son. I went to his funeral and sobbed the whole time. In my mind, we were great friends. And my relationship with the Mayor's son was a weird one, as I thought him to be a snob and privileged, but then he became a tailor and we became friends. For me, their "flatness" was less annoying than other games' stereotyped characters that I couldn't get to like. The more “personality” developers put into characters, the more flat they seem to me. I like Echoes and the Sims, because it leaves enough to the imagination that they feel more real to me instead of me relying on the creator to tell me who the people are. The characters may also be a bit flat but the dialogue is witty at times. It’s also a lot of quest fulfilling which I personally enjoy. I’m a big farm sim lover anyways so I’m happy fishing, farming, crafting to fulfil quests.

The threat of illnesses that can potentially kill half of your village (maybe your romantic interest too), the need to produce food to eat unless you want to starve, and some other "less cozy" mechanics were a fresh breath. I like farming sims, but they get boring for me when you start to set up your farm and just get tons of money that you don't even know how to spend. With Echoes, there's always something draining the money you have saved. The game has indeed a slower pace, and the beginning might seem a big grindy, but for me that's a plus, cause it means I will have things to do with my future generation. Being poor is fun, at least for me.

I enjoyed the game because I loved the art style and I just see it as a cozy game where I don’t rush to get iron, nails and stone. I quite liked the fact that I can’t rush things and I’m kinda at the mercy of what the townsfolk have to trade/sell. I go to the shop everyday and when they’re there they’re there and when not I either wait or go search for them. There’s no rush as I don’t have to immediately upgrade my house or build a barn. I don’t need an ice box yet because I get gifted enough food from the villagers and can easily dry food on the drying rack or preserve it, etc. You can make it as peaceful or “harrowing” as you like, can allow aging, diseases, poison etc. or not! You can customise it in the settings to be as challenging or cozy as you want, such as changing the lifespan, durability of tools and items, if you have an energy meter or if you pay taxes etc. The game doesn’t overly hold your hand, there’s things you can only get by trading with the townsfolk or doing quests to start with. 

This game is unlike any other, so don't go in with expectations. Like I mentioned, most farm games have well fleshed characters but in a game where one of the goals is aging and dying, it's not realistic to have fleshed out characters. Especially when characters kind of jump jobs and families (mayors wife became a lesbian butcher after her husbands death) it's immensely hard to make character backstories that would make sense. Especially when you are present for back story and like know their parents and grandparents. The characters are meant to be completely replaceable.

The way I see it is it's similar socially to Cult of the Lamb. NPC’s have some "base personality types" (as*hole, sweet, drunk) and you can have favorites and love some, but at the end of the day, even if you don't sacrifice them, they die of old age. With that in mind, I quite enjoyed the game. It's like Rimworld met Harvest Moon. There is a little excitement with trying to survive but not in the desperate Don't Starve or combat styled games. To me it's quite beautiful to see a game that shows "Rome wasnt built in a day". Like your character won't get a whole farm set up in their lifetime, but it's ok, someone will take over. And though there are some quirks, most of them have to do with the game not quite being complete.

To me, I think it is far more "original" than people credit it for. I guess that's because it contains "farming". I see it more as a survival and legacy builder game if you want to play it that way - and that's also an originality point to me. How many "cozy farming games" allow you to increase or decrease difficulty on the fly? Or give you the option to play several saves at varying difficulties so you can turn everything off and focus on the residents of Honeywood or make a new save with everything ramped up so you are challenged to survive in this 1701 era with all the hardships life can throw at you. 

If I have to find a flaw for the game, it is that it's still a young game, so it has room for improvement. I have no problem waiting for new features and content to be added, so it doesn't frustrate me that much. As for the Devs, you can really tell this was a labour of love for them and they are super active with the community- so I think it would be safe to say there’s more to come with this game. Basically, I love this game. And I highly highly recommend it. There’s a lot of typical farm stuff as well as stuff with ghosts and being able to murder your NPC’s. 

10/10

[h1][i]A very unique style of game that I think is very charming -- although a bit daunting to get into.[/i][/h1]

I've enjoyed this game, granted I still haven't gotten everything done in it. It is reminiscent of some other life simulation games such as farming games like [i]Story of Seasons[/i] and [i]Stardew Valley[/i], though it has a different take on the groundwork those familiar titles have laid. It also is weirdly reminiscent of Oregon Trail to me, in that it has a survival, historic aspect to it. I enjoy that and it's probably my favorite thing about the game. The graphics and art direction remind me a bit of [i]Paper Mario,[/i] which I find to be very unique and charming. It's definitely an art style that will stick with you as there isn't that many games like it. 

My one issue with this game is that in my opinion it is very hard to get into. I think that will put many, if not maybe even the majority, of people off the game at first. It's slow to progress and that is both I think a strength and a weakness. Strength, as it makes you slow down and appreciate the game. Weakness because in my opinion the slowness lends itself well to becoming stale a bit. 

Give it a try. I've really enjoyed it, and I think I will continue to as I progress.

review_text:
This is another review praising base PSO2 and shitting on PSO2:NGS. Scroll along, ain't nothing to see here. Game bad, community debased, and XIGNCODE3, a beautiful (not) piece of malware.

I will admit, it's a nice game to chill and relax. If you have friends, it's fun. If you don't have friends, then you can always try making some in the game. But if you're looking for content, you're in the wrong game. It is an endless grind where there's nothing to do except fight big monsters and go to virtual concerts (stan quna, cosmic twinkle night~)

I think I'm just salty that I lost a lot of progress. I lost my old account and couldn't get it back. Coincidentally, NGS came out, so I tried it. At first, it was fun! I liked slaying monsters, I liked the big raids, and I liked exploring the world and listening the music. But after awhile, it just got stale. All the events we have are just grinding events. There isn't fishing or mining mechanics, and you don't really craft armor and accessories anymore. And the story? Easily done in 5 minutes (+100 hours of bad story cutscenes, but I didn't really care too much because it's a trait for MMOs to have bad storylines). I did not care for the characters (except Nadereh, I love her concerts). This left me with nothing to do except grind, grind, and grind. I'm a casual min-max player, so I didn't mind. But as more regions came out, old equipment became obsolete and I felt like I was wasting my time just grinding all the time. I didn't even like talking to others anymore! At some point, the community got really toxic and unmoderated. My friends and I used to work together to fight tough bosses and went through so much adversaries, both in game and in real life. After the battles, we could just chill and relax, go fishing, watch the concerts, and just talk and be friends! But man, I'm not too sure what happened to the community, but it CHANGED. Friends became enemies, and I had to quit the game.

Sigh. I really used to like this game. It was my all time favorite game. I dragged irl friends into it. I even roped my siblings into playing! But now? I'm done. I can't really recommend this game anymore. If you have fun, then that's great! But I can't play this game anymore. RIP PSO2, I truly did love you (and quna)

review_text:
To save time, I'll summarize the experience I had with Pathologic 2 in bullet-points. These will cover points of contention I initially had with the game (and how they quickly turned into features which improved my experience) as well as the "best parts" of the game as a whole.

Learning Curve: I had Pathologic sitting inside of my library for nearly three months before I decided to play more than 30 minutes into the story. Before you gain an appreciation for the slow-burn timing of the game, it's going to feel somewhat agonizing. However, once you immerse yourself in the story and characters, you'll actually feel pressed on time: As though the world is moving too fast for you to keep up. Combat mechanics are straight forward but asset management takes some getting used to - The latter being essential to succeeding on a playthrough. 

Writing and Storytelling: Only second to *maybe* Disco Elysium and Knights of the Old Republic. Nothing short of fantastic, as long as you take your time to appreciate it. The story is *extremely flexible* too, with your actions having drastic consequences on the story depending on your dialogue options. What's unique about Pathologic 2, is that the consequences are *on-going* in the story, not something that arbitrarily effects a set-ending as in Disco E or KOTOR. You are altering the story, cover to cover. Also, the doesn't spell out important decisions or comments you make with obnoxious "persuasion check" or tacky coloring. Like all real-time conversations: Once it's out there, it's out there and you have no idea how it'll turn out.

Atmosphere: The game has aged amazing, given when it was made. The atmosphere can be terrifying and tranquil depending on where you are. Interactions with the characters will leave you with a sense of sonder - Craving more and more insight into who they are and what they might be thinking as they interact with you. You truly feel like an entity separate from the world around you. In the best way possible: You feel utterly out of control and helpless. More playtime rewards you with a lessened sense of helplessness, encouraging you to master the game and your playthroughs.

Overall, the game stands as one of the best titles I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. A great gift and recommendation to people who enjoy storytelling and crave that feeling of emptiness upon completing a game. A feeling which beckons you back, again and again, because you know there's nothing quite like it out there.

review_text:
There's... a LOT to say about New Genesis. I've played for 2200+ hours at this point, and while I do think there's a lot of good points in favor of this game, there's also, like, a ton of bad points.

But those 2200+ hours were also not spent entirely in NGS. So take my rating with a grain of salt, because I'm gonna review base game and NGS like they're separate games.

Let's start with base PSO2. For a game that's been in development hell for 10+ years on the global side, hearing exactly why made things... interesting. But in the 2 years I spent in base game, it was a good time! There was a huge level of customization, the content was coming out at a rather quick pace(A point I WILL brush on later), and bosses and characters that were actually fun to meet and learn about. Getting to know base game in such a short amount of time was actually somewhat daunting, but rewarding for those who wanted in for the lore. The Dark Falz in this game were all interesting concepts, including the done-again concept of fighting yourself, and how the people around the Dark Falz individuals' hosts acted when it came to those hosts was actually interesting, because it isn't like the JRPG trope of fighting a big, bad manifestation of evil and darkness that plans to destroy everything. The Falspawn, and Dark Falz by extention, prey on actual character flaws that lead to them falling to the darkness, and I loved it. Getting to fight and even redeem every single one of them by Episode 6 was super fun.

Of course, if I'm talking base game, I have to talk Episode 5. In the JP side of base game, Episode 5 was probably the worst time to be a PSO2 player. A huge deviation from Episode 4, which in itself was a deviation from Episodes 1-3, was not what the playerbase needed at the time it came out. For hardcore Phantasy Star fans, there are some fun themes in here, notably the return of Alis as a main character, but that whole story was a mess, for something that was supposed to touch upon the origins of the Photoners. There's a lot of interesting ideas in there, but not every bit of it was executed well enough. However, Episode 5 still has some great boss fights, including Masquerader, a clear highlight to the point that my old Alliance and I would run it despite Episode 6 being the endgame.

Overall, with the absolute mountain of content delivered over the course of 2 years, super fun classes and a great combat system that admittedly could be more fluid, PSO2 is an absolute blast, and if you REALLY want to get to know PSO2, I highly recommend starting here before NGS.

Because NGS was an absolute nightmare at the beginning.

I have to admit right now that NGS is way better now than it was at the start. At launch, there was practically no content, apart from Gigantix, and one episode. Just one. Now we have 7 episodes, and we're actually about to be stronger than we ever were in base game. It's gonna be interesting. But not in a good or bad way.

I want to begin here by talking about the positives I see in NGS. I love the fluidity of combat here. It's probably one of the best playing action combat systems I've played in any MMO. SEGA obviously knows how to make a great combat system in any game, but it shows here. Furthermore, I actually really like the open worlds. 4 different environments to explore with wildly changing landscapes depending on where you look, different biomes inside those 4 environments, and even the Nameless City all look great. Absolute eye candy as far as the eye can see. And lastly, I have to give praise to the improvements to the character creation system. Allowing absolute freedom in character creation means you can make literally ANYONE you want to play as. Cosplays and OCs all look absolutely fantastic, and are worth the time you put into it. Phashion, as they say, is the real endgame here.

That's the problem.

There's barely any endgame content outside of the Duel Quests, and even then, only Masquerader, the one returning endgame boss that you can take on again and again, is the only one that's actually worth it. And while we're not at the rarity of 15*, it's super noticable that the power level curve looks like a hill when you look at a player spread. While you DO have to put time into the meta, the meta's just something you do if you prefer having absolute power. 

The combat system is also limited. Less photon arts means less creative combos, and I'm getting really tired of using the same 4 moves outside of active skills, which are few and far between. Every class is guilty of this, too, and combos can become so stale after a while. 

The Gigantix are boring due to the fact that there's no unique mobs that can ONLY be Gigantix. When you fight them, they're just like the regular bosses/mobs, meaning the real challenge is just in pattern memorization. 

The story was boring, too. In a game where you're supposed to be the main character, it feels more like you're just the hard carry side character, and that's all you exist to do. It took about 5 chapters for our characters' past to become relevant, and that's if you played base game. 

It's supposed to be that our character is supposedly the actual Guardian from base game. We were somehow sent 1000 years into the future, with no objective, goal, or even our memories, starting from scratch and growing back into the warriors we used to be. But the game fails to convey ANY of that to the player until Zephetto just... hints at it. That's it. And then we don't get anything else about it until we actually fight the first Starless Dark Falz, Vael, and that's still just a hint. Just a quick flashback to who we used to be. And it kinda sucks.

PSO2 NGS suffers from uninteresting writing with baseless connections to the past, rarely any good content, and a ton of reuse at a level that would make RGG Studios cringe. With its core combat, there is very little mechanical depth, and the game can be boiled down to mash attack 1 to win.

But that core combat does feel fluid. Attacks feel good to unleash. And above all that, the eye candy is absolutely remarkable, and the character creator is absolutely amazing. It's just the most beautiful, shallow puddle of a game that could be better. And knowing SEGA, this game CAN be better.

I don't recommend NGS at all, but I highly recommend getting into base PSO2 if you want to see what we had before the utter mess that NGS is.

review_text:
It's pretty fun. Gameplay is mostly in resource management, and is like an idler version of SNKRX.

I made a list of some quality of life things I'd like to see in the full release:

- Better token signalling. It's hard to tell what gives tokens or how much. I would love to hear a token noise when monsters die or after a battle.
- More music variation, not just for battle, but switching into shops, bosses, curiosity rooms, etc
- Higher emphasis on sound effects. I had to turn down the music to even start hearing the sound effects, which weren't that punchy. For an idle battle game, I'd really love to hear some crunchy noises. There's no sound cues for many special abilities either, but when there are it makes a big difference.
- I wish we could see a keybinding list in the menu. I was wondering what hotkeys I was missing. (Like a cycle between human button?)
- I wish there was a better sense of objective. Are we trying to escape... kill the despot... is it endless? 
- More artistic chamber variation
- It's hard to tell enemy threat. With healthbars turned on, I wish enemies had a level to them.
- I wish clicking a text option had a sound effect.

Preferences:

- I wish some stats were divided by 10 or 5. I'd prefer a basic swordsman do 4.5 damage, rather than 45
- I wish leveling up healed humans
- I wish there was a scoring system to make dying in runs more fun. (New high score!)
- I wish there was an activated ability we could use -- like single use items we could buy.
- I think we get too many mutations. I would prefer starting with 2 slots for all the mutations we get, with more slots unlocked  with tokens. 
- I find tokens are a bit overused. I almost feel like there should be a third resource used for the research tree. 
- I wish WASD moved humans instead of switching chambers. I find using a mouse to reposition them somehow tedious
- I wish the humans were more active. I wish they would cheer after they win, or have conversation between them, or have a text box say "nooo!" when they die or something.
- I wish there was a better way to plan ahead, as part of the gameplay. Like, knowing you're facing a horde rather than a few tough robots would make you adjust your army a bit. As it is, since you don't know, the strategy feels independent of the game.

review_text:
It's... okay? 

The first game pulled you in with this epic intro where you meet some interesting characters and missions that were interesting. Combat was kind of janky but you could see what they were trying to do. The game world felt interesting and you cared for the plight of the refugees that escaped like you.

KCD2 is like the opposite. I don't like any of the characters I have met. Every mission I have done has been a glorified fetch quest with incredibly uninteresting characters. The map is realistic but not fun to explore, at all. I don't care even a little bit about this wedding I'm supposed to go to. Every person I meet I just hate. I get that's probably the point but... it's not fun.

My quit point was doing the mission where I need to find a missing girl. Found her on the other side of the map only for to ask me to travel all the way back to where I just was to get a "magical amulet". Might have been funny if I wasn't just thinking about how uninterested I was in this girl, her family, or the idea of travelling back to the camp to then travel back to the cave for something I do not care at all about.

review_text:
This game is a conglomeration of successes by other studios messily pasted together into something wholly disappointing. The game's enemies merge to become something better and stronger, while the studio has created a stitched and lessor version of the long list of inspirations they have.

No new ground is being broken here, and most of the game's features feel like they are tacked on. As if an alien were to attempt to imitate being a human, but really didn't know why humans do things. It mimics the voice, but it isn't human. The skin doesn't fit right, it sags and falls away, revealing cracks in the facade. There are things that are part of really great franchises present here, but the Bloober team seems to have misunderstood why they worked- only to check off items on a shopping list.

The ambient music is far too similar to themes from Silent Hill, which is then cut to a jarring synth soundscape in cut scenes.

Enemies are boring. The merging mechanic seemed interesting, but it just makes enemies more resistant to damage and knockdown.

The visuals might initially look impressive, but just don't stare too long. Anything that isn't your main character is ugly, dull, and hidden behind filters of fog or distortion.

The upgrade system feels out of place, and is also dull. Improve your accuracy, firepower, your inventory size and health. Lame. Another relic scoured from the sands of games passed, chipped, dead, and without any attempt at polishing.

The story is on the nose and edgy for the sake of being edgy. I found no attachment to the main character, and was put off by their voice- it's like a half awake teenager attempting their best Soldier 76 impression.

Nothing sticks out from any other game you have played before in the horror genre. If you have never played another video game in your life, you might be impressed.

For anyone looking for something resembling a "whole new breed of survival horror", simply save your money for something other than this failed chimera.

review_text:
I learned a lot during this game, first and foremost that I am, apparently, an unfeeling clutz because the story did absolutely nothing for me. I found the main protagonists annoying, the humor was juvenile and did not fit the theme of the story, and frankly, the story itself was also at best ok-ish. And the gameplay and mechanics are simply atrocious. 

It's a complete mystery to me why this game has an overwhelmingly positive rating. 

[h2]Story and characters[/h2]

As the blurp says, you play as two doctors who go backwards through a dying man's memories to artifically fulfill his last wish. That sounds great, but in practice it means that you visit scenes from this man's life that were significant to him but, in-game, you are just an observer, it is all very surface-level. You do not interact with the man or the other characters (with very few exceptions), you can't really investigate anything, you are just dropped into the scene, read a few lines of dialogue (no voice-over), and that's it. 

At one point, you manipulate his memories, and then skip through his life events again, this time in the right direction, to see how this manipulation affected his "life", and if you managed to "fulfill" his last wish. But, and there lies the main problem for me, it does not actually affect anything. It manipulates a dying man into misremembering his whole life (on his request). What you see didn't and does not happen, and could not have happened in reality. 

It is a bit sad if you think about it, but you do not get to know any of the characters well enough to get emotionally invested, at least in my opinion.

The memory scenes are presented through the eyes of the two doctors, who are the real protagonists, and I found them pretty much insufferable. They were clearly intended as comic relief, and they are constantly squabbling in a mean-spirited and at times childish way. I think there's supposed to be a romantic undertone but the inane dialogue completely ruins it. 

[h2]Gameplay and the rest[/h2]

The actual gameplay consists for the most part of you dropping into a scene, trying to find the very few points that you can interact with, and collect five "memento" points and a core memory. If you have found everything, you can leave the scene and have to solve a mini-puzzle. It is always the same type of puzzle, and it is neither difficult nor fun. 

There is no indication which parts of the scenery are walkable and which aren't, and there is no logic behind the mementos, so you are randomly clicking everywhere to either move somewhere else or find one of the mementos. 

This is even worse in the few "action" sequences, in which you can run around with the arrow keys. There is no excuse for having such buggy and clunky controls even in a game from 2011. 

[h2]To sum it up[/h2]

Currently, the game is tagged as "emotional". In my case, that emotion is annoyance.

I do not recommend this game.
